title: Best ever! From 14 medals to 114: How India achieved more with fewer athletes at the Asian Para Games
text: Image credit: TimesofIndia.com From 14 medals in 2010 to 114 in 2026, Indiaâs remarkable rise continued in Aichi-Nagoya as a smaller contingent surpassed its previous best, achieved 30 gold medals and secured its highest-ever finish at the continental para-sport showpiece. Indiaâs campaign at the Asian Para Games 2026 was a triumph that few would have predicted when the size of the contingent became known. With just 167 athletes travelling to Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, the prospect of repeating the 100-plus medal haul achieved at Hangzhou in 2023 appeared ambitious. The previous edition had seen India send more than 300 athletes to the competition, returning with a record 108 medals after subsequent revisions to the original tally. Watch Suchika Tariyal on her Asian Games bronze, childhood trauma, and never giving up | TOISA Spotlight But the Indian contingent defied expectations, producing an even bigger return with significantly fewer athletes. India finished the fifth edition of the Asian Para Games with 114 medals â 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze â to secure fourth place, both the highest medal tally and the best finish in the country's history at the event. The numbers tell a compelling story of progress. India improved its medal tally for the fifth consecutive edition, added to its gold-medal record and finished ahead of South Korea, which had threatened to challenge its position in the final standings. More than the record itself, the achievement highlighted how far India's para-sport movement has travelled in 16 years â from a modest 14-medal return at the inaugural edition in 2010 to a fourth-place finish among Asia's leading para-sport nations. From 14 medals to 114: India's remarkable rise India's progress at the Asian Para Games has been steady, with each edition bringing a new high in the overall medal tally. At Guangzhou in 2010, India won 14 medals â one gold, four silver and nine bronze â to finish 15th. The 2014 edition in Incheon brought a substantial improvement, with the country collecting 33 medals, including three gold, but remaining 15th in the standings. The breakthrough arrived at Jakarta in 2018. India's medal tally rose to 72, comprising 15 gold, 24 silver and 33 bronze, while its position improved to ninth. Hangzhou in 2023 marked another major leap. India crossed the 100-medal barrier for the first time, initially returning with 111 medals before the tally was revised to 108 following a doping-related disqualification and a medal reallocation. The revised haul comprised 27 gold, 32 silver and 49 bronze, with India eventually classified sixth. Aichi-Nagoya extended that upward trajectory. India added six medals to its revised Hangzhou total, increased its gold-medal count from 27 to 30 and climbed two places to fourth. India's Asian Para Games record The numbers at a glance: India's medal tally increased more than eightfold between 2010 and 2026. Its gold-medal count grew from one to 30, while its position improved from 15th to fourth. Image credit: TimesofIndia.com The rise has not been limited to the overall tally. India has improved its standing in three successive editions since 2014, moving from 15th to ninth, then sixth and now fourth. The 2026 result represents the culmination of a sustained upward trend rather than an isolated breakthrough. Smaller contingent, bigger return The most striking feature of India's latest performance was the efficiency with which its athletes converted participation into medals. India fielded 167 athletes â 111 men and 56 women â across 11 sports at Aichi-Nagoya. That was considerably fewer than the 309 athletes listed for the Hangzhou campaign in 2023, yet the team surpassed its previous best by six medals. Hangzhou vs Aichi-Nagoya The comparison is revealing. India sent approximately 46 per cent fewer athletes than it did to Hangzhou, but its medal tally increased by nearly six per cent. The gold-medal count rose by three, the silver tally by three, and the bronze count remained unchanged. Image credit: TimesofIndia.com On a simple medals-per-athlete measure, India's return increased from approximately 0.35 medals per athlete in Hangzhou to 0.68 in Aichi-Nagoya. This is an aggregate comparison, not an individual success rate, since athletes can win multiple medals and the number of events and opportunities varies across sports. Nevertheless, the figures underline the scale of the achievement. A smaller squad did not merely match the previous edition's success; it established a new benchmark for Indian para-sport. Athletics powers India's medal surge Para-athletics was the backbone of India's campaign, delivering 65 medals â 22 gold, 19 silver and 24 bronze. That represented nearly 57 per cent of the country's overall tally and made athletics the single biggest contributor to India's fourth-place finish. Para-badminton followed with 16 medals, including three gold, five silver and eight bronze. Together, athletics and badminton accounted for 81 medals, more than 70 per cent of India's total. Swimming contributed 11 medals, comprising three silver and eight bronze. Archery added six medals, including three gold and three silver, while shooting produced five, with two gold, two silver and one bronze. India's leading medal-winning sports in Asian Para Games 2026 Image credit: TimesofIndia.com Athletics' contribution also illustrates how India's progress has accelerated. At Hangzhou, para-athletics produced 52 medals, including 16 gold, 17 silver and 19 bronze. In Aichi-Nagoya, the discipline's haul rose to 65, with six additional gold medals. Badminton's contribution was different. India won 21 medals in the sport at Hangzhou, including four gold, but finished with 16 in 2026. Instead, the substantial gains in athletics and the contributions from other sports helped compensate for the decline in badminton medals. That distinction matters: the record haul reflects both the strength of India's established medal-winning disciplines and the need to broaden its success across events in future editions. Multiple medallists underline India's depth India's record was supported by athletes who delivered more than once during the competition. A total of 26 Indian athletes won multiple medals, while six athletes collected multiple gold medals, demonstrating the importance of individual excellence in a campaign involving 11 sports. Archer Sheetal Devi was among the standout performers, winning two gold medals and a silver. Her two golds came in the mixed compound and individual compound events, while the silver added to her three-medal haul. Athletics provided several other multiple gold medallists. Dilip Gavit, Nishad Kumar, Pranav Soorma and Simran Sharma each won two gold medals, while shooting contributed through Mona Agarwal, who also secured two golds. Four athletes finished with three medals apiece: Sheetal Devi in archery, Thulasimathi Murugesan in badminton, Ravi Budigina in swimming and Himanshu Nandal in swimming. Their performances illustrated how athletes winning across multiple events can make a significant difference to a country's final tally. The figures also invite comparison with Hangzhou, where 25 Indian athletes won multiple medals. The increase to 26 in 2026 was modest, but the overall tally improved despite a much smaller contingent. The result points to a campaign in which medal-winning performances were concentrated among a relatively small squad. Paralympic progress provides the wider context India's rise at the Asian Para Games has coincided with a significant improvement at the Paralympics, strengthening the country's standing in international para-sport. At Rio 2016, India won four medals and finished 43rd. Tokyo 2020 marked a breakthrough, with 19 medals â five gold, eight silver and six bronze â lifting India to 24th. At Paris 2024, India recorded its best Paralympic haul of 29 medals, comprising seven gold, nine silver and 13 bronze, to finish 18th. The progression at the Paralympics mirrors the broader trend at the Asian Para Games: larger medal returns, more gold medals and improvements in the standings. India's able-bodied contingent had also finished fourth at the 2026 Asian Games, although its 85-medal tally was below the 106 medals achieved at Hangzhou in 2023. The para contingent's performance offered a contrasting story of growth, with its medal count rising and its position improving. Fourth place sets a new benchmark China dominated Aichi-Nagoya, finishing with 435 medals, including 207 gold. Hosts Japan were second with 186 medals, while Uzbekistan finished third with 145. India placed fourth with 114, ahead of South Korea, which collected 100 medals, including 29 gold. India's final position was not guaranteed until the closing stages. South Korea remained within reach, but its final-day return of one gold and two silver left it one gold behind India. The Indian contingent held on to fourth place with 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines The gap to third-placed Uzbekistan shows that further progress will require India to expand its medal-winning strength across disciplines. Yet the immediate achievement is significant: India has moved from 15th at the first two editions to fourth, while increasing its tally at every successive Games. The challenge now is to sustain that momentum, build a deeper pool of competitive athletes and reduce dependence on a handful of disciplines. For a contingent of just 167 athletes, 114 medals represent more than a record. They mark the latest step in a 16-year transformation of Indian para-sport â one that began with 14 medals in Guangzhou and has now culminated in a historic fourth-place finish in Aichi-Nagoya. title: Hip injury, viral fever, vomiting: How Paralympic champion Praveen Kumar fought back to win Asian Para Games gold
text: Praveen Kumar (Image credit: PCI) Praveen Kumar had to fight more than his rivals to win gold at the Asian Para Games. The reigning Paralympic champion was dealing with a hip injury that had affected his jumping form for months. He was also battling fever, cold and cough during the competition in Japan. Despite these challenges, Praveen cleared 2.05m to win the menâs high jump T44/64 gold medal with a Games record on Wednesday. His jump also bettered the previous Asian Para Games record of 1.95m in the T44 category. Banti won silver with a personal best of 1.92m, while Uzbekistanâs Temurbek Giyazov took bronze with 1.86m. Watch Harita Bhadra Exclusive | 2 Asian Games Medals, Now the 22.45s World Championships Chase Praveen fights illness to win gold Praveen was not at his best physically when he competed at the Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletics Stadium. He had contracted a viral fever a few days after arriving in Japan and had been struggling with fever and a cough for most of the week. He even vomited and suffered coughing spells between attempts. However, he continued competing and secured his second successive Asian Para Games title. âWith the fever, cold and cough, training here became a difficult task, but I continued with short breaks. While my body felt fine during the final, my first jump gave me a severe headache. The mucus from my blocked nose and throat was also troubling me. I wanted to better my Asian Para Games record, and to achieve that in such a condition is a special feeling for me,â Kumar tells The Indian Express. How a hip injury affected his jumping Praveen had already proved himself on the biggest stage. At the Paris Paralympics, he won gold with a career-best jump of 2.08m, improving on the silver medal he won at the Tokyo Paralympics. His 2.08m jump remains the Asian record. However, a hip injury slowed his progress after that success. He won bronze at the World Para Athletics Championships in New Delhi last September, clearing 2.00m despite the injury. The problem continued to affect his performances, and he could not cross the 2.05m mark in the months that followed. A jump of 2.03m on the national circuit two months ago gave him hope that he was getting back to his best. Praveen was born with a deformity in his left leg. The hip injury made it harder for him to generate the power needed to take off during a jump. âI suffered a ligament tear in my hip last year, which meant I could not generate enough power from the hip during take-off. When I planted my right knee to jump, my hip would hurt a lot and I could not generate the lift. The first focus was to recover, followed by jumping exercises to strengthen the hip muscles and short sprints to build strength in my left leg. Not having a jump close to 2.05m was a bit demotivating, but I knew I had to recover and train fully to regain my old form,â Kumar says. The learning Praveen first learnt about high jump by watching videos online. He has been training under coach Satyapal Singh since 2018. When the injury disrupted his progress, the coach focused on helping him stay positive while rebuilding strength in his hip. âPraveenâs strength has always been his smooth take-off and clearance in the Fosbury Flop technique. While able-bodied high jumpers have to bend the non-leading knee during take-off, his deformity in the left leg means he does not have to worry about that aspect. He had good speed on the runway even at a young age and was also good at running the curve. His back-leaning position and flexibility during clearance were always good, and we only had to improve them with time," Singh said. "He is a short high jumper, but he compensates for that disadvantage with almost perfect technique. After the injury, I knew rebuilding strength in his hip would take time, but I kept reminding him of his best jumps. I did not want him to think negatively,â he said. Who is Praveen Kumar's inspiration? With another Asian Para Games gold medal secured, Praveen has already started thinking about the next big challenge: defending his Paralympic title at the Los Angeles Games. One athlete he continues to learn from is Canadian high jumper Derek Drouin, who won gold at the 2016 Rio Olympics with a jump of 2.38m. Praveen studies Drouinâs technique, particularly how he builds speed during his run-up and converts it into upward lift at take-off. He is also working to strengthen his left leg and make changes to his approach. âFor the last seven to eight years, I have watched videos of Derek Drouin competing at the Rio Olympics almost daily. I closely observe how he generates explosiveness from his run-up and then almost stops at take-off to create vertical lift. Even though my left leg is not as strong as my right, I have been working on building its strength. I am also aiming to increase my run-up by one or two steps. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines It will take time to adjust, but I am confident I can surpass my personal best next season and work towards defending my title at the LA Paralympics,â Kumar says. What are the T44 and T64 categories? The T44 and T64 categories are often combined in para athletics events to ensure enough athletes can compete. T64 is for athletes who run using a prosthetic lower limb. T44 is for athletes with lower-limb impairments who run using their natural limbs without prostheses. title: CM honours 419 sportspersons with Him Ratna, distributes Rs 17.85 cr
text: Himachal Pradesh CM Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu addresses athletes during Him Ratna 2026, organised in honour of sportspersons, in Shimla on Saturday Shimla : Himachal Pradesh chief minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu on Saturday honoured 419 outstanding sportspersons of the state with Him Ratna-2026 Awards, distributing cash incentives worth Rs 17.85 crore at a state-level function. Of the 419 awardees, 51 were recognised for achievements in international competitions and 368 for national-level performances. International players received Rs 13.55 crore, while national-level sportspersons were awarded Rs 4.30 crore. Athlete Sawan Barwal received Rs 2.50 crore for winning the silver medal in the menâs marathon at the Asian Games-2026 in Japan, while Seema Kumari was awarded Rs 1.50 crore for her bronze medal in the 10,000-metre race. Four Himachal players â Ritu Negi, Pushpa Rana, Jyoti Thakur and Bhawna Thakur â who were part of Indiaâs gold medal-winning womenâs kabaddi team, received Rs 1 crore each. Cricketer Renuka Thakur was also awarded Rs 1 crore. Sukhu said the govt had substantially enhanced cash awards to encourage sporting excellence. Gold medal winners at the Olympics, Winter Olympics and Paralympics will now receive Rs 5 crore, while silver and bronze medallists will get Rs 3 crore and Rs 2 crore, respectively. Asian Games gold medallists will receive Rs 4 crore. Players winning medals in team events will get at least 25% of the prescribed award money, the CM said. He also announced incentives of Rs 3 lakh each for national-level coaches and international referees. Sukhu announced that the Khelo Himachal campaign would begin in Dharamshala on Nov 20 to engage youth in sports and spread awareness against drug abuse, particularly chitta (heroin). Cricket, volleyball and kabaddi competitions will be organised for participants aged 15 to 30 years, with the toppers getting a prize purse of Rs 21 lakh. Sukhu also highlighted the development of a Rs 170-crore international-standard indoor stadium at Nadaun in Hamirpur, which will accommodate around 14 sporting disciplines. Sports minister Yadvinder Goma said the govt was committed to strengthening sports infrastructure and providing better opportunities to emerging talent. title: Asian Para Games 2026: India wins record 114 medals with just 168 athletes
text: Image credit: ANI A smaller Indian contingent has delivered a bigger return, rewriting the nationâs Asian Para Games record with 114 medals in Nagoya. Indiaâs haul of 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze is its best-ever at the continental event, with para-athletics the engine of a campaign that exceeded expectations. Only 168 Indian athletes â 112 men, 56 women â competed across 11 sports, little more than half the 303 sent to Hangzhou in 2023. Yet India has surpassed its previous best of 111 medals there, when it finished fifth and bettered the 72-medal return from Jakarta in 2018, where 190 athletes represented the country. Watch Harita Bhadra Exclusive | 2 Asian Games Medals, Now the 22.45s World Championships Chase Track and field athletes were the standout, collecting 65 medals, including 22 gold. Para-badminton was next biggest contributor with 16, meaning the two events combined for 81 medals â more than 70 percent of Indiaâs tally. The numbers underline how effectively a squad converted opportunity into podium finishes. Friday brought a flourish, with India winning nine gold medals â its best singleday gold haul of these Games. Sandeep stormed to the menâs 400m T64 title in a world-record 52.28s, while Haney won the menâs javelin F37/38 gold with a worldrecord throw of 60.49m. Sumit Antil, the Paralympic champion, defended his javelin crown in the menâs F42-44/61-64 combined event with a throw of 72.46m. It was not a record, but enough to lead an Indian sweep: Mahendra Gurjar took silver with 59.03m and Sandip Sanjay Sargar bronze with 64.48m. Pranav Soorma defended his menâs club throw F51 title with a Games-record 32.87m. Sandeepâs compatriot Ajay Kumar claimed bronze in 400m T64 in a Games-record 53.61s. Nimisha C won silver in womenâs long jump T47 with 5.37m, while Parmod Bijarnia took silver in the menâs 1500m T46 in 4:09.65. Even two would level the gold count at 30, with Koreaâs silver advantage deciding the tie-break. Whatever the final order, Indiaâs record haul has made this a landmark campaign. title: As long as I had that fire in me, I knew I could keep going: Joshna Chinappa
text: âWhen you start out at 15, youâre so excited and just happy to be there. I never thought I would still be playing even today at 40,â begins Joshna Chinappa , who won two bronze medals in squash at the recently concluded 2026 Asian Games â one in the mixed doubles (partnering with Velavan Senthilkumar) and one in the womenâs team event. Exceprts: âIâve always bounced back and focused on whatâs nextâ Although an Asian Games gold remains missing from her collection, Joshna says she does not define her career by the medal she has yet to win. âOf course, it would have been great to win gold. But medals donât define me. I love what I do and have dedicated so much of my life to it. If things donât go my way, it is disappointing, but Iâve always bounced back and focused on whatâs next,â she says. âSOmething inside me kept saying that there was more to giveâ Joshna says quitting has crossed her mind several times, but the urge to achieve more kept her going. âIâve wondered many times if this is all worth it and if I should call it a day. But something inside me kept saying there was more to give and more to achieve. I went back to training, played a few tournaments and did well. As long as I had the fire in me, I knew I could keep doing this,â she says. âHAVING A GOOD TEAM IS VERY IMPORTANTâ Having spent around 95% of her career travelling without a coach or physiotherapist, Joshna says her support system has helped her navigate the loneliness of professional squash. âI have my coach and psychologist whom I speak to. They help me get back on track, motivate me and push me to look forward to the next tournament. Even when they arenât physically with me, they are very supportive,â she says. âTHIS GENERATION IS GETTING support much sooner in lifeâ Joshna says todayâs squash players benefit from better financial backing, government support, information and coaching. âThis generation is getting support much sooner in life, and thatâs a good thing,â she says. However, she believes her generation gained valuable international exposure by spending months abroad on tour. âIf you want to be in the worldâs top 10 or 20, you have to play those tournaments and spend time away from home and family,â she adds. âWe would get along very wellâ For a dream squash doubles team featuring Indian athletes, Joshna picks tennis stars Sania Mirza and Rohan Bopanna, along with former national squash champion Ritwik Bhattacharya. âSania is a great racket-sport player, so that would be helpful. Bopanna is also a friend, so we would get along very well. I would choose Ritwik too; he was a national squash champion and reached the world doubles finals many years ago,â she adds. âIndia has a great chance to win a medalâ With squash set to make its Olympic debut at Los Angeles 2028, Joshna is optimistic about India's prospects. âItâs great that itâs finally being included; itâs about time. There is still time to prepare, and I definitely think India has a great chance to win a medal there. I hope it happens,â she says. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. title: Ashok clinches silver in men's 65kg powerlifting at Asian Para Games
text: Ashok won the silver medal in the men's 65kg powerlifting event (Image credit: X) India's Ashok won the silver medal in the men's 65kg powerlifting event at the Asian Para Games 2026 on Tuesday. The 37-year-old lifted 192kg to finish second behind China's Zou Yi, the reigning Paralympic champion, who won gold with a lift of 216kg. Indonesia's Margono claimed bronze after lifting 177kg. Watch âThis medal means a lotâ: Lovlina Borgohain on Asian Games gold & Olympic ambitions Ashok lifts 192kg to win silver Ashok started the competition with a successful 187kg lift. He then improved his performance to lift 192kg in his second attempt. However, he could not lift 201kg in his final attempt and finished with a best lift of 192kg. What is para powerlifting? Para powerlifting is a bench press event that tests an athlete's upper-body strength. Athletes compete in different weight categories, but the sport has only one discipline. The sport is open to athletes with impairments in their hips or legs. Ashok's journey Ashok hails from Gohana in Haryana's Sonipat district. He contracted polio as a child and went on to compete in para powerlifting at the international level. title: Ran for a job, found a podium
text: When the baton reached Manu Thekkinalil Saji, India was trailing in third place. Inside the roaring stadium in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, the 24-year-old did what has defined much of his journey: He held his nerve and ran without flinching. His blistering leg helped India to silver in the mixed 4x400m relay at the 2026 Asian Games. The team clocked 3:14.46 to finish just behind Bahrain, and Manu shared the podium with MR Poovamma, Vishal TK and Vithya Ramraj. A few days later, he added a bronze in the menâs 4x400m relay. Two medals at his first Asian Games. Yet his story did not start on an international track. Manu comes from Karinkanikunnu, a small hamlet near Muttil in Wayanad. It is a misty farming district, far from elite sports facilities and synthetic running tracks. No federation spotted him early. No academy groomed him. He was a BTech student at Vidya Academy of Science and Technology in Thrissur, and he started running for one reason: To get into the Army. In Wayanad, as in much of rural Kerala, an Army job means stability. For a lower middle-class family, it promises a regular income and long-term security. Athletics was simply Manuâs way to clear the physical test. âMy initial aim was to join the Army. I started training for Army recruitment. Later, with my performance in sprinting, I changed my focus to sprinting,â he said. The man who changed that focus was Rajmohan M K, an athletics coach at SAI, Thiruvananthapuram. Others saw a young man training for a job. Rajmohan saw a promising quarter-miler. No sponsors waited in the paddy fields of Wayanad. For nearly two years, Manu juggled engineering exams, hostel fees and daily training. Running was expensive. Spikes, nutrition, travel and meet entries all cost money. Every national camp meant another adjustment for his farming family. His parents never said no, even when athletics looked like a detour from a dependable job. He trained on basic tracks and often travelled to Thiruvananthapuram for better sessions. His BTech degree stayed in reserve, a safety net in case running led nowhere. His path mirrors that of many Indian track and field athletes. Javelin thrower DP Manu once trained with a bamboo spear because his school had no proper javelin. His mother sold her jewellery to buy him shoes. Manu Sajiâs rise, too, was built on sacrifice and limited resources. The breakthrough came in 2022, when he won gold in the mixed relay at the Asian U20 Championships. In 2025, he helped the Indian menâs 4x400m team win silver at the Asian Championships in Gumi. The boy who first ran for a job was now running to keep India on the podium. âI am so proud to represent India. It is my first Asian Games, and I did well. My only thought is I have to give the baton first,â he said. After his medal-winning run in Nagoya, he called his parents back in Wayanad. They broke down in tears. Back home, Muttil grama panchayat gave him a grand welcome. An autorickshaw procession set off from Edappetti, chenda melam filled the streets, and hundreds gathered at the bus stand. The panchayat honoured him with gold coins and a cash prize. The village that once watched him train for Army physical tests now celebrated an Asian Games medallist. Manu still describes his job simply: Hand over the baton in the best possible position. Disclaimer : Views expressed above are the author's own.

title: Asian Para Games: Simran Sharma, Praveen Kumar and Sachin Khilari lead Indiaâs athletics gold rush
text: Simran Sharma (Image credit: PCI) Simran Sharmaâs golden double headlined Indiaâs athletics campaign on Day 3 of the Asian Para Games, as track and field athletes collected 22 medals, including five gold, in Nagoya on Wednesday. After winning the womenâs 200m T12 title on Tuesday, the visually impaired sprinter claimed the 100m gold in a Gamesrecord 12.02 seconds, ahead of Iranâs Hajar Safarzadeh (12.30). Simran became only the fourth Indian to win two gold medals at a single Para Asiad, joining Ankur Dhama, Sheetal Devi and Nishad Kumar. Watch Harita Bhadra Exclusive | 2 Asian Games Medals, Now the 22.45s World Championships Chase Dilip Gavit supplied another track gold, winning the menâs 100m T46/47 combined event in 10.69s. Mohammed Basil Morssinganakathi, competing in T47, took silver in a Games-record 10.72s. T46 and T47 cover athletes with upperlimb impairments, differing in the nature and extent of the impairment. Field events brought three more gold. Ayush Verma topped the menâs shot put F53 with 8.16m. The class is for seated throwers with significant trunk and leg movement impairments. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Praveen Kumar defended his menâs high jump T44/64 title, clearing a Games-record 2.05m. Praveen has a lower-limb impairment -- T64 athletes use a prosthesis, while T44 covers lower-limb impairments without one. Banti claimed silver with a personal best 1.92m in the same event. Image credit: PCI Sachin Khilari completed the gold rush with a Games-record 15.87m in the menâs shot put F46, securing a podium sweep for India. Mohd Yasser won the silver at 15.06m and Parveen took the bronze at 14.94m. Other silver came from Bhagyashri Jadhav (womenâs shot put F34, personal best 8.19m), Manjeet (menâs javelin F12/13, career-best 61.03m), Preeti Pal (womenâs 100m T35), Akira Banothu (menâs 400m T35/38) and Sharath Makanahalli, whose menâs 1500m T12 medal after Uzbekistanâs winner was disqualified for obstruction. Indiaâs athletics tally has risen to 42 medals, 13 gold, 14 silver and 15 bronze, second only to China. Athletics has so far accounted for 13 of Indiaâs 14 gold medals across all sports at the Games. title: After historic best-ever medal haul, where will India finish in Asian Para Games standings?
text: Indian para-athletes Praveen Kumar and Banti (PTI Photo) NEW DELHI: India's para-athletes have scripted history at the Asian Para Games, recording their best-ever medal haul of 114 medals, including a record 30 gold, after a spectacular nine-gold flourish on Friday. But with a few events remaining on the final day, one question remains: where will India finish in the medal standings? India are currently fourth in the standings at the Aichi-Nagoya Games, having surpassed their previous best of 108 medals, including 27 gold, achieved at Hangzhou in 2023. The contingent also improved its gold-medal record by three, underlining the scale of its achievement in Japan. Watch Harita Bhadra Exclusive | 2 Asian Games Medals, Now the 22.45s World Championships Chase However, the final positions could still change when the remaining competitions conclude on Saturday. South Korea, currently fifth, are the biggest threat to India's fourth-place standing, while Iran also have a mathematical chance of moving up. There are no events left for the Indian athletes in the Games. Regardless of the final position, India are assured of their best-ever finish in terms of medal standings at the Asian Para Games. Their previous best was sixth place at Hangzhou in 2023. ALSO READ: India script history with best-ever haul of 114 medals Can South Korea push India down to fifth? India's 30 gold medals put them ahead of South Korea, who have won 28 gold, 36 silver and 33 bronze medals for a total of 97. South Korea could overtake India if they win two more gold medals in the remaining events. That would take them level with India on 30 gold, and their higher silver count â 36 to India's 35 â would give them the edge in the standings. Iran are sixth with 26 gold, 36 silver and 40 bronze medals. They would need four more gold medals to draw level with India, making a late jump above the Indian contingent a tougher prospect with only a few events remaining. India's final position will therefore depend on results in the remaining competition schedule. The standings will be confirmed once the last events are completed on Saturday. Nine golds cap India's historic campaign India's record haul was sealed by a remarkable final-day performance on Friday, when the contingent won nine gold medals â its highest single-day gold tally of this edition. Athletics remained India's biggest contributor, accounting for 65 medals, 12 more than at the previous Games. Badminton, shooting and archery added to the golden finish. The 168-member Indian contingent's performance was particularly impressive given that it was nearly half the size of the squad that competed in Hangzhou in 2023. title: Navdeep Singh credits SAI JLN Stadium support as India deliver record Asian Para Games medal haul
text: Navdeep Singh (Pic credit: SAI) NEW DELHI: Indian para-javelin star Navdeep Singh has credited the support and training facilities at the Sports Authority of Indiaâs (SAI) Jawaharlal Nehru (JLN) Stadium in New Delhi for helping the countryâs para-athletes deliver a historic performance at the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games. India finished fourth in the continental competition with a record 114 medals â 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze â its best-ever haul at the Games. Para athletics led the charge with 65 medals, including 22 gold, 19 silver and 24 bronze. Watch Suchika Tariyal on her Asian Games bronze, childhood trauma, and never giving up | TOISA Spotlight Navdeep won bronze in the menâs javelin throw F40/F41 on Friday, improving on his fourth-place finish at the 2022 edition. The Paris Paralympics gold medallist said training alongside fellow athletes at the JLN Stadiumâs main track helped him prepare for the competition environment in Aichi-Nagoya. âMost of us Asian Games-bound athletes, including me, did our preparations at the JLN Stadium for the Asian Games 2026,â said Navdeep after his medal win. âThis allowed us to acclimatise and get the feel. Despite the ongoing [Indian Super League] football matches, they kept the Asian Games a priority, which I felt was quite impressive, and that supported me,â he added. Dedicated training access helped athletes Navdeep also highlighted how access to the main track allowed athletes across disciplines to focus on their preparations without unnecessary delays. âSprinters need an empty track, so they got a good chance to train inside it. I majorly train at the SAI Regional Centres [Bengaluru, Sonipat and Gandhinagar], where there is not much crowd and I donât have to wait for other athletes to finish their throws. This all happened here at the JLN Stadium too. I could focus on my preparations rather than focusing on rotations and waiting for my turn,â Navdeep said, expressing hopes of returning to the JLN Stadium for the next season. A total of 14 para-athletics medallists from the Aichi-Nagoya Games trained at the JLN Stadium ahead of the competition. More than 50 other para-athletes also train at the facility. The silver medallists included Manjeet, Nimisha Chakkungalparambil, Varun Singh Bhati, Preeti Pal and Ajeet Singh Yadav. Bronze medallists included Sandeep Kumar in the menâs 100m T44, Sandip Sanjay Sargar in the menâs javelin combined classification event, Navdeep in the menâs javelin F40/F41 and Anubhav Choudhary in the menâs 100m T35. text: Swati Chaudhary (Image credit: PCI) Indiaâs Swati Chaudhary won the silver medal in the womenâs W1 individual archery event at the Asian Para Games on Thursday. title: âAye pehelwaan kaisi hai?â: Neeraj Yadav remembered as a friend, motivator and âzindadil insaanâ
text: Neeraj Yadav remembered as a friend NEW DELHI: "Aye pehelwaan kaisi hai?" - that is how Suvarna Raj remembers Neeraj Yadav speaking to her. The two para-athletes shared years of training, laughter and memories. For Suvarna, who won gold at the 2026 Asian Para Games, Neeraj was a 'zindadil insaan' - a person full of life who always found ways to encourage others, especially young athletes. The athletics field will no longer echo with his laughter. His fellow athletes will miss the way he waved his hands, called out to them by their familiar nicknames and brought life to every gathering. Neeraj, a three-time Asian Para Games gold medallist, was found dead in Delhi on Tuesday night. Preliminary reports suggested that he may have consumed poison, though the circumstances surrounding his death remain unclear. His body was taken to Guru Teg Bahadur (GTB) Hospital for a postmortem examination, with a police investigation underway. Watch Suchika Tariyal on her Asian Games bronze, childhood trauma, and never giving up | TOISA Spotlight For those who trained with him, he was a friend, a fellow athlete, an elder brother and a source of encouragement. The news of his death left the para-athletics community in shock. Chief coach S Satyanarayana, who was close to Neeraj, struggled to come to terms with the loss. âNeeraj has died by suicide. I was close to him. He was a very good human being. His body is at GTB Hospital. They are yet to hand over the body to us. Tough time for all of us,â Satyanarayana told TimesofIndia.com. âHe was my roommateâ For Navdeep Singh, India's Paris Paralympics gold medallist in para-javelin and a bronze medallist at the 2026 Asian Para Games, Neeraj was more than a fellow athlete. He was an elder-brother figure with whom he had shared rooms during training camps and competitions. He was asleep when his phone rang in the early hours of Wednesday. It was fellow para-javelin thrower and Paralympic champion Sumit Antil, who asked him to rush to the hospital and informed him about Neeraj. Navdeep rushed to GTB Hospital, where he learnt that Neeraj had died. The athlete's body was subsequently taken for a postmortem examination as authorities began investigating the circumstances surrounding his death. Recalling their time together, Navdeep said they had shared a room during training in Bengaluru in 2023. They had also travelled together for competitions, including the 2022 IWAS World Games in Portugal. âWe were roommates for a long time. We shared a room in Bengaluru when we were training there throughout 2023. Whenever we travelled for competitions, we stayed together. We had also gone to Portugal for the IWAS World Games in 2022,â Navdeep recalled. âWe trained together for a long time, from 2021 to 2023. We were part of the same group.â What Navdeep remembers most about Neeraj is his innocence and playful nature. Although Neeraj was older, the two shared an easy friendship filled with jokes and laughter. âHe was innocent and had a great sense of humour. He was much older than me, but we never felt that age difference. He would jokingly call me âbhai saabâ and use words for me that people usually use for someone older. We were like people of the same age when we were together. We used to joke around a lot and spend a lot of time together. There are so many memories that it is difficult to choose just one or two,â Navdeep said. âWe used to go out together whenever either of us had some work. Sometimes we would go to the market for juice or watch movies. He was very fond of films, and I also love watching them. We spent a lot of time together and shared many memories,â he said. âA zindadil insaanâ Suvarna had known Neeraj since the early years of her athletics career. She began training around 2016-17, and the two practised together before travelling to the 2018 Asian Para Games. Even shortly before leaving for the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Para Games in Japan, Suvarna was in touch with him. She needed a discus, and Neeraj had offered to help arrange one. She did not know that their conversation would be among their last. âI had spoken to him two days before I left. I needed a discus, and he said he would try to arrange one for me. I left two days later, and we did not speak again,â Suvarna recalled. Neeraj was in Sonipat at the time and had told her that he would try to arrange the equipment. âI had only two days left before leaving. He was in Sonipat and said he would try to arrange it. Now, I keep wondering what happened and why things turned out this way. It is difficult to understand because he was such a strong person,â she said. Suvarna also remembered the way Neeraj spoke to people. His familiar way of addressing her as âpehelwaanâ had become a part of their friendship. âWe practised together from the time I started my athletics career around 2016-17. We also went to Asia together in 2018. I liked the way he spoke. He had his own style and would always call me âpehelwaanâ. That was something he said regularly,â she said. âI still cannot come to terms with what has happened. Honestly, it feels as if there is something more to the story and that we are not hearing everything. It is still very difficult for me to believe,â Suvarna said. The athlete who encouraged others Neeraj competed in the F55 category and was serving a four-year suspension after testing positive for a banned substance, which ruled him out of the 2026 Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya. He was also stripped of the javelin and discus gold medals he had won at the 2023 Hangzhou Asian Para Games. The loss of those medals also meant the loss of the associated government cash reward and the prospect of a government job. Diagnosed with post-polio residual paralysis at the age of seven, Neeraj initially took up wheelchair tennis before moving to para-athletics. He won javelin gold at the 2018 Asian Para Games in Jakarta with an Asian-record throw of 29.84 metres. At the 2023 Asian Para Games in Hangzhou, he won gold in both the javelin and discus. Those medals were subsequently stripped following his doping case. For Suvarna, however, it is difficult to reconcile the circumstances of Neeraj's death with the encouragement he continued to offer other athletes. She recalled how he had recently motivated another athlete, Anmol, urging him not to give up and to work towards a comeback. âHe was such a strong person and always motivated others. We have an athlete named Anmol, whom Neeraj encouraged just three or four days ago. He motivated Anmol so much that he felt inspired to keep going,â Suvarna said. âNeeraj would tell him not to give up and would encourage him to make a comeback. He would say, âKeep doing well. Work hard. Do this, do that.â He also reminded Anmol that I had won a medal at the age of 44. And then, suddenly, we received this news.â Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Suvarna said Neeraj had also spoken about returning to competition in 2028. That conversation has made his death even harder for her to understand. âWe had never heard that he was depressed because of his sport. I spoke to Anmol early this morning, and he told me that Neeraj had been talking about 2028. He was saying, âJust wait and see what I do in 2028, how I make my comeback. Everyone will remember that comeback.â He was speaking like this only recently,â she added. Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

title: Had no clue we had emulated a 72-year-old feat: Harmeet & Yashaswini
text: Harmeet Desai and Yashaswini Ghorpade Harmeet Desai and Yashaswini Ghorpade, who created history by winning the bronze medal in mixed doubles at the Asian Table Tennis Championships, had no clue about the magnitude of their achievement until the match was over. The last time India won a medal in mixed doubles at the Asian TT Championships was in 1954, when Yatin Vyas and Meena Parande secured silver. "We did not know that India had not won a mixed doubles medal at this event after 1954. We had no clue that we had emulated a 72-year-old feat. Now that we know about it, that makes the win even more special," they tell us. 'We were just four points away from a defeat' Harmeet: In the quarterfinal against our South Korean opponents, we were trailing 1-7 in the fourth game, and just four points away from a heartbreaking defeat. In a high-pressure knockout game at a major event, youâd lose from that position nine times out of 10. Yashaswini deserves a lot of credit for raising the bar and ensuring that we never gave up. Making a comeback from that situation was an unbelievable effort. The quarterfinal match was on her birthday; so that made the medal even more special. We turned a near-defeat into a historic medal. Yashaswini: This was the best birthday gift I could have asked for! We didn't have a lot of time to recover before the semifinal, but I am happy we won the bronze medal. I want to dedicate it to my dad, who has made a lot of sacrifices to ensure that I always get the support that is so crucial for a professional sportsperson. Playing with Harmeet bhaiya is fun. We started playing together two years ago, and I have learned a lot from him. His experience always comes in handy in crunch situations. Even when we were in a tricky position in the quarterfinal, we never lost self-belief. 'Want to win many more medals for India' Harmeet: Despite my best efforts, 2026 hasn't been a great year professionally. So, this win has really boosted my confidence. If someone had told me a couple of years ago that I would win a medal in mixed doubles, I would have laughed it off. But playing mixed doubles with Yashaswini has also helped me become a better player in singles, as I have become a better counter-attacking player. She is a terrific player and has that X factor which is crucial to shine in big events. We bring out the best in each other in crunch situations. This is also my first big win since my son (Dhrishiv) was born. It hasn't been easy to stay away from him, and when results were not going my way, there were moments of self-doubt. It was disappointing to not win a medal in the doubles and men's team event at the Asian Games. I am grateful to my family and team for constantly encouraging me to keep going. My wife Krittwika deserves a lot of credit for making a lot of sacrifices and ensuring that I can focus on my sport. This medal is for all of them. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Yashaswini: We don't want to be complacent and want to win many more medals for India. In recent times, Indian players have done really well in doubles and mixed doubles at big events, and we need to keep it going. We have the ITTF (International Table Tennis Federation) Mixed Team World Cup coming up next month, and we want to do well. The biggest dream, of course, is to do well at the Olympics one day. Looking forward to celebrating Diwali at home: Harmeet Given that it is Dhrishiv's first Diwali, I am eagerly looking forward to enjoying the festival at home. But I will also stay focused and want to end the year on a high note. Hopefully, I can keep doing well and continue to be a part of the Indian team. While the year did not start on a great note, this latest victory proves that hard work, perseverance and patience are eventually rewarded. Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. title: âInjury much better nowâ: Neeraj Chopra on the path to recovery; to resume training and rehabilitation in next few weeks
text: Neeraj Chopra (PTI Photo) New Delhi: Olympic and world champion javelin thrower Neeraj Chopra said his recovery from injury is on the right path and training, rehab process will begun in the next couple of weeks. The 2020 Tokyo Olympics gold medallist has kept next year as his target after sustaining an injury, with his focus on delivering strong performances ahead of LA 2028. Chopra, who won gold at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics and silver at the Paris 2024 Olympics in men's javelin throw, has been one of India's leading figures in recent years. However, Chopra missed the recent 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya after he suffered an ankle ligament injury during a training session, which also ruled him out for the rest of the season. "My injury is much better now. I faced some issues initially in the first month and a half, but it has improved significantly. I consulted Dr. Dinshaw Pardiwala and he has advised that I can now resume training and begin proper rehabilitation. My plan is to start both in the next couple of weeks," Neeraj told SAI Media. The two-time Olympic medallist clarified that he followed complete rest as advised by his medical team. "For my injury, the doctors had advised rest, and that is exactly what I followed. With regard to competitions, TOPS (Target Olympic Podium Scheme) and SAI (Sports Authority of India) have been supporting me for years. I have been part of the TOPS Core Group for many years now, and whenever I need any support, they are there," he added. Neeraj also welcomed the Union Cabinet's approval of the Khelo India Sports Goods Manufacturing Scheme on October 28, calling it a major step for Indian sport. "The Khelo India Sports Goods Manufacturing Scheme, which was approved by the Union Cabinet, is an amazing step. Athletes face a lot of issues in procuring certain equipment in India or have to import sporting equipment from abroad. With schemes like these, as equipment will be manufactured in India, it will become much easier for them to source it," he noted. title: Who is Suvarna Raj? Asian Para Games gold medallist who is also an advocate
text: Suvarna Raj (Image credit: PCI) Suvarna Raj, a 44-year-old para-athlete from Greater Noida, won gold for India in the women's F54 discus throw at the Asian Para Games on Thursday. She finished first with a best throw of 15.66m, adding another medal to her international career. A wheelchair user, Suvarna has been competing in para-athletics since 2017. She has represented India at three Asian Para Games and several international events. Away from sports, she works to improve accessibility for people with disabilities. Watch Asmita Dey Unfiltered: Favourite Food, Match-Day Music & More | Rapid Fire | TOISA Suvarna Raj wins gold with 15.66m throw Suvarna produced a steady performance in the final, with four of her six throws going beyond 15m. Her best effort came in the fifth attempt, when she threw 15.66m to take the gold medal. Iran's Shahla Hadidi won silver with 15.45m, while Vietnam's Thi Ngoc Thuy Nguyen finished third with 14.65m. Suvarna's six attempts were 13.68m, 15.09m, 15.05m, 14.57m, 15.66m and 15.19m. Who is Suvarna Raj? Suvarna is an international para-athlete who competes in the F54 discus throw category. She is coached by Pintu Nagar and has built her career through regular training and hard work since taking up the sport in 2017. She is ranked second in Asia in the F54 discus throw, according to previously reported rankings. Her latest gold at the Asian Para Games adds to a growing list of achievements. Suvarna Raj's medals and achievements Suvarna has won medals at several international competitions. Asian Para Games: Gold in the women's F54 discus throw in 2026. Dubai World Para Athletics Grand Prix 2026: Bronze in the women's F54/55 discus throw at the 17th Fazza International Para Athletics Championship. Canberra Track Meet, Australia, January 2026: Gold in discus throw and silver in shot put. National Youth Award, 2015: Received the award from the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports. Her career reflects years of work in both training and international competition. She has carried out more than 1,000 accessibility audits across India to help identify barriers faced by people with disabilities. She has also served as the Election Commission of India's Brand Ambassador for Accessible Elections, supporting efforts to make voting easier for people with disabilities. Her training and competition expenses are supported under the government's Annual Calendar for Training and Competition (ACTC). She has received financial assistance of Rs 7,70,607 under the programme. What is the F54 discus throw category? F54 is a classification for seated field athletes whose impairments affect trunk and lower-body function. Athletes compete from a throwing chair and use their arms and upper-body strength to throw the discus. Limited trunk control can affect how they balance and generate power during a throw. title: Just 17 athletes! India prepare for Dakar 2026 Youth Olympics with smallest-ever squad: Full list and everything you need to know
text: Syndrela Das and Dhinidhi Desinghu India will have a 17-member contingent, featuring 11 women and six men, competing across 11 sports at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games in Senegal from October 31 to November 13. Table tennis player Syndrela Das, badminton talent Tanvi Patri and swimmer Dhinidhi Desinghu are among the country's leading medal prospects at the fourth edition of the Summer Youth Olympics, which will be staged in Africa for the first time. Das will take part in the women's singles table tennis competition, while Asian Under-17 badminton champion Patri will represent India in the women's singles event. Desinghu is entered in three swimming events: the women's 100m freestyle, 200m freestyle and 200m individual medley. India's participation will span athletics, archery, badminton, beach wrestling, boxing, equestrian, judo, swimming, table tennis, windsurfing and wushu. The 17-athlete squad will be the country's smallest contingent at a Summer Youth Olympic Games. The 2026 edition will be held across Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly over 15 days. Around 2,700 athletes are expected to compete in 25 sports for 153 medal events. Ten additional engagement sports will also be part of the programme, but will not offer medals. Dakar 2026 will mark the first time an Olympic sporting event is held on African soil. The Games were initially scheduled for 2022 but were postponed by four years due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The previous Summer Youth Olympics took place in Buenos Aires, Argentina, in 2018. India have collected 23 medals across the three previous editions, comprising three gold, 16 silver and four bronze. The inaugural Games were held in Singapore in 2010, followed by Nanjing in China in 2014 and Buenos Aires in 2018. title: High performance shooting centre opens in Navi Mumbai
text: shooting centre Navi Mumbai: Lakshya Shooting Club and Axis Bank inaugurated a high-performance shooting centre at CBD Belapur, the first of its kind in the MMR, to support Indian athletes preparing for international competitions, including the Olympic Games. The para-inclusive centre will provide training, coaching, sports science, nutrition, medicine and athlete-development support under one roof. This was conceptualised by Olympian shooter and Dronacharya awardee Suma Shirur, who dreamt of opening such a facility in the city to tap young talents. The six-storey centre has two dedicated 10-metre shooting ranges, strength and conditioning facilities, biomechanics assessment, physiotherapy, sports psychology and nutrition support, recovery areas and residential facilities. It will offer Elite Residency, Day Scholar and Development programmes, providing separate pathways for athletes at different stages. The centre will focus primarily on elite shooters preparing for international competitions, while Lakshyaâs wider network will continue identifying and nurturing emerging talent. Lakshya Shooting Club was established in 2006 by Indian Olympian and former national shooting coach Suma Shirur. Its athletes have competed at national and international events, including the Olympic and Paralympic Games, Asian Games, Commonwealth Games and World Championships. They include three-time Paralympic medallist Avani Lekhara , who won gold medals at Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024, and Parth Mane, the 2024 junior world champion and a team silver medallist at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games 2026. Axis Bank group head Vijay Mulbagal said the partnership sought to provide aspiring and elite athletes with access to infrastructure, coaching and technical support. Shirur, Lakshyaâs founder and high-performance director, said the centre would support every aspect of athletesâ performance as they prepared for global competition. The green-certified building was constructed to meet sustainability standards for energy and resource efficiency. title: Sexual offence charge rocks India's Asian Para Games contingent; swimmer faces lifetime ban
text: Mohammad Shams Aalam Shaikh (Image credit: Instagram) NEW DELHI: The Indian contingent at the Asian Para Games in Nagoya has been left embarrassed after para swimmer Mohammad Shams Aalam Shaikh was detained by Japanese police following allegations of sexually harassing and molesting a female hotel employee. The 40-year-old, once a world No 1 in his event, was sent back to India on Tuesday, a day after the alleged incident, and faces the prospect of a lifetime ban from the Paralympic Committee of India (PCI). A senior PCI official, who is part of the Indian delegation in Nagoya and who handled the entire situation, confirmed the development to TOI, describing the alleged misconduct as âreprehensible and intolerableâ and saying there could be âno justificationâ for such behaviour by an athlete representing the country on the international stage.â Watch Suchika Tariyal on her Asian Games bronze, childhood trauma, and never giving up | TOISA Spotlight âAalam is staring at no less than a lifetime ban for bringing disrepute to the entire Indian delegation participating at the Asian Para Games and for embarrassing the country on the world stage,â the official said. According to the official, the incident occurred on Monday at the Four Points by Sheraton hotel, where the Indian para swimming team was staying. The female employee was reportedly carrying out housekeeping duties in the swimmerâs room when the alleged misconduct took place. âThe local organising committee (LOC) informed the chef-de-missionâs (CDM) office that an alleged sexual harassment and molestation incident had occurred at the hotel and that an Indian athlete had been detained by the local police,â the official said. âWhen we reached the hotel, the police and senior hotel managers were already there. We were told that the athlete had inappropriately touched the female housekeeping staff member, made sexually coloured gestures, attempted to grope her and made sexual advances. She rushed out and informed her superiors. This is what we were told by the police and hotel staff,â the official added. The official said the delegation apologised to the hotel authorities and the employee. Following the complaint, police detained Shaikh and took him to a local police station. The official said the authorities sought his arrest and that he be formally presented before a court. The LOC subsequently intervened, with the Indian delegation asked to furnish a written apology to the employee and ensure that the athlete left Japan. Shaikh was moved to another hotel for the night and booked on the first available flight, departing Nagoya at around 2 pm local time on Tuesday, the official said. He was released after the written apology was furnished, according to the officialâs account. âThe police authorities had clearly recorded the sexual offence allegation in their formal complaint, in Japanese. We can confirm that since I saw that,â the official said. The official added the incident had diverted senior Indian officials from the contingentâs ongoing sporting campaign. âInstead of focusing on the Games and our athletesâ performances, we spent several hours at the police station and later at the hotel premises convincing the authorities. We were embarrassed in front of everyone,â the official said. He added that the employee appeared to be in deep shock when the delegation returned to the hotel. The hotel and LOC, he said, sought updates on the action India would take and warned that they could pursue formal legal proceedings if they were dissatisfied with the response. The PCI has informed the govt in New Delhi of the proposed action, the official said. After the Games, PCI officials, para swimming administrators and members of the delegation will deliberate on the matter and recommend stringent sanctions to the sports ministry and Sports Authority of India (SAI). âThe CDMâs office has already recommended a lifetime ban. A formal decision will be taken at a meeting in Delhi after we return,â the official said. Shaikh, who hails from Biharâs Madhubani district and lives with his family in Mumbaiâs Dharavi, was sent home without competing in his scheduled events on Wednesday. The incident comes close on the heels of an Indian hockey umpire and technical official Gurinder Singh Sangha was being sent home from the able-bodied Asian Games in Nagoya following sexual misconduct and harassment complaints by a Malaysian hockey official and a hotel staff member. title: From school rustication to Asian Games glory: Jay Meena's inspiring journey
text: Jay Meena (Image credit: X) For soft tennis player Jay Meena, being rusticated from school turned out to be a turning point in his life. After struggling to find admission at another school, he joined an institution run by his coach, where he discovered the sport that would eventually help him make history for India. Meena recalled his journey, including years of disappointment in quarterfinals, before winning India's first-ever Asian Games medal in soft tennis at the 2026 Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan. Watch Suchika Tariyal on her Asian Games bronze, childhood trauma, and never giving up | TOISA Spotlight Speaking at Doordarshan's sports conclave 'Khel Mahakumb' on Friday, Meena described his 16-year sporting career as a journey full of ups and downs. "The life of a sportsperson is no less than a roller-coaster ride. You will not believe it, but in these five days, I have seen the entire hard work of my 16-year career," Meena said. "It is not that I do not give 100 per cent in my first and second matches. I give my 100 per cent in every match, but the quarterfinals have been a nightmare for me, now I believe it's all a part of destiny," he added. How school rustication changed Meena's life Meena said he faced difficulties finding another school after being rusticated. He eventually joined a school run by his coach, which had two tennis courts. It was there that he came across soft tennis during the summer vacations. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Looking back, he believes the setback helped him find his path in sport. "Had I not been rusticated... I would not have become a player or made history for the country," Meena said. The 24-year-old had reached the men's singles quarterfinals at the 2023 Asian Games in Hangzhou. At the 2026 edition in Japan, he finally went beyond that stage. From quarterfinal heartbreak to a historic medal Meena defeated the Philippines' Sherwin Nuguit 4-3 in a closely fought quarterfinal. After falling behind 3-5 in the deciding game, he won four points in a row to secure his place in the semifinals. The victory guaranteed India its first-ever Asian Games medal in soft tennis. Meena later lost to Japan's Takuya Kurosaka in the semifinals but finished with a historic bronze. title: Asian Para Games: Nitesh Kumar, Thulasimathi Murugesan claim silver in badminton mixed doubles
text: Nagoya, Oct 23 (IANSâ) India's Nitesh Kumar and Thulasimathi Murugesan clinched silver in the Mixed Doubles SL3-SU5 category at the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games here on Friday. Indiaâs Nitesh Kumar and Thulasimathi Murugesan win the silver medal in the mixed doubles SL3-SU5 badminton event at the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games on Friday. The Indian pair lose 21-11, 19-21, 14-21 to Indonesiaâs Leani Ratri Oktila and Hikmat Ramdani in the final. Nitesh and Thulasimathi start strongly, winning the opening game 21-11, but their Indonesian opponents fight back to take the second game 21-19. India then lose the deciding game 14-21, settling for silver after a hard-fought contest. Watch Bombay Sport Exchange: Mustafa Ghouse on ISL, India's sporting ecosystem and grassroots problem Thulasimathi, Nitesh add to India's medal haul Thulasimathi still has a chance to win gold as she prepares to compete in the women's doubles SL3-SU5 final alongside Manasi Girishchandra Joshi. The Indian duo will face China's Yang Qiuxia and Xiao Zuxian. Earlier, Thulasimathi wins silver in the women's singles SU5 final against China's Yang Qiuxia. Nitesh, meanwhile, claims gold in the men's singles SL4 event after defeating compatriot Pramod Bhagat 21-18, 21-16 in an all-Indian final between two Paralympic champions. Nithya Sre Sumathy Sivan also takes silver in the women's singles SH6 final after losing to China's Li Fengmei 12-21, 13-21. In para badminton, SL3 is for players with significant lower-limb impairments, while SL4 is for athletes with lower-limb impairments who have better movement and balance. SU5 is for players with upper-limb impairments, and SH6 is for athletes with short stature. title: Feisty Thulasimathi Murugesan turns âalienâ tag into medal magic
text: Thulasimathi Murugesan Called an âalienâ and bullied for her dark skin and congenital left-hand deformity, Thulasimathi Murugesan has turned badminton into her most eloquent answer to those who doubted her abilities. On Friday, the 24-year-old produced a golden flourish at Asian Para Games, winning three medals in a single day to spearhead Indiaâs campaign. Thulasimathi and Manasi Joshi clinched womenâs doubles SL3-SU5 gold, beating Chinaâs Yang Qiuxia and Xiao Zuxian 21-16, 21-13. Watch Harita Bhadra Exclusive | 2 Asian Games Medals, Now the 22.45s World Championships Chase She added singles SU5 silver after losing to Yang 18-21, 11-21, before partnering Nitesh Kumar to mixed doubles SL3-SU5 silver, losing to Indonesiaâs Leani Ratri Oktila and Hikmat Ramdani 21-11, 19-21, 14-21. Born without a thumb on her left hand, Thulasimathi endured restricted movement, financial hardship and relentless teasing. Her daily-wage labourer father, Murugesan, nurtured her sporting ambitions, coaching her with his limited sports knowledge through gruelling routines despite limited resources. From inexpensive shoes and secondhand racquets to international podiums, the Kancheepuram girlâs journey continued. At Paris 2024, she became the first Indian woman to win Paralympic badminton silver, in the womenâs singles SU5 category. title: Sheetal Devi: Born without arms, she learned to shoot with her feet and became a world champion, Paralympic medallist and double gold winner at the 2026 Asian Para Games
text: A bow is usually held with one hand and drawn with the other. For Sheetal Devi , neither of those movements was an option. Born without arms, the young archer from Jammu and Kashmir had to find a way to make the equipment work with the body she had. Her answer was a technique that is now recognised around the world. She steadies the bow with her foot, uses her shoulder to draw the string and releases the arrow with the help of her mouth. It is a demanding combination of balance, strength and control. And it has taken years of practice to perfect. Today, Devi is a Paralympic bronze medallist, a world champion and one of India's most celebrated para-archers. At the 2026 Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, she added another major achievement to her record, winning two gold medals and a silver. But the medals tell only part of the story. Her journey is also about learning a skill in an entirely different way, accepting setbacks and continuing to improve. From everyday tasks to an unexpected sporting opportunity Born on January 10, 2007, in Kishtwar district of Jammu and Kashmir, Sheetal grew up in the village of Loidhar. She learnt to perform everyday activities, including writing and eating, using her feet. These early experiences helped her develop the balance and control that would later become important in archery. Her sporting journey began to take shape after she was noticed at an Indian Army camp in 2019. The Army recognised her potential and helped her access educational and medical support. She eventually joined the Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Shrine Board Sports Complex in Katra, where she was introduced to sports. Coach Kuldeep Vedwan played an important role in guiding her towards para-archery. The sport was not an obvious choice, given that conventional archery depends heavily on the use of both arms. Yet her coach and the training team worked with her to explore a method that suited her abilities. At first, even lifting and controlling the bow was difficult. She had to build strength and learn how to coordinate different parts of her body. Training included resistance-band exercises, strength work and shooting at targets placed only a few metres away. With time, she developed the balance and control required to shoot at the standard competition distance of 50 metres. The process was gradual. Each practice session helped her understand what worked, what needed to change and how to make her movements more consistent. A technique built through patience and practice Sheetal's shooting style attracts attention because it looks very different from conventional archery. However, the technique is not a shortcut. It requires precise positioning, strong leg muscles, a stable body and careful control over every movement. She holds the bow with her foot and uses her shoulder to pull the string. A release aid held in her mouth helps her release the arrow. The sequence must be repeated with accuracy, even when the weather, wind or competition pressure makes shooting more difficult. Her progress soon began to show in international competitions. At the 2023 Asian Para Games in Hangzhou, she won gold in the women's individual compound event and the mixed team event, along with a silver medal in women's doubles. She also won silver at the 2023 World Archery Para Championships. The next major milestone came at the Paris 2024 Paralympic Games. Partnering with Rakesh Kumar, she won bronze in the mixed team compound event. At 17, she became India's youngest Paralympic medallist. Although she missed an individual podium finish in Paris, the experience became another stage in her development. In an interview with World Archery in October 2025, after winning the individual world title in Gwangju, South Korea, Sheetal spoke about the doubts she had faced. "I never paid attention to them; I just stayed focused on my game," she said. She also spoke about how rewarding it was to see young girls from distant places express an interest in taking up archery after watching her. Two gold medals, one silver and a bigger message Sheetal returned to the Asian Para Games in 2026 with the aim of defending the titles she had won in Hangzhou. She delivered two gold-medal performances in Japan, retaining the women's individual compound title and winning the compound mixed team event with Toman Kumar. She also earned silver in women's doubles with Payal Nag, completing a three-medal campaign. Speaking to the Asian Paralympic Committee after the victories, she said, "I'm very happy â two gold medals and a silver in my second Asian Para Games. It feels all the hard work done in the past years was rewarded in one day. She also explained how she approached the pressure of the final: "I was just thinking to shoot my best; follow the process." It was a simple description of the focus that has shaped her career. Her story has reached people well beyond the archery field. In a 2024 interview with World Archery, Sheetal spoke about receiving messages from children with disabilities who wanted to follow her example. She said she hoped more people would believe they could achieve something despite their disabilities. She also urged parents to support their children and recognise what they are capable of. Sheetal shares updates through her Instagram account, @sheetal_archery . The belief, along with the training and support she has received, has helped her build a career on her own terms. Her achievements are not simply a story of winning despite a physical condition. They are also a reminder that sporting skill is developed through technique, coaching, practice and the willingness to keep learning. For anyone watching her take aim, the arrow reaching the target may last only a moment. The work behind it has taken years. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. title: 'One dream left': Asian Para Games double medallist Shailesh Kumar sets sights on LA 2028
text: Shailesh Kumar KOLKATA: Bihar para-athlete Shailesh Kumar returned from the 2026 Asian Para Games with a Games-record gold in the menâs high jump T63 category and a bronze in the long jump. Yet, despite finally ending his wait for a long jump medal, the 26-year-old says his focus heading into the next Paralympic cycle will remain firmly on the high jump as he chases his ultimate dream: a Paralympic medal. âI have won two medals at the World Championships and three at the Asian Games, but I donât have a Paralympic medal yet,â Shailesh told TOI in an exclusive interaction on Friday. âThat is the one dream left. Everything now is about qualifying for the Paralympics and winning a medal for India.â The high jumper cleared 1.89m to win gold and set a new Games record in Nagoya, adding to his growing collection of international medals. He also claimed bronze in the menâs long jump T42/T61/T63 event with a leap of 5.57m. The long jump medal carried special significance. At the previous Asian Para Games, Shailesh had competed in both events but finished fourth in the long jump while winning gold in the high jump. This time, he entered the competition determined to make amends. âMy main focus was always the high jump, but I really wanted a medal in the long jump because I had missed out last time in Hangzhou,â he said. The demanding schedule meant Shailesh had to compete on successive days, with the long jump followed by his main event, the high jump. While delighted with the gold, he feels there was still more in the tank. âMy personal best is 1.91m and I cleared 1.89m here. The back-to-back competitions may have had an effect. Had it been only one event, maybe I could have jumped even higher,â said the para-athlete, who is now looking forward to spending time with his family in Jamui till the Chhath Puja celebrations. Even so, he considers the two-medal haul evidence of the consistency he has developed over the last few years. âLast time, I won one gold. This time, I came back with two medals. That shows improvement,â he said. However, the reigning world champion believes there is still room for growth and plans to continue working with the same coach, Ronak Malik, who has guided his recent rise in Bengaluru. âMy coach has identified areas where I can improve. Iâve completed around 85% of that work and there is still more to do. I want to refine my technique and continue progressing,â he said. Shailesh also credited Biharâs improving sports ecosystem, particularly the efforts of Bihar State Sports Authority director general-cum-CEO Raveendran Sankaran and sports minister Shreyasi Singh, for the growing number of international athletes emerging from the state. The reception he received after returning home, meanwhile, reinforced his belief that sporting success can inspire the next generation. title: Para-cyclist Shaik Arshad fractures leg in fall; medical support missing
text: Shaik Arshad (Image credit: Instagram) NEW DELHI: Para-cyclist Shaik Arshad suffered multiple fractures to his previously operated left residual limb after a fall during the menâs time trial at the Asian Para Games in Japan on Wednesday, raising questions over the absence of dedicated medical support for the Indian team. Sources told TOI that Arshad, a 2024 Paralympian, crashed in heavy rain at the Izu Velodrome in Shizuoka, sustaining serious injuries to the above-knee amputated limb on which he relies to use his prosthesis. He requires urgent medical attention and surgery, with concerns over the implications for his future mobility. Watch âThis medal means a lotâ: Lovlina Borgohain on Asian Games gold & Olympic ambitions The cycling venue is more than 250 km from Nagoya. Sources said officials had initially asked Arshad and his support staff to travel to Nagoya for hospital admission. Following prolonged discussions, officials agreed to visit the competition venue, where the injured cyclist needed immediate attention. The incident has also raised questions about assurances regarding medical arrangements for the Indian para-cycling contingent. Sources said that at a meeting on Sept 8 at the Sports Authority of India (SAI) office here, involving Arshadâs coach Aditya Verma and SAI officials from the Teams division, with Paralympic Committee of India (PCI) officials participating through phone calls, assurances were apparently given that medical personnel would accompany the team. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines However, no dedicated medical personnel were available to attend to Arshad at the venue when the accident occurred, sources alleged. Arshadâs coach is now exploring options to travel urgently from Hyderabad to Japan and is arranging a visa to be by the athleteâs side. The injury is particularly serious because it involves Arshadâs residual limb, which is crucial for fitting and using his artificial leg. The extent of the fractures and the treatment required will determine the impact on his recovery and mobility.
