title: Asian Para Games: Sandeep, Haney strike gold with world-record feats as India hit 100 medals
text: Sandeep sets T44 world record (Image: ANI) India's golden run at the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games gathered further momentum on Friday as Sandeep and Haney clinched gold medals with world-record performances in their respective events, taking the country's overall medal tally to 100. Sandeep set a new world record in the men's 400m T64, while Haney produced a record-breaking throw in the men's javelin F37/38 final at the Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium. Sandeep sets world record, Ajay Kumar claims bronze Sandeep clocked 52.28 seconds to win the men's 400m final, finishing comfortably ahead of Saudi Arabia's Nour Alsana, who secured silver in 53.13 seconds, a season's best. India's Ajay Kumar claimed bronze in 53.61 seconds, setting a Games record, while China's Huang Ruihua finished fourth with a personal-best time of 54.39 seconds. In the men's 400m, athletes from the T44 and T64 classifications competed together. While Sandeep and Alsana belong to the T44 category, Ajay Kumar competes in T64. Both classifications cover athletes with lower-limb impairments. Haney breaks world record with 60.49m javelin throw Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Haney followed with a world-record throw of 60.49 metres to claim gold in the men's javelin F37/38 event, earning 1,116 Raza points. Iran's Hormoz Seidikazpounji took silver with a personal-best throw of 50.68 metres, earning 1,009 points, while China's Yu Chengjie secured bronze with an Asian-record effort of 53.66 metres and 943 points. The combined F37 and F38 javelin categories are decided using Raza points, which account for the different classifications. This explains why Seidikazpounji finished ahead of Yu despite recording a shorter throw. India reach 100-medal milestone The double world-record triumph marked another significant milestone for India, whose overall medal tally crossed 100 at the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games. title: Meet India's flag-bearers at closing ceremony: Asian Para Games double gold medallists Mona Agarwal and Nishad Kumar
text: Nishad Kumar and Mona Agarwal (Pic credit: X) NEW DELHI: Double gold medallists Mona Agarwal and Nishad Kumar will be India's flag-bearers at the closing ceremony of the 2026 Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya on Saturday, following outstanding campaigns in shooting and para-athletics. Both athletes won two gold medals each at the continental event, with Mona producing a record-breaking performance in shooting and Nishad excelling in the high jump and long jump. Their selection as flag-bearers recognises their achievements as India prepare to bring the Games to a close. Watch Suchika Tariyal on her Asian Games bronze, childhood trauma, and never giving up | TOISA Spotlight Mona's record-breaking run in shooting The 38-year-old Mona opened India's medal account in shooting by winning gold in the women's 10m air rifle standing SH1 event with a Games-record score of 250.0 points. She edged compatriot Avani Lekhara by 0.4 points to secure the title, as India completed a one-two finish. Mona staged an impressive comeback in the final, climbing from sixth place to claim gold, while two-time Paralympic champion Avani settled for silver. The para-shooter continued her remarkable campaign by winning gold in the women's 50m rifle 3 positions SH1 event on Friday. She recorded 357.5 points to set a world record, surpassing the previous mark of 356 set by Sweden's Anna Benson in July 2026. Mona contracted polio at the age of nine, affecting both her lower limbs and leaving her dependent on a wheelchair. Her two gold medals at the Games added another significant milestone to her career. Poll Vote & Share your view Should more opportunities be provided for para-athletes in India? Yes, absolutely! No, current support is enough. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion Nishad's golden double in athletics Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Nishad, 27, also enjoyed a memorable campaign, winning gold in the men's long jump T47 and high jump T47 events. He opened his account in the long jump with a best effort of 7.11 metres, before adding another gold in the high jump. He cleared 2.04 metres to set a new Games record in the latter event. The double-gold performance placed Nishad among a select group of Indian athletes to win two gold medals in a single edition of the Asian Para Games, joining para-runner Ankur Dhama and armless archer Sheetal Devi. Nishad's journey to the top has been marked by resilience. His right arm was severed by a grass-cutting machine at his family's farm in Himachal Pradesh when he was six years old. He went on to establish himself as one of India's leading para-athletes, particularly in the high jump. With two gold medals apiece, Mona and Nishad will lead India's contingent at Saturday's closing ceremony, providing a fitting conclusion to their impressive campaigns in Aichi-Nagoya. title: Who is Mona Agarwal? Paralympics medallist sets Asian Para Games record to win gold
text: Mona Agarwal won gold in the women's 10m air rifle standing SH1 event. (Image credit: X) NEW DELHI: Mona Agarwal made a strong start to India's campaign at the 2026 Asian Para Games by winning gold in the women's 10m air rifle standing SH1 event on Monday. She finished ahead of fellow Indian shooter Avani Lekhara , who took silver, to give India a memorable one-two finish. Mona scored 250.0 points in the final at the Aichi Prefectural General Shooting Gallery to set a new Asian Para Games record. She broke the previous record of 249.6 points, set by Avani at the 2022 Hangzhou Games. Watch âThis medal means a lotâ: Lovlina Borgohain on Asian Games gold & Olympic ambitions The final was closely contested, with Mona holding a narrow lead of 239.2 points against Avani's 239.1 before the final shots. Mona eventually finished with 250.0 points, while Avani ended with 249.6. South Korea's Yunri Lee won the bronze medal. The gold medal adds to Mona's growing list of achievements in para shooting and highlights her rise among India's leading rifle shooters. Who is Mona Agarwal ? Mona Agarwal is an Indian para shooter from Jaipur, Rajasthan. Born on August 11, 1987, she competes in the SH1 category in rifle shooting. She trains in Jaipur under coach Yogesh Kumar and competes in the women's 10m air rifle standing SH1 and women's 50m rifle three positions SH1 events. Mona has built her career through consistent performances at national and international competitions. Her success at the Asian Para Games is another major achievement in a career that has seen her compete against some of the world's best para shooters. Mona reached a major milestone at the Paris 2024 Paralympic Games, where she won bronze in the women's 10m air rifle standing SH1 event. The medal brought her international recognition and established her as one of India's leading para rifle shooters. At the Paris Games, she competed in the same event in which she has now won gold at the Asian Para Games. Her latest performance shows her ability to compete at the highest level and challenge experienced shooters. Mona continued her good form in the lead-up to the 2026 Asian Para Games. At the 2026 World Shooting Para Sport Championships in Changwon, South Korea, she won one gold and one silver medal. She also secured a quota place for India for the Los Angeles 2028 Paralympic Games. Her achievements at World Cup events include two gold, two silver and one bronze medal, adding to her experience at international competitions. These results have helped Mona establish herself as an important member of India's para shooting team. SH1 is a classification for para shooters who have lower limb impairments or impairments that do not require them to use a shooting stand to support the rifle. In the women's 10m air rifle standing SH1 event, shooters aim at a target from a distance of 10 metres. title: India script history with best-ever fourth-place finish and record 114 medals at Asian Para Games
text: NEW DELHI: India signed off from the Asian Para Games 2026 in Aichi-Nagoya with a historic performance, securing their best-ever finish of fourth place and their biggest medal haul across the five editions of the continental event. With the competition concluding on Saturday and only the Closing Ceremony remaining, India finished with a record 114 medals, including 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze. The fourth-place finish also marked a new high for the Indian contingent at the Asian Para Games, underlining the progress made by the countryâs para-athletes on the continental stage. Watch Suchika Tariyal on her Asian Games bronze, childhood trauma, and never giving up | TOISA Spotlight India had entered the final day in fourth place, but their position was not confirmed as South Korea remained within striking distance. The Korean contingent needed two more gold medals to draw level with Indiaâs tally of 30, with their superior silver count potentially pushing them ahead. South Korea threaten, but India hold on to fourth South Korea added three medals on the final day, taking their overall tally to 100. However, they won only one gold, along with two silver medals, and finished fifth with 29 gold, 38 silver and 33 bronze. That left South Korea one gold short of India, ensuring the Indian contingent retained fourth place. Iran, who finished sixth with 26 gold medals, were also unable to mount a late challenge to Indiaâs position. Indiaâs final tally of 114 medals surpassed their previous best of 108 at the 2022 Asian Para Games in Hangzhou. The 30 gold medals also set a new benchmark for the country at the event. The performance was built on strong contributions across disciplines, with athletics, badminton, archery and shooting among the key medal-winning sports. Indiaâs athletes produced several standout performances and record-breaking efforts during the week-long competition. China dominate as Japan and Uzbekistan complete top three China topped the standings by a substantial margin, finishing with 217 gold medals and 435 medals overall. Hosts Japan placed second with 186 medals, including 64 gold, while Uzbekistan took third with 145 medals, including 45 gold. title: My hard work paid off at the 2026 Asian Games: Suraj Kumar Chand
text: Suraj Kumar Chand Written By: Harsh Kashiv Squash sensation Suraj Kumar Chand, who made India proud by winning a bronze medal at the 2026 Asian Games, recently visited Ahmedabad for an event. Earlier this year, Chand scripted history by becoming the first Indian to win gold at the FISU World University Championship Squash. A video of him taking off his shirt in celebration after winning a thrilling final also went viral on Instagram. In a chat with us, the young athlete talks about his journey, future goals, and more. âI have it in me to win more medals for India' Recalling his Asian Games experience, Chand says, âWinning an Asian Games medal was a long-term dream, and I really worked hard for it. The last two years were really tough, but after winning the medal, I felt that all the hard work paid off. After the Asian Games, I feel even more motivated. I believe I have it in me to win more medals for India, perhaps silver or gold next time.â With several tournaments lined up, Suraj is already back to training. He adds, âHopefully, I can make it to the Olympics or win a gold medal at the Asian or Commonwealth Games. The Commonwealth Games will be held in Ahmedabad in 2030, and I hope to win a medal there.â âQualifying for the Olympics will be a big dealâ With squash set to make its Olympic debut at the 2028 Olympics, Chand says, âThe qualification criteria are very difficult. You have to maintain your ranking and be among the top 20 or top 16 players in the world. I still have a year or more, and there might also be a qualifying event starting in 2027. I am training for that and will try my best to make it. If I get into the Olympics, that will be a big deal for me." Talking about the 2030 Commonwealth Games, he adds, âSquash has been part of the Commonwealth Games for a long time, and it is a very important sport for India. We have won medals in squash. This time, with the CWG happening in Ahmedabad, more people will be able to watch us and there will be greater home support. I think we can win more medals. Hopefully, I will be part of the team and win a medal for India." 'More people in India know about squash now' Chand believes squash still has considerable ground to cover in India. âThere is still a big gap between squash and cricket in India. But since squash has been included in the Olympics, more people know about the game now. Anahat Singh won the World Junior Championships this year, and I won the World University Championship, becoming the first Indian to do so. After these two big wins, more people in India know about squash and are supporting it. More viewership means more support,â he says. He adds, âI think the game will improve in India. More people will start playing and more will participate at the grassroots level. We need to develop the game in schools and colleges. For instance, Egypt has the game at every level, with more than 200 players in every category. Right now, India is nowhere close to them, but we are getting there. That is a good sign, and I look forward to seeing us develop good players like Egypt. " âGujarat's sports infrastructure is really goodâ Chand, who has visited Gujarat a couple of times for tournaments, feels, "If you compare the infrastructure with what we had five years ago, it is really good now. The setup here during the National Games was very good. Gujarat has excellent infrastructure and can host big tournaments. I can see squash becoming a big thing in Gujarat over the next two to three years." He has also observed a shift in the ambitions of young players. âWhen I was a junior, very few children wanted to play professionally or enter the professional circuit. Now, under-17 and under-19 players are entering the professional squash circuit and competing in PSA (Professional Squash Association) tournaments. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines That is a big difference,â he says. âI watch Bhaag Milkha Bhaag for motivationâ Away from the court, Chand keeps his routine simple. Despite the demands of training, travelling and competing on the international circuit, he prefers spending his free time with his family. He says, âWhenever I need some motivation, I watch Bhaag Milkha Bhaag . It is my favourite movie. I can watch it a thousand times. I follow Virat Kohli a lot. His discipline, both on and off the field, has motivated me a lot." Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news , check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule . title: Why India slipped in Asian Para Games standings despite 24 medals, five golds as China extend lead
text: Simran and Pranav Soorma NEW DELHI: India enjoyed a spectacular medal rush at the Asian Para Games 2026 on Tuesday, winning 24 medals, including five golds, but the impressive haul was not enough to prevent the country from slipping from fourth to sixth in the standings as rivals also enjoyed a bumper day in Aichi-Nagoya. India finished Day 2 with 35 medals â nine gold, 11 silver and 15 bronze â after adding five gold, six silver and 13 bronze medals to Monday's tally. However, the medal table is ranked primarily by the number of gold medals won, followed by silver and bronze, rather than the overall medal count. That distinction proved crucial. South Korea moved to fourth with 12 gold medals, while Iran climbed to fifth with 10. India, with nine golds, dropped to sixth despite having more medals than South Korea. Watch Asian Games gold medallist Sujeet Kalkal on fatherâs influence and how he turned final around China widen gap as Uzbekistan overtake Japan China continued to dominate the competition, extending their lead at the top with 70 gold medals and 149 medals overall. The gap between China and the chasing nations remained substantial, with Uzbekistan in second place on 17 golds and 56 medals. Hosts Japan, despite having 63 medals â seven more than Uzbekistan â occupied third place with 16 golds. Uzbekistan's superior gold count kept them ahead. Thailand were seventh with 41 medals, including eight golds. Kazakhstan, Indonesia and Malaysia completed the top 10 in the standings. India's position was therefore not a reflection of a poor day. Rather, the competition at the top intensified as rival nations accumulated gold medals at a faster rate. ALSO READ: Indiaâs medal storm! 24 medals, five golds as Nishad Kumar, Deepthi Jeevanji shine Nishad, Deepthi lead India's golden charge India's five gold medals on Tuesday came through an outstanding athletics performance, led by Nishad Kumar and Deepthi Jeevanji. He became only the third Indian to win two gold medals in a single edition of the Asian Para Games. Simran claimed the women's 200m T12 title in a Games-record 24.80 seconds, while Pranav Soorma won the men's discus throw combined F51/52/53 event with an Asian-record effort of 11.66m. title: Roman Reigns inspired his punches; Andre Russell earned him a nickname: Meet Army havaldar and Asian Games medallist Kapil Pokhariya
text: Kapil Pokhariya's fascination with pro-wrestler Roman Reigns was well known in his locality. (Image credit: Special arrangement) NEW DELHI: Jumping on cotton-filled mattresses, punching pillows, throwing them over walls and hitting a homemade punching bag filled with mountain soil - Kapil Pokhariyaâs childhood was all about pro-wrestling. His fascination with pro-wrestler Roman Reigns was well known in his locality. He would skip meals, playtime, and outings to watch WWE programming on television. Once the show was over, he would try to copy the moves and punches at home. Watch Suchika Tariyal on her Asian Games bronze, childhood trauma, and never giving up | TOISA Spotlight Little did he know that this childhood fascination could one day bring him his biggest recognition. Today, Kapil - an Indian Army havaldar - is an Asian Games medallist. Kapil won bronze in the menâs 90kg boxing event at the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan. âI never knew that copying Roman Reigns and practising those punches would bring me this far. I used to save recordings of his videos, and I still have them. I am really proud of where I am today. Honestly, I started learning how to throw punches by copying Roman Reigns (laugh),â Kapil told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interview. "My favourite was WrestleMania and Money in the Bank," he said. From Khatima to the Asian Games podium Kapil hails from Chakarpur village in Khatima, Uttarakhand, far from the major boxing centres that have produced several Indian stars. His father, Narendra Singh Pokhariya, served in the Indian Army. He wanted his son to study well and join the Army as a commissioned officer. Boxing, however, was never part of the original plan. Kapil Pokhariya with his father (Image credit: Special arrangement) Narendra often watched his son copy WWE stars at home. Initially, he would scold and even beat him for damaging things around the house. But his view slowly changed when he saw Kapil putting sand into a thick sack after returning from school and punching it with all his strength. âA teacher used to teach boxing at a nearby school. I saw the students punching a bag and decided to make one myself. My father scolded me in the beginning, but later he took me to a training centre and got me admitted there. That is how I got into boxing,â Kapil said. From a small training ground to the boxing ring Kapil did not begin his boxing journey at a big academy. His first steps came at a small training ground, where he practised alongside boys of his age and those who were older. After a few months, he began training under a coach. âI come from a small village where boxing was never a popular sport. Pooran Bohra sir was there. He trained a small group of boys for just a few hours on selected days of the week. But I was interested in learning. I listened to him carefully and repeated everything he taught me when I returned home,â Kapil said. With time, Kapil developed as a boxer and competed in his first state-level competition in 2015. He went into the tournament with excitement but came away disappointed. His first competitive bout ended in defeat in the opening round. âI was really disappointed. It was the first bout of my life, and I was seeing such a large crowd for the first time. I lost in the first round. But that competition and the defeat taught me a lot. My interest in boxing grew even stronger after that,â he said. Kapil Pokhariya (Image credit: Special arrangement) Kapil returned with a different mindset at the national-level competition. This time, he did more than win his bouts - he also claimed the gold medal. The prize money was followed by a job in the Indian Army. He joined the force in April 2017 and was appointed as a havaldar. His boxing career took a big step forward after that. The Army gave him opportunities to improve his skills and compete at a higher level. He began training more seriously, took part in Services competitions, won medals and continued to grow as a boxer. âMy father wanted me to study and join the Army as a commissioned officer. He joined as a sepoy and retired as a havaldar. But he wanted me to reach a higher rank if I joined the Indian Army,â Kapil said. âHe was very happy. The day I won a national medal, he hugged me. That was when I realised that I had achieved something big in my life,â Kapil said. âNow, after winning this Asian Games medal, I will be promoted to naib subedar. Papa said, âAb tu mera senior ho gaya haiâ,â the Indian boxer recalled with a smile. Kapil Pokhariya (Image credit: Special arrangement) The â Andre Russell â of Khatima Like many children in India, Kapil also grew up playing gully cricket. He even played inter-village cricket in Uttarakhand. His height, muscular build and powerful hitting made him a popular figure on the local cricket grounds. His ability to hit big sixes earned him the nickname âRussellâ, after West Indies power-hitter Andre Russell. âI loved Andre Russell. I also liked Hardik Pandya. People used to call me âKhatima ka Russellâ because of my power. The boys wanted me in their team because I could hit big sixes,â he said, laughing. Kapil Pokhariya (Image credit: Special arrangement) The Road Ahead and LA 2028 Dream For Kapil, the Asian Games bronze is only the beginning. His biggest dream is to represent India at the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics and win a medal. The tournament is scheduled for April and will be the first qualifying event in boxing for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games. Kapil knows there is still a long road ahead. âRukna nahi hai ab, bas aage dekhna hai,â he said. âThe Olympics is the ultimate dream. I want to go there, represent my country and win a medal. That is the only thing on my mind right now. I am preparing for the World Championships in April,â he added. Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

title: Anahat Singh scripts history, storms into maiden PSA Gold semi-final after thrilling comeback
text: India's Anahat Singh (ANI Photo) Indian squash sensation Anahat Singh continued her giant-killing run at the Silicon Valley Open 2026, producing a remarkable comeback to defeat Egypt's Salma Hany in a five-game thriller and book her maiden semi-final berth at a PSA Gold-level event. The 18-year-old World No. 15 recovered from a 1-2 deficit to register a 4-11, 11-8, 4-11, 11-2, 11-5 victory over the sixth-seeded Egyptian in 42 minutes in Redwood City, California. Anahat showed tremendous resilience after twice falling behind in the contest, raising her level in the final two games to complete an impressive turnaround. Having conceded the opening and third games, the Indian dominated the closing stages, dropping just seven points across the last two games to seal a landmark win. The victory marks another significant milestone in Anahat's burgeoning career and comes on the back of her stunning second-round upset of eight-time world champion and World No. 3 Nour ElSherbini. Anahat rallies from behind to seal historic victory Hany made a strong start, capitalising on Anahat's errors to take the opening game 11-4. The Indian responded with an improved performance in the second, winning it 11-8 to restore parity. However, the Egyptian regained control in the third game, cruising to another 11-4 win to move within a game of victory. With her quarter-final hopes hanging in the balance, Anahat produced a superb response, stepping up her intensity to dismantle Hany 11-2 in the fourth game. The teenager carried that momentum into the decider, maintaining her composure and dictating the rallies to close out the contest 11-5. Her emphatic finish underlined her ability to respond under pressure against an experienced opponent. The win ensures Anahat reaches the last four of a PSA Gold event for the first time in her career, further strengthening her growing reputation on the international squash circuit. Asian Games final rematch awaits Anahat in semi-finals Anahat's reward for the hard-fought quarter-final victory is a semi-final showdown against Malaysia's World No. 4 Sivasangari Subramaniam, who booked her place in the last four with a straight-games win over compatriot Rachel Arnold. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines The clash will renew a rivalry established at the 2026 Asian Games, where Sivasangari defeated Anahat 3-0 in the women's singles final to claim gold, leaving the Indian with silver. Anahat had made history at the continental event by becoming the first Indian woman to reach the squash singles final. Anahat has enjoyed an impressive campaign in Redwood City. She began by defeating Egypt's Nour Aboulmakarim 11-8, 11-8, 12-10 in the opening round before producing one of the biggest wins of her career against ElSherbini, beating the top-tier Egyptian 11-8, 11-8, 11-7. title: Asian Para Games 2026: India races past 50 medals as Simran and Dilip Gavit deliver gold in 100m events
text: Dilip Gavit won gold medal in men's 100m T47 event, while Mohammed Morssinganakath clinched silver (Photo/Screengrab) Dilip Gavit won gold in the men's 100m T47 event, while Mohammed Morssinganakath took silver in the same race as India's medal tally crossed the 50 mark at the Asian Para Games in Nagoya on Wednesday. Gavit competes in the T46 classification. Athletes of two or more classifications can be clubbed together in a combined event to ensure that there are enough number of participants. T46 and T47 categories are for athletes with upper limb impairment. The primary difference between T46 and T47 comes down to the severity and location of the upper limb impairment. T46 applies to athletes with a more severe unilateral or bilateral impairment affecting the shoulder or elbow -- roughly equivalent to an above-elbow amputation -- whereas T47 is for athletes with a less severe impairment affecting the wrist or below the elbow -- roughly equivalent to a below-elbow amputation. title: Double gold, Games record! Nishad Kumar joins elite Indian club with historic Asian Para Games feat
text: Nishad Kumar NEW DELHI: Nishad Kumar scripted history at the Asian Para Games 2026 on Tuesday, winning his second gold medal in as many days to become only the third Indian to claim two golds in a single edition of the continental para-sport showpiece. The two-time Paralympic silver medallist clinched the men's high jump T47 title with a Games-record effort of 2.04m in Aichi-Nagoya, a day after winning gold in the men's long jump T47 event with a best effort of 7.11m. Watch Suchika Tariyal on her Asian Games bronze, childhood trauma, and never giving up | TOISA Spotlight Nishad's double-gold performance puts him in an elite club alongside Ankur Dhama and armless archer Sheetal Devi, who had both won two gold medals at the 2023 Asian Para Games in Hangzhou, China. Dhama won the men's 5000m T11 and 1500m T11 titles, while Sheetal struck gold in the women's individual compound open and mixed team compound open events. Nishad breaks Games record after long jump triumph Known primarily for his high-jump exploits, Nishad demonstrated his versatility by adding the long jump crown to his collection before returning to his speciality on Tuesday. His 2.04m clearance secured the gold and established a new Games record in the men's high jump T47 category, which is meant for athletes with upper-limb impairments. The Indian's latest triumph adds to an impressive career that includes a silver medal at the Paris 2024 Paralympics and a world championship gold in the high jump. Nishad's journey has been marked by extraordinary resilience. His right arm was severed by a grass-cutting machine at his family's farm in Amb, Himachal Pradesh, when he was just six years old. Winning a Gold on his debut in this event makes the achievement even more special. His versatility, determination and sporting excellence are truly inspiring. Wishing him the very best for the endeavours ahead," PM Modi was quoted as saying in a post by PMO India. The Prime Minister's message came after Nishad delivered a commanding performance in the long jump, recording 7.11m twice in the final. With two gold medals and a Games record, Nishad has emerged as one of India's standout performers in Aichi-Nagoya. title: Asian Para Games conclude in Nagoya: India sign off with record 114 medals, finish fourth
text: India finish fourth as China lead medal standings at Asian Para Games. NEW DELHI: India signed off from the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games with their best-ever medal haul of 114 medals as the week-long continental competition concluded with a closing ceremony at the Mizuho Park Athletics Stadium in Nagoya, Japan, on Saturday. Double gold medallists Nishad Kumar and Mona Agarwal led the Indian contingent as flag-bearers at the ceremony, marking the end of a landmark campaign in which the country's para-athletes delivered historic victories, world-record performances and podium sweeps across disciplines. Watch Asian Games gold medallist Sujeet Kalkal on fatherâs influence and how he turned final around India finished fourth in the overall standings with 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze medals, surpassing its previous best of 108 medals at the 2022 Hangzhou Games. Held in Japan for the first time, the fifth edition of the Asian Para Games brought together around 4,000 athletes and staff from 45 countries and regions. The competition featured 18 sports, with more than 20 world records reportedly set during the seven-day event. ALSO READ: India script history with best-ever fourth-place finish India finish fourth as China lead medal standings China topped the medal table with 435 medals, including 207 gold, while hosts Japan finished second with 186 medals â 64 gold, 60 silver and 62 bronze. Uzbekistan emerged as the third-ranked nation, collecting 145 medals, including 45 gold. India's fourth-place finish was particularly significant given the size of its contingent. A total of 168 para-athletes represented the country at Aichi-Nagoya, compared with 309 at the previous edition in Hangzhou. President Droupadi Murmu congratulated the Indian contingent on its record performance, saying the achievement reflected the athletes' hard work, perseverance and self-belief. In a post on X, Murmu said the unprecedented medal haul would inspire young people to dream big, work with dedication and remain positive in the face of challenges. She also extended her congratulations to the entire Indian contingent. Para athletics leads India's medal charge Para athletics was India's biggest medal contributor, accounting for 65 medals â 22 gold, 19 silver and 24 bronze. Para badminton followed with 16 medals, including three gold, five silver and eight bronze. India also won 11 medals in para swimming, seven in para table tennis, six in para archery and five in para shooting. The contingent added two medals each in para judo and para powerlifting. Doha to host next edition in 2030 The closing ceremony brought together athletes, officials and dignitaries to mark the conclusion of the Games. Asian Paralympic Committee president Majid Rashed declared the event closed, highlighting the growing strength of para sport across Asia and its role in building a more inclusive society. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi also praised the athletes' determination, teamwork and sportsmanship, describing their performances as a reminder of the âprofound beautyâ of para sports. The Asian Para Games began in Guangzhou, China, in 2010, evolving from the Far East and South Pacific Games Federation for the Disabled. The Aichi-Nagoya edition was the fifth staging of the event, with Doha, Qatar, scheduled to host the sixth in 2030. For India, the closing ceremony marked the end of a historic campaign â one that raised the country's medal benchmark and showcased the depth and growing strength of its para-sport movement. title: 24 wins, seven titles, one heartbreaking defeat: Wrestler Sujeet Kalkal's winning streak ends
text: Sujeet Kalkal (Image credit: X) Sujeet Kalkalâs wait for a World Championships medal continued as the Indian wrestler suffered a heartbreaking defeat in the menâs 65kg quarterfinals on Thursday. Sujeet lost 3-3 on criteria to Tajikistanâs Abdulmazhid Kudiev, bringing his 24-match winning streak to an end. The defeat was a major setback for Sujeet, who had enjoyed an impressive run over the past year. He won seven titles during this period, including the U23 World Championships, the 2026 Asian Championships and the Asian Games. His last defeat before Thursday had come in the repechage round of the World Championships in Zagreb last year. The loss to Kudiev also ended Indiaâs hopes of seeing a second world champion after Sushil Kumar, who won the title in 2010. Watch Asian Games gold medallist Sujeet Kalkal on fatherâs influence and how he turned final around Kudiev turns the tables on Sujeet Sujeet had beaten Kudiev in the Asian Games final after making a remarkable comeback. Trailing 2-9, the Indian scored eight straight points to secure the gold medal. However, the Tajik wrestler had the last laugh this time in a closely fought quarterfinal. Sujeet conceded the first point for passivity but moved ahead 2-1 with a takedown just five seconds before the end of the first period. Kudiev was then penalised for passivity, allowing the Indian to increase his lead to 3-1. The contest took a dramatic turn in the final 30 seconds. Sujeet attempted a takedown near the edge of the mat but could not put Kudiev in a danger position. The Tajik wrestler then countered with a takedown of his own. The mat referee did not award Sujeet two points for his move, but the chair umpire gave him the points. Kudiev was also awarded a point for a step-out, leaving Sujeet ahead 5-2. The Tajik corner challenged the decision and won. Sujeetâs two points were cancelled, while Kudiev received two points for his takedown. The score was level at 3-3. Sujeet needed a decisive move in the final seconds but could not find a way past Kudiev. The Tajik wrestler held on to win on criteria because he had scored the last point. Sujeet had started with two convincing wins Before the quarterfinal, Sujeet had looked in control of his campaign. He opened with a commanding 12-1 win over Switzerlandâs Nino Leutert by technical superiority. He then defeated Belarusâ Islam Guseinov 4-0 to reach the quarterfinals. But his winning run ended against the same wrestler he had beaten for Asian Games gold, leaving him still searching for his first senior World Championships title. Tanu enters bronze medal bout, Manisha reaches semifinals India had some positive results in the womenâs events, with Tanu Sharma advancing to the bronze medal bout in the 72kg category. title: PV Sindhu, Mirabai Chanu, Harmanpreet Singh among 12 candidates cleared for IOA Athletes Commission election
text: Olympic medallists PV Sindhu and Mirabai Chanu (Agency Images) NEW DELHI: The nomination papers of all 12 candidates, including Olympic medallists PV Sindhu and Mirabai Chanu , have been declared valid following scrutiny for the Indian Olympic Association's (IOA) Athletes Commission election. Electoral Officer (Returning Officer) Sanjay K. Srivastava issued the final list of validly nominated candidates on Thursday. The election to select 10 members â five men and five women â for the 2026â2030 term will be held on November 3. Watch Kynan Chenai: The 38-Year-Old Gun Barrel, Asian Games Gold and the LA 2028 Dream | TOISA Spotlight The list remains unchanged from the draft nominations released on October 22, with all 12 sportspersons clearing scrutiny. Besides Sindhu and Chanu, the candidates include men's and women's hockey captains Harmanpreet Singh and Salima Tete, shooter Swapnil Kushare, fencer Bhavani Devi, athletes Sudha Singh and Tajinderpal Singh, former archer Bombayla Devi, shuttler Kidambi Srikanth, swimmer Sajan Prakash and Manjeet Singh from kayaking and canoeing. Sindhu, Chanu and Bhavani Devi are also members of the outgoing Athletes Commission, headed by celebrated boxer MC Mary Kom. Earlier, on October 16, Srivastava had released a list of 34 members of the electoral college, comprising two representatives each from 17 National Sports Federations (NSFs). The 10 members of the new Athletes Commission will be elected from this electoral college. The All India Football Federation (AIFF), the All India Tennis Association (AITA), the Boxing Federation of India (BFI) and the Table Tennis Federation of India (TTFI) were not represented in the electoral college. Article 10.3 of the IOA Athletes Commission Rules, ratified in September, states: "Only those NSF Members which have established an Athletes Commission shall be allowed to appoint their athletes' representatives through their respective Athletes Commissions." Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines The rules also lay down eligibility requirements for the elected members. Two members of the Athletes Commission â one man and one woman â will be inducted into the IOA Executive Council. Of the 10 elected members, six â three men and three women â must have participated in at least one of the last three editions of the Olympic Games at the time of their election. The remaining four members â two men and two women â must have won at least one medal at any of the last three editions of the Asian Games, Commonwealth Games, World Championships/Cups or the National Games. title: Gr Noida para-athlete defies spinal pain, competes wearing neck brace
text: NOIDA: Para-athlete Suvarna Raj won her maiden Asian Para Games gold in discus throw after battling a severe spinal condition, chronic pain and an emergency hospitalisation just two days before the event in Japan. After two unsuccessful attempts at Asian Para Games, Suvarna had decided this would be her final shot, and she would move on from the sport if she failed to win a medal in Japan. Asian Para Games 2026 hopes also appeared to have been dashed at the eleventh hour when she fainted due to acute spinal and cervical pain and told her team she could not compete. But with support from her husband Pradeep Raj, a former national-level para table tennis player himself, the couple's 15-year-old son and coach Robin Singh, she went ahead, wearing a neck belt. The hospital scare also disrupted her routine in Japan. Raj could not eat normally because of her condition and had to depend on juices and fruits. "At that point, I genuinely felt that I could not compete. I told my team that my body was not allowing me to continue. Every movement was difficult, but I kept reminding myself that I had waited for this moment for years. I had competed at the Asian Para Games several times without winning a medal. I wanted to return with a medal for my country, and I knew this could be my last chance," she said. The 44-year-old threw 15.66m in the women's F54 discus event at Aichi-Nagoya Asian Para Games 2026. F54 discus throw classification is meant for seated field athletes with impairments affecting trunk and lower-limb function. Raj had represented India at 2014 Asian Para Games in Incheon, South Korea, and the 2022 edition in Hangzhou, China (held in 2023), without winning a medal. "There comes a point when you start questioning yourself, especially when you keep trying but the result does not come. Winning gold has changed that feeling completely," she said. The gold is her biggest win in a career that includes bronze in the women's F54/55 discus throw at Dubai World Para Athletics Grand Prix 2026 and gold at Canberra Track Meet in Australia. She received National Youth Award from Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports in 2015. Raj, who hails from Nagpur in Maharashtra and lives in Greater Noida and trained at Gautam Buddha University, contracted polio at the age of two in 1984. The condition affected her spine, leaving her with a severe curvature and problems with body balance. She continues to live with persistent pain and requires medication, insulin and assistance with some daily activities. Her preparation at GBU involved three to four support personnel, including physiotherapists and medical professionals. "People see an athlete on the field and judge the performance by the distance or the medal. They do not always see what happens before the competition or after training. Preparing for an international competition means managing treatment, physiotherapy, medication and training together. I do not want my disability to be the only thing people associate with me. I want to be recognised for what I can achieve as an athlete," she said. She hopes to undergo spinal surgery, using the cash from her medal win. Robin said he had seen her struggle through training sessions, but the way she held herself together in Japan was exceptional. "She was emotionally exhausted and told us she would not be able to throw. We knew how much this competition meant to her, so we kept encouraging her to give it one last attempt," he said. Javelins to barbells: How Raj is helping budding athletes Raj founded Association for Disabled People (ADP) in 2021 to open a route into competitive sport for persons with disabilities, especially those from difficult backgrounds. About 50 persons now train at its ground in GBU, where javelins, discus and barbells share the space. Arun Pratap Singh (32), a five-time UP state javelin champion, ran a contracting business until a road accident on the Aligarh-Mathura bypass in 2020. During his recovery, a conversation with an international para-athlete drew him towards adaptive sport. He trained at Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium in Delhi before joining ADP and won five state golds in the F57 category despite two to three further surgeries and repeated injuries. "I realised that I could still set goals and work towards something meaningful," Arun said. His focus is now the national championship. "I want to test myself against the best athletes in the country and see how far I can go." Lucky, a Class XII student who lives near Dankaur railway station, joined after his father, an auto-rickshaw driver, read about ADP in a newspaper. Born with a disability, he travels nearly 13km every morning to reach the ground between 6.30 am and 7.30 am, training in discus and javelin under coaches Haider and Robin. He has won two junior national silver medals in about one-and-a-half years. "I travel every morning for training, and even during my board examinations, I come to practise after finishing my paper," Lucky said. His aim is a Paralympic gold. "I know it may take years of hard work and consistency, but I want to keep improving," he said, adding that he draws inspiration from Raj. title: Asian Para Games: Sheetal Devi's double gold, Shailesh Kumar-led podium sweep headline India's best day yet
text: India enjoyed a podium sweep in the high jump T63 event. Shailesh Kumar led the way with a Games-record effort of 1.89m. (Pic credit: PCI) NEW DELHI: India enjoyed its best day at the Asian Para Games 2026 on Thursday, winning 26 medals, including seven golds, as a remarkable medal rush across athletics, archery, swimming, badminton and table tennis took the country's overall tally to 88. Armless archer Sheetal Devi led the charge with two gold medals in less than two hours, while the track-and-field contingent remained India's biggest contributor. Suvarna Raj, Shailesh Kumar, Anjanaben Bumbadiya, Dilip Mahadu Gavit and Solairaj Dharmaraj were among the other gold medallists on a memorable day for the Indian contingent. India's tally now stands at 21 gold, 26 silver and 41 bronze medals. The seven golds helped the country reclaim fourth place in the standings after it slipped to sixth on Day 2 and fifth on Day 3. Watch Suchika Tariyal on her Asian Games bronze, childhood trauma, and never giving up | TOISA Spotlight Sheetal Devi strikes twice, Swati Chaudhary makes history Sheetal, the 19-year-old reigning world champion and world No. 1, began her golden run by teaming up with Toman Kumar to defend India's mixed team title. The Indian duo beat Indonesia's Teodora Audi Ayudia Ferelly and Ken Swagumilang 151-148. Less than two hours later, Sheetal returned to the range for the women's individual final. After overcoming a four-point deficit, she defeated Singapore's Alim Nur Syahidah 142-139 to repeat her triumph from the Hangzhou 2023 Asian Para Games. India also celebrated a historic achievement in archery as Swati Chaudhary won the country's first-ever Asian Para Games medal in the W1 category. She settled for silver after losing 4-6 to China's Cen Mengkan in the women's individual final. ALSO READ: Where India stands in medal tally after best day with 26 medals, including 7 golds Athletics powers India's seven-gold haul The day began with Suvarna Raj winning gold in the women's F54 discus throw with a best effort of 15.66m. The 44-year-old wheelchair athlete recorded four throws beyond 15 metres to secure the biggest win of her career. India then enjoyed a podium sweep in the men's high jump T63 event. Shailesh Kumar, who had won bronze in the long jump on Wednesday, led the way with a Games-record effort of 1.89m. Former Paralympic bronze medallist Varun Bhati took silver with a season's best of 1.84m, while Rahul completed the all-Indian podium with a jump of 1.81m. Anjanaben Bumbadiya won the women's 400m T47 gold in 59.97 seconds, with compatriot Jayanti Behera taking silver in 1:00.65. Dilip Mahadu Gavit, who had won the men's 100m T47 gold on Wednesday, added another title by winning the men's 400m T47 final in 48.27 seconds. Solairaj Dharmaraj provided a fitting finish to the day's athletics action, successfully defending his men's long jump T44/T62/T64 title with an Asian-record effort of 7.15m. Malaysia's Eddy Bernard won silver with 6.34m, while Japan's Yuma Tamaki took bronze with a personal-best 6.89m. Tejalben Damor also added to India's medal count, winning silver in the women's 400m T12 in 57.60 seconds. The visually impaired athlete had earlier claimed bronze in the 200m T12 event. Four more swimming medals, Ravi Budigina completes hat-trick India added four medals in the pool, taking its overall swimming haul to 10, although a gold remained elusive. Eighteen-year-old Ravi Budigina secured bronze in the men's 50m freestyle S13 with a time of 25.89 seconds. It was his third medal of the Games, following silver-medal finishes in the 100m backstroke and freestyle events. Kapil Kumar won silver in the men's 400m freestyle S10 in 4:38.44, finishing behind Japan's Akito Minai, who set a Games record of 4:27.44. Swatik Patil claimed bronze in the men's 100m breaststroke SB9 in 1:13.77, while Tejas Nandakumar took bronze in the men's 100m backstroke S7 with a time of 1:18.58. Indian shuttlers assured of multiple badminton medals India's para-shuttlers also enjoyed a productive day, with Pramod Bhagat and Nitesh Kumar setting up an all-Indian men's singles SL3 final. Six-time world champion and Tokyo Paralympic gold medallist Bhagat survived a marathon two-hour-and-nine-minute semifinal against South Korea's Lee Seunghu, winning 16-21, 21-18, 21-17. Paris Paralympic champion Nitesh had earlier defeated Indonesia's M Imran 21-19, 21-16 to reach the final. He also advanced to the mixed doubles SL3-SU5 final with Thulasimathi Murugesan after the Indian pair beat China's Li Mingpin and Xiao Zuxian 21-19, 14-21, 21-17. Naveen Sivakumar reached the men's singles SL4 final, while Indian shuttlers collected five bronze medals across other events. Bhavina Patel, Subham Wadhwa win table tennis bronze India's medal rush extended to para-table tennis, where Bhavina Patel and Subham Wadhwa secured bronze in mixed doubles XD7. China continued to dominate the overall standings, crossing 300 medals to reach 313, including 149 golds. Hosts Japan were second with 136 medals, including 40 gold, while Uzbekistan occupied third place with 117 medals, including 37 gold. India's seven-gold day lifted the contingent back to fourth place, with 88 medals overall and momentum building across multiple disciplines. title: 'Sports ek tapasya hai' - Boxer Parveen Hooda's fight: A 22-month ban, a father battling cancer, then Asian Games gold
text: Parveen Hooda won gold in the womenâs 65kg category at the Asian Games (Image credit: TimesofIndia.com) NEW DELHI: âSports ek tapasya hai,â says Indian boxer Parveen Hooda, reflecting on a period that saw her miss the Paris Olympics because of a 22-month ban, deal with her father's battle with cancer, and eventually return to the ring to win an Asian Games gold medal. At 23, Parveen has already experienced the disappointment of losing an Olympic opportunity she had worked years to earn. She had secured a quota for Paris when a suspension for three whereabouts failures ruled her out of the Games. She was also stripped of the bronze medal she had won at the 2022 Asian Games. Watch Suchika Tariyal on her Asian Games bronze, childhood trauma, and never giving up | TOISA Spotlight Her father, Lakhpat Hooda, has been battling stage-three throat cancer and heart problems. The family has also faced financial difficulties in the past, with her mother, Neelam Devi, having supported the household by selling milk from two buffaloes when Parveen was growing up. Through the suspension, Parveen continued training despite having no competition to prepare for. Her return culminated in gold in the women's 65kg category at the Asian Games, where she defeated Chinese Taipei's Nien-chin Che in the final. âNow, when I look back at those day, I feel very proud of myself because I did not give up. I continued training. I am grateful to the people who stood by me during this journey,â Parveen told Timesofindia.com in an exclusive interview. âThis journey has made me very strong, both mentally and physically. I am grateful that I went through that phase because it helped me become a better person.â The pressure of an Asian Games final Parveen entered the Asian Games final having beaten opponents from China and Uzbekistan previously. She was confident about her preparation, but the expectations surrounding her were difficult to ignore. âI was confident because I had beaten both my opponents from China and Uzbekistan. But there was also a lot of pressure in the final because so many expectations were attached to me. Once I reached the final, everyone expected me to win gold,â she said. Image credit: Special arrangement It had been a long time since she had competed in a final at a major event. The prospect of winning gold brought its own nerves. âI was a little nervous because I was competing in a final at such a big event after a long time. But beating those opponents had also increased my confidence, and my preparation was very good. I felt confident going into the final bout. I thanked God and felt happy that we had come so far in this journey. I had reached the final, and so many people were congratulating me. There were also a lot of outside distractions,â she said. Parveen had analysed her opponent's bout before the final. The challenge was to keep her attention on the fight amid the activity around her. âMy mindset was to put everything aside and focus only on the final bout. I had analysed my opponentâs bout. It was a little difficult to concentrate because so many people from the Boxing Federation of India were also there. There were distractions, so keeping myself focused was the main thing for me.â When the result was announced, Parveen folded her hands and looked up at the sky. She then ran towards her coach, took the Indian flag and draped it around her shoulders. Tears rolled down her cheeks as she completed a lap of honour. For Parveen, the victory came after months in which she had been unable to compete and had watched the Paris Olympics from home. Image credit: PTI When a 22-month ban ended her Paris Olympics hopes Parveen had secured a quota for the Paris Olympics when she was handed a 22-month suspension following three whereabouts failures. Under the anti-doping whereabouts system, athletes included in a registered testing pool must provide accurate location information, including a designated 60-minute daily window during which they can be located for testing. A combination of three missed tests or filing failures within a 12-month period can constitute an anti-doping rule violation. Parveen admits she had not paid enough attention to the requirements. âI learnt that we take things too casually. We players mostly focus on training, but we do not always learn enough about these other things. I was also casual about whereabouts and did not properly learn how it worked. We should be educated and have knowledge about these things. If I am part of the whereabouts system, I should know how it works. Many athletes take these things very casually,â she said. The suspension left her without a clear target. For someone accustomed to preparing for tournaments, continuing the same training routine without knowing when she would compete again became difficult. âI needed to be mentally very tough at that time because there was no goal in front of me. Usually, we prepare for something specific in training. But at that time, there was no target. Motivation remains very low because you keep thinking, âWhat are we doing this for?â There is no aim ahead,â she said. Parveen Hooda with her family members (Image credit: Special arrangement) âMy mind did not want me to train even for one day, but I did not miss a single day of training. Somewhere, I had made that commitment to myself. I believed in myself. I knew that I had achieved so much in this journey and that I could do it again. I knew the basics and how to get things done. That was my mindset,â she said. Parveen spent more time at home during the suspension. She listened to motivational songs, prayed, recited the Hanuman Chalisa and continued working on her boxing. She also tried to concentrate on what remained within her control. âWhen bad times come, that is when you find out about your champion mindset. You learn how you handle negative situations. I focused more on the things I should be grateful for. I was fit, I had no injury, and my family was doing well. I accepted that this had happened because of my mistake and that I would correct it going forward. But that did not mean I should sit back and stop training,â she added. Watching the Paris Olympics was particularly difficult. Her friends were competing at an event where she had expected to represent India. âI felt sad because my friends were competing there while I was sitting at home watching their bouts. I felt that I should also have been there, competing. But I never thought of quitting,â she said. Fatherâs cancer battle weighed on Parveen during Asian Games camp While Parveen was working towards her return, her family was dealing with Lakhpat's illness. He had been diagnosed with stage-three throat cancer and was also suffering from heart problems. His health had affected his ability to work, adding to the family's financial difficulties. During the Asian Games, Lakhpat was hospitalised while Parveen was at the training camp. She kept in touch with him through video calls. âI was at the camp during the Asian Games, and my father was hospitalised. I felt very bad that I was not with him at that time. I was in touch with him on video calls. A glimpse of him and his smile were enough to motivate me,â she said. âI cried during practice, and all I wanted was to regain my pride and make my father and mother proud once again.â The family travelled to different hospitals in search of treatment, including facilities in Chandigarh and Mohali. Parveen was involved in finding medical care for her father and spent time with him during her suspension. âWe travelled from one corner to another to take my father to various hospitals. We consulted doctors in Chandigarh and Mohali as well. I just wanted him to recover. Thankfully, all our efforts helped improve my fatherâs health. So, in a way, it was a good opportunity because I could be with him,â she said. âAchha, theek ho gaya betaâ When Parveen returned home from the Asian Games with the gold medal around her neck, her mother was overcome with emotion. âMy mother was very emotional when I entered the house with the gold medal around my neck. She was with me throughout the struggle and would always say, âYou work so hard.â She cried a lot that night,â Parveen said. Parveen Hooda with her father, mother and brother (Image credit: Special arrangement) Her father's reaction was rather understated. âWhen I told my father that I had won gold, he just said, âAchha, theek ho gaya betaâ (Okay, thatâs good, child). He was happy, but he does not express his emotions much,â she said with a laugh. Los Angeles 2028: Another shot at the Olympics The Paris Olympics remain a painful memory for Parveen, but her next target is already set. She wants to qualify for the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028 and win a medal for India. Her Asian Games gold has restored her confidence ahead of another Olympic cycle. She continues to rely on prayer and meditation, practices she says helped her through the suspension. âThis period gave me a lot of strength. I am stronger now, both physically and mentally. I listen to the Hanuman Chalisa, worship and recite mantras. Meditation helped me a lot. It gives me positive energy and makes me feel that Godâs blessings are with me. I am sure Los Angeles will be mine,â she said. Image credit: Special arrangement Back home in Rurki village, Parveen sometimes sits quietly in front of a small temple and thinks about the period when she continued training despite having no competition in sight. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Asked what she would say to the younger version of herself who went through those difficult months, she had a simple answer. âI want to say thank you to that Parveen. She faced so much struggle to make the Parveen I am today. She worked hard and did not give up,â she said. And then she returned to the words she had heard from her earlier coaches, words that she says she now understands better. âPeople say that sports is a tapasya. I had heard this from my earlier coaches, but now I have felt it myself. It is truly a tapasya,â Parveen signed off. title: Who is Deepthi Jeevanji? Indian para-athlete wins 400m T20 gold with Games record
text: Deepthi Jeevanji (Image credit: X) NEW DELHI: Deepthi Jeevanji continued her impressive run in para athletics by winning gold in the women's 400m T20 event at the Asian Para Games on Tuesday. The Indian clocked a Games record time of 56.36 seconds to defend her title. The 23-year-old from Telangana finished ahead of Japan's Niina Kanno, who won silver in 58.92 seconds. Kanno's compatriot Akane Kato took bronze with a time of 1:00.26. Deepthi, who also holds the Asian record, has established herself as one of India's leading para-athletes with her performances at major international events. Watch Harita Bhadra Exclusive | 2 Asian Games Medals, Now the 22.45s World Championships Chase Who is Deepthi Jeevanji ? Deepthi hails from a remote village in Warangal, Telangana. Her parents are small farmers who have also worked as labourers in their village. Her talent for running was spotted when she was young. According to her athlete profile, Sports Authority of India coach N Ramesh first noticed her during a state-level athletics meet when she was 15. He recognised her potential and began training her. Deepthi later received support from badminton great Pullela Gopichand. At his suggestion, she underwent testing for intellectual disability in Hyderabad. Her journey in para athletics began to gain attention after she competed at the Asian Youth Championships in Hong Kong in 2019, where she won bronze. From a village in Telangana to the international stage Deepthi continued to improve through competitions organised by the Athletics Federation of India between 2019 and 2022. She also won gold medals in the 100m and 200m events at the Khelo India Youth Games in Guwahati in 2020. Her breakthrough at the senior international level came at the Asian Para Games in 2023, where she won gold and set Games and Asian records in the women's 400m T20 event. She went on to win gold at the 2024 Para Athletics World Championships, setting a world record of 55.07 seconds. She also won a bronze medal in the same event at the Paris Paralympics in 2024. Deepthi added another achievement to her career by winning silver at the 2025 World Championships. She has also won gold at the Indian Open in 2025 and 2026. What is the T20 category? Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines T20 is a classification for athletes with intellectual impairments. Athletes in this category may face challenges with processing information, concentration and following race plans or tactical strategies. The role of her parents in her journey Deepthi's success has come with strong support from her parents. She has spoken about how they stood by her ambitions even when people in their village taunted them for supporting her sporting dreams. Their support, along with years of training and hard work, has helped Deepthi rise from a village in Telangana to the top level of international para athletics. Her latest gold at the Asian Para Games, achieved in a Games record time of 56.36 seconds, is another milestone in her remarkable journey. title: Paralympian Suvarna Raj Named Delhiâs State Commissioner For Persons With Disabilities
text: New Delhi: Paralympian and Asian Para Games 2026 gold medallist Suvarna Raj has been named the state commissioner for persons with disabilities. She was chosen by LG TS Sandhu from a panel of three candidates recommended by a search-cum-selection committee. The post had remained vacant after the previous commissionerâs tenure ended. An earlier selection process initiated in 2024 had concluded without any candidate being selected. Fresh applications were invited through newspaper advertisements in Hindi, English and other regional languages in July 2026. The social welfare department received 18 applications, of which 15 candidates were found eligible after scrutiny. The committee, headed by the chief secretary, met on Aug 20 and interviewed 13 candidates who appeared before it. After assessing their qualifications, experience, understanding of disability rights and welfare, and suitability, it unanimously recommended three candidates to LG. Under Section 79 of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, state govt appoints the commissioner. Under the Delhi Rights of Persons with Disabilities Rules, 2018, the post is full-time for three years from assuming office or until the age of 65, whichever comes first, subject to the rulesâ maximum tenure. title: Who is Himanshu Nandal? The para-swimmer who won a hat-trick of bronze medals at Asian Para Games in Japan
text: Himanshu Nandal (PTI Photo) NEW DELHI: Indian para-swimmer Himanshu Nandal made his mark at the Asian Para Games 2026 in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, completing a hat-trick of bronze medals with another podium finish in the men's 100m freestyle S11 event on Friday. The 22-year-old clocked 1 minute 5.90 seconds to finish third, behind Japan's Uchu Tomita, who won gold in a Games-record time of 58.22 seconds, and China's Chuanzhen Sun, who took silver in 58.70 seconds. Nandal's latest medal added to his earlier bronze finishes in the men's 400m freestyle and 100m breaststroke S11 events. He became one of India's standout performers in para swimming, matching compatriot Ravi Budigina's three-medal haul at the Games, which comprised two silver medals and a bronze. Watch Suchika Tariyal on her Asian Games bronze, childhood trauma, and never giving up | TOISA Spotlight Who is Himanshu Nandal? Born blind due to optic nerve failure, Nandal grew up in a sports-oriented family in Rohtak, Haryana. His father had played hockey at the national level, and sport became part of his life from an early age. At four, Nandal moved to Delhi and joined the National Association for the Blind, where he learnt Braille. He initially took up judo and went on to win medals at the national level before switching to swimming in 2021. The change opened a new chapter in his sporting journey, as he quickly progressed from domestic competitions to the international stage. From Paris Paralympics qualification to Asian Para Games medals Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Nandal achieved a significant milestone in 2024 when he became the first Indian blind swimmer to meet the Minimum Qualification Standard for the Paris Paralympics. A political science graduate from the University of Delhi's Atma Ram Sanatan Dharma College, he continued to build his experience against international opposition. In 2025, he reached two finals at the World Para Swimming Championships in Singapore. At the Asian Para Games, Nandal began his medal-winning run on Tuesday, clocking 5:10.91 to secure bronze in the men's 400m freestyle S11 event. He followed it up with another third-place finish in the 100m breaststroke before completing his hat-trick in the 100m freestyle on Friday. The S11 classification is for swimmers with visual impairment, including those with very low visual acuity or no light perception. Nandal's three-medal campaign in Japan marks another milestone in his progress as an Indian para-swimmer and adds to his growing experience at major international competitions. title: Sheetal Devi strikes double gold again! Indian archer repeats 2023 Asian Para Games medal feat in 2026
text: Indian para-archer Sheetal Devi wins three Asian Para Games medals again. NEW DELHI: Indian para-archer Sheetal Devi once again proved her mettle on the biggest continental stage, winning two gold medals at the Asian Para Games for the second consecutive edition after clinching the women's individual compound title on Thursday. The 19-year-old armless archer from Jammu and Kashmir produced a stunning comeback to defeat Singapore's Alim Nur Syahidah 142-139 in the final at Okazaki Chuo Sogo Park Multipurpose Square, successfully defending the individual title she won in Hangzhou in 2023. Watch Suchika Tariyal on her Asian Games bronze, childhood trauma, and never giving up | TOISA Spotlight The victory completed a memorable double-gold day for Sheetal, who had teamed up with Toman Kumar to win the compound mixed team gold earlier in the day. She also secured a silver medal in the women's compound doubles event alongside Odisha's quadruple amputee archer Payal Nag. With three medals â two golds and a silver â Sheetal has replicated her medal tally from the 2023 Asian Para Games, where she also won two gold medals and a silver to announce herself as one of India's brightest para-sporting talents. Sheetal turns the tide to defend individual crown Sheetal had to dig deep to retain her individual crown, with Alim initially putting the Indian under pressure in their gold medal clash. The Singaporean archer established a four-point advantage after the opening two ends, leaving Sheetal with plenty of work to do. However, the Indian mounted an extraordinary recovery, firing six 10s, including three Xs â arrows landing closest to the centre of the target â across the next two ends. The remarkable sequence helped Sheetal overturn the deficit and take a two-point lead into the final end, setting up a tense finish. With the gold medal on the line, Sheetal maintained her composure, scoring three 9s for 27 points in the final end. Alim, meanwhile, managed scores of 9, 8 and 9 for 26 points, allowing the Indian to seal a 142-139 victory. The triumph was particularly significant as it came less than a couple of hours after Sheetal had won the mixed team gold with Toman, underlining her ability to deliver under pressure across multiple events. Three medals again, just like Hangzhou Sheetal's campaign in 2026 has followed a familiar pattern from her breakthrough performance at the 2023 Asian Para Games in Hangzhou, China. At the previous edition, she won gold in the women's individual compound event and the compound mixed team competition alongside Rakesh Kumar. She also claimed silver in the women's team event with Sarita. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Three years later, Sheetal repeated that medal-winning feat, this time collecting individual and mixed team gold medals alongside a silver with Payal Nag in the women's compound doubles. The Indian duo had topped the ranking round in the doubles event but lost 141-150 to China's Xueqing Xu and Jing Zhao in the final on Wednesday. Sheetal's latest triumph further strengthens her reputation as a leading figure in Indian para-archery. Having already made history in Hangzhou by becoming the first Indian woman to win two gold medals in a single edition of the Asian Para Games, she has now successfully repeated the feat in 2026. At just 19, Sheetal continues to turn extraordinary personal determination into landmark sporting achievements, delivering another golden chapter for India on the para-sporting stage. Former Paralympic bronze medallist Varun took silver with a season's best jump of 1.84m, while Rahul won bronze after clearing 1.81m. With this result, India repeated its podium sweep from the 2022 edition in the men's high jump T42/T63 event, once again claiming all three medals. The T63 classification is for athletes with an above-knee amputation or limb deficiency, who compete using a lower-limb prosthesis with a knee joint for running and jumping. The Indian high jump trio usually competes in the T42 category, which covers lower-limb deficiency, leg-length difference, impaired muscle power or limited passive movement affecting hip and knee function. title: Asian Para Games: Where India stands in medal tally after best day with 26 medals, including 7 golds
text: Sheetal Devi and Toman Kumar (Image credit: PCI) NEW DELHI: India enjoyed its best day at the Asian Para Games 2026 on Thursday, winning 26 medals, including seven golds, to reclaim fourth place in the standings. The haul took India's overall tally to 88 medals â 21 gold, 26 silver and 41 bronze â with para-athletics continuing to lead the country's charge. India had finished the opening day in fourth place before slipping to sixth on Day 2 and fifth on Day 3. Thursday's medal rush helped the contingent climb back to fourth, ahead of South Korea, who also have 21 gold medals but fewer silver and bronze medals. Watch Suchika Tariyal on her Asian Games bronze, childhood trauma, and never giving up | TOISA Spotlight Sheetal Devi strikes double gold, athletics lead charge Armless archer Sheetal Devi reaffirmed her status as one of India's standout athletes, winning two gold medals in less than two hours. The 19-year-old reigning world champion and world No. 1 first teamed up with Toman Kumar to defend the mixed team title, beating Indonesia's Teodora Audi Ayudia Ferelly and Ken Swagumilang 151-148. Sheetal then came from four points behind to defeat Singapore's Alim Nur Syahidah 142-139 in the individual final, repeating her triumph from Hangzhou 2023. India's day began with Suvarna Raj winning gold in the women's F54 discus throw with a best effort of 15.66m. The 44-year-old wheelchair athlete recorded four throws beyond 15 metres to secure the biggest win of her career. Dilip Gavit also claimed his second gold of the Games, winning the men's 400m T47 final in 48.27 seconds and defending the title he won in 2023. Solairaj Dharmaraj capped the day with gold in the men's long jump T44/T62/T64 final, setting an Asian record of 7.15m. title: India's Yuki Bhambri wins  Almaty Open title; triumph offers timely boost after medal-less Asian Games
text: India's number one doubles player Yuki Bhambri won his first ATP Tour title of the 2026 season, partnering American Ryan Seggerman to clinch the Almaty Open India's top-ranked doubles player Yuki Bhambri won his first ATP Tour title of the 2026 season after teaming up with American Ryan Seggerman to claim the Almaty Open on Sunday. The fourth-seeded Indo-American pair defeated top seeds Lucas Miedler and Neil Oberleitner of Austria in a closely fought final in Almaty. Bhambri and Seggerman won 7-6(3), 6-7(1), [10-2] to secure the ATP 250 title and give Bhambri his fifth career doubles crown on the ATP Tour. Watch Indian tennis star Shrivalli opens up on injuries & comeback journey The victory added to Bhambri's collection of ATP titles. He had previously won ATP 250 tournaments in Mallorca in 2023, and Gstaad and Munich in 2024, before claiming the ATP 500 title in Dubai in 2025. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines The 34-year-old will take confidence from Sunday's win, especially after returning from the Asian Games in Japan without a medal despite being expected to finish on the podium. It was Bhambri's second ATP final of the season. He had finished runner-up at the ATP 250 Geneva Open earlier in the year, partnering New Zealand's Michael Venus. Bhambri reached a career-high ranking of 18 in February but gradually slipped out of the top 40. His 2026 Grand Slam campaign included a third-round appearance in men's doubles at the Australian Open with Sweden's Andre Goransson. He was then knocked out in the second round of the French Open before suffering first-round exits at Wimbledon and the US Open, where he partnered Venus. Bhambri's best Grand Slam result came in 2025, when he and Venus reached the US Open semifinals. He also won the prestigious ATP 500 title in Dubai that year, partnering Australia's Alexei Popyrin. title: Asian Para Games: Nishad Kumar leads Indiaâs 14-medal athletics haul with double gold
text: India's Nishad Kumar (AP/PTI) Indiaâs track and field athletes turned grit into glory on Tuesday, collecting five gold, four silver and five bronze medals at the Asian Para Games in Nagoya to take their athletics tally to 20. The 14-medal haul featured record-breaking performances, emotional comebacks and podium sweeps, proof that determination can outpace the toughest odds. Nishad Kumar stood tallest, literally and figuratively. The Himachal Pradesh high jumper cleared 2.04m to win the menâs T47 gold with a Games record, adding to the long jump title he claimed on Monday. He became only the third Indian to win two gold medals at a single Asian Para Games, joining runner Ankur Dhama and armless archer Sheetal Devi. T47 is for athletes with upper-limb impairments. Deepthi Jeevanji launched Indiaâs gold rush by defending her womenâs 400m T20 crown in a Games-record 56.36 seconds. The 23-year-old from Telangana, who has an intellectual impairment, is also a world champion and Paralympic bronze medallist. Raised by small-farmer parents in a village in Warangal, she pursued running despite social taunts directed at her family for supporting her ambitions. A school physical education teacher first spotted her talent; later, coach N Ramesh and badminton coach Pullela Gopichand helped her journey gather pace. Simran claimed her maiden Para Games gold in the womenâs 200m T12, clocking a record 24.80 seconds. The sprinter, who has a moderate visual impairment, is rebuilding with guide Shivam after her previous guide, Umar Saifi, was banned for a doping violation. Debutant Tejalben Damor took bronze in 25.23 seconds, drawing confidence from the medal despite her familyâs financial struggles. In the menâs combined F51/52/53 discus, Pranav Soorma won gold with an Asian record of 11.66m, while fellow F51 athlete Ram Ratan Singh secured silver with 10.35m. The seated F51 classification involves significant movement limitations in the trunk, legs and hands. Placings in combined classes use the Raza points system, which enables fair comparisons between athletes with different levels of impairment.
