title: Silver lining! Preethi Pal wins second silver at Asian Para Games with sprint double
text: Preethi Pal (PTI Photo) NEW DELHI: India's Preethi Pal continued her impressive run at the Asian Para Games 2026, clinching her second silver medal of the continental event with a runner-up finish in the women's 100m T35 race on Wednesday. Preethi clocked 13.98 seconds to secure silver, adding to the medal she won in the women's 200m T35 event on Tuesday. The double podium finish further underlined the Indian para-athlete's consistency on the track. Watch Harita Bhadra Exclusive | 2 Asian Games Medals, Now the 22.45s World Championships Chase From rural Uttar Pradesh to the international podium Preethi has overcome significant physical challenges to establish herself among India's leading para-athletes. Born into a farmer's family in rural Uttar Pradesh, she faced difficulties from birth because of weakness in her legs and an irregular leg posture. Her legs were plastered for six days after she was born, and she underwent traditional treatments in an effort to strengthen them. At the age of five, she began wearing callipers, which she continued to use for eight years. Her introduction to para-sports came at the age of 17, when videos of the Paralympic Games on social media sparked her interest in athletics. Her journey gained momentum after she met Paralympian and mentor Fathima Khatoon, who encouraged her to compete at district, state and national levels. Preethi made her international debut at the Hangzhou Asian Para Games in 2023 before making a major breakthrough at the 2024 World Para Athletics Championships, where she won bronze medals in both the 100m and 200m events. She became the first Indian woman to win two track-and-field medals at a single Paralympic Games. Her achievements also include a silver and three bronze medals at the World Para Athletics Championships, four gold medals at Indian Open tournaments and a gold at the New Delhi Grand Prix. With two silver medals already secured at the Asian Para Games, Preethi has added another significant chapter to her career, demonstrating the resilience and consistency that have marked her rise in international para-athletics. title: 'I have no expectations, I just want to play my game': Diksha Dagar ahead of Womenâs Indian Open
text: Diksha Dagar (ANI Photo) NEW DELHI: Having fulfilled a long-cherished dream of winning an Asian Games medal in 2026 at Aichi-Nagoya, Japan where Indian golfer Diksha Dagar won the team silver with Pranavi Urs and Aditi Ashok , she is approaching the Womenâs Indian Open with a clear mindset, focus on her game, take every shot as it comes and let the result take care of itself. With some of the worldâs leading women golfers set to compete at the prestigious tournament at the DLF Golf and Country Club in Gurugram from Oct 22-25, Diksha is looking forward to testing herself against an international field on home soil. The golfer from Jhajjar, Haryana, believes that playing regularly against strong opposition this year has helped her prepare for the challenge, but she is not putting herself under pressure to deliver a particular result. âI donât have much of an expectation at the Womenâs Indian Open. I am just going to go there and play my game,â she said. She played the pro-am on Wednesday. âI am going to get a feel for the golf course and focus on every shot,â she said. For Diksha, the tournament also offers an opportunity to welcome players she has competed against on the international circuit. She is particularly excited about the prospect of seeing the European golfers take on the demanding DLF Golf and Country Club course, widely regarded as one of the toughest tests on the women's professional circuit. âI would like to see my friends playing here and share ideas about the course,â she said. Competing at her home course makes the occasion even more special for Diksha, who sees the tournament as an opportunity to showcase Indian golf to visiting players while measuring herself against some of the best in the business. The confidence with which she is approaching the tournament comes after an emotionally significant Asian Games campaign, where she achieved a milestone she had been chasing for years. For the golfer, the medal was not merely another addition to her achievements but the fulfilment of a personal ambition that had remained with her since she turned professional. The experience also brought back memories of her previous outing at the Asian Games in 2018 in Jakarta . Having missed out on the opportunity to achieve her target in the earlier edition, Diksha was determined to make the most of her chance this time around. She recalled being in good form before the previous Asian Games, including winning the Ladies European Tour's Czech Ladies Open, but the desired Asian Games result had eluded her. Returning to the competition years later gave her a fresh perspective on the responsibility of representing the country. Diksha said, âI approached the event with the understanding that opportunities to compete at the Asian Games do not come around often, making it important to give everything on the course.â âWhen I got there, sometimes I had a flashback of the first time I played in the 2018 Asian Games. It is always great to be back and represent your country. You are carrying the flag and have the responsibility to perform well,â she said. She added, âI played there as if it was my last day of golf. I gave everything because it is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. It happens once in four years, and you never know what might happen in the future. To me, it was a blessing that I was able to achieve what I wanted. I am grateful for it.â The Asian Games experience has come at a time when women's golf in India is gaining greater visibility, with Indian players increasingly competing on international tours and testing themselves against established names. Diksha believes the improvement in performances over the years reflects the progress the sport has made, while major international tournaments hosted in India can further accelerate that growth. She also welcomed the growing opportunities for younger players, pointing out that children are taking up golf at an early age and getting chances to compete in tournaments. However, she believes the next stage of development will depend on making the sport more accessible to families across different economic backgrounds. According to Diksha, reducing the cost of playing and improving access to facilities could help uncover a larger pool of talent. The Asian Games medal has given her a moment to cherish, but the next opportunity to compete on home soil presents another chance to demonstrate how far Indian women's golf has come. And as she prepares to take on the demanding DLF course, Dikshaâs approach remains refreshingly uncomplicated: stay patient, commit to every shot and allow her golf to do the talking. title: Seven medals for Army para athletes in Japan; Subedar Dharmaraj Solairaj retains long jump gold with new Asian record
text: Subedar Solairaj Dharmaraj successfully defended his menâs long jump title in the combined T44/T62/T64 event Pune: Athletes from Indian Armyâs Paralympic Node (APN) secured seven medals, including a historic gold by Subedar Dharmaraj Solairaj, at Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, which concluded on Saturday. Despite fielding a lean squad of only 10 athletes this time, the contingent successfully matched its previous editionâs medal tally. Solairaj (32) successfully defended his menâs long jump title in the combined T44/T62/T64 event. He set a new Asian record with a spectacular leap of 7.15 metres on Thursday. With this victory, the Tamil Nadu-born athlete, who competes in T64 classification, became the first Army para-athlete to win two gold medals at Asian Para Games. Solairajâs achievement builds on his steady, inspiring progress since returning to the track following a life-altering injury. Recruited into the Madras Regiment in 2013, he underwent a transtibial amputation in 2018 after serving in a high-altitude area along Indiaâs northern border. Initially fearing he would be permanently confined to a wheelchair, he found renewed purpose after interacting with fellow para-athletes at the Armyâs Artificial Limb Centre (ALC). His performance has improved consistently through focused training on his run-up, jumping technique, balance, and physical conditioning. In 2025, he had set a national and continental record of 7.32 metres in the T64 category at Indian Open Para Athletics International Championship in Bengaluru. Another major highlight for the Army contingent was the bronze medal clinched by Paris Paralympics bronze medallist Hokato Sema. The 43-year-old registered a throw of 14.65 metres in the menâs F57 shot put event, demonstrating his elite competitiveness against a much younger field. âAge is a crucial factor in this competition, but Sema has once again proven the old adage that age is just a number,â an official noted. Army officials stated that the seven-medal haul is highly commendable given their reduced representation. Strict entry caps imposed by the organisers prevented the Army from fielding its core para-rowers and athletes in canoeing and kayaking. âWe could have won significantly more medals had our rowers and kayakers been permitted to participate,â the official added. The contingentâs performance also brought to light the technical challenges faced by para-athletes, particularly those using running prostheses. Fine-tuning prosthetics and sockets to different competition surfaces and unpredictable weather conditions remains a critical challenge, as even microscopic variations can heavily impact balance, comfort, and final performance. Housed on the campus of Bombay Engineering Group and Centre, APN trains and supports injured soldiers looking to rebuild their lives through competitive sports. Officials noted that Solairajâs journeyâfrom an injury that threatened to derail his sporting ambitions to successfully defending his continental titleâunderscores the crucial role of sustained coaching, rehabilitation, and structural physical conditioning. PM appreciates Solairajâs achievement Prime Minister Narendra Modi took to his official X platform to praise the long jumperâs landmark victory, writing: âSolairaj Dharmaraj has delivered an exceptional performance in the menâs long jump T44/T62/T64 event at Asian Para Games 2026, winning gold with a phenomenal jump. By surpassing his own Asian record, he has once again demonstrated his tremendous skills and determination. Congratulations to Solairaj on this outstanding triumph. May he continue to achieve greater heights.â Medal winners: Long Jump (Final): Solairaj Dharmaraj: Gold Discus throw : Rakesh Kundu : Silver 100mtr freestyle: Kapil kumar : Silver Shot put: Hokato Sema: Bronze Discus throw: Pradeep Kumar: Bronze T64 400mt: Ajay Kumar: Bronze 100mtr breast stroke: Rohit kumar (Indian Navy) : Bronze You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Pune | Silver Rate in Pune | Bank Holidays in Pune | Public Holidays in Pune | Petrol Price in Pune | Diesel Price in Pune | CNG Price in Pune | LPG Price in Pune Stay updated with the latest Pune news. title: Super Sunday for India! Lakshya Sen ends year-long title drought as PV Sindhu completes Hylo Open double delight
text: Lakshya Sen and PV Sindhu (Video grabs) NEW DELHI: Indian badminton enjoyed a memorable Super Sunday at the Hylo Open 2026 as Lakshya Sen ended his year-long wait for a BWF World Tour title, joining PV Sindhu in winning the men's and women's singles crowns at the Super 500 tournament in SaarbrÃ¼cken, Germany. Lakshya produced a commanding performance to defeat Indonesia's fourth seed Jonatan Christie 21-17, 21-10 in the men's singles final, bringing an end to his title drought that had stretched back to the Australian Open in November 2025. Watch Kynan Chenai: The 38-Year-Old Gun Barrel, Asian Games Gold and the LA 2028 Dream | TOISA Spotlight Earlier, double Olympic medallist Sindhu had clinched the women's singles title with a dominant 21-12, 21-14 victory over Denmark's Line HÃ¸jmark KjÃ¦rsfeldt. The two straight-game victories ensured India walked away with both singles trophies, capping a remarkable campaign at the USD 500,000 event. For Lakshya, the victory was particularly significant after a season disrupted by injuries and inconsistent performances. The 25-year-old had reached the All England Championships final earlier this year but had struggled to maintain that level in subsequent tournaments. Lakshya dominates Christie to end title drought The men's singles final initially developed into a closely fought contest, with both players engaging in fast-paced rallies and exchanging powerful smashes. Lakshya made an aggressive start to take an 8-4 lead, using sharp cross-court angles and attacking strokes to push Christie around the court. The Indonesian, however, responded with a five-point run to move ahead 9-8. The Indian recovered his composure and gradually regained control through solid defence, deceptive net play and well-directed smashes. He held his nerve in the closing exchanges to take the opening game 21-17. The second game was far more one-sided. Lakshya raised his intensity, capitalising on Christie's unforced errors while controlling the rallies with excellent movement and shot selection. The Indian repeatedly neutralised the Indonesian's attacking strokes and turned defence into counter-attacking opportunities. Christie struggled to find answers as Lakshya extended his advantage and eventually sealed the game 21-10 to secure the title. The victory also levelled Lakshya's career head-to-head record against Christie at 4-4. Sindhu leads India's double title celebration Sindhu had set the tone for India's title-winning Sunday by defeating KjÃ¦rsfeldt in the women's singles final . It was Sindhu's second title of the season after her Japan Open triumph in July. She had also finished runner-up at the French Open last week, making the Hylo Open victory another significant boost to her late-season campaign. The Indian's title run also earned her 9,200 ranking points, keeping her in contention for qualification for the season-ending BWF World Tour Finals. Lakshya had also spoken about rediscovering his rhythm after an injury-interrupted period following his semifinal victory. "I've had a few niggles here and there, and I was out for some time. At certain tournaments, I wasn't really 100 per cent. But I'm happy with the way I've played here. It's a really good confidence booster because I haven't played this many matches in a row over the last couple of months," he had said. Since the All England Championships, I think this is the first time I've felt that I was playing really well again. I can feel myself getting back into rhythm and playing good badminton." With Sindhu and Lakshya both finishing on top of the podium, India secured a memorable double at the Hylo Open, with the two leading shuttlers delivering a timely boost ahead of the closing stretch of the badminton season. title: Asian Para Games 2026: Pradeep Kumar wins silver, Ayush Verma takes bronze in javelin
text: Pradeep Kumar (Image credit: ANI) India's Pradeep Kumar and Ayush Verma won silver and bronze medals respectively in the men's javelin throw F53/54 event at the Asian Para Games 2026 on Tuesday. Pradeep, competing in the F54 category, finished second with a personal best throw of 27.45 metres. It was his second successive silver medal at the Asian Para Games. Ayush, who competes in the F53 category, secured bronze with a throw of 17.88 metres. His performance earned him enough Raza points to finish on the podium. Iran's Erfan Bandori wins gold Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Iran's Erfan Bandori successfully defended his title with a Games record throw of 30.24 metres. Thailand's Sahar-dam Yaena finished behind Ayush despite throwing the javelin 23.31 metres. Ayush secured the higher position because the Raza points system takes the athletes' level of disability into account when different classifications compete in the same event. What is the Raza points system? The Raza points system converts athletes' performances into scores based on their classification and level of disability. It allows athletes from different classifications to compete in the same event on a comparable basis. What are the F53 and F54 classifications? The F53 category is for athletes who have good arm and hand function but limited trunk control and no sitting balance because of reduced abdominal and lower back muscle function. The F54 category is for athletes who have good arm strength and some or full trunk muscle power, although their trunk and leg movements remain significantly affected. title: A leap from the seaâs edge
text: Before sunrise, the fishing village of Nattika in Thrissur is already awake. The air is thick with the briny smell of raw fish as wooden boats ride the glistening waves and fishermen bring the nightâs catch ashore. This unassuming hamlet is the last place one would expect to find a world-class athlete. Yet from the loose, shifting sands of Nattika beach has emerged Ancy Sojan. Last month, the 25-year-old stood on the podium at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, with her second Asian silver. In Aug, at the National Inter-State Senior Athletics Championships in Bhubaneswar, she leapt 6.88m to wipe out Anju Bobby Georgeâs 22-year-old national record in the womenâs long jump. Earlier this week, as Durga Puja celebrations were in full swing, every road into Nattika was clogged. Children ran alongside the procession and old fishermen walked up from the shore as drumbeats mixed with the smell of the sea. Locals had organised her felicitation at the Triprayar Sports and Games Association stadium. This was the girl who once ran along Nattikaâs coastline at dawn with her father, Sojan ET, an autorickshaw driver. Now the whole town had turned out to see its biggest star. Loud applause greeted Ancy as she walked to the podium. She spoke frankly about her hormonal issues and the sleepless nights spent fighting her weight. âThe season began with a bronze at the Asian Indoor Championships in Tianjin, and ended with a silver at the Asian Games in Japan,â she said. Missing gold in Aichi-Nagoya by 2cm still hurts. âWhen I was younger, my dream was to fill my trophy cabinet with national medals. Now, I want to fill it with international medals, irrespective of the colour,â she said. Beyond that sits a bigger target. âI want to become the first Indian woman to jump 7m.â After breaking the national record, Ancy had told sports minister OJ Janeesh that the state's athletes do not get the recognition they deserve. Janeesh, at Triprayar to felicitate her, backed her with figures. âBetween 2018 and 2026, the previous govt has not disbursed funds worth Rs 13 crore to its athletes who participated at various national and international meets,â he said. The sports council, he said, had no details of the state's athletes despite writing twice to associations. Payments to around 300 athletes, including Ancy, are pending. The govt owes her Rs 3 lakh, which he said would be paid in a couple of months. âI am Ancy's debtor,â the minister said. Following criticism over disparities with other states, the cabinet recently doubled cash awards for Commonwealth Games medallists. Under the Pinarayi Vijayan govt, CWG medallists received Rs 5 lakh for gold, Rs 3 lakh for silver and Rs 2 lakh for bronze. The benefits now extend to coaches and athletes who narrowly missed medals, Janeesh added. Ancyâs story is also the story of Nattika. Nattika has produced several Olympians and international athletes. Besides P Ramachandran, who ran in the 4x400m relay at the 2000 Sydney Olympics, Nattika has seen the rise of track athlete Anjali PD and discus thrower Athulya P. But none has burst into the national consciousness like Ancy. âI trained on a mud track when I started. Today, Nattika Fisheries School has a synthetic track, and Thrissur also has its own synthetic track for school events. I am happy that the coming generations will get the opportunities and infrastructure I never had,â she said. Ancy has put Nattika on Indiaâs sporting map. Indiaâs next Olympic winner may not come from big metros or posh academies, but from forgotten coastlines that carry the briny smell of raw fish. title: Three medals in a day! Thulasimathi Murugesan caps Asian Para Games campaign with gold
text: Thulasimathi Murugesan NEW DELHI: Thulasimathi Murugesan produced a memorable triple-medal performance at the Asian Para Games 2026 on Friday, winning gold and two silver medals as India's para-badminton contingent enjoyed a productive day in Aichi-Nagoya. The 24-year-old Paris Paralympics silver medallist capped her campaign with gold in the women's doubles SL3-SU5 event, partnering Manasi Joshi to defeat China's Yang Qiuxia and Xiao Zuxian 21-16, 21-13 in the final. The Indian pair wrapped up the contest in just 28 minutes. Thulasimathi had earlier settled for silver in the women's singles SU5 final, losing 18-21, 11-21 to China's Yang. She then teamed up with Nitesh Kumar in the mixed doubles SL3-SU5 final, but the Indian combination went down 21-11, 19-21, 14-21 to Indonesia's Leani Ratri Oktila and Hikmat Ramdani. Watch Suchika Tariyal on her Asian Games bronze, childhood trauma, and never giving up | TOISA Spotlight Nitesh, Naveen strike gold for India Nitesh, the Paris Paralympic champion, enjoyed a successful day of his own, winning gold in the men's singles SL3 event before adding mixed doubles silver with Thulasimathi. The 31-year-old defeated compatriot and Tokyo Paralympic gold medallist Pramod Bhagat 21-18, 21-16 in the men's singles final. "Last time I was close, I was leading 19-16 in the third set, and then I lost. So this time, winning it and again winning in two sets against Pramod is, of course, very special, and I think it's one of the rarest of the rare things to see," Nitesh said after his victory. Naveen Sivakumar added another gold for India, beating Indonesia's Fredy Setiawan 21-9, 21-17 in the men's singles SL4 final. Making his Asian Para Games debut, Naveen completed the win in 36 minutes. Pramod had to settle for silver after winning gold in the 2018 and 2022 editions. India's Nithya Sre Sumathy Sivan also claimed silver in the women's singles SH6 final after losing to China's Li Fengmei. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines India close in on best-ever medal tally India continued to collect medals across disciplines on Friday. Para shooter Mona Agarwal won her second gold of the Games in the women's 50m rifle 3 Positions SH1 final, setting a world record with 357.5 points. She finished 3.8 points ahead of China's Cuiping Zhang. In para archery, Harvinder Singh and Vijay Sundi won gold in the men's recurve doubles event. Sandeep claimed the men's 400m T64 title, while Haney won gold in the men's javelin throw F37/38 event. India also added silver medals through Nithya Sre Sumathy Sivan, Pooja Jatyan and Bhawna Choudhary in women's recurve doubles, Parmod Bijarnia in the men's 1500m T46 and Nimisha Suresh in the women's long jump T47. Jehan Madan and Shubham Wadhwa secured bronze in men's doubles para table tennis MD4. India's tally stood at 106 medals â 28 gold, 34 silver and 44 bronze â with the country fourth in the standings. title: âDemands comprehensive federal responseâ: 105 US lawmakers urge FBI to probe Hindu temple shooting plot amid hate crime concerns
text: Alexandros Paporakis, 19, arrested in alleged temple shooting plot. A group of 105 US lawmakers has urged the FBI to investigate an alleged shooting plot at a Hindu temple in Aurora, Illinois, as a potential federal hate crime, citing concerns about anti-Indian, anti-Hindu and broader anti-South Asian hostility. Led by Indian American Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi, wrote to FBI Director Kash Patel on Tuesday, asking for an update on the investigation into the alleged plot at the Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) temple and the bureauâs efforts to address credible threats against South Asian communities. Krishnamoorthi and his family were worshipping at the temple when the alleged incident occurred on October 11. Watch âPajeet, Dirtyâ: Racist Videos, Temple Attacks, Slurs: Americaâs Shocking Anti-India Hate Wave âThe alleged combination of targeted racial hatred, a religious setting, and preparations for mass violence demands a comprehensive federal response,â the lawmakers wrote. The group included the entire Illinois House Democratic delegation, every Indian American member of Congress, and Senators Dick Durbin, Tammy Duckworth, Andy Kim and Chris Van Hollen. Alexandros Paporakis, 19, was arrested on October 11 in connection with the alleged plot. According to prosecutors, he attempted to shoot a man outside the temple, but his rifle jammed. He fled the scene and later communicated plans to return, prompting a co-worker to alert police, who arrested him that day. Prosecutors allege that Paporakis, who identified himself as a neo-Nazi, wrote an eight-page white supremacist manifesto describing violence against people of Indian descent at a Hindu place of worship. Investigators recovered a rifle, hundreds of rounds of ammunition, body armour and white supremacist imagery, as per the press release. The letter asks whether the FBI is examining potential racial, ethnic and religious bias in the case and whether online platforms or other individuals may have helped facilitate the alleged plot. The lawmakers also want to know whether the bureau is coordinating with the Justice Departmentâs Civil Rights Division and the relevant US Attorneyâs Office. The request comes amid concerns about online hate targeting South Asians in the US. The lawmakers cited a September 2026 report that identified more than 542,000 anti-South Asian hateful posts on X between January 2025 and June 2026. The monthly volume reportedly rose by about 240% between January 2024 and June 2026. They also cited a Carnegie Endowment survey in which 48% of Indian American respondents said they had encountered racist posts targeting their community very or somewhat often since the start of 2025. One in four respondents reported being called a slur. The letter criticised messages posted by Trump administration agencies that the lawmakers said risk reinforcing racial and religious stereotypes. Examples included a Department of Homeland Security post targeting a Sikh man with a remark about driving and a Department of Education post declaring âMake College Football Great Againâ after a Texas Republican complained about South Asians attending a University of Texas football game. The lawmakers argued that political debates over immigration and public safety should not lead to collective suspicion of Indian, Sikh, Hindu or other South Asian communities. They have asked the FBI to clarify how it distinguishes protected speech, including offensive expression, from credible threats that warrant investigation. They also want details of how actionable intelligence is shared with local law enforcement and potentially targeted places of worship. Other questions concern whether the bureau has sufficient personnel, language expertise and analytical resources to assess threats involving anti-Indian, anti-Hindu and broader anti-South Asian bias. The lawmakers requested a written response by October 29, to the extent permitted by the ongoing investigation. They urged the bureau to examine all relevant evidence, pursue applicable offences and explain what steps are being taken to protect affected communities. You use AI every day. title: Opaque selection, forced doubles pairing: Para-shuttlers challenge Para Asian Games non-selection in Delhi HC
text: Chirag Baretha NEW DELHI: Chirag Baretha is a two-time Asian Games medallist, having won silver in 2023 and bronze in 2018. Instead of focusing on the upcoming Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, which begin on October 18, he is running from pillar to post, trying to keep his fading dream of representing India alive. The 29-year-old has also won bronze medals at the 2024 BWF Para Badminton World Championships, the 2025 Asian Para Badminton Championships, and the 2026 World Para Badminton Championships. Baretha, alongside fellow para-shuttlers Shashank Kumar, Ammu Mohan and Manisha Patel, has filed a petition in the Delhi High Court against the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports (MYAS), the Paralympic Committee of India (PCI), the Badminton Association of India (BAI) and the Sports Authority of India (SAI) over their non-selection. Watch Suchika Tariyal on her Asian Games bronze, childhood trauma, and never giving up | TOISA Spotlight In the petition, accessed by TimesofIndia.com, the para-shuttlers argue that they meet the selection criteria set by the Sports Ministry, which require them to be ranked in the top six in Asia. Baretha and Mandeep Kaur were ranked World No. 6 in the SL3-SU5 category on July 14, 2026, when the rankings were considered for the Asian Para Games. Subsequently, the petition argues that " Rakesh Pandey has not obtained or won any medal in the last 12 months or have ranking less than the petitioners in the international athlete ranking. Moreover, he was debarred for 4 years for failing the Anti-Doping Test." The men's doubles pairing of Rakesh Pandey and Dev Rathi was ranked World No. 3 in the SU5 category on the cutoff date. However, Rakesh is set to partner Umesh Vikram Kumar in men's doubles at the Asian Para Games, while also finding a spot in the men's singles discipline. This, too, has a layer of intrigue. In an email sent to qualified para-shuttlers on August 25, K Prabhakar Rao , the chairman of para-badminton at the Badminton Association of India (BAI), made it clear that "for a pair to be considered valid for recommendation, separate emails must be received from both players, with each player naming the other as their partner for the concerned event." In response, Baretha, who was named in the Badminton World Federation's (BWF) entry list, registered for singles (SU5 category), men's doubles (SU5 with Hardik Makkar) and mixed doubles (SL3-SU5 with Mandeep Kaur). However, Vikram, Pandey's partner at the Asian Para Games, expressed displeasure at his name being added to the doubles draw without his consent. "Sir, I have not given consent to participate in MD SL3 SU5. How can I [sic] my name appear in doubles? Please make sure to remove my name from doubles without affecting my singles entry," he wrote in a WhatsApp group for Asian Para Games athletes. He addressed the message to Prabhakar Rao and coach Venkata Murali Krishna. However, his plea was not entertained. "Vikram, we can discuss this in a physical meeting at hotel. At this stage, no modification is allowed. We already discussed with referee, ABC [Asian Badminton Confederation] persons." Not satisfied, Vikram responded, "Sir, I will be arriving at hotel late tonight and by that time draw will be announced. Without my consent, my name should not be entered. Pandey bhaiya can play with Hardik (Makkar)." For Vikram, there is no way out. The rules stipulate that if a player withdraws from one discipline, they withdraw from the entire tournament. We are fighting on a merit basis. We are medal holders. We are rank holders. We followed the guidelines of SAI. But Mr Prabhakar Rao has tricked us and affected our career and effort of four years. Chirag Baretha This sequence of events, and the eventual loss of his place in the contingent, has left Baretha distraught. "We are (fighting) on a merit basis. We are medal holders. We are rank holders. We followed the guidelines of SAI. But Mr Prabhakar Rao has tricked us and affected our career and effort of four years," Baretha told TimesofIndia.com. "I am Asia No. 6 and have qualified through my ranking. Even if you ignore that, I meet another clause of being a medallist from previous Games." The Badminton Association of India didn't have a say in this. We didn't include or exclude an athlete as per our choices. We got this list from SAI, and we followed it. K Prabhakar Rao "Before my name was withdrawn at the manager's meeting, the draw was such that I was destined to reach the final. Except for one player, I have been able to beat everyone. I could guarantee the country a silver medal," he added confidently. K Prabhakar Rao said the squad selection was not theirs to make in the first place. "The Badminton Association of India didn't have a say in this. We didn't include or exclude an athlete as per our choices. We got this list from SAI, and we followed it," he told TimesofIndia.com. The exclusion of former head coach Gaurav Khanna is believed to have been a major factor in the entire selection fracas. Khanna, who established India's first para-badminton academy (Gaurav Khanna Excellia Badminton Academy), has the likes of Suhas and Baretha under his wing. Baretha alleged that senior para-shuttlers were instrumental in creating a negative impression of Khanna among officials at SAI. "They keep going on about the academy, but at least look at my credentials. Look at my medals, my ranking. I am talking about my achievements." In the days following the squad announcement and Baretha's omission on October 12, Baretha, Shashank Kumar and Ammu Mohan approached the Delhi High Court and met Dr Pallavi Rai, SAI's director (TEAMS Division), but failed to receive a satisfactory response. Their repeated attempts to seek clarity from BAI secretary Sanjay Mishra and K Prabhakar Rao have also failed to yield results. The para-shuttlers are not the only aggrieved group of Indian athletes. Para-shooters and para-cyclists, too, had demanded a fairer and more transparent selection process. They held a protest during the send-off ceremony on October 8. India has sent a 281-member contingent to the Asian Para Games, which includes 168 athletes. title: 2 points from a medal, Anjali scripts Indian Boccia history at Asiad
text: âNext time, straight for gold,â Anjali said, setting her sights on the Los Angeles 2028 Paralympics. Chandigarh: Two points separated Anjali Devi from a medal at the 2026 Asian Para Games. For the Himachal Pradesh athlete, who spent four years largely confined to home after a road accident left her quadriplegic, the fourth-place finish marked the best-ever performance by an Indian in Boccia at the Asian Games. âNext time, straight for gold,â she said, setting her sights on the Los Angeles 2028 Paralympics. Anjaliâs performance marked the deepest run by an Indian Boccia player at the continental event. She topped her pool, beating Japan 9-0, Singapore 3-2 and China 5-3, though she lost 0-8 to South Korea. She then reached the medal stages but lost both her gold and bronze medal matches by two points. The result was a remarkable turnaround for someone who had to rebuild her life after a devastating accident in 2018. Anjali was returning home with her uncle around 1am during heavy monsoon rain when their car plunged nearly 250 feet down a ditch. The crash caused a spinal cord injury. She spent two to two-and-a-half months in the ICU at PGI before returning home for physiotherapy. âI had lived 18 years of a normal life, and suddenly I was in a wheelchair. That was the biggest shock,â she recalled. For four years, she remained largely at home, trying to adapt to a life radically different from the one she had known. A visit to Chandigarh Spinal Rehab Centre in Nov 2022, however, opened up a new possibility. Introduced to Boccia during rehabilitation, Anjali was initially sceptical. The sport seemed to involve little more than throwing balls. She soon discovered that its apparent simplicity concealed a demanding contest of precision and strategy. âIt is a complete mind game, just like chess. You have to calculate angles, speed, trajectory and measurements,â she said. Within 10 days of taking up the sport, she won gold at the national level. Within six months, she was representing India at the 2023 Asian Games, where she finished eighth despite having no prior international experience. Her progress has exposed the challenges facing Boccia in India, where the sport remains relatively unknown and facilities are scarce. Anjali estimates that the country has only two-three dedicated Boccia courts, forcing many athletes to practise in multipurpose halls or on surfaces not designed for the sport. She believes awareness camps in schools, special schools and communities at district and state levels could help introduce Boccia to more people with disabilities and identify talent early. Dedicated facilities would then give emerging players the opportunity to develop their skills. The resource gap extends to international competition. Anjali has seen rival teams arrive with physiotherapists, dietitians, observers, camera operators and analysts who record and review matches. The Indian team, she said, has far fewer support personnel, with one coach handling four players. âThose small things also matter. The other teams have their entire team behind them, with everyoneâs efforts going into their performance. In India, the player often has to do all these things themselves,â she said. In a sport where a slight error in angle, speed or distance can decide a match, such support can prove crucial. Anjaliâs two-point defeats in the medal matches brought that margin into sharp focus.Personal sponsors helped her undertake two training trips to Thailand before the Asian Para Games. Her sister, Priyanka Thakur, has been her biggest source of support and also serves as her ramp operator in the BC3 category. title: For mom, for India: The making of a para champion
text: Shubham Wadhwa won two medals in the Asian Para Games in Japan Chandigarh: For nearly three years, Shubham Wadhwa lay bedridden, uncertain of what life held for him after a bike accident changed everything. Today, the Ludhiana-born para table tennis player has two Asian Para Games bronze medals to his name, along with a promise to his mother that he has fulfilled. Making his debut at the Asian Para Games 2026 in Japan, Wadhwa won bronze in menâs doubles with Jehan Dorab Madan in the MD4 category and in mixed doubles with Bhavina Patel in the XD7 category. Both podium finishes created history for India, marking the countryâs first-ever medals in menâs doubles and mixed doubles at the Asian Para Games. âBefore coming to Japan, I had told my mom that I will give my best and make my dream come true,â Wadhwa told TOI. âI had to fulfil this promise, and so I did. This is for my mother.â It is the family support he says because of which he could make a comeback at life. For his family, the medals mark the end of a difficult chapter that began in 2016, when a bike accident left Wadhwa with a spinal cord injury, paralysed below the chest. A national-level table tennis player during his school days, he had stepped away from the sport to pursue modelling. The accident forced him to rebuild his life from scratch. âWhen I was lying bedridden, I had no idea life was going to turn out this way,â he told TOI. For three years, even the simplest daily activities required assistance. His mother, Poonam Wadhwa, stood by him through the long period of treatment and recovery. âMy husband and son both used to go for work. I used to be there to take care of Shubham when he was bedridden,â she told TOI. Recalling the accident, she said her son had returned home at night when a friend called him to accompany him to the market. Within those 10 minutes, their lives changed forever. âI sometimes sit and think, had he not gone back to the market that day, things would have been so different,â she said. âThose three difficult years, we kept faith in God and did our best for his treatment.â Wadhwa credits his family for helping him find his way back. His friends, too, refused to let him give up on table tennis. They helped him discover a scholarship opportunity at Lovely Professional University, encouraged him to return to the sport and even came home to practise with him for hours during the Covid pandemic. He joined LPU in 2018 to pursue computer science engineering and gradually rebuilt his sporting career, returning to the table around 2019-20. Since then he has won 10 national gold medals and earned international recognition, including a gold and two bronze medals at the ITTF World Para Future in Gold Coast, followed by silver in mixed doubles and bronze in menâs singles at the ITTF World Para Elite in Taipei City. At the Asian Para Games, partnerships built over years also paid off. Wadhwa has played alongside Madan for two to three years and with Patel for about a year and a half. Their combined efforts brought India two historic podium finishes. Poonam broke down in tears when she learnt of her sonâs achievement. âNow my son is unstoppable. Table tennis is his whole life. He derives his lifeâs meaning from it,â she said, thanking those who supported him during his recovery. Wadhwa, however, is already looking ahead. He is the only Indian athlete in the menâs category to have qualified for the ITTF World Para Table Tennis Championships in Thailand. âWhen I come back to India, I wonât be able to go home. First, Iâll report for practice and then leave for the World Championships within 10 days,â he said. title: Asian Para Games: 1-2 for India! Pranav Soorma, Ram Ratan Singh clinch discus gold and silver
text: Pranav Soorma NEW DELHI: India continued to swell their medal tally at the Asian Para Games 2026 as Pranav Soorma and Ram Ratan Singh secured a memorable one-two finish in the men's discus throw combined F51/52/53 event on Tuesday, with Soorma setting a new Asian record to clinch gold. Iran's Alireza Hemami, competing in the F53 classification, finished with the bronze medal after recording a throw of 20.20m in the fourth round. Raza points system decides final standings Although Hemami registered a longer distance than both Indian athletes, he finished third because the combined event's standings were determined using the Raza Point System. The system adjusts performances according to athletes' disability classifications, converting results into standardised points to allow fair comparisons between competitors with different levels of impairment. The F51 classification includes athletes with significant limitations in trunk, leg and hand movement, alongside varying restrictions in arm function. Events may combine athletes from different classifications when participation numbers are limited. The F51-F57 categories cover seated throwing events for athletes with various lower-body impairments, limb deficiencies and limitations in muscle power or range of movement. title: 'How long will Mirabai Chanu alone keep winning medals for us?' Sports Ministry reviews Asian Games performance; questions injuries, lacklustre show
text: The meeting was attended by Minister of State for Sports Raksha Khadse, Indian Olympic Association (IOA) President P T Usha, Sports Secretary Hari Ranjan Rao and NSF representatives. NEW DELHI: India's sub-par medal haul in disciplines like athletics and badminton came under scrutiny during the Sports Ministry's review of the country's Asian Games performance on Thursday. In a meeting with the National Sports Federations (NSFs), Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya questioned athlete injuries upon reaching Aichi-Nagoya and the lacklustre effort of some high-profile athletes. India finished fourth in the medal tally at the 2026 Asian Games, pulling ahead after a gold-laden show in the last two days. India bagged 85 medals at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, including 21 golds, significantly lower than the 106 medals it won at the previous edition in Hangzhou, China. Watch Harita Bhadra Exclusive | 2 Asian Games Medals, Now the 22.45s World Championships Chase The meeting was attended by Minister of State for Sports Raksha Khadse, Indian Olympic Association (IOA) President P T Usha, Sports Secretary Hari Ranjan Rao and NSF representatives. The Minister also called for greater responsibility from the NSFs on the sporting performance. He reiterated the need to work with further synergy to sustain Indiaâs sporting excellence. Mandaviya stressed that India needs a continuous pipeline of athletes rather than relying on a handful of medal winners. âHow long will Mirabai Chanu alone keep winning medals for us? We need to produce 10 more Mirabai Chanus. Every federation must take this responsibility seriously. We have to identify talent, provide the right training and create an environment in which athletes can progress to the highest level,â the Sports Minister said. As TimesofIndia.com had reported last week, injuries to athletes like hurdler Jyothi Yarraji and triple jumper Praveen Chithravel were brought to attention during the meet. The topic was raised by PT Usha when Athletics Federation of India (AFI) advisor Adille Sumariwalla presented his performance analysis. However, the topic wasn't elaborated on further, with the objective being an overall look at the performance rather than isolated cases. Runner Avinash Sable's fitness came under scrutiny after he failed to start the 5000m, having finished fourth in his pet event, the 3000m steeplechase. He was the defending champion in the steeplechase and had won 5000m silver in Hangzhou. Overall, athletics' gold count fell from six to one this time, while the discipline's total haul of 24 medals was five fewer than at the previous Games. The Boxing Federation of India (BFI), basking in a landmark performance that included an unprecedented three golds, promised more if given "continued institutional support." The organisation's current power struggle between President Ajay Singh and Secretary Pramod Kumar, who have suspended each other over multiple alleged violations, was not discussed. Besides athletics and shooting, badminton has come under scrutiny after producing just one men's team bronze. A major disappointment was defending men's doubles champions Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty crashing out in the first round â a result partly blamed on hectic scheduling that forced players into more than one match within 24 hours. Focus on LA 2028 Beyond Asian Games 2026, the platform was also used to assess preparations for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics, the 2030 Commonwealth Games and the 2030 Asian Games in Doha. As a path forward, Mandaviya emphasised the need for more sports psychologists, sports science experts and high-performance mental trainers to mitigate the loss of focus that athletes go through when competing on major international stages. He also urged every NSF to introduce more competitions, strengthen athlete preparation, work with dedicated commitment, as well as carry out honest assessment of gaps in performance and administration. For the 2030 Commonwealth Games, we must break our own record from the 2010 Commonwealth Games and finish among the top three. Since we are hosting the Games, every NSF must take the competition seriously and prepare accordingly. We must treat this as a challenge and work towards it from now,â he said. title: Asian Para Games: Sheetal Devi, Swati Chaudhary storm into archery finals, eye gold medals for India
text: Sheetal Devi and Swati Chaudhary NEW DELHI: India's para archers Sheetal Devi and Swati Chaudhary stormed into the finals of their respective events at the Asian Para Games 2026 on Tuesday, assuring the country of at least two medals and setting up opportunities to add to India's tally. Defending champion Sheetal continued her impressive run in the women's compound category, defeating Japan's Shinohara Aya 145-137 in the semifinal. The 19-year-old will face Singapore's Alim Nur Syahidah in the gold-medal match on October 22. Swati, making her debut at the continental multi-sport event, also booked her place in the final after beating South Korea's Lee Eunhee 6-2 in the women's W1 semifinal. She will take on China's Mengkan in the gold-medal contest, with both Indian archers now assured of at least silver medals. Watch Asian Games gold medallist Sujeet Kalkal on fatherâs influence and how he turned final around Sheetal continues record-breaking run Sheetal, who was born without arms and shoots using her feet and shoulder, has been one of India's standout performers in para archery. The Jammu and Kashmir archer equalled the world record and set a new Asian record during qualification, underlining her credentials as she seeks to defend her title. She continued her dominant campaign in the elimination rounds, defeating Hong Kong's Chan Yuen Wah 149-134 in the pre-quarterfinals and the Philippines' Agustina Bantiloc 147-135 in the quarterfinals before overcoming Shinohara in the last four. Sheetal had also produced a record-breaking 149 against Chan, surpassing the previous world record of 148 held by Britain's Jessica Stretton. The world No. 1 will now look to cap her campaign with another gold medal. She is also scheduled to compete in the compound women's doubles semifinals alongside Payal Nag. However, the day brought disappointment in several individual events. Harvinder lost 5-6 to China's Yun Duo in a shoot-off in the men's recurve quarterfinals, while Bhawna went down 2-6 to Mongolia's Selengee Demberel in the women's last eight. In the men's compound event, Toman suffered a 144-149 semifinal defeat to China's Ai Xinliang and will compete for bronze. Shyam Sundar Swami had earlier lost 146-147 to Ai in the quarterfinals. With Sheetal and Swati now one victory away from gold, India will look to convert their strong performances into top-podium finishes as the para archery competition progresses. title: Asian Para Games: Thulasimathi clinches silver in women's singles SU5, remains in contention for two more golds
text: Thulasimathi Murugesan India's Thulasimathi Murugesan added another medal to her growing collection at the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games, settling for silver in the women's singles SU5 badminton event after losing to China's Yang Qiuxia in the final on Friday. The 24-year-old, who won silver at the Paris 2024 Paralympics, went down 18-21, 11-21 against the Chinese shuttler at the Ichinomiya City Municipal Gymnasium. However, Thulasimathi's campaign is far from over, with the Indian still in contention for two more gold medals in the mixed doubles and women's doubles events. She will look to make amends in the remaining finals as India aim to add to their medal tally. Thulasimathi falls short against Yang after impressive semi-final comeback Thulasimathi, currently ranked World No. 2, could not overcome Yang in the title clash, with the Chinese player securing the gold medal in straight games. The Indian had produced a fighting performance in the semi-finals, rallying from a game down to defeat compatriot and World No. 1 Manisha Ramdass 19-21, 21-15, 21-13 and book her place in the final. The silver medal adds to Thulasimathi's impressive record in para-badminton, following her breakthrough performance at the Paris 2024 Paralympics, where she finished runner-up in the women's singles SU5 category. Two more gold medal opportunities await Thulasimathi will have two more chances to finish her campaign on a high. She has partnered Nitesh Kumar to reach the mixed doubles SL3-SU5 final, where the Indian duo will face Indonesia's Leani Ratri Oktila and Hikmat Ramdani. The Indians booked their place in the final after overcoming China's Li Mingpan and Xiao Zuxian in a hard-fought 42-minute semi-final. Nitesh and Thulasimathi prevailed 21-19, 14-21, 21-17 to secure their place in the gold medal match. Later, Thulasimathi will team up with Manasi Girishchandra Joshi in the women's doubles SL3-SU5 final. The Indian pair will face China's Yang Qiuxia and Xiao Zuxian, giving Thulasimathi another opportunity to challenge for gold against the Chinese shuttler who defeated her in the singles final. title: Asian Para Games: Can Indiaâs para-athletes script another 100-medal triumph despite a smaller contingent?
text: Archer Sheetal Devi from India prepares to fire during the Paralympic Games in Paris on Thursday, Aug. 29, 2024. (File Photo/ AP) Indiaâs para-athletes will look to build on the countryâs remarkable rise in international para-sports as the fifth edition of the Asian Para Games gets underway in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, on October 18. After Indiaâs fourth-place finish at the Asian Games 2026, the para contingent will aim to continue the countryâs impressive medal-winning run at the continental event. India will be represented by 166 athletes across 10 disciplines at the October 18-24 event. The contingent features several Paralympic medallists, world champions and emerging talents, including archer Sheetal Devi, badminton stars Pramod Bhagat and Suhas Yathiraj, and para-table tennis player Bhavina Patel. Watch Suchika Tariyal on her Asian Games bronze, childhood trauma, and never giving up | TOISA Spotlight Indiaâs recent performances at the Asian Para Games and Paralympics have established the country as an increasingly competitive force in para-sports. From 14 medals at the inaugural edition in 2010 to a record 108 in Hangzhou in 2023, the progress has been remarkable. The challenge in Aichi-Nagoya will be to build on that foundation and demonstrate that the momentum can continue, even with a smaller contingent. Can India cross the 100-medal mark for the second consecutive edition? While the size of this yearâs squad makes comparisons with Hangzhou particularly interesting, Indiaâs established medal-winners and growing strength across disciplines provide reasons for optimism. 166 athletes across 10 disciplines: Indiaâs medal prospects Indiaâs contingent comprises 111 male and 55 female athletes, alongside 94 team officials and support staff and 15 contingent staff members. Para-athletics accounts for the largest share, with 62 athletes, followed by para-badminton with 28 and para-swimming with 16. Para-shooting has 13 athletes, while para-archery and para-table tennis have 11 and 10, respectively. The remaining disciplines are blind football (10), para-powerlifting (eight), para-judo (seven) and para-cycling (one). The squad brings together established international performers and athletes looking to make their mark at the continental level. Sheetal, Pramod, Suhas and Bhavina are among the prominent names to watch, while para-athletics is expected to play a central role in Indiaâs medal campaign. From 14 medals to 108: Indiaâs remarkable rise Indiaâs journey at the Asian Para Games offers a compelling picture of sustained improvement. The country won 14 medals at the inaugural edition in 2010, comprising one gold, four silver and nine bronze, to finish 15th in the standings. Four years later, India retained 15th place but more than doubled its tally, winning 33 medals - three gold, 14 silver and 16 bronze. The breakthrough came in 2018, when India secured 72 medals, including 15 gold, 24 silver and 33 bronze, to climb to ninth place. At Hangzhou in 2023, the contingent took another giant leap, winning 108 medals (27 gold, 32 silver and 49 bronze) to finish fifth. The progression across four editions reflects the growing depth of Indian para-sports: India has improved its medal tally in every edition so far while also making significant gains in the standings. The jump from 72 to 108 medals between the 2018 and 2023 editions was particularly impressive, taking the country past the 100-medal mark for the first time. Aichi-Nagoya offers the next opportunity to extend that progress and build on the foundations established over the previous decade. Paralympic success underlines Indiaâs growing potential The rise at the Asian Para Games has been accompanied by a remarkable improvement in Indiaâs performances at the Paralympics. India finished 43rd at the Rio Paralympics in 2016 with four medals. At Tokyo 2020, the country won 19 medals - five gold, eight silver and six bronze - to finish 24th. The momentum continued at Paris 2024, where India achieved its best-ever Paralympic haul of 29 medals, including seven gold, nine silver and 13 bronze, to finish 18th. These results underline the progress made by Indiaâs para-athletes and have helped raise expectations ahead of the Aichi-Nagoya Games. Can India repeat its 100-medal achievement? Indiaâs record-breaking 108-medal performance at Hangzhou has naturally raised expectations ahead of the Aichi-Nagoya Games. However, the contingent this time comprises 166 athletes, compared with 309 at the previous edition. That represents a reduction of 143 athletes, or approximately 46%. The smaller squad makes a repeat of the previous tally a demanding target, but it does not diminish the significance of the opportunity before the contingent. Indiaâs able-bodied athletes also competed with a smaller contingent at the 2026 Asian Games, with the squad size falling from 661 in Hangzhou to 495 in Aichi-Nagoya. India finished with 85 medals (21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze) after winning 106 at the previous edition. The 21-medal decline came alongside a reduction of around 25% in the number of athletes. The comparison offers an interesting reference point, although it cannot be directly applied to the para contingent because the two competitions have different event structures, athlete profiles and medal opportunities. If the relationship between contingent size and medal output at the Asian Games were used purely as a mathematical illustration, the 46% reduction in Indiaâs para contingent could suggest a medal tally of around 68. Such a figure, however, would be only a theoretical estimate, not a reliable prediction of the outcome. A more encouraging perspective comes from Indiaâs own history at the Asian Para Games. The country won 72 medals with 211 athletes in 2018 before improving to 108 medals with 309 athletes in 2023. Those results demonstrate that medal conversion depends on far more than the size of the contingent. The quality and competitive experience of the athletes, their event specialisations and their ability to deliver on the day will all influence Indiaâs final tally. A smaller squad can still produce an impressive return if its members make the most of their medal opportunities. The Asian Para Games present a fresh opportunity for India to underline the breadth of its sporting progress. The countryâs para-athletes have steadily improved their medal totals, climbed the continental standings and carried that momentum onto the Paralympic stage. The immediate target will be to produce strong performances across the 10 disciplines and make the most of the opportunities available. A second consecutive 100-medal finish would be a landmark achievement, while another strong overall showing would further consolidate Indiaâs position among Asiaâs leading para-sport nations. The numbers suggest that matching Hangzhou will be challenging, but the bigger story is the remarkable journey that has taken India from 14 medals in 2010 to 108 in 2023. title: From personal battles to sporting glory: Punjabâs athletes at Para Asian Games 2026
text: Table Tennis player Shubham Wadhwa Shubham Wadhwa : From a Bedridden Life to the Table Tennis Table, a Dream to Win for India In 2016, a bike accident changed Shubham Wadhwaâs life in ways he could not have imagined. A spinal cord injury left the Ludhiana-born athlete paralysed below the chest and confined to bed for nearly three years. A national-level table tennis player during his school days, Wadhwa had stepped away from the sport to pursue modelling. The accident brought that chapter to an abrupt end, forcing him to rebuild his life from scratch. âFor three years, I was bedridden. Friends kept reminding me of table tennis. When I finally returned to the table in 2019-20, it gave me a new life,â he told TOI. With his familyâs support, Wadhwa began finding his footing again. A scholarship opportunity at Lovely Professional University (LPU) in 2018 opened another door, allowing him to pursue Computer Science Engineering. It was also where he discovered a renewed purpose in table tennis, this time as a para-athlete competing in the menâs Class 3 category. âAfter the accident, I had to start from zero. Table tennis gave me direction again,â he told TOI. What followed was a journey of rebuilding, having to constantly push himself each day. Now a 10-time national gold medallist, Wadhwa has carried his game onto the international stage. In 2026, he won a gold and two bronze medals at the ITTF World Para Future in Gold Coast, followed by silver in mixed doubles and bronze in menâs singles at the ITTF World Para Elite in Taipei City. Away from the table, he has also revisited wheelchair modelling, an interest he developed during his university years. At the Asian Para Games 2026 in Japan, Wadhwa is making his debut, competing in singles, doubles and mixed doubles. âFor me, spending three years bedridden, now the goal is to win a medal for India.â From fighting her own battles to lifting Indiaâs hopes: Jaspreet Kaur For Jaspreet Kaur, 32, from Bathinda, the road to international para-powerlifting began with a warning that forced her to rethink her life. Having contracted polio at the age of three, she went on to complete an MTech and work as a software engineer. But long hours at a desk saw her weight climb to nearly 80kg, putting increasing strain on her body. Determined to reclaim her health, she left her job, joined a gym and discovered a sport that would change her direction. âI discovered para-sports while trying to lose weight,â she recalls. In 2021, learning about powerlifter Rajinder Singh Rahelu deepened her interest in the sport. What began as an effort to regain her health soon became a pursuit of excellence. After shedding nearly 40kg in 18 months, Jaspreet turned her focus to powerlifting, training in Gandhinagar, Gujarat, in the 45kg category. Her progress has since translated into medals and records. She won gold at the Khelo India Para Games 2025, setting a national record with a lift of 101kg, and claimed bronze at the Asia-Oceania Open Championships in Bangkok in 2026. She also won silver at the Brazil Open Para-Powerlifting Championship and represented India at the 2026 Commonwealth Games. The journey, however, has not been measured only in kilograms lifted. Travelling alone, particularly by train, once meant dealing with physical difficulties, stares and social stigma. âEarlier, travelling alone, especially by train, was physically tough. The stares and social stigma hurt, but sports has lifted my confidence, it has built my confidenceâ she told TOI. Her decision to leave UPSC preparation initially worried her parents, but their concern has since turned to pride. â Itâs a journey I have consciously chosen every day,â she told TOI. Now for her second Asian Para Games outing, Jaspreet says her preparation has been good. She is eyeing a medal, hoping to deliver her personal best and make India proud. Once stopped from pursuing sports to making her mark: Seema Rani For 40-year-old Seema Rani, the road to para-powerlifting began with a life that had already demanded more of her than most. A fever when she was three, followed by an injection that affected both her legs, left her with a 79 percent disability and dependent on a wheelchair. Growing up in Haripur Khalsa, she had spent most of her life within the familiar boundaries of home, in a joint family where stepping out on her own was not something she had known. Her father a labourer and mother a housewife. When Seema first expressed an interest in sport, her family was reluctant to let her pursue it. âFor someone who had rarely left home, the prospect of training and competing meant challenging not just physical limitations, but years of hesitation and uncertainty,â she told TOI. When Parmjeet Kumar , a para-powerlifter from her village, was welcomed back with the entire village celebrating his historic medal at the World Championship, that is what ignited a spark in her. In 2019 she began practising but it was only in 2022 when she was selected to train at the SAI centre in Gandhinagar, under the guidance of coach Rajinder Singh Rahelu, that she began her formal career. In 2025, Womenâs elite 61 kg category, Seema had made a national record in Khelo India Para Games, lifting 97kgs. Now, Seema is looking ahead, determined to improve with every competition. Her ambition is to keep pushing her limits and work towards the biggest stage in sport. She told TOI, â I believe in my preparation and all I want to do is perform better than ever.â Parmjeet Kumar: From a Village Gym to the World Stage, Chasing a Paralympic Dream For Parmjeet Kumar, 34, the journey to international para-powerlifting began with curiosity. Growing up in Haripur Khalsa in Punjab , he had little access to sporting facilities. But in 2004, a gym set up in a local haveli caught his attention. He would watch with interest, unaware that the weights inside would one day become his livelihood and his identity. Born with a disability after an injection administered during a fever when he was two, Parmjeet has both legs affected. His introduction to powerlifting was far from easy. The first time he tried lifting a 20kg bar, he struggled to raise it, with balance posing another challenge. Today, he has lifted 177kg at the Asia-Oceanic Championship in Bangkok, where he won silver in April. His journey has been shaped by years of discipline and the guidance of coach Rajinder Singh Rahelu, under whom he trained for nearly a decade. From Gandhinagar to Delhiâs Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium, Parmjeet has spent years building his strength. âInspiration is for a short time. Discipline is what is most needed. Motivation does not last long, but routine does,â he told TOI, is the philosophy he lives by. In 2021 Parmjeet made history after lifting 158 kgs securing bronze, becoming the first Indian to clinch a medal in the World Para Powerlifting Championships. After finishing fourth at the 2023 Asian Para Games, Parmjeet has continued to push forward. He competed at the Paris Paralympics in 2024 but suffered a hand injury. He recently represented India at the CWG 2026. Parmjeet is determined to give his best. His goal is simple, âimprove on my previous performance and change the colour of his medalâ, he told TOI. Mohd Yasser : 3rd Asian games outing, Chasing Olympic Dream For Mohd Yasser, 32, the journey from the fields of Malerkotla to the international athletics arena has been shaped by family support and the determination to keep going, even when setbacks derailed his ambitions. Yasser, who hails from Malerkotla in Punjab, suffered an impairment in his left hand at the age of eight. Growing up in a farming family, he had the unwavering support of his parents, who stood by him as he found his footing in sport. Athletics entered his life during his college days, when he participated in a meet in Malerkotla. It was there that coach Harminderpal Singh Ghuman spotted him, opening the door to a career he had not initially envisioned. The shot-putter gradually made his mark on the international stage. At the 2018 Asian Para Games in Jakarta, Yasser won bronze in the F46 category, establishing himself as a competitor to watch. He added another milestone at the World Para Athletics Grand Prix in Dubai in 2021, winning gold with a throw of 14.58m. But the journey has not been without its disappointments. At the 2023 Asian Para Games, an injury prevented him from delivering the performance he had hoped for. He went on to represent India at the Paris Paralympics, gaining further experience on the sportâs biggest stage. Now preparing for his third Asian Para Games outing, Yasser is focused on making the opportunity count. With his parents continuing to support him, he hopes to deliver his best performance and take another step towards his Olympic dream. title: Asian Para Games: Kokila assures India of judo medal, sets up gold-medal clash
text: Kokila assures India of judo medal (Image - X) Indiaâs Kokila secured a medal in para-judo at the Asian Para Games on Monday after defeating Chinaâs Yi Liu in the semifinals of the womenâs J2 -52kg category. The visually impaired judoka edged past her Chinese opponent 1-0 at the Aichi Prefectural Martial Arts Hall to book her place in the final, where she will compete for gold against Kyrgyzstanâs Aibike Ulanbek Kyzy later in the day. Kokila registered one waza-ari, the second-highest technical score in judo, and one yuko for an effective technique during the semifinal. Liu also managed one waza-ari, while the Indian received a shido penalty for a minor rule infringement. The result guarantees Kokila at least a silver medal, improving on her performance at the previous edition in Hangzhou, where she won bronze in the -48kg category. Hailing from Kasun village in Haryanaâs Jind district, Kokila was also part of Indiaâs campaign at the Paris 2024 Paralympics. The J2 classification is for judokas with varying degrees of visual impairment. Kapil Parmar to fight for bronze Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Indiaâs Kapil Parmar, meanwhile, will compete for bronze in the menâs J1 -70kg category after losing his semifinal against Indonesiaâs Junaedi by a score of 0-1. Parmar will face another Indonesian, Ahnaf Rafli Shidqi, in the bronze-medal playoff later on Monday. The J1 category is for athletes with severe visual impairments, ranging from total blindness to minimal light perception. Sheetal Devi equals world record in archery Earlier on Monday, Indiaâs para-archer Sheetal Devi delivered another standout performance, equalling the world record in the womenâs compound archery ranking round. Competing at the Okazaki Chuo Sogo Park Multipurpose Square, Sheetal scored 704 points out of a possible 720 to match the world record jointly held by Turkeyâs Oznur Cure. The record-equalling effort added to Indiaâs encouraging start at the 2026 Asian Para Games, with athletes making their mark across multiple disciplines. title: Para Asian Games 2026: Mona Agarwal storms back from sixth to win gold, Avani Lekhara takes silver
text: Mona Agarwal (Image credit: X) Mona Agarwal began the final as the top qualifier. A few rounds later, she was in sixth place, while compatriot Avani Lekhara had taken the lead. Then the standings began to shift. As the elimination rounds unfolded, Mona worked her way back into contention. By the final shot, she held a narrow lead. Mona scored 10.8. Avani followed with 10.5. The difference across the final was 0.4 points: Mona finished with 250, a Games record, while Avani took silver with 249.6. South Koreaâs Lee Yunri won bronze with 227.9. âI kept faith in the process, stayed relaxed and continued to trust myself,â Mona said. âI donât quit when the chips are down. Instead, I try to regain control of the situation and make up for lost ground.â This was a different ending from Monaâs last Asian Para Games final. She finished sixth in Hangzhou in 2022 and later said she had learned from the experience. Her route into shooting was itself a series of turns: she won gold in para-athletics throwing events, pursued powerlifting and captained Rajasthanâs womenâs sitting volleyball team to a national championship in 2019. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines She took up rifle shooting in Dec 2021 and won bronze at the Paris Paralympics in 2024. Mona has said that a reaction to polio drops affected both her legs. She has also balanced training with raising two children and studying for a masterâs degree in psychology. She dedicated Mondayâs gold to her mother-in-law, who cared for the children while she competed. âBecause of her, I was able to focus on my performance,â she said. For Avani, the silver adds another medal to a career that includes Paralympic golds at Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024. A wheelchair user since a car accident, she had arrived in Nagoya as the defending Asian Para Games champion. The one-two finish also secured a second quota place for India at the 2028 Los Angeles Paralympics, adding to the place Mona had earned at the World Shooting Para Sport Championships in Changwon last month. title: Asian Para Games 2026: Ayush Verma adds shot put gold to javelin bronze
text: Ayush Verma (Image credit: SAI) Indiaâs Ayush Verma won the gold medal in the menâs shot put F53 event at the Asian Para Games on Wednesday. Ayushâs best throw of 8.16m came in his fifth attempt and helped him finish first in the event. Iranâs Alireza Hemami won the silver medal with a throw of 8.09m. Kazakhstanâs Makhambet Serikkaliyev took bronze with 6.81m. Watch âThis medal means a lotâ: Lovlina Borgohain on Asian Games gold & Olympic ambitions Second medal for Ayush Ayush added a second medal to his tally at the Games. He had won bronze in the menâs javelin throw F53/F54 event on Tuesday. What is the F53 category? The F53 category is for athletes who have limited movement in their trunk and legs, while their hand grip is less affected. Athletes compete from a seated position and use their chest, upper back and shoulders to generate force for their throws. title: New guide, new glory! Simran storms to Games-record gold as Tejalben adds bronze at Asian Para Games
text: Simran (PTI Photo) NEW DELHI: India's Simran scripted a golden comeback at the Asian Para Games 2026, setting a new Games record to win the women's 200m T12 title with her new guide Shivam, while compatriot Tejalben Damor added a bronze to complete a memorable outing for the country on Tuesday. The 26-year-old Simran clocked 24.80 seconds to claim her maiden gold at the continental showpiece, finishing ahead of Iran's Hajar Safarzadeh, who took silver in 25.02 seconds. Tejalben, making her debut at the Asian Para Games, secured bronze with a time of 25.23 seconds. The T12 classification is for athletes with moderate visual impairment. Watch Suchika Tariyal on her Asian Games bronze, childhood trauma, and never giving up | TOISA Spotlight Simran shines with new guide after difficult transition A bronze medallist at the 2024 Paris Paralympics, Simran has been rebuilding her campaign with Shivam after her previous guide, Umar Saifi, was banned for a doping violation. She had won silver in the same event at the 2023 Hangzhou edition, making Tuesday's record-breaking performance a significant milestone in her comeback. Simran, however, admitted that fatigue and recovery issues had affected her preparations. Her personal Asian record of 24.46 seconds remained beyond reach, but she was delighted to secure the gold. "My body was not feeling good, in fact, it felt tight because the recovery has not been great. I was very tired after my heat race," she said. The sprinter also spoke about the challenge of finding suitable vegetarian food at the Games, adding with characteristic humour: "Otherwise, we Indians can run on willpower too." Simran will next compete in the women's 100m, an event in which she won silver at the previous edition. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Tejalben's bronze boosts confidence ahead of 400m Tejalben's podium finish provided another boost to India's medal campaign. The 24-year-old said her journey had been shaped by financial hardships faced by her family and that she had arrived with considerable determination. "My parents have struggled financially for most of their lives and I would even die to get a medal," she said. The bronze has strengthened her confidence ahead of the women's 400m, which she considers her strongest event. "My next race is 400m and that is my best event and this medal has given me a lot of confidence for that event," Tejalben added. With Simran's gold and Tejalben's bronze, India enjoyed a double-podium finish in the women's 200m T12, highlighting the country's growing strength in para-athletics.
