title: Perfect pairing? Why India must stick with Abhishek Sharma and Vaibhav Sooryavanshi
text: Abhishek Sharma and Vaibhav Sooryavanshi (BCCI Photo) With the T20I series against New Zealand already sealed, the pressure on India to pick the safest XI might have eased. Maybe the team management can focus on a more important question: what should Indiaâs batting order look like two years from now, when the 2028 T20 World Cup is held in Australia and New Zealand? Vaibhav Sooryavanshiâs explosive 45 off 19 balls in the third T20I in Wellington has added to Indiaâs selection headache. Itâs a happy problem. Handed an opportunity after Ishan Kishanâs injury, Sooryavanshi initially struggled at No. 3 in Christchurch as he batted outside the Powerplay. But when India pushed him up to open alongside Abhishek Sharma in Wellington, the 15-year-old was back at his belligerent best. He smashed the first ball to the boundary and never looked back. Watch Bhuvneshwar Kumar press conference: Abhishek Sharma's fearless batting, T20 mindset and more While Abhishekâs century was the headline act, Sooryavanshiâs fearless approach set the tone. The pair raced to a stunning 133-run stand in just seven overs, blowing New Zealand away. The Abhishek-Sooryavanshi partnership also offered a glimpse into the mindset of a new generation of T20 batters, one that sees every ball as a scoring opportunity. The innings also carried a significant subplot. To accommodate Sooryavanshi at the top, Sanju Samson willingly moved down to No. 3 despite enjoying tremendous success as opener. Since returning to the side midway through the T20 World Cup, Samson has formed one of Indiaâs most productive opening partnerships alongside Abhishek. Together, they have scored 1,166 runs in 37 matches and become permanent fixtures at the top of the order. Abhishek was quick to acknowledge the sacrifice. âThe way Sanju bhai batted in the last game, it is not easy to let go of oneâs familiar batting position. That showed his character. Someoneâs going for his position but everyone is selfless and happy for each other, which is the hallmark of a great team,â he said in a BCCI video. The comment revealed an increasingly important characteristic of this Indian side. Unlike previous eras where players were tied to specific positions, this Indian team, under coach Gautam Gambhir , appears willing to embrace flexibility if it benefits the larger cause. That larger cause may now involve finding out just how good a Vaibhav-Abhishek opening pair can become. The youngster himself admitted that batting at No. 3 in Christchurch had forced him away from his natural game. âLast match, I went against my grain as to how I play in T20s. This game, I wanted to give a quick start so that it becomes easy,â Sooryavanshi said. His Wellington knock backed up that assessment. As an opener, there was visible clarity in his approach. He did not have to assess conditions or pace an innings. It was just all out attack. Abhishek, too, felt the impact from the other end. âWhen Vaibhav hit the first ball, he showed aggression. I saw that at the nonstrikerâs end and when you see such a shot, you also feel pumped up. Special mention and credit to Vaibhav for how he played,â Abhishek said. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines The challenge now is fitting everyone into the same side when India are back at full strength. Sooryavanshiâs emergence during IPL 2026 makes it increasingly difficult to keep him on the bench. Yet India already have established performers in Samson and Kishan. However, the debate need not be framed as Vaibhav versus Sanju or Vaibhav versus Kishan. Head coach Gautam Gambhir has repeatedly maintained that only the top two batting positions are fixed and the rest of the order remains flexible. Kishanâs adaptability strengthens that approach. His matchwinning 80 off 46 balls at No. 5 during the Asian Games semifinal vs Sri Lanka showed he can thrive even when he is kept away from the opening slot. It also provided a possible blueprint on how all four batters can feature in the playing XI. With the series result already decided, India can afford to think beyond just the next game. title: Asian Para Games: Mona Agarwal, Avani Lekhara secure one-two finish in 10m air rifle qualification
text: Avani Lekhara and Mona Agarwal Indiaâs Mona Agarwal and Avani Lekhara dominated the womenâs 10m Air Rifle Standing SH1 qualification at the 2026 Asian Para Games in Nagoya on Monday, finishing first and second respectively to put themselves in a strong position ahead of the final. Agarwal topped the standings with 629.1 points from six series, setting a new Asian Para Games qualification record and breaking the previous mark held by Chinaâs Zhang Cuiping. The Indian shooter narrowly missed out on the world record of 629.4 points, which is jointly held by compatriot Lekhara and Slovakiaâs Veronika Vadovicova. Lekhara secured second place with 626.4 points, completing a one-two finish for India in the qualification round. With both shooters advancing in impressive form, India will now look to translate the strong showing into two medals in the final. The result also brought together two of Indiaâs established names in para shooting. Avani and Mona had won gold and bronze medals respectively at the 2024 Paris Paralympics. India also qualified two shooters for the menâs 10m Air Rifle Standing SH1 final. Rakesh Nidagundi finished seventh with 619.3 points, while Swaroop Unhalkar claimed the eighth and final qualifying position with 617.4 points. Anandha Krishnan, however, missed out on the final after finishing 13th with a score of 605.2. title: Drawn in same group, India-Pakistan set to clash on November 22 in Rising Asia Cup
text: India's and Pakistan's fans carry their national flags as they wait for the Asia Cup cricket final between India and Pakistan to begin at Dubai International Cricket Stadium, United Arab Emirates, Sunday, Sept. 28, 2025. (AP File Photo) The Asian Cricket Council (ACC) has announced the schedule for the 2026 Rising Asia Cup in Doha, with India A and Pakistan A drawn in the same group alongside Nepal and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The two sides will face each other on November 22 at the West End Park International Cricket Stadium. India A will open their campaign against Nepal on November 20 before taking on Pakistan A two days later. They will play their final group-stage match against the UAE on November 24. Rising Asia Cup 2026: Groups and format Eight teams have been divided into two groups for the tournament. Group A features Sri Lanka A, Bangladesh A, Afghanistan A and Hong Kong, China, while Group B comprises India A, Pakistan A, Nepal and the UAE. Each team will play the other three sides in its group in a single round-robin format. The top two teams from each group will advance to the semi-finals, scheduled for November 26 and 27. The final will be played on November 29. Teams generally field their 'A' sides in the Rising Asia Cup. In the 2025 edition, Jitesh Sharma captained India A, with Vaibhav Sooryavanshi also part of the squad. The West End Park International Cricket Stadium will host most of the tournament's matches, including the final. The remaining games will be played at the University of Doha for Science and Technology (UDST) Cricket Ground, which will host the opening match on November 19. How India A fared in the 2025 Rising Asia Cup India A began their 2025 campaign with a 148-run win over the UAE in their opening Group B match in Doha. title: Election of IOA Athletesâ Commission: 9 sports, 10 seats and uneven representation
text: PV Sindhu is in the fray for one of the ten elected positions in the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) Athletesâ Commission NEW DELHI: With 12 athletes from nine sports in the fray for 10 elected positions in the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) Athletesâ Commission, the application of a key provision in the election rules has emerged as an important consideration -- how to ensure maximum representation of different sports in the Commission. Rule 8.6 of the IOA Athletesâ Commission Rules, 2026 states that, âas far as practicableâ, the composition of the Commission should seek âmaximum representation from all sports affiliated with IOAâ. It adds that, as a guiding principle, âan endeavour shall be made to ensure that there is not more than one Athlete from any one particular sportâ. Watch Harita Bhadra Exclusive | 2 Asian Games Medals, Now the 22.45s World Championships Chase The provision assumes significance in the ongoing election, with the draft list of nominations showing candidates from nine sports competing for 10 positions â five male and five female. The 12 nominees are Manjeet Singh (kayaking and canoeing), Swapnil Suresh Kusale (shooting), Harmanpreet Singh (hockey), Sajan Prakash (swimming), Kidambi Srikanth (badminton) and Tajinderpal Singh Toor (athletics) in the male category. The female nominees are PV Sindhu (badminton), Salima Tete (hockey), Mirabai Chanu (weightlifting), L Bombayla Devi (archery), Sudha Singh (athletics) and Bhavani Devi (fencing). Athletics, badminton and hockey have candidates in both the male and female categories. The remaining six sports have one nominee each. An opportunity to maximise diversity The current nomination pattern presents an opportunity to give representation to all nine sports in the 10-member Commission, with one sport having two representatives. Such a composition would align with the guiding principle under Rule 8.6, provided the mandatory eligibility and category requirements are met and the outcome is consistent with the prescribed election process. The provision does not, however, establish a separate quota for each sport or specify which sport should have two representatives. Nor does it expressly authorise the Electoral Officer (Returning Officer) to override the election outcome to achieve a preferred composition. Instead, the wording places emphasis on what is practicable and calls for an endeavour to avoid multiple representatives from the same sport. Mandatory requirements remain central The Rules also prescribe specific requirements for the Commissionâs composition. Under Rule 8.1, the 10 elected members must comprise five male and five female athletes. Rule 8.2 provides that six of the elected members must have participated in at least one of the last three editions of the Olympic Games. Rule 8.3 specifies that these six must include three male and three female athletes. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines The remaining four members, under Rule 8.5, must feature two male and two female athletes who have won at least one medal in any of the last three editions of the Asian Games, Commonwealth Games, World Championship/Cup or National Games. Rule 8.4 further states that, as far as practicable, the Olympic-category composition should include at least one athlete from an individual sport and at least one from a team sport. The final composition must give effect to these requirements alongside the guiding principle of maximum sporting representation. Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

title: From sleeping on Mumbaiâs streets to building Indiaâs esports future: Santanu Basuâs journey
text: In 2007, competitive gaming in India had no leagues, few sponsors and very few paid players. Tournaments came and went. Players paid their own way to reach them, and most quit when the money ran out. That year, a young football gamer arrived in Mumbai for a national qualifier with barely enough money for the trip. He had travelled part of the way in a train's toilet compartment. He couldn't afford a room, so he slept on the city's streets. Then he finished third. That player was Santanu Basu, and the event was the World Cyber Games India qualifiers. The result earned him a job and a sponsorship with a gaming company, which was rare for Indian gamers at the time. It also began a career that has now run for almost two decades. Over the next decade, Basu built one of the longer competitive careers in Indian football gaming. He represented India in FIFA tournaments abroad, with third-place finishes in China, France and Malaysia. He signed with US-based esports organisation Tempo Storm as its only Indian player, and stayed for seven years. AMD named him its first gaming brand ambassador in India, and Sony PlayStation made a documentary on his life. Alongside competing, he started building for others. Basu has organised or taken part in more than 500 college events, from Mizoram to Chennai. In 2013, he launched the Asian Football Gaming Championship (AFGC), which has since sent more than 27 Indian players to compete abroad*. In 2018, he founded LetsGameNow (LGN). The company started with football gaming events, then expanded to other titles and began developing its own mini-games. The move from player to organiser changed the job. Instead of preparing for his own matches, Basu was building teams, running events and finding partners. His years as a competitor gave him a clear brief: players need access, exposure, regular competition and a credible route to international events. Watch #PlayStationGamerTales | Two Ends -  How gaming can change your life His latest project is the most ambitious. The Indian Super Gaming League (ISGL) was launched in 2026 as a franchise-based national esports league 1 . Eight teams compete across five titles: FC 26, Cricket 26, Call of Duty: Mobile, chess and table tennis. Teams include Indian Super League clubs Mumbai City FC, Kerala Blasters FC, Chennaiyin FC and FC Goa, and Pro Kabaddi side Puneri Paltan. The league runs city qualifiers to find new players, and has drawn investment from Anand Mahindra's family office. The early results are encouraging. Saransh, who played for Mumbai City FC in ISGL's first season, went on to represent India at the Esports World Cup in Paris. We spoke to Basu about what the league offers young players, and where he wants it to go. ISGL has permanent teams and seasons, not one-off tournaments. What does that mean for a young player? It gives them consistency, and a real scope for long-term career development. Players get to build teams and work as teams. Regular competitive matches mean regular practice, so skills keep improving. Most of all, it creates a structured ecosystem. Players can develop professional skills and build a reputation, which is what a sustainable career in competitive gaming needs. Saransh went from ISGL to the Esports World Cup in Paris. Can other players follow that route? Saransh's journey shows the opportunity the league creates for Indian talent: visibility, and access to bigger competitive platforms. Every player will have a different journey. But the league aims to create international opportunities for all its players. ISGL intends to build an ecosystem that identifies talent, nurtures it and gives it exposure to compete at the highest level. LetsGameNow has also built a game, Bharat Run. What is it, and what else is LGN working on? With Bharat Run , we want to create an educational and engaging experience that is deeply rooted in Indian identity and culture. More broadly, LGN is building a gaming and digital ecosystem that connects entertainment, technology, commerce and community. Our e-commerce platform will help gaming communities discover and access relevant products. Beyond tournaments, we want to develop original gaming experiences and create opportunities for talent. We see gaming as a platform for entertainment, innovation, learning and economic opportunity. Watch Bharat Run What is the bigger vision for ISGL? To build a world-class esports ecosystem in India. One that nurtures talent, creates global opportunities, and gives competitive gaming the professional recognition and sustainability of traditional sports. Starting your journey to compete on the streets of Mumbai, today you are building a national esports league. What does this journey mean to you? It reminds me of the extent to which Indian esports have come and how far it can go ahead. At one point of time, I fought for my own opportunity. So, today I want to build a system for the next generations where they can get the chance without having to fight this hard. After the decades of gaming experiences you had, what are the achievements you are most proud of and what according to you remains unfinished? Iâm most proud to move beyond competition and being able to create opportunities for others. From AFGC, to LGN and ISGL, my goal has always been bigger than just one player or one tournament. I think, the mission to make India a global esports powerhouse for talents to build long-term sustainable careers and compete internationally is yet unfinished but in progress. Where do you see the league in three years? As one of India's leading esports and gaming properties, recognised for its professional standards, its ability to develop talent, and its business model. We want a strong, loyal fan base and sustainable careers for players, coaches and other esports professionals. Above all, we want ISGL to be recognised as a pathway for Indian talent to reach international stages. For a player who once had to find his own way to a tournament, the aim now is to make that route easier for the next generation. title: Asian Para Games: Himanshu Nandal wins bronze, gives India second swimming medal
text: Himanshu Nandal NEW DELHI: Indian para-swimmer Himanshu Nandal clinched a bronze medal in the men's 400m freestyle S11 event at the Asian Para Games 2026 on Tuesday, securing India's second medal in swimming at the continental showpiece. The 22-year-old from Rohtak clocked 5 minutes and 10.91 seconds to finish third in the four-swimmer field. China's Chuanzhen Sun won gold with an Asian-record performance, while Japan's Uchu Tomita claimed silver. Nandal's podium finish added to India's growing medal tally in Nagoya and came a day after he narrowly missed out on a medal in the men's 100m backstroke S11 event, finishing fourth. Watch Suchika Tariyal on her Asian Games bronze, childhood trauma, and never giving up | TOISA Spotlight From judo to swimming , Nandal makes his mark Nandal, who has been blind since birth due to optic nerve failure, has taken a distinctive route to international para-swimming. A political science graduate from Delhi University 's Atma Ram Sanatan Dharma College, he initially pursued judo and won medals at the national level before switching to swimming in 2021. He competes in the S11 classification, which is for swimmers with near-total visual impairment. His bronze on Tuesday marked a significant achievement after his fourth-place finish in the backstroke event a day earlier. Budigina misses out after silver-medal success Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines India's Ravi Karthik Budigina also competed in the men's 400m freestyle, finishing outside the medal positions in the S13 category with a time of 5:41.70. Budigina had delivered India's first swimming medal of this edition on Monday, winning silver in the men's 100m freestyle S13 event with a time of 56.68 seconds. Uzbekistan's Egor Bolotov took gold in 52.90 seconds, while Kazakhstan's Viktor Volkov claimed bronze in 57.23 seconds. The S13 classification is for athletes with a vision impairment who have the least vision loss among eligible competitors in para-swimming. India add to their medal tally Nandal's bronze gave India another boost at the Asian Para Games, following Budigina's silver on Monday. India's para-swimmers will look to build on the early success as the competition continues in Aichi-Nagoya. The Indian contingent has so far won five gold, eight silver and 11 bronze medals, taking its overall tally to 24. title: Asian Para Games Medal Tally: Where does India stand after a bumper 11-medal haul on Day 1?
text: Javelin thrower Rinku and middle-distance runner Soumya celebrate after winning gold medals in their respective events. (Pic credit: X) NEW DELHI: India made a strong start to the Asian Para Games 2026, winning 11 medals, including four gold, five silver and two bronze, on the opening day to occupy fourth place in the overall standings on Monday. India's four gold medals came through shooter Mona Agarwal, long jumper Nishad Kumar, middle-distance runner Soumya and javelin thrower Rinku. The opening day also saw India register three 1-2 finishes, with compatriots sharing gold and silver in shooting, athletics and javelin. Hosts Japan were second with 27 medals, including eight gold, while Uzbekistan occupied third place with 23 medals, including six gold. India followed in fourth place with 11 medals, ahead of Kazakhstan, who had 14 medals, including three gold. South Korea and Iran also won three gold medals each to occupy sixth and seventh positions respectively. Thailand, Indonesia and Mongolia completed the top 10. Nishad Kumar won gold in the men's T47 long jump with an effort of 7.11m, while Soumya claimed the women's 1500m T12/T13 title in a personal-best 5:12.39. Venkatesh Radha took silver in the same event, completing India's second 1-2 finish. Rinku secured India's fourth gold in the men's F46 javelin throw with a season-best 65.11m. title: Asian Para Games: Simran, Praveen Kumar, Sachin Khilari shine as India's medal tally swells to 62
text: Simran, Praveen Kumar and Banti (PTI Photo) NEW DELHI: India enjoyed a memorable Day 3 at the Asian Para Games 2026, with its athletics contingent leading the charge with five gold medals among 18 podium finishes to help the country swell its overall medal tally to 62 and climb to fifth in the standings. Sprinter Simran, high-jumper Praveen Kumar and shot-putter Sachin Khilari set new Games records in their respective events, while Dilip Gavit and Ayush Verma also struck gold as Indian athletes dominated the track and field competitions in Aichi-Nagoya on Wednesday. Watch Suchika Tariyal on her Asian Games bronze, childhood trauma, and never giving up | TOISA Spotlight India's overall tally stood at 14 gold, 22 silver and 26 bronze medals, with athletics accounting for 13 gold, 14 silver and 15 bronze. Beyond athletics, India also added medals in para-archery, para-swimming and powerlifting, while the badminton contingent assured itself of further podium finishes. Simran's record-breaking double, Gavit and Praveen shine Simran was among India's standout performers, winning the women's 100m T12 gold in a Games-record time of 12.02 seconds. The visually impaired sprinter had also claimed the women's 200m T12 gold with a Games record on Tuesday, completing a memorable sprint double. She finished ahead of Iran's Hajar Safarzadeh, who clocked 12.30 seconds, while Indonesia's Made Ni Putri took bronze in 12.51 seconds. Dilip Gavit won the men's 100m T47 gold in 10.69 seconds, leading a one-two finish for India. Mohammed Morssinganakath Basil took silver in 10.72 seconds, a Games record, while China's Kangjun Shi secured bronze in 10.80 seconds. Praveen Kumar won gold in the men's high jump T44/64 event with a Games-record performance, while Sachin Khilari claimed the top spot in the men's shot put F46. Ayush Verma also won gold in the men's shot put F53 event. India collected four athletics silver medals in the morning session through Banti in the men's high jump T44/64, Bhagyashri Jadhav in the women's shot put F34, Mohd Yasser in the men's shot put F46 and Manjeet in the men's javelin F12/13. The bronze medallists included Anubhav Choudhary in the men's 100m T35, Parveen in the men's shot put F46 and Rakeshbhai Bhatt in the men's 100m T37. Preethi Pal adds second silver; athletics haul reaches 42 Preethi Pal continued her impressive campaign by winning silver in the women's 100m T35, adding to the silver she claimed in the 200m T35 on Tuesday. The double bronze medallist at the 2024 Paris Paralympics was among three Indian athletes to have won two medals at the Games so far. India's athletics contingent had accumulated 42 medals by Wednesday, keeping it on course for its ambitious target of winning medals in 60 of the 62 events it is contesting. Sheetal Devi, swimmers and powerlifter add to India's tally Armless compound archer Sheetal Devi and Payal Nag won silver in the women's doubles event after losing to China in the final. In para-swimming, visually impaired Ravi Kartik Budigina secured his second silver of the Games, finishing runner-up in the men's 100m backstroke S13 in 1:10.10. Himanshu Nandal also won his second medal, taking bronze in the men's 100m breaststroke S11 in 1:20.72. Powerlifter Kasthuri Rajamani claimed silver in the women's 67kg category, marking the biggest achievement of her career. In badminton, India's men's singles SL4 campaign was guaranteed at least three medals after defending champion Suhas L Y, Naveen Sivakumar and Abhijeet Sakhuja advanced to the semifinals. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines The SL4 classification covers athletes with moderate lower-limb impairments. Krishna Nagar and Sivarajan Solaimalai secured silver in the men's doubles SH6 category. With four pairs competing in a single group, medals were awarded according to the final group standings rather than through knockout matches. India builds momentum with more medals in sight India's strong showing across disciplines has strengthened its position in the overall standings, with athletics providing the biggest boost. The five gold medals won on Wednesday took the country's gold tally to 14, while the overall count reached 62. With more competition remaining before the event concludes on Saturday, India will look to build on its momentum and add to its medal haul across athletics, badminton, swimming and other disciplines. title: Asian Para Games: Why was Rakshitha Raju disqualified despite a faster time as Ravanni Valasanaini won bronze?

title: From selling vegetables to Commonwealth medal: Now Jhandu Kumar dreams of Asian Para  Games glory
text: Jhandu Kumar Kolkata: Not too long ago, Jhandu Kumar used to sell vegetables and drive an e-rickshaw to meet his own expenses and help run the family household. Today, the Bihar para-powerlifter is a Commonwealth Games bronze medallist, has secured a government job and is preparing to represent India at Asian Para Games. For Jhandu, who finished on the podium in the menâs heavyweight para-powerlifting event at the 2026 Commonwealth Games with a 190kg lift, the transformation still feels like a dream. âYes, absolutely. It feels like a dream. A boy from a village who worked hard is now making a name for himself across the country,â Jhandu told TOI from Aichi-Nagoya. âI cannot express how happy I am. Words fail me. Now I have another opportunity at the Asian Para Games to represent my country.â The athlete from Harnaut village in Biharâs Nalanda district will compete in the 72kg category on Tuesday. He continued his training for the Games at the National Centre of Excellence in Gandhinagar under coach Rajinder Singh Rahelu. More than making drastic changes to his training, he concentrated on strengthening the self-belief that has driven his rise. âThe basic approach remains the same. For me, it is about maintaining that inner drive and staying motivated. I have this determination within me: âI will do it, I will definitely succeed,ââ said the 29-year-old. âThat has been my main focus, to perform even better.â However, Jhandu knows there will be little margin for error in a competitive field. Asked what sort of lift could put him in medal contention, he said the numbers alone would not determine the outcome. âA medal could come at 200kg, 205kg or even 190kg. During competition, the mind works differently. You have to manage everything, and there is pressure,â he said. âYou have to handle that pressure, and then it depends on how your body responds and how much you can push yourself.â Irrespective of the numbers, Jhandu expects stiff competition and is relishing the challenge. âThere are many strong competitors. Lifter from China and Malaysia will be among them, apart from athletes from several other countries. Competition is inevitable. In fact, without competition, it would not be exciting,â Jhandu said. Despite all that he has achieved, Jhandu admits his journey still feels surreal. âHonestly, I never imagined that I would one day compete at Commonwealth Games or Asian Para Games. My focus was simply on working hard and winning a medal for my country,â he said. That hard work has paid off, and the medal in Glasgow did more than establish Jhandu on the international stage. It changed his life back home, too. The reception he received and the support from the Bihar govt, including a govt job, have given him even greater motivation to succeed. None of it, he believes, would have been possible without his familyâs support. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines âMy family has always been a huge source of motivation and support. They supported me even when I was selling vegetables and driving an e-rickshaw,â said the para-lifter, who was affected by polio at the age of five. âIt is difficult to put into words how much my family has done for me.â The Asian Para Games may be the immediate assignment, but Jhandu already has a bigger destination in mind. âMy main target is the Paralympics. I am determined to win a Paralympic medal for India,â he said. âI am prepared to put in whatever hard work is required.â For the boy from a small village in Bihar, the journey that once seemed unimaginable has only made him dream bigger. title: Indiaâs medal storm! 24 medals, five golds as Nishad Kumar, Deepthi Jeevanji shine at Asian Para Games
text: Nishad Kumar and Deepthi Jeevanji (PTI Photo) NEW DELHI: India produced a stunning medal rush on Day 2 of the Asian Para Games 2026, collecting 24 medals, including five golds, as athletics powered the country's campaign in Aichi-Nagoya on Tuesday. Nishad Kumar headlined the action with a second gold in as many days, while Deepthi Jeevanji reaffirmed her continental supremacy with a Games-record triumph. At the end of the day's competition, India occupied sixth place in the standings with 35 medals â nine gold, 11 silver and 15 bronze. Athletics accounted for 20 of India's medals so far, underlining its importance to the country's campaign. Alongside the established stars, emerging athletes also delivered encouraging performances, while archery and badminton provided further reasons for optimism by assuring India of more medals in the coming days. Watch Asian Games gold medallist Sujeet Kalkal on fatherâs influence and how he turned final around Nishad, Deepthi lead India's golden charge Nishad became only the third Indian to win two gold medals in a single edition of the Asian Para Games after adding the men's high jump T47 title to his long jump gold from Monday. The two-time Paralympic silver medallist cleared 2.04m to establish a new Games record. He joined Ankur Dhama and armless archer Sheetal Devi, who had each won two golds at the 2023 Hangzhou edition. Deepthi set the tone early, winning the women's 400m T20 title in a Games-record time of 56.36 seconds. The 23-year-old from Telangana, a former world champion and Paris Paralympics bronze medallist, secured her second consecutive Asian Para Games gold in the event. The golden run continued with Simran winning the women's 200m T12 title in a Games-record 24.80 seconds. Despite struggling with fatigue and limited vegetarian food options, the Paralympic bronze medallist delivered a commanding performance. Games debutant Tejalben Damor added bronze in the same event with a personal-best 25.23 seconds. Pranav Soorma claimed gold in the men's discus throw combined F51/52/53 event with an Asian-record effort of 11.66m, while compatriot Ram Ratan Singh took silver with 10.35m. Devender Kumar completed India's five-gold haul for the day by winning the men's discus throw F44/64 event. Shooting, powerlifting and swimming add to the haul India collected two medals in shooting, with Manish Narwal winning silver in the men's 10m air pistol SH1 event and Shrishti Arora taking bronze in the women's 10m air pistol SH1 competition. Narwal, a Paris 2024 Paralympics silver medallist, shot 233.7 in the final to finish behind South Korea's Jo Jeongdu. His performance also secured India a quota place for the Los Angeles 2028 Paralympics. India's shooting tally rose to four medals after two days, comprising one gold, two silver and one bronze. In powerlifting, Ashok Kumar Malik won silver in the men's 65kg category with a best lift of 192kg. The 37-year-old from Haryana improved on the bronze he won at the previous edition. Swimming contributed two more bronze medals. Himanshu Nandal, who was born blind due to optic nerve failure, clocked 5:10.91 to finish third in the men's 400m freestyle S11 event. Niranjan Mukundan followed with bronze in the men's 200m individual medley SM7, finishing in 2:57.01. Para table tennis also delivered a landmark performance. Ravi Baby Sahana and Prachi Pandey became the first Indian players to win medals in the standing category at the Asian Para Games. They were joined on the podium by Paralympics medallist Bhavina Patel, Sonalben Patel and Jehan Madan, taking India's haul to five bronze medals in the competition. Bhavina lost to China's Zhang Bian in the Class 4-5 semifinal, while Sonalben went down to South Korea's Jiyu Yoon in Class 3. Sahana lost to China's Mao Jingdian in Class 9, and Prachi was beaten by Iraq's Najlah Al-Dayyeni in Class 6. Archery assures five medals; badminton stars reach last four India's medal tally is set to grow further, with para archery assuring the country of at least five medals through finalists across individual, doubles and mixed-team events. Defending champion Sheetal Devi stormed into the women's compound final after defeating Japan's Shinohara Aya 145-137. Sheetal, who equalled the world record and set a new Asian record in qualification, will face Singapore's Alim Nur Syahidah for gold. Games debutant Swati Chaudhary also assured India of at least silver after beating South Korea's Eunhee Lee 6-2 in the women's W1 semifinal. India's women's compound doubles pair of Sheetal and Payal Nag defeated Thailand's Phannibha Srathongmaew and Wasana Khuthawisap 151-135 to reach the gold-medal match. Pooja and Bhawna advanced to the women's recurve doubles final with a 6-2 win over Iran's Mohadeseh Babahabib and Rahimi Ghahderijani Somayeh. Harvinder Singh and Vijay Sundi also progressed to the men's recurve doubles final after edging South Korea 5-4. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines The recurve mixed team of Harvinder and Bhawna defeated Thailand 6-0 to reach the semifinals, while Sheetal and Toman Kumar advanced in compound mixed team after beating Japan 154-147. Badminton also guaranteed India more medals. World champion Pramod Bhagat defeated Japan's Daisuke Fujihara 21-12, 21-10 to reach the men's singles SL3 semifinals, extending his record of podium finishes at the Para Asiad to five consecutive editions. He will face South Korea's Lee Seunghu on Thursday. Paralympic gold medallist Kumar Nitesh also advanced to the last four after beating compatriot Vikram Kumar 21-8, 21-8. He will meet Indonesia's Al Muh Imran in the semifinal. With five golds already secured on Tuesday and more medals assured in archery and badminton, India ended Day 2 with momentum firmly on their side as the campaign gathered pace in Aichi-Nagoya. title: Asian Para Games: Kokila wins silver in Judo after stunning reigning world champion in semifinals
text: Kokila secures silver (Agency Images) Indiaâs Kokila upgraded her bronze medal from the previous Asian Para Games to silver at the 2026 edition in Aichi-Nagoya, overcoming reigning world champion Yi Liu in the semifinals before falling to Kyrgyzstanâs Aibike Ulanbek Kyzy in the womenâs J2 -52kg final on Monday. The Indian judokaâs title hopes, however, ended abruptly as Ulanbek Kyzy secured an ippon in just 21 seconds at the Aichi Prefectural Martial Arts Hall to clinch gold. Watch Suchika Tariyal on her Asian Games bronze, childhood trauma, and never giving up | TOISA Spotlight Kokila stuns reigning world champion to reach final Kokila produced one of the standout performances of her campaign in the semifinals, defeating Chinaâs Liu to book her place in the gold-medal bout. The Indian registered a waza-ari and a yuko in a closely contested encounter, while Liu also scored a waza-ari. Kokila received a shido penalty for a minor rule infringement but held on to secure a memorable victory. However, she was unable to carry that momentum into the final, where Ulanbek Kyzy delivered a decisive finish almost immediately to deny the Indian a continental title. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Indian judoka improves on Hangzhou bronze Despite the disappointment of missing out on gold, Kokilaâs silver medal marks a step forward from her bronze in the womenâs -48kg category at the previous Asian Para Games in Hangzhou. Competing in the -52kg division this time, she progressed to the final and improved her medal standing at the continental event. A visually impaired judoka from Haryanaâs Jind district, Kokila has also represented India at the Paris 2024 Paralympics. She competes in the J2 classification, which accommodates judokas with varying degrees of visual impairment. Her victory over Liu, the reigning world champion, underlined her ability to challenge the leading names in international para-judo. Although the final proved a brief and difficult outing, Kokila leaves Aichi-Nagoya with silver and another significant milestone in her international career. title: No Sharath Kamal, no Nikhat Zareen: Major shake-up in IOA Athletesâ Commission
text: Sharath Kamal New Delhi: The Indian Olympic Associationâs (IOA) Athletesâ Commission is set for a change of guard, with former vice-chairperson Sharath Kamal and two-time World champion boxer Nikhat Zareen missing from the electoral list for the Nov 3 elections. The development also marks the end of Mary Kom âs tenure as chairperson, with neither of the two outgoing office-bearers in contention for the new commission. The elections for the 2026-30 term will precede the IOA Executive Council (EC) polls on Dec 5. The commissionâs chairperson and vice-chairperson have voting rights in the EC, making their positions significant in the Olympic bodyâs decision-making structure. Sharathâs absence stems from a technical issue with his nomination, sources familiar with the matter told TOI. The former India table tennis captain had submitted his application to contest as a Sportsperson of Merit, with the form routed through the ad-hoc committee currently administering the Table Tennis Federation of India (TTFI). Watch Tilak Varma on batting at No. 5 and 6: âI want to finish games for the countryâ The application, however, was rejected by the Returning Officer (RO) after it reportedly reached the electoral authority without the signature of the competent official in the ad-hoc committee. The election rules provide for rejection, without further notice, of incomplete or unsigned nomination forms. Sharath, who served as vice-chairperson in the outgoing commission, will consequently miss the race. His absence is particularly striking, given that he recently served as deputy chef-de-mission (CDM) at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games. The nomination process has also affected boxing. The names of Nikhat and Narendra Berwal, who recently won bronze at the Asian Games, were reportedly forwarded for consideration but were not accepted because the IOA does not recognise the Boxing Federation of India (BFI) as a member national sports federation. The BFI is currently not recognised by either the IOA or the sports ministry amid governance concerns and internal disputes. The TTFI, meanwhile, was suspended by the ministry over governance failures and administrative lapses. Mary Komâs name was not forwarded by the BFI. Sources said her reduced involvement in Indian boxing, business interests and television commitments were among the factors. The IOA was also reportedly unhappy after she initially accepted, then declined, the chef-de-mission (CDM) role for the Paris Olympics 2024. Six must have competed at one of the last three Olympic editions, while the remaining four must have won medals at specified major competitions, including the Asian Games, CWG, World Championships or National Games. While the RO is empowered to scrutinise nominations, the exclusions raise questions about ensuring athletes are not disadvantaged by administrative disputes involving their federations. title: I want to build on what I have achieved this year: Dhiraj Bommadevara
text: Pics: Sanjana Pulugurtha Dhiraj Bommadevara has had a year to remember. He won two gold medals at the Archery World Cup Stage 3 in Antalya, clinched the menâs individual recurve title at the Archery World Cup Final in Mexico and returned from the Asian Games with two silver medals. ââI still have a lot of room for improvement, but this yearâs achievements have really motivated me, and Iâm going to push myself even harder,â says the 25-year-old archer from Vijayawada. In a candid chat with Hyderabad Times, Dhiraj reflects on his breakthrough year, the sacrifices that shaped his journey, the lessons he has learnt from setbacks and his ambitions for Indian archery. Dhiraj and Kumkum Anil Mohod with their recurve mixed team silver at the Asian Games. Dhiraj also won silver in the menâs team event âI wanted gold, but Iâm happy with two silver medalsâ Reflecting on his performance at the recently concluded Asian Games in Japan, Dhiraj says, âCompared to the last Asian Games, where I won one silver medal, this time I came back with two silvers. Even though I wanted the gold, itâs okay, I have two medals.â He adds, âI have a lot of room for improvement, and I can push myself forward during my upcoming training days. The Asian Games medals are a motivation for that next step. â Young Dheeraj in 2006 âI took the positives from Paris Olympics and pushed myself furtherâ For Dhiraj, finishing fourth in the mixed team event at the Paris 2024 Olympics was a significant moment in his career, despite missing out on a medal. âFinishing fourth was still a positive result, as no Indian archer had ever achieved that position before. I took a lot of positives from that,â he says. However, the hard work did not immediately translate into results in 2025. âGoing into 2025, I did everything I needed to do behind the scenes. I really put in the hard work and did everything. But 2025 didnât bring me many results,â he adds. Despite not getting the results he had hoped for, Dhiraj continued to trust the process and remain consistent with his training. His perseverance has paid off, making 2026 a landmark year in his career. âWhen things werenât working out, I didnât give up on them. Thatâs why I think this year has been very special for me,â he says. âIndian archery is only moving forwardâ While Indian archery continues its pursuit of an Olympic medal, Dhiraj believes the teamâs progress over the years offers reason for optimism. He says the focus should be on measuring progress against past performances. âIf we compare Indian archery today with where it was in the past, weâre only moving forward,â he says. Pointing to recent milestones, Dhiraj highlights the teamâs achievements at the Asian Games. âIt was the first time an Indian woman won an individual gold medal in recurve archery. It was also the first time we won silver in the mixed event. During the qualification round at the Asian Games, I broke the previous record held by South Koreaâs Lee Woo Seok,â he says. âOf course, we havenât won that Olympic medal, but with every win and every learning experience, weâre moving towards that medal,â he adds. âSharing a team with international archers helps us improveâ Dhiraj also values the opportunity to learn from fellow archers. Competing in the franchise-based archery league in Hyderabad, he says, allows Indian archers, both established and emerging, to gain insights into the mindset and match-day approach of international competitors. âWhen a foreign archer is part of our team, we understand how they think during a match and approach different situations. We also learn how they analyse their performances, win or lose. These insights have helped us at several championships, where we went on to win titles,â he says. Following the conclusion of the tournament in Hyderabad, Dhiraj will return to the Army Sports Institute in Pune, where he trains, to focus on the next phase of his preparation. âThe next three months are all about preparation. We have some national tournaments and Iâll focus on my preparation for the next World Championships cycle,â he says. During the Asian Games in Japan âThere was a time I almost gave up archeryâ Behind Dhirajâs rise is a story of sacrifice and perseverance. Nearly a decade ago, his mother, Revathi, sold her jewellery to buy him a second-hand bow as the family struggled to afford his equipment. At 16, he came close to giving up archery amid financial difficulties. âIâm happy that I was able to go through all of it,â he says, adding, âIn 2017, when I was 16, my family had run out of everything. But somehow, both my parents stood by me, and my sponsors have helped me a lot. â - Biswajit Talukdar You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. title: IND vs NZ: Shreyas Iyer on verge of breaking Rohit Sharma's unique T20I captaincy record
text: Rohit Sharma, Shreyas Iyer Shreyas Iyer is closing in on a record held by Rohit Sharma and will have a chance to become India's highest run-scorer as T20I captain in a calendar year when the team faces New Zealand in the second match of the five-match series on Saturday (October 24) at Hagley Oval in Christchurch. Iyer, who took over as India's T20I captain from Suryakumar Yadav in June, has scored 632 runs in 22 matches as skipper this year. He needs 25 runs in Saturday's match to go past Rohit's tally of 656 runs, which the former India captain scored in 29 T20Is in 2022. Watch Sitanshu Kotak Press Conference: Update on Ishan Kishan, Vaibhav in Playing XI and more Rohit led India to the T20 World Cup title in 2024. However, the record for the most runs by a captain in T20Is in a calendar year belongs to Pakistan's Babar Azam , who scored 939 runs in 29 matches as skipper in 2021. Japan's Kendel Kadowaki-Fleming is second on the list, having scored 860 runs in 20 T20Is as captain in 2024. Iyer batted at No. 4 in India's series opener against New Zealand on Thursday and scored 42 off 28 balls during the chase of 226 runs. India won the match by four wickets. The Punjab Kings captain in the IPL also has a chance to break another record in T20 cricket this year. Iyer has scored 1,130 runs as captain across T20 matches in 2026. He needs 96 runs in Saturday's match to go past Babar's tally of 1,225 runs, which the Pakistan batter scored in 35 matches as captain in 2021. title: Injured Ishan Kishan ruled out of 2nd T20I, paves way for Vaibhav Sooryavanshi's return to playing XI
text: Ishan Kishan, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi (PTI Photo) India's teenage sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi could get another opportunity in the playing XI after wicketkeeper-batter Ishan Kishan was ruled out of the second T20I against New Zealand with a low-grade right adductor strain. The injury has opened up a selection question for India ahead of Saturday's encounter at Hagley Oval in Christchurch, with the team management weighing its options after a record-breaking chase in the series opener. Watch Glenn Phillips press conference: What went wrong for New Zealand, India batting and more The Board of Control for Cricket in India ( BCCI ) confirmed that Kishan sustained the injury during the first T20I. The BCCI medical team is monitoring his progress, but the wicketkeeper-batter will miss the second match as India look to extend their 1-0 lead in the five-match series. Sooryavanshi, who was part of India's squad but missed the opening match, is among the possible options to replace Kishan. The 15-year-old has already made his senior international debut and represented India at the 2026 Asian Games, where he was part of the gold-medal-winning men's cricket team. His inclusion against New Zealand would therefore mark a return to the playing XI. Finn Allen contributed 45 off 24 deliveries, while Bevon Jacobs added a brisk 31 off 16 as the hosts built a formidable total. India responded with an explosive opening partnership between Sanju Samson and Abhishek Sharma. title: Where India stands in Asian Para Games medal tally after 27-medal rush, including five golds
text: L-R: Sheetal Devi, Payal Nag; Mohd Yasser, Sachin Sarjerao Khilari, and Parveen NEW DELHI: India returned to the top five of the Asian Para Games medal standings after another bumper day on Wednesday, adding 27 medals, including five gold, to take their overall tally to 62 after three days of competition in Aichi-Nagoya. After slipping to sixth despite winning 24 medals on Day 2, India leapfrogged Iran to claim fifth place, with 14 gold, 22 silver and 26 bronze medals. Athletics once again led the charge, accounting for 18 medals on Wednesday, including five gold, as India crossed the 50-medal mark comfortably. China continued to dominate the continental event, crossing the 100-gold mark and taking their overall tally to 226. Their 107 gold medals alone were more than second-placed Japanâs overall count of 100, underlining the hostsâ commanding lead. Watch Asian Games gold medallist Sujeet Kalkal on fatherâs influence and how he turned final around India climb to fifth as China extend dominance Japan occupied second place with 100 medals, while Uzbekistan slipped to third despite having the same 29 gold medals as the hosts. Japanâs superior silver and bronze counts kept them ahead. South Korea remained fourth with 46 medals, including 15 gold. India, Thailand and Iran had 14 gold medals apiece, with silver counts determining their positions in the standings. Thailand moved to sixth, pushing Iran, who were fifth after the second day, down to seventh. Kazakhstan, Indonesia and Iraq completed the top 10 after the third day. Indiaâs 27-medal haul on Wednesday took their total from 35 after the first two days to 62. The five gold medals also brought the countryâs gold tally to 14, keeping India firmly in contention for a strong overall finish. ALSO READ: Simran, Praveen Kumar, Sachin Khilari shine as India's medal tally swells to 62 Athletics power India's medal rush Indiaâs athletics contingent delivered another outstanding performance, winning 18 medals, including five gold. Simran, Praveen Kumar and Sachin Khilari set new Games records, while Dilip Gavit and Ayush Verma also finished on top of the podium. Simran won the womenâs 100m T12 gold in a Games-record time of 12.02 seconds, adding to her 200m title from Tuesday. Praveen triumphed in the menâs high jump T44/64, while Sachin won the menâs shot put F46. Ayush claimed gold in the menâs shot put F53, and Gavit topped the menâs 100m T47 in 10.69 seconds. His compatriot Mohammed Morssinganakath Basil secured silver in 10.72 seconds. Athletics has now contributed 42 medals, including 13 gold, 14 silver and 15 bronze, making it the driving force behind Indiaâs campaign. Medals across archery, swimming, powerlifting and badminton Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines India also collected medals in other disciplines. Compound archers Sheetal Devi and Payal Nag won silver in womenâs doubles, while swimmer Ravi Kartik Budigina secured his second silver of the Games in the menâs 100m backstroke S13. Himanshu Nandal added a bronze in breaststroke, and powerlifter Kasthuri Rajamani won silver in the womenâs 67kg category. India were also assured of three medals in menâs singles SL4 badminton after defending champion Suhas LY, Naveen Sivakumar and Abhijeet Sakhuja advanced to the semifinals. title: âI got it late, but I got itâ: Told she was too old, Suchika Tariyal went from judo, kurash and ju-jitsu to Asian Games MMA bronze
text: Suchika Tariyal The gym where Suchika Tariyal trains is modest: a single floor, a makeshift mat, a cage and the equipment needed to prepare for mixed martial arts. It is owned by Vikas Dahiya, an MMA fighter himself. When Dahiya is out of town, the keys are with Tariyal and her husband, Kapil Hooda. The couple have become so invested in the place that it is more than a training facility. It is part of the routine around which they have organised their lives, with Kapil closely watching his wife's preparation and sharing the emotional highs and lows of her career. Watch Suchika Tariyal on her Asian Games bronze, childhood trauma, and never giving up | TOISA Spotlight For years, that routine was built around a goal that kept slipping out of reach. Tariyal moved from one combat sport to another, dealt with selection hurdles, and came close to walking away more than once. The medal she had chased since childhood finally arrived at 36, when she became India's first Asian Games medallist in MMA. âFor me, it's more than my life. Because I had a dream since childhood, which has come true today. I mean, I got it late, but I got it. I am very happy about it. I can't believe I have achieved it. I still can't believe it. But I feel like I have to do more. That's what's in my mind.â The bronze was a first for Indian MMA. Tariyal, though, was still thinking about the final she had missed. The semifinal against Singaporeâs Hui Hoon Teo went to an additional round and was decided by a weigh-in tiebreak. Tariyal was 700 grams heavier and missed the final. âBut I missed a gold medal. I was very sad. I had planned to win gold. But it did not happen. I am very sad about it.â The disappointment was familiar. Her sporting career had been marked by moments when she came close to a breakthrough, only for circumstances to push her towards another route. Judo had been her first sport, followed by kurash and ju-jitsu, before MMA gave her another chance at an Asian Games medal. Suchika Tariyal The medal also carried the memory of a time when she had considered walking away altogether. âI had a desire from my childhood, which I made my life and I didn't achieve - either Commonwealth or Asian Games or Olympics. I wanted to get a medal. I wanted people to know about my struggling life, or how I reached here, or how my family helped me reach here.â The girl who wanted to learn how to fight Tariyal grew up in Chhawla, near Najafgarh in Delhi, one of four sisters. Her introduction to combat sports came not from a dream of winning medals or building an international career, but from an experience that left her feeling vulnerable as a child. When she was around 12 and sporting a âboy cutâ, a barber at a salon touched her inappropriately. She returned home without telling her family what had happened, frightened and unsure how to process the incident. The experience stayed with her and eventually shaped her decision to learn how to fight back. âThe barber touched me wrongly. I felt very bad. I did not know what was going on. I did not know why this happened to me.â âI did not tell anyone. I did not tell my family. I did not want to go out. I did not want to play. I did not know what to do. I wanted to learn a fighting game, so that if this happens again, I can do it.â Her mother eventually enrolled her in judo. Tariyal had wanted to learn boxing, but she took to judo quickly. âI was crazy about it. I didn't want to study or do anything. I just wanted to play judo. I wanted to give my 100% in judo.â She became an eight-time national judo champion. She won silver at the 2018 Commonwealth Judo Championships, gold at the 2019 edition and gold at the 2019 South Asian Games. Tariyal spent 15 years in judo and tried to qualify for the Olympics, but the Covid-19 pandemic disrupted that pursuit. At the 2022 Commonwealth Games in Birmingham, she lost the bronze-medal bout in the final seconds. The route to the Asian Games through judo had also become difficult. Ranking requirements made selection challenging, so she turned to kurash, which offered another pathway. She trained for around a year and won the selection trials, but her name was not cleared for the 2023 Asian Games in Hangzhou until the final days before the competition. âDue to two federations, we were left behind. I didnât have my name on the list. At that time, Mr Anurag Thakur was the sports minister. He helped us a lot. He made us understand. He listened to us. I got my name in the last moment, but I didnât get enough training because we were running to get my name cleared.â She competed in kurash at Hangzhou but lost. Another sport, another beginning After leaving kurash, Tariyal took up ju-jitsu and became a world champion in 2024. But the achievement did not guarantee a clear path forward, with the sportâs recognition in India remaining an obstacle. MMA offered another route, giving her a fresh opportunity to pursue the Asian Games medal she had long wanted. Suchika Pooja Tomar and Himanshu Kaushik encouraged her to try the sport. Tomar is a trailblazer in Indian MMA: she became the first Indian woman to compete in the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) in June 2024, and the first Indian fighter to win a bout in the promotion. Kaushik also guided Tariyal towards the sport. Suchika MMA Tomar's presence is not limited to that early advice. She lives one floor above Tariyal and Kapil in their apartment complex on the outskirts of Gurugram. The proximity is part of the small circle around the fighter, a network of people who have encouraged her to continue when other routes have closed. Because of her judo background, she was comfortable with grappling but had to develop her striking. âI am a grappler. I have a judo background. It was difficult for me. I wanted to learn striking,â she said. She gradually worked on the new skills and that transition also opened a route into professional MMA. Tariyal signed a five-fight deal with BRAVE Combat Federation, making her promotional debut at BRAVE CF 92 in Bahrain in December 2024. The deal offered a way to continue competing professionally while she pursued the Asian Games pathway. Tariyal said she had completed two fights under the contract, with three remaining. Her judo background also shaped her choice of traditional MMA for the Asian Games, where the use of a gi (Judogi) and the emphasis on grappling and throws suited her strengths. Tariyal's career has involved repeated reinvention and each change required her to adapt her training and start again, often without the certainty that the new discipline would bring the medal she wanted. But the setbacks were not only about results or injuries. As she grew older, she began hearing a different kind of criticism: that she was too old to continue. When they stopped asking for help Kapil, who works in Manesar, had seen how much Tariyal had given to sport. By the time they married, she had a job and a home, but years of chasing a major medal had left her close to giving up. Kapil urged her to continue, even as the financial burden of keeping her career going grew. Suchika with her husband Kapil âMy husband had faith in me. I had given up. I was married and had a good job. I had a house and a husband. Then he believed in me, that I can do it. âI have seen you doing it,ââ Tariyal said. Keeping her career going cost money. She took unpaid leave from work to train and compete, while overseas camps and travel had to be paid for without any guarantee of a result. âHe spent from his pocket, took loans and he trained me. He sent me to Bali. I went there three-four times for two months. I have a job, and when I go for training, I go without pay. I don't get paid. Whatever I needed, he spent it.â Kapil approached people for financial help, but was repeatedly told that Tariyal was too old to continue. Eventually, he stopped asking and concentrated on doing what he could himself. Tariyal also looked for ways to find sponsors. During COVID-19, she appeared on reality television, hoping the exposure might help fund training and competition. âI thought if I do two-four events, I might get a sponsor,â she said. âIf I get a sponsor, I will do it.â However, she dislocated her elbow during one of the shows. The injury put her preparation for the 2022 Commonwealth Games at risk. Even though she recovered in time to compete, she decided not to return to reality shows until she had achieved her sporting goals. âI decided I won't go to such reality shows until I achieve. I have to focus on my work,â she said. The doubts about her age continued. Tariyal said she heard at training camps that she should step aside and give younger athletes a chance. âA lot of people meet me and say that you have become so old. You have become 30 years old. You canât play [the sport],â she said. âWe still get to hear in the camps that you are too old. You shouldn't play now. You should drop now. You should give a chance to the youth ahead. So, I have heard this many times.â Her response was to keep competing. âAs long as my body is working or I want to play, I can play. And you have seen that I have won a medal,â she said. âThe more demotivating people I met in my life, the more motivated I got.â When she moved into MMA, Tariyal said, the federation - MMA-SFI (Mixed Martial Arts Sports Federation of India) - helped with training, food and other requirements and allowed her to use its gym without monthly fees. âI haven't seen such a federation,â she said. She credits Kapil with helping her stay in sport long enough to reach the Asian Games podium. âI would like to thank him. That's why I reached here. It was his dream, which I fulfilled.â The 700 grams At Aichi-Nagoya, the pressure of the opening bout was clear to Tariyal. She admitted to her coach that she was scared, only for him to tell her that he felt the same way, but believed she would do well. âI was very nervous at that time. I told my coach that I was scared. He said, âIt's fair. You are scared, so you are telling the truth.â I said, âYes, I am scared.â He said, âIt's okay, I am scared too. But you will do well. I know you have worked very hard.ââ Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines She focused on winning the quarterfinal and securing a medal. âI had a belief that I have to win this round. Only then I will be able to secure a medal. I played all out. I don't know how I performed in the first round. I was very disturbed. Will my body work or not? What kind of performance will come? I played and I won. I was very happy.â Suchika first Indian athlete to win an Asian Games medal in Mixed Martial Arts (MMA) The win assured her of bronze. The semifinal tiebreak kept her out of the final by 700 grams. At 36, Tariyal had finally won the Asian Games medal she had wanted since childhood. For now, Tariyalâs focus shifts to the World Championships in November. She will travel to Mumbai to prepare for the event, while the two remaining bouts on her BRAVE Combat Federation contract remain on the back burner. title: Rakesh Nidagundi designs his destiny from graphics to Asian Para Games
text: Rakesh Nidagundi PUNE: Destiny works in mysterious ways. With his legs affected by polio since childhood, Hubballiâs Rakesh Nidagundi, thought a career in graphic design, would suit him better. Until 2017, he had no idea that it would only open doors to bigger opportunities and a sporting life that he had never thought of. Watch Class topper, wooden gun, Nano rides: How Shapath Bharadwaj reached the Asian Games On Wednesday, the Karnataka shooter, 38, will travel to Japan for the Asian Para Games, his first multi-sport event since he started shooting in 2021. âI am very excited and prepared for the Asian Para Games. I have worked hard for this, and I am hoping to do well,â the rifle shooter told TOI. The Karnataka shooter will participate in the 10m air rifle SH1 category at the Aichi-Nagoya Games. Shooting happened to Rakesh by chance. While at his office, he got an order to design a creative publishing material for a shooting academy in Hubballi. âThat was the first time I got to know about shooting. The coach at the academy, Ravichandra Balehosur, asked me to visit his academy and try out the sport," Rakesh, who now trains and is sponsored by the Vijayi Bharat Foundation in Ahmedabad, said. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines âI didnât think of trying the sport then, but during the Covid-19 lockdown in 2020, I had no work, so I decided to try it once the lockdown was relaxed. I fell in love with the sport and started competing in 2021,â Rakesh said. After he started competing, his life changed after he won medals at the Khelo India Games. âI was supported by the government through the National Centre of Excellence and VBF also came forward to help me. Since then, I have been improving consistently and have won medals at the World level,â said the shooter, who won silver at the World Shooting Para Sport (WSPS) in Changwon, last month. title: 'India-Pakistan flavour will be missed': Suraj Karkera on rivals' withdrawal from Asian Champions Trophy
text: Suraj Karkera reacts to Pakistan's ACT withdrawal (Image: Instagram/ @surajkarkera7) The absence of an India-Pakistan clash may take away some of the intensity and excitement from the upcoming Asian Champions Trophy (ACT) Punjab 2026, but defending champions India remain focused on retaining their title, goalkeeper Suraj Karkera has said. With Pakistan withdrawing from the continental tournament and Bangladesh stepping in as their replacement, the Indian team will turn its attention towards continuing its dominance in Asian hockey. Pakistan's withdrawal leaves India-Pakistan rivalry on the sidelines Pakistan's withdrawal has ruled out a potential India-Pakistan showdown at the Asian Champions Trophy, scheduled to be held from October 27 to November 5 across Jalandhar and Mohali in Punjab. Bangladesh have replaced Pakistan in the six-team tournament after the Pakistan Hockey Federation's participation remained subject to government clearance. PHF president Mohyuddin Ahmed Wani had earlier indicated that the federation would follow the government's decision regarding the team's proposed visit to India. India and Pakistan share one of the most intense rivalries in international hockey, with their encounters traditionally drawing considerable attention from fans. However, the recent head-to-head record has heavily favoured India. In their last 20 meetings since 2016, India have won 18 matches, while the remaining two ended in draws. Pakistan are yet to register a victory during that period. Their most recent encounter came in the semifinal of the 2026 Asian Games, where India edged Pakistan 4-3. 'India-Pakistan flavour will be missed' - Karkera Karkera acknowledged that fans would miss the fierce rivalry between the two neighbours, but stressed that players have little control over decisions surrounding participation in international tournaments. The Indian team, he added, would concentrate on performing to the best of its ability. âThey are a good team, and athletes never want to pull out of a tournament, but these are things beyond our control. We're just there to go and perform to the best of our ability, and I think the result will take care of itself. The India-Pakistan flavour will be missed by the people, but it is something that is way beyond our say,â Karkera told ANI. The Indian goalkeeper was speaking on the sidelines of a felicitation ceremony where Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth interacted with and felicitated Indian Army sportspersons who participated in the 2026 Asian Games. India aim to defend Asian Champions Trophy title With Pakistan out of the tournament, the competition will feature India, Malaysia, Japan, South Korea, China and Bangladesh. India will enter as defending champions, reigning Asian Games gold medallists and the highest-ranked team in the field. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines The Indian men's hockey team arrives in Punjab on the back of another successful Asian Games campaign in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, where it successfully defended its gold medal with a commanding 5-1 victory over Malaysia in the final. The triumph marked India's fifth men's hockey gold at the Asian Games, following their victories in 1966, 1998, 2014 and 2022. It also marked a historic edition for Indian hockey, as both the men's and women's teams won gold medals at the same Asian Games for the first time. India, five-time winners of the Asian Champions Trophy, will now look to carry that momentum into the continental competition and strengthen their position among Asia's leading hockey nations. title: When R Madhavan said son Vedaant was still far from the Olympics, revealed how he taught him the difference between success, fame and popularity: âIt is wrong to compare kidsâ
text: Actor R Madhavan's son Vedaant is an athlete and quite popular, however, the actor has always made sure to keep him grounded with reality checks time and again. The actor also acknowledged that Vedaant receives considerable media attention because of his celebrity status, something both father and son are conscious of. Vedaant is a swimmer and has often represented India at several global platforms. He was recently a part of Asian Games 2026 and competed in the men's 4x200m freestyle relay, the 200m freestyle, and the 200m backstroke. However, in an interview few years back, Madhavan had revealed how he is still far from Olympics. âHis achievements are good but he is nowhere close to the Olympics,â Madhavan said in an earlier interview with Lallantop Cinema. âBecause he is my son, he is getting a lot of attention, which both of us realise. He realises it, so he is keeping his head low.â Watch R Madhavan Reacts To Padma Shri Win, Says The Honour Will Shape His Choices Going Forward The actor also recalled advising Vedaant to understand the difference between sporting success and the attention that comes with it. He said he wanted his son to remain grounded after winning a medal at an international competition brought him into the spotlight. âI am more of a philosophical friend, less of his father,â Madhavan said. âFor example, he won a medal and he got very popular. So I explained it to him that there is a huge difference between success, fame and popularity. Donât consider fame and popularity to be yours, because at his age it is very easy to confuse each thing. You still have a long way to go for success.â Madhavan also spoke against the tendency to compare celebrity children, pointing out how such comparisons can affect young people who are still finding their feet. He believes children should be allowed to grow at their own pace instead of being judged against their peers based on their appearance, career choices or early accomplishments. âI believe it is wrong to compare kids between each other. It breaks their hearts. It feels very wrong,â Madhavan said. âYou canât just put kids of the same age in a mould and compare, saying theyâll become successful or not. Star kids are kids after all. It is very important to protect and safeguard them. My family doesnât like these comparisons. We donât engage with it or encourage it.â Born in 2006, Vedaant is the son of R Madhavan and his wife, Sarita Birje. He began training in competitive swimming at a young age and has represented India at several international junior-level competitions. In 2022, when he was 16, Vedaant won a silver medal in the 800m freestyle at the Danish Open in Copenhagen, bringing him considerable attention across the country. Madhavan has previously spoken about the familyâs decision to move to Dubai to ensure that Vedaant had access to better swimming facilities and coaching infrastructure. The move also involved a significant personal and financial commitment from the family to support his sporting ambitions. While the actor frequently attends his sonâs competitions and shares updates about his progress on social media, he has maintained that Vedaant must carve out his own path. For Madhavan, the focus remains on allowing his son to develop as an athlete without letting public attention get ahead of his achievements. Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more.
