title: From introduction to skeet gun at 13 to Asian Games bronze: Parinaaz Dhaliwalâs journey of precision, perseverance and the right support
text: Parinaaz Dhaliwal NEW DELHI: For Parinaaz Dhaliwal, success in skeet shooting is about much more than hitting targets. It is a combination of technical precision, mental strength, financial backing and the ability to find balance under pressure. After years of investing in her game, the Asian Games medallist believes experience, the right coaching environment and an unwavering support system have helped her take significant strides forward. When Parinaaz looks back at her journey in shooting, she does not attribute her progress to one competition, one coach or one breakthrough moment. Instead, she sees it as an evolution shaped by years of training, international exposure and lessons learnt along the way. The bronze medal in the womenâs skeet team event at the Asian Games 2026 at Aichi-Nagoya in Japan alongside Raiza Dhillon and Maheshwari Chauhan, was a significant milestone in that journey. Watch Asian Games gold medallist Sujeet Kalkal on fatherâs influence and how he turned final around âIt was bits of everything, to be honest,â she says, reflecting on the difference between her previous Asian Games appearance and the latest campaign. âYou evolve with every single competition. You learn something or the other. You win or you donât win, but you always learn.â The medal was the culmination of a more comprehensive preparation programme, one that she believes made a tangible difference. Ahead of the Games, the Sports Authority of India (SAI), in coordination with the National Rifle Association of India (NRAI), organised two preparatory camps. The first, held in Aug, focused on fundamentals, while the Sept camp concentrated on fine-tuning and final preparations. The support structure, she says, was also stronger than before, with foreign coaching expertise and a larger team of support staff contributing to the preparations. An important part of that preparation was the presence of her personal coach, Anthony, an Olympic medallist from France. She received permission from the federation to have him join the national camp and accompany her to Japan, where he worked alongside national coaches and foreign coach Riccardo Filippelli. For her, the arrangement was about more than technical advice. A personal coach who has worked with an athlete over an extended period understands the individual beyond the shooting range, including their habits, temperament and response to pressure. âMy personal coach might have seen my tantrums or might have seen a lot,â she says with a laugh. âHe has seen various sides of me because I train with him a lot more than I do with my national coach.â She is particularly appreciative of the cooperation between the coaches, describing the atmosphere as one without ego or insecurity. Anthony, she adds, was equally conscious of respecting the national coaching structure. Her introduction to shooting began well before she took up skeet seriously. Growing up around firearms, she was familiar with the sport, and her father, Ratandeep Dhaliwal, encouraged her to learn how to use a weapon. At Mayo College Girlsâ School in Ajmer, she participated in open-sight shooting competitions and school-level events. When she turned 13, her father suggested that she explore shotgun shooting. She initially tried trap, but it was an unexpected session at the skeet range that changed her trajectory. During a week at home to prepare for a state competition, her mentor, Amarjang Singh Sidhu, suggested that she try a station of skeet. She hit a couple of targets and immediately found herself drawn to the discipline. âI looked at my dad and said, âPapa, I think I want to do skeet.â He was like, âHuh?ââ she recalls. Her father discussed the decision with her grandfather, and by the following day, she had a skeet gun. âIt turned out to be a great decision,â she says. While she remains close to several trap shooters, skeet is the discipline she finds more engaging. The experience reinforced a lesson she considers fundamental to sporting success: an athlete must enjoy what they do. Behind the medals, however, lies a challenge that is often overlooked: the financial demands of competitive shooting. Shotgun shooting, she explains, can be particularly expensive, making financial stability and institutional support crucial for aspiring athletes. Equipment, training and travel can place a substantial burden on families, while sponsorships often arrive only after an athlete has established a record. Despite having competed at the previous Asian Games, she says she relied on her family to fund her development for years, even while working with internationally accomplished coaches, fitness professionals and sports psychologists. She is grateful for the backing, but is equally conscious of the sacrifices that preceded it. Her father had travelled with her to competitions and camps, both in India and abroad. This year, however, he stepped back from travelling because her grandparents were unwell and needed family support. âI said, for me and for my mental sanity, itâs just better that you are at home with my grandparents. And Iâm fine,â she says, drawing on the independence she developed during her years at boarding school. For young shooters, she believes, understanding the financial realities of the sport is as important as recognising their own potential. Parinaazâs preparation has evolved beyond technique and equipment. Over the past three years, she has worked extensively on fitness and the technical aspects of her shooting, while also consulting a sports psychologist based in the UK. At the elite level, she believes, every component matters. âYou cannot leave anything unattended at all,â she said. One incident from the World Cup in Lonato, Italy, illustrates the importance she places on mental preparation. After the first four rounds, she was uncertain about her standing and found herself worrying about the competition. Anthony responded by taking her out for dinner rather than allowing her anxiety to dominate the evening. She was initially concerned about losing sleep ahead of the following morningâs round. Her coach, however, believed that continuing to dwell on the competition would be counterproductive. The evening continued with a walk by the lake and gelato, helping her shift her attention away from the scoreboard and reconnect with the reasons she had taken up shooting. Anthony, she said, believes strongly in maintaining balance and reminding athletes why they compete in the first place. The next day, she shot a perfect round of 25, her best of the competition, which helped her reach a shoot-off. âThese are the small things that coaches with experience can teach you,â she said. At the Asian Games, the women's team faced a difficult opening day, but the athletes concentrated on their individual routines rather than becoming distracted by the collective result. Skeet may have a team component, but the discipline demands individual accountability. Each shooter must execute their own process, manage pressure and remain focused on the target in front of them. The team's positive atmosphere helped them persevere, while the men's skeet team also produced a strong finish. India ultimately returned with medals in both the men's and women's team events. For her, the result reflected not only individual ability but also the value of a supportive environment in which athletes and coaches worked towards a common objective. She also believes India's development in skeet coaching needs greater attention. While the country has several accomplished coaches in trap, she sees a relative shortage of experienced specialists in skeet. International coaches, despite their high fees, can offer technical knowledge and an understanding of competitive pressure acquired through years at the highest level. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines At the same time, she acknowledges that being an accomplished shooter does not automatically make someone an accomplished coach. Coaching, she says, is a discipline in itself. Looking ahead, she intends to continue building on the progress she has made through competition experience, technical refinement and mental preparation. Her latest Asian Games performance is a milestone, but not the end of the journey. For a shooter whose career began with a spontaneous decision at 13, the larger lesson remains remarkably simple: excellence comes from getting the fundamentals right, learning from every competition and finding the people who help you become better. And perhaps that is what defines Parinaazâs journey best. The targets may be fleeting, but the work behind each shot is anything but. title: âEvery time Iâm playing, itâs almost a win for meâ: Yuki Bhambri on injuries and gratitude
text: Yuki Bhambri (Image credit: X) ALMATY: Yuki Bhambriâs smile is revealing. It belongs to someone who has learnt to accept what life throws at him, not with resignation, but with the understanding that there is little point railing against what cannot be changed. You work with what you have, make the best of it and move on. The 34-year-oldâs Zen-like equanimity has been forged in the storms he has weathered through much of his adult life. He began the 2026 season with good reason for optimism. Fresh off a first Grand Slam semifinal at the 2025 US Open, alongside close friend Michael Venus, Bhambri carried that momentum into the new year, climbing to a career-high No. 18 in the rankings in February. Then tennis did what life so often does, complicate plans. An elbow injury that required surgery kept Venus off the Tour, and when the New Zealander returned in March, the pair needed time to find their stride again. In August, at Winston-Salem, Bhambri injured his quad and heâs yet to regain full fitness. Watch Indian tennis star Shrivalli opens up on injuries & comeback journey âThatâs tennis for you,â Bhambri told TOI at the Almaty Arena. âThat's why you have to respect players who are able to stay on Tour for so long. It's so difficult to do it year after year, to maintain a ranking, keep improving, keep playing and chasing those Grand Slams and Masters titles.â For Bhambri the injury has meant a step back, his ranking has slipped to No. 46. Heâs playing the Almaty Open this week with American Ryan Seggerman, the duo are seeded four. Next he plays a Challenger in Seoul and will finish the season at the Paris Masters. âI've been in these situations before because of injuries, where you play for a year, a year and a half, and then have to stop,â he says. âBut this time it's a little different. I've been able to play, but I haven't performed exactly as I would have liked. So it's been a learning curve, almost a fresh start to get back to competing for important events.â Starting over is a familiar exercise for Bhambri. Once Indian tennis's teenage prodigy, he won the Australian Open junior title at 16, became the junior world No. 1 and claimed a silver medal at the Youth Olympics. After he turned pro his singles journey was repeatedly interrupted by tendonitis in both knees. Some three years ago, he switched his focus to doubles. The Asian Games was a goal this year and Bhambri and Dhakshineswar Suresh were billed medal prospects. Bhambriâs movement was hampered by injury, and the pair bowed out in the quarterfinals. âIt's disappointing how it panned out,â he says, a flicker of a smile on his face. Bhambri knows what an Asian Games medal feels like. At the 2014 Asian Games, he won two bronze medals, one in singles and the other in doubles. âI feel very fortunate that I did it a long time ago,â he says of the medals. âHopefully, I'll get another chance four years down the line to improve on that.â There is a telling distinction in the way Bhambri talks about his career. He does not pretend that losing is easy, or that ambition has somehow evaporated with experience. He still wants to win, climb the rankings and compete at the biggest tournaments. But the years spent watching his career stall because his body was wounded may have altered his perspective. âEvery time I'm playing, it's almost a win for me,â he says, his eyes following the players around him at the Almaty Arena. âSomewhere at the back of my mind, there's gratitude that I'm still here, still competing. You want to win everything, of course, but a small part of me considers just being here, competing at these events, a little win in itself.â Was there anger before the gratitude? âI've had different setbacks, but a lot of them have been about not being able to play,â he said. âMaybe it goes back to growing up in a country where a lot of these things weren't accessible. I was always handed down racquets from my sisters. You learnt quite early that if you broke one, you couldn't necessarily expect to get another. So breaking racquets or getting angry on court wasn't really an option, because you might not have anything to play with. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Maybe some of that has stayed with me.â Perhaps that is where Bhambri's composure is tethered, not in some grand philosophy of sport or life, but in the practical understanding that what you have is worth looking after. The racquet had to last. The opportunity to play could not be taken for granted. Years later, the stakes are different, the racquets are his own and the ambitions considerably larger. Yet the instinct to work with what is in front of him remains. Injuries may have cost him time, momentum and ranking points, even switching lanes, from singles to doubles, but it has not diluted the desire to compete. title: Kumkum Mohod sets sights on LA Olympics after historic Asian Games gold
text: Kumkum Mohod (Image credit: X) NEW DELHI: For years, South Koreaâs dominance in recurve archery was taken for granted. Kumkum Mohod had heard enough. At 17, the teenager from Maharashtraâs Amravati did not want to be intimidated by reputation; she rewrote the record books by winning an individual gold at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya instead, finishing with two gold and one silver medal. âEveryone keeps talking about Korea. But they also have to shoot a 10, and I have to shoot a 10. So why think about who is standing opposite me? I just have to focus on my shot and give my best,â Kumkum said on Friday. Watch Asmita Dey Unfiltered: Favourite Food, Match-Day Music & More | Rapid Fire | TOISA Her defiance translated into history in Japan. She became the first Indian woman to win individual recurve gold at the Asian Games, overcoming South Koreaâs Oh Yejin in a nerve-racking final that went into a shoot-off at 5-5. When it mattered most, the Indian teenager struck a perfect 10. Her opponent managed an eight. The individual triumph followed gold in the womenâs team event, alongside Ankita Bhakat and Kirti, ending South Koreaâs remarkable run of seven consecutive Asian Games titles. Kumkum also claimed mixed team silver with Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Dhiraj Bommadevara , completing a three-medal debut that announced her arrival on the continental stage. âEveryone thought Koreans were unbeatable, which is why this gold is so important,â she said during an interaction facilitated by Sports Authority of India (SAI). Yet, for all the composure she displayed under pressure, Kumkum knows her craft remains a work in progress. Even after the biggest victory of her young career, her hand can still tremble while releasing the arrow. Technical refinement, physical strength and mental conditioning remain priorities. âI need to improve on technical aspects and work on my strength. I also want to become mentally stronger,â she said. That composure was tested in the shoot-off, when her heartbeat raced. Breathing exercises, self-motivation and visualising the perfect shot, however, helped her settle the nerves. title: All-time great! An Se-young scripts history, ends Susi Susantiâs 29-year reign with record 47th badminton title
text: An Se Young of South Korea celebrates winning the women's singles final at the Denmark Open in Odense. (AP/PTI Photo) South Korean badminton superstar An Se-young has rewritten the history books, becoming the most decorated womenâs singles player in international badminton and ending Indonesian legend Susi Susantiâs nearly three-decade reign at the top. The Olympic champion achieved the landmark with a hard-fought 21-23, 21-14, 21-18 victory over Japanâs Akane Yamaguchi in the Denmark Open final in Odense on Sunday. The triumph took Anâs tally to 47 international titles, surpassing Susantiâs record of 46, which stood since the Indonesian great retired in 1997. The Badminton World Federation (BWF) confirmed the milestone, noting that its records, maintained since 1989, exclude titles won at regional games. The governing body hailed the 24-year-old South Korean as âan all-time greatâ. Watch Suchika Tariyal on her Asian Games bronze, childhood trauma, and never giving up | TOISA Spotlight Anâs record-breaking run ends legendary reign Susanti, one of badmintonâs most celebrated figures, had held the record for the most international womenâs singles titles for almost 29 years. Anâs latest triumph has now taken her past the Indonesian icon, underlining her remarkable consistency at the highest level. âI want to make a lot of history and break records but I focus on one match at a time,â An said after her victory, reflecting on the achievement. âThat is my motivation. The crowds turn out for me and Iâm happy people enjoy every match I play.â The world No. 1 has occupied the top ranking for 105 consecutive weeks, establishing herself as the dominant force in womenâs singles badminton. She won a record 11 titles in a single season in 2025 and is building another extraordinary campaign this year. Comeback victory despite ankle scare Anâs record-breaking achievement came after a demanding final against Yamaguchi, who took the opening game 23-21. The South Korean responded strongly to win the second 21-14 and force a decider. The final game presented another challenge when An trailed 11-5 and appeared to injure her right ankle after slipping on the court. Despite the setback, she recovered her rhythm, capitalised on the slower side of the court and completed the comeback with a 21-18 win. âItâs a little bit bad,â An admitted after the match. âThe court conditions were difficult and I slipped. I will check my body and talk to my [coaches]. In the final game, I was on the slower side of the court, and I was more confident.â The victory secured her second consecutive Denmark Open crown and ninth individual title of the season. A season of remarkable dominance Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Anâs latest achievement adds to a season in which she has won six BWF World Tour singles titles and claimed major honours at the Asian Championships, World Championships and Asian Games, alongside success in team competitions. Her only defeat of 2026 came in the All England Open final in March, where she lost to Chinaâs Wang Zhiyi. Anâs rivalry with Yamaguchi has also become one of the defining contests in womenâs badminton. The South Korean has now won their last 10 meetings in succession. âI think sheâs my best rival. I always want to win against her. She motivates me to train harder,â An said. âWang Zhi Yi and Chen Yu Fei are rivals too and Iâm happy to have them. Rivalry makes you better.â With the record now hers, An has moved beyond chasing individual titles to establishing a legacy that could define an era of womenâs badminton. title: When and where to watch IND vs NZ first T20I: Match date, time, venue and live streaming details
text: Shreyas Iyer, Mitchell Santner India, led by Shreyas Iyer, will look to extend their unbeaten run in T20I series in New Zealand as they begin a five-match rubber against the hosts on Thursday. The visitors, despite having limited time to rest, acclimatise and train after their arrival, will rely on their batting strength to take on the home side. India's most recent T20I series in New Zealand was in 2022. The match in Napier ended in a tie under the Duckworth-Lewis method after rain interrupted play. India went on to win the series, claiming victory in the only match that was not affected by rain. Watch Shreyas Iyer press conference: On Sanju Samson v Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, Bhuvneshwar Kumar and more Only four batters in India's squad have played T20Is in New Zealand before â captain Iyer, Ishan Kishan, Sanju Samson and Shivam Dube. While Abhishek Sharma, Tilak Varma and 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi bring plenty of attacking options, they will need time to adjust to the pace and seam movement expected in local conditions. For Iyer, the series is an opportunity to prove himself on an overseas tour after his tenure as captain began with consecutive defeats in Ireland and England. Mitchell Santner's New Zealand side will look to put India under pressure. Iyer arrives after leading India to their second consecutive gold-winning campaign at the Asian Games and a hard-fought home series against the West Indies that ended in a draw. However, if the series follows the pattern of India's tour of the UK earlier this year, scrutiny of Iyer's leadership is likely to increase. He is expected to lead India at the T20 World Cup in Australia and New Zealand in two years. India will be without two key players in all-rounder Hardik Pandya, who is injured, and pace spearhead Jasprit Bumrah, who will feature only in the ODI and Test legs of the tour. title: EXCLUSIVE | 'Fear may never completely go away': Sujeet Kalkal on turning Olympic heartbreak into Asian Games gold
text: Sujeet Kalkal (Image credit: PTI) NEW DELHI: Two years ago, Sujeet Kalkal was stranded at Dubai International Airport, watching his Olympic dream slip away with every passing hour. On his way to Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, for the Asian Olympic Qualifying Tournament, Kalkal was stuck in Dubai for three days after floods disrupted his travel plans. By the time a flight was arranged, it was too late. He could not reach Bishkek in time, and with it went his chance to qualify for the Paris Olympics. Watch âThis medal means a lotâ: Lovlina Borgohain on Asian Games gold & Olympic ambitions Two years later, the disappointment of Dubai has been replaced by an Asian Games gold. Kalkal, the world No. 2 in the men's 65kg category, fought back from 2-9 down against Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev in the final to win 10-9, ending India's eight-year wait for a wrestling gold at the Games. The comeback was symbolic of what Kalkal's career has looked like since that Olympic setback. He has had to rebuild, compete through the disappointment and find a way back to the biggest stages. On Sunday, he did that with an Asian Games title. When the final whistle came, Kalkal folded his hands, looked up and thanked God. He then took a lap of the arena with the Indian tricolour draped around his shoulders, tears and a broad smile. For a wrestler who had once been denied even the chance to fight for an Olympic place, the moment carried a little more weight than an Asian Games gold. "This gold means a lot to me. Not just because it is an Asian Games gold, but because there is so much behind this medal. The last few years have had many ups and downs, and I missed a few opportunities, but I never lost belief in myself," Kalkal told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interview on his way back to Imlota village in Bhiwani, Haryana, where his parents were waiting to welcome him. Sujeet Kalkal (Image credit: PTI) The Dubai episode, he says, is now behind him. What remains is the lesson from it - and a much bigger target. "Paris was very difficult for me to miss, but that experience made me stronger instead of breaking me. LA 2028 is obviously a very big goal for me," Kalkal said. And he is clear about what he wants from that opportunity. "Olympics mein jaana hai toh sirf participate karne ke liye nahi jaana, bhaisaab. Gold ke liye jaana hai [âIf youâre going to the Olympics, donât go just to participate, brother. Go there to win gold]." India had not won a wrestling gold at the Asian Games since 2018. Kalkal's victory ended that wait and added another major title to a career that already includes an U23 World Championship crown, Asian Championships success and a Zagreb Open triumph. "India has won a wrestling gold at the Asian Games after eight years, so being a part of it is very special for me. This medal reminds me that if you keep working hard, your time will come," he said. The road to the Asian Games gold was not easy for Kalkal. He had a challenging draw, but handled each bout with confidence. After a comfortable opening victory, he made a statement in the quarterfinals by throwing Iran's Abbas Ebrahimzadehsavadkouhi from a standing position within the opening 20 seconds. The semifinal brought an even bigger test, but Kalkal overcame Olympic champion Kotaro Kiyooka to reach the gold medal bout. Then came the final against Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev, and it looked like the toughest challenge of them all. Instead of allowing the deficit to affect him, Kalkal fought his way back into the contest. He produced eight points to turn a seven-point deficit into a 10-9 victory and seal the Asian Games title. "The simple plan was to wrestle my own way and not be impressed by my opponent's name. Whether he is an Olympic champion, a world champion or anyone else, everyone starts from zero on the mat. I just trusted my preparation and my strength. I knew that if I executed my best, I could beat anyone. Instead of thinking too much during the match, I just had to fight for every single point," he said. Sujeet Kalkal during his gold medal bout (Image credit: PTI) Kalkal also dedicated the gold to the country and remembered his father, who stood by him throughout his journey. "I dedicate this gold to the whole of India. Of course, my first call was to my father. He has supported me tremendously throughout this journey, and without his support, it would have been impossible for me to reach this point. His support will always remain with me," the Indian wrestler said. The final also reflected the mental change Kalkal says came from the disappointment of 2024. "Fear may never completely go away, but now I know how to fight with fear. When you go through tough situations in life, small things stop bothering you. What happened in Dubai, missing the Olympic qualifiers - every experience taught me something," the Indian wrestler said. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines "Now I don't run away from pressure. I enjoy pressure because those are the moments when you realise how strong you actually are," Kalkal said. The Asian Games gold now joins an already impressive list of achievements for Kalkal, but he is not dwelling on the medals he has already won. The next target is Los Angeles. And this time, he wants to get there on his own terms. "Gold ke liye jaana hai." Poll Vote & Share your view Which factor do you think played the biggest role in Kalkal's comeback? title: Asian Games 2026 Medal Tally: Golden run in hockey, cricket, wrestling, archery takes India into top 4

title: How Neeraj Chopra's javelin helped Rohit Yadav win Asian Games bronze
text: Rohit Yadav (Image credit: X) NEW DELHI: When Rohit Yadav stepped onto the field in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, for the Asian Games javelin final, he carried more than a piece of sporting equipment. In his hand was a signed javelin belonging to Olympic and world champion Neeraj Chopra â a quiet gesture of support that would accompany him to an international podium. The story began in June, when Yadav struck gold at the National Inter State Senior Athletics Championships in Bhubaneswar with a personal best of 87.05m. Upon returning to his training base in NIS Patiala, he discovered that his preferred javelin had bent, apparently during air transit in its protective PVC tube in the aircraftâs cargo hold. Watch Lovlina Borgohainâs golden birthday: Asian Games medal after comeback Yadav subsequently competed at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow with a borrowed implement, finishing seventh with 81.56m in cold, windy conditions. With the Asian Games approaching, he faced the prospect of competing without his trusted javelin. âFor the Asian Games, I didnât have my own javelin. My preferred one was damaged and had bent. While coming to Delhi from Patiala for the Indian Athletics Final Series on Sept 10, I spoke to Neeraj bhai,â Yadav told TOI. âWe have been in regular touch. I knew he had returned to India for rehabilitation. I told him I didnât have a javelin of my own for the Asian Games. He immediately came to my rescue and sent me one of his signed javelins through a private taxi service to the Jawaharlal Nehru (JLN) stadium,â he added. Chopra had withdrawn from the remainder of the season, including the Asian Games, to recover from an ankle ligament injury. His absence left India without its two-time defending champion, but his gesture ensured that a fellow Indian thrower had the equipment he needed. There was, however, a catch. Yadav could not use the javelin in Delhi because it had not been registered with the Technical Information Centre (TIC) for inspection. He borrowed another registered implement for the event, then carefully packed Chopraâs gift for Japan. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines âAt the Asian Games, I registered two javelins with the TIC. But I used the one Neeraj bhai gave me. I had a good grip and hold over it, and with that javelin I made the winning throw to secure bronze with 84.35m,â he said. âI will remain thankful to Neeraj bhai. I have kept that javelin with me and will use it in future competitions as well.â After his competition, Rohit listened to Chopraâs congratulatory voice message. âHe told me to enjoy the win and savour my first big international medal. He said that when he returns fully fit, we will compete together, and that I have a long way to go.â Back home in Uttar Pradeshâs Jaunpur, Yadav is taking the off-season to spend time with family until Diwali. âI want to earn a Diamond League entry, compete internationally and qualify for the World Championships next year. The ultimate target remains the Los Angeles Olympics,â he added. Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news , check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule . title: Women's India Open: Vani Kapoor makes herself heard but Phatlum has last word
text: Indian Finishes Second As Thai Invitee Makes It Four Triumphs At Women's Indian Open GURUGRAM : The autumn leaves were falling on the vantage point, where many had gathered for a glimpse of the ninth hole at DLF G&CC. Overnight leader Vani Kapoorâs rousing birdie on the eighth kept her one ahead of the experienced Thai, Pornanong Phatlum, already a three-time winner at the venue, although on the old Arnold Palmer-designed layout. People could sense a turning point as the LPGA golfer collected her fifth birdie of the day. The home pro stood over her small pressure putt, studying the lines over and over again, taking a step backwards, playing it in her mind, then attempting again. Finally she hit, it was a miss! A leaf fell again on the shoulder. Was it natureâs way of saying that the hopes had withered too? The spectators remained still, in disbelief, then politely clapped in admiration as the calm Thai caught up with the home challenger. Maybe that elusive Hero Womenâs Indian Open trophy had slipped out of our hands again. Onto the par-4 10th, and Vaniâs second shot was short, and her wedge failed to find the right spot on the green. As Phatlum settled for her two-putt par, Vani's putter missed the target again for a bogey. The narrative had changed. This is the club where Vani, a star student of the DLF Academy, had grown up. A casual walk here would often lead to one bumping into the little confident girl whose dreams were big. Older now at 32, her expectations were now tempered with a sprinkling of reality. But despite all the disappointments home and away, she carried on with a happy demeanour. In golf, you could be second but you were still a winner but only one could walk away with the prize, and that person needed a little bit of luck, she had said before. The stumbles on the back-nine ensured that Vani came second. Yes, she was still a winner. But champion Phatlum made her own luck. When the Indian came out, all irons blazing, with four birdies in five holes, the Thai managed three of her own, adding two more before the turn. Pars can be powerful if you are ahead, and others are not making their moves. Phatlum was creating her own new chapter with two more birdies after the lull under the strong afternoon sun for a final-day bogey-free seven-under 65, and a magical fourth triumph by four strokes. Vani quietly accepted her lot with her round of 70, as her bogey tumbles on the return journey set the tone for the unhappy conclusion. âI think this year I was much more confident, and more anchored. I had much more clarity in my head and a sense of purpose,â she shared her positive notes. But she had felt the pressure. âSome shots you donât have exactly have the yardage you want, and you have to think about where you can miss the ball. Those are stressful, so there were little mistakes there.â But where the margins are minute, especially on the slopey greens of the Gary Player course, little could become large when you are fighting for the championship. âI donât think I could have done anything more. I made a lot of birdies, especially considering the amount of pressure there was. I made a couple of mistakes too, but thatâs part of the game.â Golf can be cruel, it can also be rejuvenating. For the petite Thai conqueror with an infectious smile, this is the end of a long drought. Phatlum, who has returned to India after 14 years on an invite, had her first look at the changed environment and used all her experience on American shores to plot her way around the course where âevery shot countsâ. With soft skills to match the Mudmee silk her hometown of Khon Kaen is famous for, Phatlum steadily improved with rounds of 72, 71, 69 as her understanding of the playground grew, to finish on a high of 65. With a solo second at the 2018 Womenâs British Open in her resume, the Womenâs Indian Open champion of 2008, 2009 and 2012 had seen better years on the LPGA. With the 2026 crown, her love affair with the tournament continued. âI think I could live in India,â the 36-year-old said, giggling. Stomach bug Pranavi's biggest challenge The Indians are getting closer to that hallowed trophy, which Aditi Ashok won in 2016. A second place finish is as good as it gets for now. âIt was Pornanongâs experience which came clutch today,â explained Pranavi Urs, who finished tied-fourth. It was a week the Asian Games gold medallist was looking forward to. âWith the way Iâve been playing, I thought I would have a chance.â The biggest obstacle was not the course, but her stomach. Not having a proper meal since Pro-Am day, the breathless figure could be seen struggling as the day progressed. Despite the trouble, the Mysuru girl finished with a 72 and a total of three-under. title: Vithya Ramraj on newfound fame: 'I'm still far away from reaching world standards'
text: Vithya Ramraj (Image credit: PTI) CHENNAI: With three medals and newfound recognition, Vithya Ramraj returned home from the Asian Games with plenty to celebrate. People at petrol bunks, airports and bus stands have started recognizing her, but it has left the 28-year old, who broke P T Ushaâs 400 metre 42-year-old hurdles record, slightly surprised. âPeople are recognising me now and Iâm happy athletics is growing. Iâm also thinking about the recognition I am getting. Is it because of the relay medals or because I broke the record? Why have I become famous? That is one constant thing on my mind. Iâm still far away from reaching world standards, and my coach was not happy with the timing. Watch âThis medal means a lotâ: Lovlina Borgohain on Asian Games gold & Olympic ambitions âPersonally, I didnât get the satisfaction even though people celebrated. I think of how Neeraj Chopra is celebrated, and if I reach his level, then more people will know me,â Vithya told TOI. What worked for Vithya in 400m hurdles was that she brought down her stride count from 17 to 16 between hurdles 5 and 6. âIn the bend from the fifth to the sixth hurdle, I used to take 17 strides, but I have now reduced it to 16. We have been working on it since Nov last year. That helped me going into the home stretch.â Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Going into the Asian Games, Vithya did not dip below 56 seconds even once this season. While she bagged gold at the Federation Cup and Inter-state athletics meet, her coach Nehpal Singh, who has been a strong source of support, was not satisfied with the medals. âMy coach told me, âDid I train you to run 56 seconds? What performance have you put in?ââ What Vithya felt helped her in the run-up to the Asian Games was the training stints she had in Poland and the Czech Republic with Nehpal. âI used to sleep for 10 hours for three months during the stint abroad, but in India, I used to sleep only for 7-8 hours. In India, I cannot train at 10 am due to the climate, but the sleep cycle in Poland helped me. In India, I train from 5:30am to 8:30am,â she said. title: Other side of India's Asian Games success: 201 athletes won just 6 bronze, 137 returned empty-handed
text: AP Photo NEW DELHI: Indiaâs 85-medal haul at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games was its secondbest finish, but the headline numbers donât reveal everything. A sport-by-sport audit by TOI shows that 137 Indian athletes across 16 disciplines returned empty-handed, exposing persistent gaps in the countryâs medal ambitions. Watch Asmita Dey Unfiltered: Favourite Food, Match-Day Music & More | Rapid Fire | TOISA Indiaâs pruned-down 495-member contingent competed across 36 sport disciplines and finished fourth with 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals. Yet 137 athletes across 16 disciplines won nothing. Another 64 athletes across six sports managed six bronze â one each in kurash, mixed martial arts, rowing, sepaktakraw, soft tennis and wushu. The zero-medal list included canoeing (19 athletes), cycling (14), equestrian (7), esports (15), fencing (20), gymnastics (1), judo (3), karate (2), rugby sevens (13), sport climbing (2), surfing (4), swimming (12), taekwondo (3), tennis (7), teqball (3) and volleyball (12). The six-bronze group comprised kurash (6 athletes), MMA (2), rowing (22), sepaktakraw (21), soft tennis (6) and wushu (7). In all, 201 athletes accounted for just six bronze medals across the 22 disciplines mentioned above. In other prominent sports with sizable athlete numbers, table tennis sent 10 athletes and returned with one bronze and badmintonâs 20-member contingent managed one bronze in the menâs team event. Together, the two sent 37 athletes and produced only two bronze. India contested in 259 medal events in AichiNagoya and won medals in just 20, a 7.7% eventpodium conversion rate. Of 356 medals available in which India featured, the nation collected 85, a conversion rate of only 23.9%. The spending breakdown The govt spent Rs 259.69 crore on 19 sports as part of the overall total expenditure during the current Asian Games cycle (Nov 2023-Aug 2026), led by badminton (Rs 49.26 cr), cycling track (Rs 35.9 cr), fencing (Rs 28.2 cr), table tennis (Rs 25.3 cr), tennis (Rs 22.4 cr) and canoe/kayak (Rs 20.1 cr). Other allocations included rowing (Rs 13.8 cr,) swimming (Rs 10.8 cr), gymnastics (Rs 10.49 cr), judo (Rs 8.05 cr), wushu (Rs 7.8 cr), volleyball (Rs 6.5 cr), sepaktakraw (Rs 5.7 cr), equestrian (Rs 3.7 cr), rugby (Rs 3.63 cr), surfing (Rs 2.9 cr), karate (Rs 1.99 cr), soft tennis (Rs 1.6 cr) and kurash (Rs 1.6 cr). On three sports â MMA, eSports and sport climbing, the govt spent no money. As per the govtâs own estimates, it spent approximately Rs 703 cr across 30 disciplines during the Nov 2023-Aug 2026 preparation cycle. The Rs 703 cr included about Rs 118 cr for domestic training and national coaching camps, Rs 40 cr for overseas training, Rs 252 cr for international competition exposure, Rs 89 cr for equipment, Rs 86 cr for foreign coaches/support staff and Rs 118 cr for other expenses, including Indian experts, championships, competitions in India, grassroots and coach development. Also, a total of 427 athletes who were part of the govtâs various programmes and schemes participated in the Games, including 77 athletes from Target Olympic Podium Scheme (TOPS) Core group, 78 from TOPS Development 78, 48 from Target Asian Games Group (TAGG), 65 Khelo India Athlete (KIA), 25 from National Centre of Excellence (NCoE) and 134 from National Coaching Camps (NCCs). The Glasgow comparison is revealing, though not like-for-like. India had 122 athletes and para-athletes in 10 sports at the curtailed 2026 Commonwealth Games and won 39 medals â 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze â also finishing fourth. The Asian Games contingent was 4.06 times larger, but its 85-medal haul was only 2.18 times Glasgowâs. Medal efficiency was 17.2 per 100 athletes in Aichi-Nagoya against 32 in Glasgow. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines The message is that at this level, the medal base remains concentrated. For a country investing Rs 703 cr across a multi-year cycle, the next challenge is clear: turn wider participation, exposure and support into wider podium conversion. title: 'My father has never watched me play at the stadium': Harmanpreet eyes memorable homecoming as hockey returns to Punjab after 17 years
text: Indian Men's Hockey captain Harmanpreet Singh (ANI Photo) India men's hockey captain Harmanpreet Singh is eagerly awaiting a rare homecoming as the defending champions prepare to compete in the Men's Asian Champions Trophy 2026 in Punjab from October 27 to November 5. With international hockey returning to the state after 17 years, the tournament will carry special significance for the Indian skipper, who is set to represent the country in front of his family on home soil for the first time. Watch Suchika Tariyal on her Asian Games bronze, childhood trauma, and never giving up | TOISA Spotlight International hockey returns to Punjab after 17 years The Men's Asian Champions Trophy 2026 will bring international hockey back to Punjab, with Jalandhar and Mohali set to host the six-team tournament. India will compete against Malaysia, South Korea, China, Japan and Bangladesh as they look to defend their title. The tournament marks the second time India will host the men's edition of the Asian Champions Trophy, following Chennai's hosting in 2023. The return of international hockey to Punjab is expected to generate considerable excitement in a state where the sport has deep cultural and sporting roots. 'It's going to be special' For Harmanpreet, the occasion will be particularly emotional as his father is expected to watch him play an international match at the stadium for the first time. The Indian captain believes the tournament will be a memorable experience not only for him but also for the players from Punjab, a state that has played a significant role in shaping Indian hockey. âItâs going to be a special occasion for the entire team, especially for the players who belong to Punjab because itâs the first time that we will be wearing India jersey at an international tournament in Punjab,â Harmanpreet said. âMy entire family is expected to be at the stadium watching me play an international match together from the venue for the first time, including my father who has never seen me play for the country while sitting inside the stadium,â he added. Jalandhar to host opening ceremony, Mohali to stage medal matches The tournament will be played across two venues in Punjab, with Jalandhar hosting the opening ceremony and the league-stage matches from October 27 to November 2. The Olympian Surjit Singh Hockey Stadium at Burlton Park will be the centre of action during the initial phase of the competition. The tournament will then move to Mohali's Olympian Balbir Singh Senior International Hockey Stadium for the knockout stage. The semi-finals and medal matches are scheduled for November 4 and 5, when the participating teams will compete for the continental title. The tournament is also expected to give local supporters an opportunity to watch India's leading hockey players in action, adding to the significance of the event for the state. title: MLBx Mumbai: Suryakumar Yadav, Shardul Thakur and four other Indian cricketers take on World Series champions
text: Suryakumar Yadav has built a career on hitting the ball where nobody expects it. Scoops over fine leg, ramps over the keeperâs head and flicks that travel almost backwards earned him the â360-degreeâ tag. In baseball, most of those shots would not count. The sport allows only a 90-degree wedge of fair territory in front of the batter. Anything behind or wide of it is a foul ball. That is only the first adjustment. There is no bounce to read and no pitch to play off, and the bat is round. For bowlers, the rulebook flips the other way: the straight-arm rule that defines cricket bowling does not exist on the mound. Fielders canât stop the ball with their pads either. They get a leather glove instead. On 24 October, six of Indiaâs best-known cricketers will find out how quickly they can adapt. Suryakumar will be joined by Shardul Thakur, Jitesh Sharma, Kashvee Gautam, Radha Yadav and Deepak Chahar at Mumbai Football Arena, Andheri Sports Complex, where they will line up alongside World Series champions and elite softball players in a short, fast 3-on-3 format. The event, MLBx: Mumbai, is Major League Baseballâs first MLBx event in India. Four teams will carry the colours of four of the sportâs most famous franchises, each pairing an MLB legend with an Indian cricketer and an Athletes Unlimited Softball League (AUSL) star. The teams New York Yankees: Nick Swisher, Suryakumar Yadav, Rachel Garcia Los Angeles Dodgers: AdriÃ¡n GonzÃ¡lez, Jitesh Sharma, Jordan Woolery Chicago Cubs: Jake Arrieta, Shardul Thakur, Radha Yadav Boston Red Sox: Jonny Gomes, Kashvee Gautam, Deepak Chahar The cricketers stepping up to the plate Shardul Thakur brings big-match experience. The seam-bowling all-rounder has played all three formats for India, won the IPL twice with Chennai Super Kings and played a key part in Indiaâs 2020-21 Test series win in Australia, including the Gabba Test. At the Cubs, he will share a dugout with one of the top pitchers of his generation. Jitesh Sharma, the aggressive wicketkeeper-batter, may have the most familiar role. Standing behind the stumps is the closest cricket gets to a baseball catcher. He was part of the Royal Challengers Bengaluru squad that won the IPL in 2025 and Indiaâs gold medal-winning team at the 2022 Asian Games. Kashvee Gautam made history in 2020 as the first Indian woman to take all 10 wickets in an innings in a BCCI domestic tournament, a spell that included a hat-trick. Radha Yadav, the Mumbai-born left-arm spinner known for her sharp fielding, was part of Indiaâs 2025 Womenâs ODI World Cup-winning squad. She started out playing tennis-ball cricket with boys in her apartment building. The other side of the diamond The baseball line-up carries serious silverware. Nick Swisher won the 2009 World Series with the New York Yankees and was an All-Star in 2010. AdriÃ¡n GonzÃ¡lez is a five-time MLB All-Star and four-time Gold Glove winner, the award for the gameâs best defenders. Jonny Gomes played 13 MLB seasons and was part of Bostonâs 2013 World Series-winning team. Jake Arrieta won the 2015 National League Cy Young Award as the leagueâs best pitcher and helped the Chicago Cubs win their historic 2016 World Series. The softball stars are just as decorated. Rachel Garcia is a two-time NFCA National Player of the Year, an Olympic silver medallist and the first overall pick in the inaugural AUSL Draft. Jordan Woolery is the 2026 Softball America and Big Ten Player of the Year. Built for big moments The 3-on-3 format keeps games short and fast, with little time to settle in, which is a test of adaptability for every player on the field. Around the action, the event will bring together music, food and entertainment. Badshah and KR$NA will perform, and Mumbai-based DJ OG SHEZ will play her genre-blending sets. title: New beginnings, new heroes: Women lead India's charge as a new generation shines in Nagoya
text: Lovlina Borgohain and Neeru Dhanda (Image credit: X) As Neeru Dhanda led the Indian contingent out for one last time at the Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium on Sunday night, it was symbolic of how Indiaâs Asian Games campaign had unfolded over the past two weeks. The women had come to the fore - packing punches, vaulting to new heights, lifting weights, taking aim, towering over opponents with sixes, blazing the track, finding the fairway and hitting the back of the net. Indiaâs final tally of 85 medals, including 21 gold, may represent a drop from the 106 medals and 28 golds won in Hangzhou. But numbers alone cannot tell the story of these Games. Watch Lovlina Borgohainâs golden birthday: Asian Games medal after comeback There were path-breakers everywhere, athletes who pushed through glass ceilings that had stood for years. The aftermath will bring reviews, reflections, deliberations and reports. But before the analysis begins, it is only fair to celebrate those who made these Games count. For almost 12 days, the Indian gold rush had remained subdued. Then, just as the sun finally began showing up in Nagoya, the floodgates opened. Eleven gold medals came in the final two days, transforming what had threatened to become a disappointing campaign into a collection of stories about guts, resilience and glory. Dhanda, the 26-year-old from Sangatpura in Haryana, had set the tone by winning Indiaâs first individual gold of these Games in the womenâs trap event. The women went on to win 11 gold medals, apart from the three secured in mixed events. The contingent had 83 debutants, who accounted for 41 of Indiaâs 85 medals â a clear indication of a changing guard across several sports. But if one athlete were to be picked as the face of that change, it would be difficult to look beyond 17-year-old Kumkum Mohod. The Maharashtra archer won two gold medals and a silver, but her biggest achievement went beyond the medal tally. She ended South Koreaâs two-decade domination of the womenâs recurve events by becoming the first Indian to win individual recurve gold at the Asian Games. It did not take her long to make the biggest stage of her young career her own. Even her Korean opponent Oh Ye-jin, whom Kumkum beat for the individual gold, was left impressed. âFor a 17-year-old, she is very composed and has a very bright future,â Oh said. Another teenager, Prithika Pradeep, also emerged with two gold medals, adding to the sense that a new generation is beginning to announce itself. Pranavi Urs became the first Indian woman to win an Asian Games golf gold. Behind every medal was a story of humble beginnings, survival in sport, societal pressures overcome and personal tragedies endured. That made the successes more than just entries in a medal table. The comeback girls They were not newcomers to the big stage. They had competed at the biggest of them all â the Olympics. But Nagoya offered unfinished business. Lovlina Borgohain had contemplated walking away from boxing after a difficult phase post the 2024 Paris Olympics. Instead, she returned to punch her way to gold. Parveen Hooda, returning after a doping ban, produced her own golden comeback. The bronze she had won in Hangzhou and subsequently lost became gold in Nagoya. Mirabai Chanu did not win gold, but her silver in the 49kg category had the weight of a championâs achievement. It also completed her Asian Games medal collection. Golden standards The womenâs kabaddi team survived a tense battle against Iran. The womenâs hockey team ended a 44-year wait for Asian Games gold. And Harmanpreet Kaur and her team ensured that cricketâs gold returned to India. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Among the men, too, there were performances that demanded attention â Aman Sehrawat in wrestling, Ankush Panghal in boxing and Gulveer Singh in long-distance running among them. Yet, for all the celebration, there were glaring blanks. Manu Bhaker, one of Indiaâs biggest sporting heroes, returned without a medal. There were plenty of nearmisses and some disastrous outings. Indiaâs badminton return of a solitary bronze was another disappointment, particularly with a strong menâs doubles combination of Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty, PV Sindhu and Lakshya Sen in the squad. Table tennis also raised questions, while equestrian had its own share of run-ins between administrators and riders, alongside selectionrelated concerns but failed to add to the medal count. title: 46,500 youth recruited on merit in 2 years: Saini
text: CM Nayab Singh Saini addresses mediapersons on the occasion of the two-year completion of the third consecutive term of the BJP govt in Haryana, in Chandigarh on Saturday Chandigarh: Marking the completion of two years of the BJP govtâs third consecutive term, Haryana chief minister Nayab Singh Saini said 46,500 youth had been recruited to govt services through a transparent, merit-based system. Highlighting key policy decisions, Saini announced 20% horizontal reservation for former Agniveers in direct recruitment to identified govt posts, including those of police personnel, forest guards and mining guards. Eligible candidates will also be exempted from written examinations for certain Group-C posts. He said 2.7 lakh youth had received around Rs 657.2 crore under the Saksham Yuva Yojana, while placement drives had provided jobs to more than 11,000 youth in the private sector. Focus on sports and youth development Highlighting Haryanaâs sporting achievements, Saini said the state had distributed Rs 147.1 crore in cash awards to 1,319 medal winners over two years and established 2,000 sports nurseries in rural areas. He also highlighted the performance of Haryana athletes at international sporting events, claiming that they won 32 of Indiaâs 85 medals at the Asian Games in Japan and 11 medals at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Womenâs empowerment Saini said more than 10 lakh women had benefited from the Deen Dayal Lado Lakshmi Yojana, which provides Rs 2,100 per month, with Rs 2,466.63 crore disbursed under the scheme. Additionally, around 2.9 lakh women had become âLakhpati Didis,â while 33% reservation had been provided to women in ration depot allotments. Healthcare expansion The number of medical colleges in Haryana has increased from six in 2014 to 18, Saini said. Free dialysis services are now available at all district hospitals and medical colleges, while the Ayushman Bharat-Chirayu scheme has been expanded to cover higher-income families. Education boost The govt has established 250 Chief Minister Excellence and Early English (CM-EEE) schools, while information and communication technology (ICT) labs have been approved for 900 govt schools under the PM SHRI initiative. Saini reiterated that merit-based governance, accessible healthcare and womenâs economic self-reliance would remain key priorities for the state govt. title: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi is Indiaâs youngest Asian Games gold medallist, but do you know who is the worldâs youngest?
text: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, 15, is Indiaâs youngest Asian Games gold medallist, while Yuki Kurihara, 11, is the youngest ever. At 15, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi has already made history at the Asian Games . The young Indian cricketer became the youngest Indian to win an Asian Games gold medal after India defeated Pakistan by 19 runs in the menâs cricket final at the 2026 Aichi-Nagoya Games. But there is an even younger name at the top of the Asian Games record books. Just days before Sooryavanshiâs historic gold, 11-year-old Japanese esports player Yuki Kurihara became the youngest gold medallist in Asian Games history . He achieved the feat in a sport very different from cricket - the puzzle game Puyo Puyo Champions - defeating South Koreaâs 24-year-old Kang Dongshin 10-2 in the final. Who is Yuki Kurihara? Yuki Kurihara won gold in Puyo Puyo Champions at the age of 11. Kurihara is an elementary school student from Japan who competed in the esports competition at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games. At just 11, he was also reported to be the youngest competitor at the Games. His gold-medal run was remarkable not only because of his age, but also because of the experience of some of the opponents he faced. In the semi-final, Kurihara defeated Thailandâs 28-year-old Tanarak Wongkitkun 10-1, ensuring himself at least a silver medal. He then faced South Koreaâs Kang Dongshin in the gold-medal match. Kurihara initially fell 1-0 behind in the final. He then responded with a string of wins and eventually closed out the match 10-2 to claim the gold on home soil. The Olympic Council of Asia described the victory as a record-setting achievement, confirming that Kurihara had become the youngest champion across all editions of the Asian Games. The young player appeared remarkably composed after the victory. Speaking after his win, Kurihara said he felt âa bit embarrassedâ and found it difficult to show much emotion. But the significance of the moment was not lost on him. âI'm really happy. The gold medal is really beautiful, shiny and heavy,â he said. From a Christmas present to an Asian Games gold Kuriharaâs association with Puyo Puyo began when he received Puyo Puyo Tetris 2 as a Christmas present about five years ago. He became fascinated by the game's chain mechanics and went on to compete in tournaments. According to The Japan Times , he began playing during his first year of elementary school and later earned a professional licence in April 2026. He had already won the elementary school division of the 2024 SAGA National Prefectural eSports Championship and the open division of a 2025 SHIGA championship before arriving at the Asian Games. His preparation is also unusual for a child his age. Reports have noted his love of eel, which he eats as part of his preparation for competitions. Despite the demanding training schedule, Kurihara continues his school education alongside esports. The Associated Press reported that he trains for around eight hours a day while keeping up with his studies. He was facing players more than twice his age The age difference between Kurihara and his opponents was one of the most striking aspects of his campaign. His semi-final opponent Wongkitkun was 28, meaning Kurihara was less than half his age. In the final, he faced 24-year-old Kang. Yet the youngster did not appear overawed by the difference in experience. After losing the opening game of the final, Kurihara recovered and gradually took control. His eventual 10-2 victory gave Japan a gold medal and placed his name in the history of the Asian Games. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. title: Chinese father, 41, walked his 21-year-old daughter down the aisle, but guests thought he was her brother; his three daily habits are surprising and...
text: Dad and Daughter duo (Instagram) A wedding is generally a bride and groomâs moment to shine. But the wedding that happened in Chinaâs Chaozhou, Guangdong province, it was the brideâs father who took away all the attention for all the right reasons! Meet the brideâs father, Zheng who at 41 looked so amazingly young standing beside his 21-year-old daughter that he became an overnight viral sensation on social media. The fun part began when some viewers mistook him as the brideâs brother, turning an emotional family moment into a viral talking point about aging and fitness. The viral wedding video The wedding video attracted global attention in late August 2026. It showed Zheng with his daughter on her special day. His youthful appearance and stylish outfit left viewersâ shocked with happiness. Some were even joking that he looked more like her older brother or a boyfriend than the man walking her down the aisle. But the surprise did not end with the wedding footage. According to reports, Zheng said that he and his daughter are frequently mistaken for siblings when they go out together. On some occasions, people have even assumed that they are a couple. His son-in-law was also surprised by his young appearance when they first met, too. But for Zheng, the attention was normal. What many viewers found astonishing was something he had grown accustomed to: looking younger than his age. The secret behind his youthful appearance When asked about his youthful appearance, Zheng did not point to an extensive exercise regime or a carefully curated meal or an elaborate skincare routine. Instead, his reason was simple. He shared three habits: getting plenty of sleep, exercising regularly and keeping calm. The first, he said, is maintaining a relaxed state of mind. He says that he tries not to get angry easily and keeping calm is important. His second habit is likely to surprise people who struggle to get enough rest. Zheng said he sleeps for around 10 to 12 hours every day. While that is considerably longer than the amount of sleep recommended for most adults, he says getting plenty of rest is part of his routine. The third is playing badminton. He says he plays the game three to four times a week. The game combines movement, agility, coordination and cardiovascular exercise. Taken together, these habits paint a picture of someone who prioritises rest, regular movement and a relatively untroubled approach to everyday life. They may help explain why Zheng appears energetic and fit, although his story does not establish that these habits alone are responsible for his youthful looks. Can sleep, exercise and a calm mind really make a difference? According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), adults aged 18 to 60 generally need at least seven hours of sleep a day. Good-quality sleep supports emotional wellbeing, helps regulate mood and contributes to overall health. Zhengâs reported 10 to 12 hours, however, should not be treated as a target everyone needs to achieve. Physical activity also offers benefits that go beyond appearance. The CDC says regular exercise can improve sleep, support brain health, reduce feelings of anxiety and help people maintain their physical abilities as they age. Zhengâs badminton sessions are one example of how exercise can become a regular part of life without necessarily revolving around a gym or a strict fitness programme. Still, looking young is not a straightforward measure of health. Genetics, sun exposure, skin care and lifestyle also matters. The internetâs fascination with ageing He is 41 and the daughter is 21 Zhengâs story also reflects the internetâs enduring fascination with people who appear younger than their years. Social media frequently celebrates so-called age-defying looks, turning ordinary moments into conversations about skincare, fitness, diet and lifestyle. In this case, the setting made the contrast particularly striking. A father accompanying his daughter at her wedding is a familiar family milestone, but the relatively small age gap of 20 years and Zhengâs youthful appearance gave the moment an unexpected twist. Reports say the father and daughter are accustomed to being mistaken for siblings, making the wedding video another instance of something they have experienced in everyday life. The viral attention may have focused on his appearance, but the story also offers a reminder that wellbeing is often shaped by ordinary habits rather than dramatic transformations. Finding time for physical activity, getting sufficient sleep and learning to manage everyday stress can all contribute to a healthier life. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. title: Ban threat on para shooters for challenging PCI in court
text: Imag credit: X NEW DELHI: With Indiaâs Asian Para Games preparations already marred by selection disputes and court battles, the Paralympic Committee of India (PCI) has landed in another controversy over a para shooting policy that threatens athletes with lengthy bans for challenging its decisions in court. A clause in the PCI governing body-approved 2026-27 national selection policy for para shooting prescribes a three-year ban if a shooter or their parents initiate legal action against the association and the case is dismissed. A repeat offence could invite a lifetime ban, according to the 16-page policy, a copy of which is with TOI. Watch Harita Bhadra Exclusive | 2 Asian Games Medals, Now the 22.45s World Championships Chase âAny para shooters/coaches/parents going to the courts or taking any legal action against the association and further if the case is dismissed by the court, the para shooter would be banned for at least three years and in case of repeated offence, ban could go for lifetime as well,â the clause states. The provision raises questions about athletesâ right to seek judicial redress in selection disputes, potentially exposing para shooters to severe sporting sanctions for challenging the PCIâs decisions. A senior PCI official told TOI that the clause was damaging and should never have been included. The official said directions had been issued to amend the policy and that a corrigendum would be uploaded. However, since the policy was approved by the governing body, a formal amendment may be necessary. It is learnt that some shooters unhappy with their exclusion from the Asian Para Games squad refrained from approaching the courts for fear of being banned. Boccia dropped, contingent shrinks to 10 sports The controversy comes amid further reductions in Indiaâs contingent for the Games. After para fencing, boccia has become the latest discipline to be dropped, with the sports ministry withholding clearance for the two-member team of Sachin Chamaria and Anjali Devi. India, initially scheduled to compete in 12 sports, will now participate in 10. The ministry cleared 166 athletes late Monday evening, taking the delegationâs strength to 275, including 94 team officials and support staff and 15 contingent staff. The Games begin in Nagoya on Oct 18. Para athletics accounts for the largest share of the contingent, with 62 athletes, including 46 men, along with 36 support staff. Para shooting chief coach JP Nautiyal has not received clearance despite representations from nine of the 13 selected shooters. Jeevan L Rai and Rakesh Singh will oversee the team. Nautiyal has faced allegations of violating selection criteria and demanding kickbacks. Cyclistsâ hopes end with DRM The final Delegation Registration Meeting (DRM) in Nagoya on Monday has effectively closed the door on additional entries. Para cyclists awaiting court relief against their exclusion will miss the Games even if they secure a favourable order later. Only Arshad Shaik will compete, while six other cyclists selected by the Cycling Federation of India and the PCI were omitted for allegedly failing to meet the prescribed criteria. Baretha questions Suhasâ inclusion Para badminton player Chirag Baretha has questioned the last-minute inclusion of LY Suhas, citing his absence from national and international competition since the Paris Paralympics in 2024. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Baretha, a two-time Asian Para Games medallist, was excluded after the ministry ruled that he did not meet the selection criteria. âHow a player can be qualified and sanctioned in the events at the Asian Para Games, he has never played a single game in the events he is qualified. Arbitration in sports can be visibly seen with the sanction issued for upcoming Games,â Baretha wrote on X. Manisha Patel, Shashank Kumar, Ammu Beulah Mohan and Rachna Patel were also denied clearance by the ministry. title: Sports Ministry revises funding rules for federations, mandates advance selection policies
text: Union sports minister Mansukh Mandaviya NEW DELHI: National Sports Federations (NSFs) will have to publish athlete and coach selection policies well in advance of major international competitions, while those seeking to host international events in India will be eligible for financial assistance under revised Sports Ministry's guidelines aimed at strengthening the country's sporting ecosystem. The assistance scheme stands for the period of 2026-27 to 2030-31 (16th Finance Commission Cycle) at a total outlay of Rs 7,386.74 crore. Under the revised Scheme of Assistance to National Sports Federations (NSFs), selection policies must be announced at least one year before continental or world championships and at least two years before multi-sport events involving quota or qualifying systems. Watch Suchika Tariyal on her Asian Games bronze, childhood trauma, and never giving up | TOISA Spotlight The guidelines also provide for financial assistance to federations hosting international tournaments in India, with the amount determined by the scale and importance of the event, India's performance in the sport and the level of international participation. India are scheduled to host the 2030 Commonwealth Games in Ahmedabad and have also expressed interest in staging the 2036 Summer Olympics. Additionally, India has also submitted a formal Expression of Interest (EoI) to the Olympic Council of Asia to host the 2038 Asian Games in Ahmedabad. The changes form part of a broader framework covering athlete preparation, grassroots development, coaching, sports science and the administration of national federations. Selection policies and international event hosting The requirement to publish selection policies in advance is intended to establish a clear and transparent framework for choosing athletes and coaches for international competitions. It comes on the heels of controversies surrounding squads for the Commonwealth Games, the Asian Games and the Asian Para Games. The guidelines call on federations to ensure that their selection procedures are fair and publicly communicated within the stipulated timelines. The provision assumes particular significance for multi-sport events where athletes must navigate qualification systems and quota allocations. For international event hosting, the guidelines allow assistance for eligible tournaments conducted in India. The prescribed ceilings vary according to the category and scale of the competition, with certain world championships in Olympic sports eligible for assistance of up to Rs 50 crore. Proposals will be assessed by a designated committee, which will recommend assistance based on the event's requirements and the applicable conditions. The framework is intended to strengthen India's capacity to host prestigious international competitions and provide domestic athletes with greater opportunities to compete at home. Greater emphasis on grassroots development The guidelines require national sports federations to earmark at least 20% of their annual budget under the scheme for grassroots development through affiliated units. They also call for structured junior development programmes and measures to prevent early specialisation, age fraud and overtraining. Federations are expected to identify promising senior and junior athletes and strengthen their development pathways through coaching, specialised equipment and sports science support. Olympic Training Centres and coaching support The Ministry has also outlined plans for sport-specific Olympic Training Centres equipped with modern facilities, specialised equipment and sports science services. The centres are intended to reduce Indian athletes' reliance on overseas training facilities. Federations can engage foreign coaches and high-performance specialists within the prescribed funding framework. At least five Indian coaches are expected to remain with a foreign coach during the coaching assignment, with the objective of developing domestic expertise and reducing long-term dependence on overseas coaches. Performance-linked bonuses for foreign coaches may be capped at 20% of their annual salary. Medical support and financial oversight The guidelines require federations to establish sport-specific protocols for injury management and return to training. Proposals from federations that have not defined these protocols will not be considered for funding. Athletes are also required to undergo quarterly assessments covering medical condition, fitness, biomechanics and other relevant parameters. On expenditure, the scheme permits up to 10% of the funding provided to be allocated to administrative manpower and support. A separate provision allows expenditure of up to 2.5% of the annual scheme budget on specified administrative and legal expenses, including governance-related activities and the engagement of specialised professionals or interns. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines The guidelines also require federations to follow prescribed financial procedures for equipment procurement and submit utilisation certificates certified by a chartered accountant empanelled with the Comptroller and Auditor General. Support for indigenous sports and international cooperation The revised framework provides for assistance to promote indigenous and traditional sports internationally, including through competitions, international recognition and the establishment of federations in other countries. It also envisages cooperation with countries in the Global South by facilitating training opportunities for athletes and coaches at Indian high-performance centres. The measures collectively seek to strengthen the administration of national federations, improve athlete preparation and expand India's presence in international sport. Their impact will depend on implementation, including compliance with selection-policy deadlines, the delivery of planned training infrastructure and the effective use of public funding. title: Asian Para Games: Defending champion Shailesh Kumar ready for another big jump
text: Shailesh Kumar KOLKATA: There was a time when people in his village wondered what future awaited him. Unable to walk properly since childhood after being diagnosed with polio in his right leg, Shailesh Kumar, a resident of Islamnagar village in Biharâs Jamui district, often faced doubts about what he could achieve. Watch Suchika Tariyal on her Asian Games bronze, childhood trauma, and never giving up | TOISA Spotlight Today, the same people urge him to bring glory to the country, thanks to the success he has achieved in para-athletics. The T63 high jumper heads to the Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, as the defending champion, carrying not just expectations but also the confidence that comes from changing lives, including his own. âLife has changed significantly, both financially and socially. Earlier, people would wonder what I could achieve because I couldnât walk properly. Today, their mindset has changed. They see that a para athlete can represent the country and achieve success,â Shailesh told TOI ahead of the Games. Since winning gold with a Games record at the 2023 Asian Para Games in China, the 26-year-old has added several major titles to his rÃ©sumÃ©, including gold medals at 2025 World Para Athletics Championships and 2026 World Para Athletics Grand Prix. Training under close friend and coach Ronak Malik in Bengaluru since Jan 2025, the 26-year-old is now focused on defending his high jump title. He enters the competition after overcoming knee issues that troubled him earlier in the season, but Malik is confident his ward can retain the gold medal in high jump and also contend for a podium finish in long jump. âIf everything goes according to plan, he has the potential to win medals in both events. Gold is definitely a possibility. He has already set records at the World Championships and Asian Championships and has achieved personal best performances,â said Malik, a former national-level high jumper. Training a para athlete requires a different approach from coaching able-bodied athletes, and Malik regularly consults experienced jump coach GV Gaonkar to fine-tune Shaileshâs programme. While Malikâs guidance has proved hugely beneficial on the field, their friendship has also played a key role in Shaileshâs resurgence, particularly after Paris Paralympics, where he narrowly missed a medal and finished fourth. âAfter beginning his training in Sonipat in 2019, Shailesh moved to SAI Gandhinagar under coach Vinod Chauhan. Unfortunately, Vinod sir passed away in a road accident in April 2023. It was a difficult phase for Shailesh and he wasnât in the best frame of mind going into the Paris Paralympics,â Malik said. It was after Chauhanâs death that Shailesh reconnected with Malik. Together, they are now targeting success not only at the Asian Para Games but also at next yearâs World Championships and, ultimately, the Paralympics in LA. But as Malik says, none of it would have been possible without the discipline and dedication of Shailesh, who chose sport even as his family hoped he would focus on studies and secure a stable job. âPeople had different opinions about me, so I wanted to do something different. My family stood by me throughout and today they are very proud,â said Shailesh. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines But as he prepares for another Asian Para Games campaign, he remains determined not to be weighed down by expectations. âI am the defending champion, but I am an athlete first. When you represent the country there is pressure, but I try to keep it to a minimum and perform freely,â he said. For Shailesh, though, the biggest motivation remains the journey itself. From being doubted because of his disability to becoming a champion who inspires others, he believes para-sports have given him a life he never imagined, and he intends to make the most of it.
