title: India's golden Saturday at Asian Games: Hockey, cricket, wrestling, golf and archery deliver golds
text: India's medal tally now stands at 85 medals â 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze. (Image credit: Agencies) India produced one of their biggest medal hauls of the Asian Games on Saturday, with gold medals coming in men's hockey, T20 cricket, wrestling, golf and archery. The men's hockey team capped the day by beating Malaysia 5-1 in the final to retain their Asian Games title and book a place at the 2028 Olympics. India's medal tally now stands at 85 medals - 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze. Hockey delivers another golden moment Captain Harmanpreet Singh led from the front with two goals as India beat Malaysia 5-1 to win the men's hockey gold. Harmanpreet scored in the 11th and 57th minutes, while Jugraj Singh, Hardik Singh and Shilanand Lakra also found the net. Malaysia's only goal came from Shello Silverius in the 14th minute. Harmanpreet finished as the tournament's top scorer with 12 goals. India also earned 14 penalty corners compared to Malaysia's two. Watch Asmita Dey Unfiltered: Favourite Food, Match-Day Music & More | Rapid Fire | TOISA The victory gave India their fifth Asian Games men's hockey gold, after previous triumphs in 1966, 1998, 2014 and 2022. India also became only the second country after Pakistan to win back-to-back Asian Games men's hockey golds. Harmanpreet became the first Indian men's hockey captain to lead the team to two Asian Games gold medals. The triumph came a day after the women's team beat defending champions China 1-0 to win their first Asian Games gold in 44 years and secure an Olympic berth. It was the first time that both Indian hockey teams finished on top of the podium at the same Asian Games. Aman wins wrestling gold, Antim settles for silver Aman Sehrawat upgraded his bronze from the 2023 Hangzhou Games to gold by beating North Korea's reigning world champion Chong Song Han 10-7 in the men's 57kg final. The 23-year-old was initially frustrated by Han's defensive approach but took control after being put on the clock. He built a 6-1 lead before Han fought back to move 7-6 ahead. Aman responded with two more takedowns to seal the gold. It was India's second wrestling gold of the Games after Sujeet Kalkal's title on Friday. Antim Panghal, meanwhile, had to settle for silver after losing 1-9 to Japan's 2024 world champion Mei Miyooka in the women's 53kg final. Antim could not find a way through Miyooka's defence and attack. Deepak Punia added a bronze in the men's 97kg category after beating Mongolia's Gankhuyang Ganbataar 2-1. India finished the wrestling competition with six medals â two gold, two silver and two bronze. Abhishek, Tilak power India to cricket gold India retained their Asian Games men's T20 cricket title after beating Pakistan by 19 runs in the final. Abhishek Sharma smashed 61 off 28 balls, hitting seven sixes, while Tilak Varma produced an unbeaten 51 off 22 balls as India posted 211/6. Pakistan fought back through Hasan Nawaz, who scored 96 off 51 balls, but India held their nerve to restrict them to 192/6. The victory also extended India's head-to-head dominance over Pakistan to 6-0 since the start of the 2024 T20 World Cup. Pranavi makes history in golf Pranavi Urs became the first Indian woman to win an individual Asian Games golf gold. The 23-year-old held her nerve despite a triple bogey on the third hole and recovered with three birdies to finish the final round at even-par 70. She finished at 15-under 265, one stroke ahead of China's Yin Ruoning. Pranavi's gold also helped India win the women's team silver, with Aditi Ashok and Diksha Dagar completing the team. It rounded off India's best Asian Games golf performance in 44 years. Kumkum creates recurve archery history Teenager Kumkum Mohod produced another landmark performance by winning India's first-ever Asian Games individual women's recurve gold. Her run to the final also secured an individual quota place for India at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. The quota belongs to India, while the final selection of the athlete will be decided through the federation's trials. Neeraj wins men's recurve bronze Neeraj Chauhan completed a memorable day for Indian recurve archery by beating compatriot Dhiraj Bommadevara 6-4 for the men's individual bronze. Neeraj fought back from 2-4 down before winning the deciding set. He became only the second Indian male archer after Tarundeep Rai to win an individual recurve medal at the Asian Games. title: The freedom to roam
text: The Chinnakkanal tragedy reveals how encroachments and blocked elephant passages endanger both wildlife and communities living alongside it By: Dr TV Sajeev When a wild tusker killed a tribal farmer in Idukki , his neighbours did not just ask for compensation. They demanded the removal of illegal resort fences blocking the elephantâs pathâand proved a vital ecological truth: Wildlife needs the freedom to move. On the morning of Sept 23, 2026, a 47-year-old tribal farmer from the Panthadikkalam settlement near Chinnakkanal in Keralaâs Idukki district stepped onto the road outside his workplace shed. The previous night, the formidable wild tusker locally known as Chakkakomban had entered his farmland, prompting the forest departmentâs rapid response team (RRT) to warn residents to stay indoors. Believing the elephant had retreated into the forest by daybreak, the farmer ventured out. Instead, he walked straight into Chakkakomban. Before he could flee, the tusker charged and trampled him to death. In the hills of the Western Ghats, such tragedies usually follow a familiar bureaucratic script: Officials arrive, announce modest solatium, promise to chase the animal back into the woods, and remove the body. At Panthadikkalam, however, the victimâs neighbours and relatives refused to let the authorities take his body. For five hours, tribal residents held their ground. Alongside compensation and livelihood support for his bereaved family, they made a demand that cut to the ecological core of the crisis: Dismantle the illegal solar fences, steel cables, and resort enclosures that had choked the elephantsâ traditional movement routes. That five-hour protest at Panthadikkalam should force a national reckoning with how India understands humanâelephant conflict. We habitually frame this crisis as a story of wild animals trespassing into human settlements. Yet as the events in Chinnakkanal reveal, the conflict is equally a consequence of human infrastructure that fragments habitats, severs historic migratory corridors, and traps wide-ranging animals inside lethal cul-de-sacs. A Landscape Carved into Traps To understand why Chinnakkanal has become a crucible of humanâelephant conflict, one must look at both the casualty ledger and the map. Official data compiled by the Idukki district administration shows that between 2015â16 and 2026â27, humanâwildlife conflict across the district claimed 81 human lives and left 486 people injured. Crucially, while annual fatalities hovered between four and ten over the decade, non-fatal encounters surged dramatically in the years immediately preceding the Chinnakkanal interventionârising from 28 injuries in 2019â20 to 79 in 2023â24 (when deaths peaked at 10) and 103 injuries in 2024â25. Within the first nine months of 2026â27 alone, five people were killed and 13 injured in the district. In ecology, a sharp spike in human injuries alongside persistent fatalities is a classic symptom of spatial compression: Humans and elephants are colliding with growing frequency in shrinking, overlapping spaces. Chinnakkanal panchayatâa 66.74-square-kilometre mosaic of tea estates, eucalyptus coupes, cardamom plantations, tribal hamlets, and booming high-range tourism resortsâsits wedged between the Anamalai hills and the Mathikettan Shola National Park. Over recent years, private resorts and estate encroachers erected a labyrinth of high-voltage solar fences, trenches, and even heavy steel wire ropes strung between giant trees across govt and revenue land. According to the forest department, three primary natural elephant passages in Chinnakkanal had been obstructed: The route linking MathikettanâThondimala to Chinnakkanal, the passage from Shankarapandyamettu to the PPK Estate, and the link between Devikulam and Old Devikulam. Because of these barriers, Chakkakomban had been unable to exit the Chinnakkanal pocket for a year and a half. The famous 2023 capture and translocation of another Chinnakkanal tusker, Arikomban, had already shown the futility of removing individual bulls without fixing a broken landscape. Blocked from returning to the contiguous forests of Mathikettan Shola, Chakkakomban was effectively corralled among tribal settlements and estate lanesâturning every dusk and dawn into a game of Russian roulette for local residents. The Intervention and the Proof in the Footprints Confronted with the Panthadikkalam protest on Sept 23, Idukki district collector, acting as chairperson of the district disaster management authority (DDMA), ordered the forest department and local authorities to clear unauthorised structures, steel ropes tied to trees, and illegal fences obstructing elephant movement paths in identified hotspots. Five days later, on Sept 28, the collector issued a companion advisory through plantation inspectors in Munnar, Peermade, and Udumbanchola, instructing estates in conflict hotspots to halt worker movement and plantation operations between 6pm and 6am when RRT warnings are active. A four-member expert committee was also appointed to recommend long-term solutions. Acting on the directive, forest department teams dismantled an unauthorised solar fence installed on encroached revenue land near the RS Estate close to Panthadikkalam, cleared an encroachment blocking elephant movement near the Anayirankal reservoir, and removed a barrier along National Highway-85 between Mathikettan and Chinnakkanal. What happened next offered a striking field test of the tribal residentsâ ecological hypothesis. As has been documented, once the unauthorised fence near RS Estate was dismantled, Chakkakombanâwhich had been stuck in the human-dominated pocket for 18 monthsâwalked straight through the reopened natural passage into the Mathikettan Shola National Park. In the immediate aftermath of the barrierâs removal through early Oct, officials reported a halt to the daily conflict encounters that had plagued the settlement. Scientific honesty requires us not to overstate this outcome as a permanent âzero-conflictâ miracle. The initial post-intervention observation window was barely a fortnight, tracked through field sightings rather than satellite telemetry, and by Oct 10 the forest department had to issue legal notices to 16 violators who brazenly re-erected illegal fences and solar barriers across the Chinnakkanal corridor. Yet Chakkakombanâs immediate departure into Mathikettan Shola once the fence came down demonstrated a vital mechanism: The tusker was not lingering in Panthadikkalam out of malice, but because its exit had been walled off. How Misinformation Clouded an Ecological Debate Rather than welcoming the reopening of a blocked passage, powerful commercial, agrarian, and political lobbies erupted in protest, fuelled by a wave of social-media distortion. Three misleading narratives dominated the backlash. First, viral social-media posts, local merchant associations, and political leadersâincluding the local member of Parliamentâclaimed or expressed alarm that the collector had imposed a blanket 6pm to 6am night curfew across the entire Idukki district, violating citizensâ fundamental freedom of movement. On Sept 30 and Oct 2, the district collector and a local MLA publicly refuted this falsehood: The Sept 28 letter to plantation inspectors was strictly a safety advisory limited to designated conflict-hotspot plantations during active wildlife alerts, with zero restrictions on public night travel in the district. Second, leaders of major political parties, local MLAs, various farmer associations, and representatives of local religious bodies alleged that the administration was demolishing protective solar fences on farmersâ legal patta (title-deed) lands while locking citizens indoors. Both the collector and the govt chief whip clarified that farmers retain every right to protect legal patta holdings with solar fences; the demolition drive targeted only illegal fences, steel tree-ropes, and unauthorised resort structures on encroached govt and forest land. Third, a district-level leader of a major political party argued that the collector was inventing ânon-existent elephant corridors,â pointing out that the Union govtâs 2023 âElephant Corridors of Indiaâ report lists 150 corridors nationally (and six in Kerala) but none in Idukki. It was argued that elephants enter Chinnakkanal solely because forests lack food and water. While it is true that the 2023 central inventory does not list a macro-corridor in Idukki, using that administrative omission to deny local elephant movement routes is ecologically fallacious. Macro-surveys map narrow bottlenecks between major forest divisions; within a fragmented forest-plantation mosaic like MunnarâChinnakkanal, elephants rely on fine-scale functional passages to move between shola patches, grasslands, and reservoirs. The forest minister stood at the forefront to demolish this false narrative. The Science of the Freedom to Move Decades of peer-reviewed research on Asian elephants (Elephas maximus) explain why blocking these local passages is disastrous. An elephantâs home range in the Western Ghats spans 100 to over 600 square kilometres. Elephants do not use space randomly; they follow multigenerational spatial memory along topographical contoursâgentle valley gradients, saddle points, and riparian stripsâto track seasonal forage, minerals, and water while avoiding human disturbance. As famously said, elephants are not forest species, they are landscape species. Not every fence is harmful. Properly designed community solar fencing that rings a compact human hamlet or legal homesteadâwhile leaving adjacent valley passages openâcan protect lives and crops. Conflict explodes when resorts, large estates, and encroachers erect uncoordinated, linear barriers across valley floors and ridge saddles. In landscape ecology, this creates a âfunnelâ or âpinballâ effect: An elephant encountering an electrified wire or steel cable along its traditional path is deflected laterally into the path of least resistanceâwhich is frequently a public road or an unfenced tribal settlement like Panthadikkalam. This brings us to a deeper ecological truth that conventional wildlife management routinely misses. Public debate in Kerala endlessly repeats the clichÃ© that elephants leave the forest only because they lack food and water inside. Invasive weeds like Senna spectabilis and Lantana camara, along with colonial eucalyptus monocultures, have undoubtedly degraded forage quality in our forests. Yet even where food and water exist, a wide-ranging herbivore cannot survive in a gilded cage. Elephants require landscape connectivity to rotate across seasonal feeding grounds, prevent localised overbrowsing, regulate social and musth dynamics among bulls, and escape human stressors. Providing food patches or waterholes inside a fragmented pocket cannot compensate for severing the corridors that allow animals to navigate the wider landscape. Two Lessons from Panthadikkalam The Chinnakkanal intervention is still fragile, as the rapid re-erection of barriers by 16 violators in Oct shows. Yet those few days in late Sept offer two indispensable lessons for Indian conservation policy. First, we must learn from the people who know the forest. When political parties and commercial lobbies demanded that wildlife be âconfined to forest limitsâ or translocated, it was the tribal residents of Panthadikkalam who stood beside their neighbourâs body and diagnosed the actual structural cause of their vulnerability. Their lived familiarity with terrain and animal behaviour identified what years of administrative inertia had overlooked: That illegal resort barriers were trapping Chakkakomban in their midst. Indigenous and local ecological knowledge should not require a funeral and a five-hour road blockade to be heard; tribal communities must have a permanent, statutory seat at the table when land-use and conflict-mitigation decisions are made. Second, wildlife needs room to move. You can fill a forest with waterholes and bamboo, and you can ring every estate with high-voltage wire, but a landscape stripped of connectivity will always bleed conflict. For a creature built by evolution to walk across mountain ranges, food and water keep the body alive, but movement is what keeps the ecosystem whole. Conservation is not the art of walling nature into shrinking reservations; it is the courage to step back, pull down our illegal fences, and restore to wild creatures the ancient freedom to move. (The author is chief scientist at Kerala Forest Research Institute. text: Para-badminton player Pramod Bhagat, para-archer Rakesh Kumar, para table tennis player Bhavina Patel, and others during the send-off ceremony. (PTI Photo) NEW DELHI: The Sports Ministry has dropped under-fire para-shooting coach Jai Prakash Nautiyal from India's contingent for the Asian Para Games 2026, approving a 166-athlete squad for the continental event in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, amid a controversy-marred selection process that triggered protests by shooters and cyclists. The Games are scheduled to begin on October 18, with India set to compete across 10 disciplines. Long-serving national coach Jeevan L Rai has replaced Nautiyal in the squad following allegations of irregularities in the selection process. Watch Asian Games gold medallist Sujeet Kalkal on fatherâs influence and how he turned final around As per a PTI report, Nautiyal had faced allegations of not following established selection criteria and demanding kickbacks in exchange for selecting shooters. Several athletes protested outside the Sports Authority of India (SAI) headquarters, demanding his removal and an investigation into the charges. The aggrieved shooters also met Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya to present their grievances after attempting to disrupt the contingent's send-off ceremony last week. With 166 athletes approved, India will have a total contingent of 275, including 94 team officials and support staff and 15 contingent staff members. Controversial shooting selection; cyclists' protest fails to change squad The 13-member shooting squad, which has been at the centre of the controversy, features Paralympic gold medallist Avani Lekhara and Mona Agarwal, among others. Agarwal recently secured a silver medal at the World Championships in Korea, earning India a quota place for the 2028 Los Angeles Paralympics. The Ministry has also resisted pressure for last-minute additions to the cycling squad despite protests by omitted athletes. Only Paralympian Arshad Shaik was approved from among those in contention, having comfortably met the selection criteria. Six other cyclists had been selected by the Cycling Federation of India and the Paralympic Committee of India (PCI), but were subsequently left out for failing to satisfy the prescribed criteria. The decision comes amid questions over the selection process, with athletes seeking greater transparency in the composition of the Indian contingent. Sheetal Devi, Bhavina Patel among India's medal hopes Para-athletics forms the biggest part of India's contingent, with 62 athletes, including 46 men, and a support staff of 36. World Championships medallist Simran, a visually impaired sprinter, is also part of the squad. After her previous guide, Umar Saifi, was caught in a doping case, she will compete with a new guide, Shivam. Former world No. 1 and Tokyo Paralympic gold medallist Pramod Bhagat and former Paralympic silver medallist Suhas Yathiraj headline the badminton squad, which has been allocated 11 support staff members. title: AI is changing Asiaâs jobs market: What it means for India
text: AI is changing Asiaâs jobs market Asia has a tricky tightrope to walk as artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes its job market: creating enough jobs for a growing workforce while ensuring workers donât get left behind as technology changes the rules of the game. The challenge is particularly significant for India, Indonesia and the Philippines, where expanding working-age populations need productive employment even as AI transforms industries expected to provide those jobs. The International Monetary Fundâs (IMF) October 2026 Regional Economic Outlook: Asia and Pacific points to a shift in employer demand since the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022. An analysis of approximately 40 million online job postings across 19 Asian economies found that demand for jobs more exposed to AI had declined by nearly 10 per cent compared with occupations less exposed to the technology. However, the trend does not suggest that AI is simply eliminating jobs. The report found that the decline in demand for workers in highly exposed occupations appears to have stabilised, despite significant advances in AI capabilities. Part of the changing employment landscape is being driven by demand for new technical skills. Prompt engineering, retrieval-augmented generation and AI agent development are among the areas creating new employment opportunities. Employers are looking for people who can put AI to practical use in business operations, integrate it into existing processes and improve productivity. Businesses using AI see stronger labour demand How companies use the technology is emerging as an important factor in determining its employment impact. Around 6 per cent of firms in Asia explicitly seek AI skills in their job advertisements, according to the IMF report, highlighting the uneven pace of adoption across businesses. Firms that have adopted AI are seeing stronger growth in labour demand than those that have not. This pattern also holds for occupations highly exposed to automation, indicating that the technology can support human capabilities even as it reduces the demand for certain tasks. The employment effects of AI, therefore, vary according to how businesses incorporate it into their operations. Alongside the decline in demand for some AI-exposed occupations, the report identifies stronger labour demand growth among firms adopting the technology. Lower AI exposure may not be an advantage for India in the long run Emerging Asian economies, including India, may initially face less disruption because many workers are employed in agriculture and other sectors less exposed to AI. But this could create a longer-term difficulty if the technology makes it harder for workers to move into higher-productivity manufacturing and services. For countries with growing working-age populations, the challenge extends beyond protecting existing jobs. They must also create productive employment opportunities and enable workers to move into occupations that can support higher productivity. India, Indonesia and the Philippines will need to navigate these pressures as AI reshapes the sectors expected to employ their expanding workforces. The pace and effectiveness of adaptation by businesses, workers and economies will be crucial to how this transition unfolds. Skills and preparedness will shape the employment outlook The IMF report places the emphasis on preparing workers and institutions for the changes ahead, rather than focusing solely on the adoption of AI. Education reform, reskilling, digital infrastructure and stronger labour-market institutions will be central to this effort. Businesses will need to invest in workers as they integrate AI into their operations. Governments, meanwhile, will have to prepare younger populations for changing skill requirements and evolving occupational opportunities. Asiaâs ability to manage the transition will depend on how well it combines technological progress with workforce preparedness. Timely investment in skills could help the region use AI-driven changes to support productivity, innovation and sustainable employment, while keeping inclusive growth within reach. title: 'Are they so afraid of me?': Bhagwant Mann hits out at Centre after HC clears France trip
text: Bhagwant Mann said he wanted to travel to bring investment to Punjab. CHANDIGARH: The Punjab and Haryana high court on Friday allowed Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann âs plea challenging the Centreâs decision to deny political clearance for his proposed visit to France to attend SIAL Paris 2026, an international food trade exhibition, news agency PTI reported. The Punjab government had approached the court seeking the quashing of the Ministry of External Affairsâ (MEA) decision, describing it as âarbitraryâ. The visit was scheduled from October 15 to 21, while the exhibition is being held from October 17 to 21. Punjab additional advocate general Ferry Sofat, one of the lawyers representing the state government, said a bench of Justice Tribhuvan Dahiya allowed the plea after hearing the matter. A detailed order is awaited, he said, according to PTI. Sofat said the Centre, in its reply before the court, cited two reasons for denying clearance: security concerns and the absence of an invitation for the chief minister. The state government submitted that the invitation had been attached when it applied for permission. On the security issue, the government argued that it had sought clearance well in advance and that the Centre could not rely on this ground to deny permission, Sofat said. In its 56-page petition, the Punjab government stated that Mannâs visit was proposed in connection with the participation of the Punjab State Cooperative Supply and Marketing Federation Ltd. (MARKFED), the stateâs apex cooperative, in SIAL Paris 2026. According to the petition, MARKFEDâs stall had been allotted under the APEDA India Pavilion by the Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA), a body under the Union Ministry of Commerce and Industry. The plea also stated that the Indian Mission in France had been consulted, administrative approval and cadre clearance had been granted, and MARKFED would bear the entire expenditure for the visit. Speaking to reporters in Phillaur, Mann expressed gratitude to the high court for allowing him to travel. He questioned why he had to approach the court to obtain permission for a visit intended to promote Punjabâs interests. âThe high court has granted me permission to go... But why should we have to obtain permission from the high court for this? Do we now have to approach the court for everything?â he said. Criticising the Centreâs decision, Mann contrasted the restrictions on his travel with the Prime Ministerâs overseas visits. He said he wanted to travel to bring investment to Punjab and participate in a food trade exhibition where MARKFED would set up a stall, rather than attend a political rally. âWe are going there to promote Punjabâs interests, not to hold a political rally,â Mann said. He also questioned the denial of permission for his proposed visit to Japan last month for hockey events at the Asian Games. Mann said officials were granted permission to travel, while he was not, and reiterated that his proposed overseas engagements were connected to Punjabâs interests. title: Asian Games: Japan signs off, Doha takes the 2030 baton
text: Qatar will host the 2030 Games. (Image credit: X) NAGOYA: It has been a testing three weeks for Japan. Accommodation woes, transport and logistical nightmares, mismanagement and weather that refused to cooperate â the challenges the Asian Games organisers faced were plenty. Yet, as the Games drew to a close, there was enough to celebrate. Records were broken, medals won, friendships forged and, on Sunday, the baton was passed to Doha as Japan bid farewell to representatives from 44 countries at the Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Watch Asmita Dey Unfiltered: Favourite Food, Match-Day Music & More | Rapid Fire | TOISA India finished fourth in the medals tally, while China topped the standings by a distance, collecting 341 medals, including an astonishing 169 golds. Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) president Sheikh Joaan bin Hamad Al Thani described the Games as an event that would âshape the next generation of Asian sportâ before welcoming the next chapter to his home country. âTonight, as we lower the flag on Aichi-Nagoya 2026, we close these Games, but we raise the bar for Asian sport,â he said. âOver 350 records have been broken, including more than 50 world records. Forty out of the 45 NOCs achieved medals. This is a record for our Asian Games,â the 40-year-old added. In a symbolic handover to the next hosts, Qatarâs equestrian rider Jassim Al Kuwari, entered the stadium on horseback and received the OCA flag on behalf of Doha, which will host the 2030 Games. title: 'Your success is not just yours': PM Modi meets Asian Games medal-winners, lauds India's sporting achievements
text: Prime Minister Narendra Modi is presented a jersey by Indian women's cricket team captain Harmanpreet Kaur during an interaction programme with the athletes of the Asian Games 2026, in New Delhi. (PTI Photo) Present at the event were the entire men's T20 team, led by Shreyas Iyer, which played the fourth T20I against West Indies on Wednesday evening and is scheduled to play the fifth and final match against them in Bengaluru on Saturday, along with the women's team, which is due to face Zimbabwe in a T20I in Raipur on Friday, as Prime Minister Narendra Modi met India's Asian Games medal-winners at the Major Dhyan Chand Stadium in New Delhi on Thursday. title: âOlympic gold jeetna haiâ: Kumkum Mohodâs big dream after ending Koreaâs stranglehold in archery at Asian Games 2026
text: Kumkum Mohod NEW DELHI: For years, Kumkum Mohod had watched South Korean archers closely, studying their technique and trying to understand what made them so dominant in recurve archery. She observed their movements, learnt from their approach and looked at the qualities that had made them role models for young Indian archers like her. But when the 17-year-old stood on the shooting line at the Asian Games , just seconds away from releasing her arrow, she had a message for herself: the Koreans were not unbeatable. Watch Harita Bhadra Exclusive | 2 Asian Games Medals, Now the 22.45s World Championships Chase âMaine match shuru hone se khud ko bol diya tha, woh 10 maarte hain, to mujhe bhi 10 hi maarna hai [I told myself before the match began: they shoot 10s too, so I have to shoot 10s as well],â Asian Games 2026 gold medallist archer Kumkum Mohod told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interview. The 17-year-old made history by winning the womenâs individual recurve gold at the Asian Games, beating the Republic of Koreaâs Oh Yejin in the final. In doing so, she ended South Koreaâs hold on the individual recurve gold at the Games and helped India secure a quota place for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics. Before leaving for Aichi-Nagoya, Kumkum had already imagined herself standing on the top of the podium. She had also visualised beating her inspiration, South Koreaâs Kang Chaeyoung, whom she eventually defeated in the quarterfinals on her way to the historic gold. Kumkum became the first Indian to win an individual recurve gold at the Asian Games. She also won gold in the womenâs recurve team event and silver in the mixed team event with Dhiraj Bommadevara, finishing the Games with three medals. âUntil now, no one had managed to do it. But we Indians have done it. We have put the Koreans on a pedestal, as if they are the only ones who can do it and hit those scores. Before the match began, I told myself that they shoot 10s too, and we have to shoot 10s as well,â she said. Kumkum Mohod Manifestation: âI had been visualising this for a yearâ For Kumkum, the feeling of becoming an Asian Games champion is still sinking in. The young archer said the result did not come as a complete surprise because she had been visualising the moment for a year, even before she stepped onto the field in Japan. For a year leading up to the Asian Games, she repeated the same words five times before going to sleep: âKumkum, Asian Games gold jeetna haiâ (Kumkum, you have to win Asian Games gold). She would then say âHare Krishnaâ, reflecting her devotion to Lord Krishna. Her belief was tested against some of the world's best archers. Kumkum defeated South Koreaâs reigning world champion and Olympic medallist Kang Chaeyoung 6-3 in the quarterfinals before beating Chinaâs Zhu Jingyi 6-2 in the semifinals. In the final, she held her nerve against South Koreaâs Oh Yejin. The contest ended 5-5 after five sets, forcing a shoot-off. Oh shot an eight, while Kumkum hit a 10 to seal the gold medal. Kumkum had been trailing during the match and needed to win the fifth set to stay in contention. She responded by shooting a perfect 30 to force the shoot-off before producing the decisive 10. âThe final went really well. I was trailing, but I remained strong. I believed in myself and knew I could do it because I had been visualising this for the past year. I kept imagining that I would face Kang in a match and that it would be a final,â Kumkum said. When Oh shot an eight in the shoot-off, Kumkum had to focus on her own shot rather than the possibility of winning. She knew she had to deliver, regardless of what her opponent had scored. âI had made up my mind that day that I had to prove myself. My first thought was, âKumkum, you still have to shoot a good shot.â Even if she had shot a 10, I was very confident at that moment,â she said. âI enjoyed that moment while shooting. There is always some pressure, but I tried to reduce it. Anyone who says there is no pressure is absolutely wrong. Sport is about nerves and thrilling moments. There is always adrenaline, and you have to overcome it. The person who manages to do that wins,â she said. Kumkum Mohod (AP Photo) Road to the final: Learning from the best, then beating her Kumkum's journey to the gold medal included victories over some of the world's leading archers. But one of the most memorable moments for her was beating Kang, an archer she had admired and learnt from since the beginning of her career. Kang had been Kumkum's inspiration because of her technique, focus, composure and ability to deliver under pressure. Kumkum paid particular attention to her release and follow-through, as well as the way she maintained her technique in crucial moments. At the Asian Games, however, the young Indian found herself competing against the very archer she had looked up to for years - and came out on top. âKangâs shooting technique is very good. Her release is excellent, and she does not drop her bow after the follow-through. Her shooting is very strong,â Kumkum said. So, the victory carried special meaning. After the match, Kumkum exchanged a high-five with her opponent and told her, âGood shooting, good shooting.â Kang smiled and congratulated her. âI have learnt a lot from her, and I was happy. She is a legend of the sport. She has made her country proud by winning medals, and now I have done the same. I am proud that I have made my country proud,â Kumkum said. âMy family always supported meâ Behind Kumkumâs success is a family that continued to believe in her, even when her performances were not going as planned. Her father, Anil Mohod, runs a business making sweet boxes. As Kumkum was good at academics, her father initially wanted her to focus on her studies. But when he saw her growing interest in archery, her family supported her sporting ambitions while ensuring that she did not neglect her education. Kumkum is the coupleâs only child and is currently in Class 12. âI joined archery, and within six months, I won a medal. After that, I learnt about the Olympics and understood what the sport could lead to. I also learnt that India had not won a medal in this event. My interest grew, and I started working harder,â she said. Her familyâs faith in her remained strong even during difficult periods. âWhen I was not doing well, my family told me that I could do it. They have supported me a lot, and I never faced any problems because of them,â she said. Now, following her historic achievement, the Mohod household has been welcoming a steady stream of visitors. Neighbours, friends, relatives, sports associations and fellow sportspersons have been arriving to congratulate the family. Kumkum said the celebrations have kept everyone busy, with little time to rest. âIt feels like a wedding atmosphere at home. People keep coming and going, and we are hardly getting any sleep. All thanks to Krishna ji,â she said. Gold medallist India's Kumkum Anil Mohod, Ankita Bhakat and Kirti celebrate on the podium during the victory ceremony. (Reuters Photo) Beyond archery: Drawing, crafts and a dream before sleep Away from the archery range, Kumkum enjoys spending time with a paintbrush and a colour palette. Drawing and craftwork are among her favourite hobbies, giving her a break from the demands of training and competition. âI like drawing and crafting. I also enjoy making things with my hands,â she said. She also enjoys watching television shows and films. Her favourites include Taarak Mehta Ka Ooltah Chashmah and sports-based films such as Dangal, Mary Kom, Ghoomer and Bhaag Milkha Bhaag. Unlike many teenagers, Kumkum has never had Facebook or Instagram accounts. She also disabled YouTube a few months before the Asian Games. Drawing, craftwork and reading are among the activities she enjoys away from the range. âI never had Facebook or Instagram. I also disabled YouTube a few months before the Asian Games. My crafts, drawing and reading books help me a lot,â she said. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines The ultimate dream: Olympic gold Kumkum has already achieved a major milestone by winning three medals at the Asian Games and helping India secure a quota place for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics. But she has a bigger dream â winning India's first Olympic gold medal in archery. The words she repeated before going to sleep for a year - âKumkum, Asian Games gold jeetna haiâ - now reflect a new ambition: âKumkum, Olympic gold jeetna hai.â At home, a small message on the wall serves as a reminder of what she wants to achieve. âLA 2028 gold is the target. That is the dream. I do not want to think too far ahead just yet, but that is the target. I will work hard for it and strengthen myself mentally,â Kumkum signed off. title: Asian Games 2026 India medal winners: Full list of athletes and medals till October 3
text: India's women's hockey team clinch Gold(IANS) Indiaâs medal-winning campaign at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games 2026 has reached 80 medals, with the contingent winning 18 gold, 26 silver and 36 bronze medals. India are currently fifth in the overall medal standings. Indiaâs medal tally received a major boost over the last two days, with the contingent adding gold medals across boxing, wrestling, archery, hockey and golf. Lovlina Borgohain, Parveen Hooda, Ankush Panghal, Sujeet Kalkal, the Indian womenâs hockey team, Kumkum Mohod and Pranavi Urs have all contributed gold medals to Indiaâs latest surge. Kumkum also won silver alongside Dhiraj Bommadevara in the mixed recurve team event, while Indiaâs womenâs golf team of Pranavi Urs, Aditi Ashok and Diksha Dagar secured silver. title: Hokato and Soman chase Asian Para Games gold
text: (From left) Soman Rana with Hokato Hotozhe Sema and coach Rakesh Rawat KOLKATA: Nagalandâs Hokato Hotozhe Sema heads into the Para Asian Games carrying both confidence and a touch of uncertainty. The world No. 2 shot putter in the F57 category was in good shape before an injury disrupted his preparations. âIt was a minor injury near the hip region. I did the required exercises and itâs fine now. I am confident of achieving my personal best,â said the Paris Paralympics bronze medallist. While he may not have had the smoothest build-up to the Games, 2026 has still been a memorable year for Hokato. The 42-year-old became world No. 1 in his category and also set a national record with a massive throw of 15.21m at the Indian Open Para Athletics Championships in Bengaluru. But Hokato knows that if he is to stand atop the podium, he may have to get past a familiar face: Soman Rana. Ranked world No. 3, 43-year-old Soman Rana arrives at the Asian Para Games as the reigning Commonwealth Games champion and a two-time World Championships silver medallist, having finished runner-up in 2024 and 2025. The pair have trained together at the Army Paralympic Node in Pune since 2017 under coach Rakesh Rawat, developing both a strong friendship and a fierce rivalry. âWeâre very close friends. We eat together, train together and spend a lot of time together. Our coordination is excellent,â said Soman, who suffered a mine blast injury while serving with the 2/8 Gorkha Rifles along the Line of Control in Jammu & Kashmir on Dec 1, 2006. For Hokato that friendship comes with an added competitive edge. âThere is definitely a lot of competitiveness. We train together and help each other improve, but once competition starts, everyone wants to win,â he said. Rawat believes that rivalry has been one of the biggest reasons behind their development on the international stage. âThey motivate each other a great deal,â Rawat said. âTraining together gives them valuable experience. They are friends and support each other, but once competition begins, friendship takes a back seat and they become rivals. The one who performs best on the day wins.â The coach expects both throwers to be in contention for medals and insists there is little to separate them. âThe rivalry between them has helped both improve. They are very closely matched. On the day, it could go either way,â he said. Soman agrees, although his Commonwealth Games gold is likely to provide an added boost. âThe gold gave me a lot of confidence. But Iâve been in this sport for many years. My confidence was already there and winning the medal only strengthened it,â he said. While both athletes believe a podium finish is within reach, neither is willing to predict who will come out on top. For Hokato, however, a gold medal would carry special significance. Since winning bronze in Paris, the road has not been easy. His father passed away last Dec, while he has also been overseeing the construction of a house in his village of P. Vihoto in Nagaland and supporting his daughter, who recently began an MBA programme in Pune. Yet, despite the setbacks, Hokato has remained focused on recovery and training. âRecovery is crucial. If you donât recover properly, thereâs no point competing. You can travel all that way and still return empty-handed,â he said. Now, he is eager to return to competition and renew his rivalry with Soman on one of para athleticsâ biggest stages. For India, it could be an ideal scenario: two close friends pushing each other every day in training before battling for continental glory when it matters most. title: Major team overhaul ahead of 2028 Olympics: RP Singh
text: RP Singh Lucknow: Following Indiaâs gold-medal success in menâs and womenâs hockey at the Asian Games , Hockey India selection committee chairman RP Singh has set his sights on the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics, hinting that some players could be replaced in the run-up to the Games. âSome players from the current Asian Games team may not be able to continue until 2028. The time has come to look for their replacements and accord them a respectful retirement,â RP Singh told TOI. He added, however, that the immediate focus was on the Menâs Asian Champions Trophy 2026, to be held in Jalandhar and Mohali from Oct 27 to Nov 5. âMajor changes have to be made within the next month or two. If we delay, we will be behind by the time the 2028 Olympics arrive. India are champions in Asia at present, but the next target is to become champions against European teams as well,â he said. Asked whether captain Harmanpreet Singh could remain part of the squad for the Los Angeles Olympics, RP Singh said the defender was currently fit and available. âHarmanpreet is fit at the moment and has no issues right now, but anything can happen in sport. Fitness is crucial for every player. Whoever remains fit and performs well will be considered for the Los Angeles Olympics,â he said. India will hold two camps this month. The India A team camp will begin in Bengaluru on Oct 11 ahead of its tour of New Zealand, while the camp for the Asian Champions Trophy will start in Jalandhar on Oct 18. Most players who featured in the Asian Games are expected to attend the Jalandhar camp. RP Singh also said Hockey Indiaâs top officials should not have aired internal matters on social media during the Asian Games. He said such remarks affected the players, but both the menâs and womenâs teams remained focused and went on to win gold. On the Senior National Hockey Championship, RP Singh said the senior menâs event, beginning in Jhansi on Oct 10, was initially scheduled to be held in Odisha a week earlier. Team camps had already been set up in Odisha, but the Odisha Hockey Association declined to host the 2026 Senior Menâs National Hockey Championship. Uttar Pradesh then stepped in to host the event, making the necessary arrangements at short notice. Hockey India elections were initially scheduled for Nov 7, but the timeline was extended because of the upcoming sports bill. The process of forming Hockey Indiaâs new executive body is underway. All state units have been asked to send two nominations each by Nov 15 â one man and one woman â who will serve as voters. The new executive body is expected to be formed by Dec 5. title: Ravindra Jadeja, Yashasvi Jaiswal dropped! Indiaâs big ODI calls ahead of 2027 World Cup
text: Yashasvi Jaiswal and Ravindra Jadeja (Agency Image) Indiaâs ODI plans for the 2027 World Cup continue to evolve, with the selectors making several changes to the squads for the upcoming five-match series against New Zealand. The Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) on Friday announced separate squads for the first three and final two matches, with the split aimed at giving Test regulars time to prepare for the two-match red-ball series, which begins just four days after the ODIs. The selections have raised questions over the futures of some established players, with Ravindra Jadeja emerging as the biggest omission from the squad for the first three matches. The veteran allrounder has struggled for form over the past several months, and his exclusion could be a significant setback to his hopes of making Indiaâs squad for the 2027 World Cup. Watch Morne Morkel on India's bowling concerns ahead of 5th T20I vs West Indies Axar Patel has been brought in as a like-for-like replacement for Jadeja. The left-arm allrounder last played an ODI in July against England and will now have an opportunity to strengthen his case for a place in the team for the marquee tournament in Africa. Another notable omission is Yashasvi Jaiswal , who has been left out of both squads for the New Zealand series. The decision means the opener will miss an opportunity to partner Rohit Sharma at the top of the order after Shubman Gill leaves the ODI squad to prepare for the Tests. Gill is set to depart after the first two matches. The BCCI has not provided an explanation for Jaiswalâs exclusion. Wicketkeeper Dhruv Jurel has also been left out and replaced by Ishan Kishan, despite not getting an opportunity to play in the first four ODIs against West Indies. Kishan, along with Shreyas Iyer and Arshdeep Singh, returns to the fold after missing the West Indies series due to the 2026 Asian Games. There has also been a change in the pace department. Auqib Nabi, who featured in the first ODI against West Indies in Guwahati, conceded 84 runs without taking a wicket and has been replaced by Anshul Kamboj for the first three matches against New Zealand. The arrangement will be reversed for the final two ODIs, with Kamboj leaving for Test preparations and Nabi returning to the squad. The squad will undergo further changes after the first three ODIs, with Shubman Gill, KL Rahul, Anshul Kamboj and Prasidh Krishna leaving to focus on preparations for the Test series. title: From Asian glory to tractor duty, hockey star Jarmanpreet drives home a message
text: Attachment Hockey star Jarmanpreet ploughs his family farm Attachment Hockey star Jarmanpreet ploughs his family farm Attachment 1 2 Amritsar : From hockey fields to his familyâs field, Olympian Jarmanpreet Singh is balancing national duty while staying rooted to tradition. The Indian defender, who returned home with an Asiad gold medal, recently shared a video of himself driving a tractor and ploughing his fields in Razadan village, around 50km from Amritsar, with a Sidhu Moosewala song playing in the background and the caption: âNation duty â home dutyâ. He is prepping the family land for sowing of wheat, around a fortnight from now. Jarmanpreet is also an income-tax officer posted in Bengaluru but when heâs back home, he is his element. The six-footer, whose towering presence is unmistakable on the blue turf, has no hesitation in doing his part for the family. âEvery child should fulfil their responsibilities towards their parents and spend enough time with the family,â was his message to the youth. Every time there is a break between tournaments, he makes it a point to return to his roots. âYour parents always stand by you, so must you. Spend time with them,â is his message to youngsters. Jarmanpreetâs sporting achievements include gold medals at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou, China, and the 2026 Asian Games in Japan, a silver medal at the 2022 Commonwealth Games in Birmingham, and bronze at the 2024 Paris Olympics. Jarmanpreet will now prepare for the next Asian Champions Trophy campaign being hosted by the Punjab govt and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. title: âWe have made our mark, but do we have any support yet?â: Quimcy DâSouzaâs fight to put Indian teqball on the map
text: Quimcy DâSouza (AP/PTI) NEW DELHI: When Quimcy DâSouza first picked up a teqball ball in August 2022, she had no coach, no established training system and little idea of how far the sport could take her. A footballer already, she had discovered teqball after watching a reel of Brazilian football legend Ronaldinho. What began as curiosity quickly turned into something much bigger. âI managed to put the ball back on the first goal. I think that clicked everything for me,â she recalls. Within two months, DâSouza had competed at the national championships and won. Four years later, she is a seven-time national champion, has competed in more than a dozen international tournaments and has established herself among Indiaâs leading teqball players. Watch Harita Bhadra Exclusive | 2 Asian Games Medals, Now the 22.45s World Championships Chase Her fourth-place finish at the Asian Games in Japan in 2026 has helped introduce the sport to a wider Indian audience. Yet, for DâSouza, the achievement comes with a difficult question: how further could Indian teqball go if its athletes did not have to fight for financial support alongside their opponents? âI started playing in 2022, and nobody followed the sport. Nobody knew who Quimcy was, nobody knew what teqball was,â she says. âToday, after my first two matches and when I made it to the semifinals at this yearâs Asian Games the internet actually boomed. People started knowing what teqball was.â For a sport that combines footballing technique with the precision of table tennis, the sudden attention has been significant. DâSouza believes that even getting more people to recognise the sport is an achievement in itself. Sport was never an afterthought for DâSouza. Growing up watching her father play football, she inherited a passion that eventually became a personal mission. âHe always dreamt one day to play for India, and I wanted to kind of fulfil it,â she says. Her sporting journey began on the athletics track. Competing for Maharashtra, she ran the 1,500m and 3,000m at the national level. She later took up competitive football, representing Maharashtra at the Under-19 level. An ACL tear, however, forced her to reconsider her playing career. At a time when access to rehabilitation and sports medicine was more limited, continuing football became difficult. Rather than leave sport behind, she chose to study sports management, hoping to contribute to the industry beyond the field. She worked with Decathlon while continuing to explore opportunities in sport. Teqball arrived during this period, opening a new competitive avenue. In 2023, DâSouza moved to Bengaluru with her colleague Chelsea, with whom she founded Teqball Club of Bangalore. At the time, Maharashtra and Gujarat were the sportâs dominant centres in India, with relatively few players competing across other states. The move was about more than pursuing her own ambitions. It was an attempt to build something that could outlast her individual career. The club went on to develop national-level players, including three athletes under the age of 16 who progressed to represent India at the Asian Youth Games in Bahrain. All three subsequently became national champions. For DâSouza, that development is among the most rewarding parts of her journey. Some young players have even moved away from football to concentrate on teqball, while parents have shown an encouraging willingness to prioritise their children's sporting ambitions. The challenge now is to turn that enthusiasm into a wider movement. DâSouzaâs progress has come at a considerable personal cost. Without a coach to guide her, she learnt by watching videos, studying other players and recording international opponents to analyse their techniques later. She saved money to compete abroad, treating each tournament as both a competition and an opportunity to learn. âIâm 24 now. I started when I was 21. From 21 up until 24, all my savings have been teqball,â she says. In four years, she has competed in 12 international tours, funding the trips herself. Her father supported her ambitions, but family circumstances made it important for her to become financially independent. The international exposure was crucial. Her performances and world ranking helped her meet the selection criteria for the Asian Games, which required players to be among Asiaâs top eight. Without the money to travel, compete and gain ranking points, the Asian Games opportunity might never have materialised. What makes her story particularly striking is that the situation has barely changed despite the breakthrough. âJust to answer your very last question in short, it is the same even now,â she says when asked whether funding has improved. DâSouza says the sport's governing structure in India is yet to secure the necessary recognition from the Sports Authority of India or the sports ministry. Without that institutional backing, athletes continue to shoulder the cost of competing internationally. With world championships approaching, the uncertainty remains. âWeâve made our mark, but do we have any support yet? No, because weâre still thinking about how to save money,â she says. It is a sobering reality for an athlete who has already demonstrated that Indian players can compete with established international opponents. The Asian Games exposed both the potential of Indian teqball and the distance the country still has to travel. DâSouza identifies Thailand as a major force in the sport, while pointing to the strength of the Asian competition more broadly. She was particularly struck by Myanmar and Indonesia, whose players, she says, had received substantial govt support and access to international coaches in the lead-up to the Games. Their preparation offered a glimpse of what sustained investment can achieve. For athletes balancing employment, training, travel arrangements and tournament preparation, such support can make an enormous difference. DâSouzaâs own routine involves strength training two or three times a week and table sessions four days a week, including drills, technical work and match practice. As a major tournament approaches, she reduces gym work to concentrate on table training. But training is only one part of the equation. An athlete who must also arrange funding, plan international travel and work without a dedicated coach is carrying responsibilities that have little to do with performance. Indian teqball has nevertheless expanded beyond its original strongholds. DâSouza says around 15 states now compete at the national level, compared with the handful that dominated when she began in 2022. The Asian Games exposure, she hopes, will encourage more states to enter the sport and give young players a reason to take it seriously. DâSouzaâs message to potential sponsors is direct: Indian teqball has already shown what it can do without a support system. âWe have reached a level like this, where we are top four in Asia and in the top 30s in the world,â she says. âIf we can do this by ourselves without any support, I think with support, we will only get better.â She is not asking for recognition based on potential alone. The results are already there, along with a growing player base and a club that is producing national champions. What remains missing is the structure that allows athletes to concentrate on becoming better rather than constantly wondering how they will afford the next tournament. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines For DâSouza, the Asian Games were proof that India belongs in the conversation. The next step is ensuring that the achievement becomes a beginning rather than a one-off moment of attention. Her journey began with a reel of Ronaldinho and a ball that bounced back onto a curved table. It has since taken her to international competitions, national titles and the brink of a breakthrough for Indian teqball. Now, she wants the country to look beyond the novelty of the sport and recognise the athletes building its future. The message is simple: India has shown it can compete. The question is whether the people and institutions capable of helping it go further are finally ready to back the players who have brought it this far. title: Gukesh, Praggnanandhaa get Rs 15 lakh each as Tamil Nadu awards Rs 60 lakh to Chess Olympiad medallists
text: Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay honoured the state's chess players (Special Arrangements) NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay honoured the state's chess players for their performances at the 2026 Chess Olympiad, awarding a total of Rs 60 lakh to five recipients at a ceremony in Chennai on Thursday. World champion D Gukesh and R Praggnanandhaa received Rs 15 lakh each, while Savitha Shri B, R Vaishali and Indian Open team captain Srinath Narayanan were awarded Rs 10 lakh each. Watch Harika Dronavalli Exclusive: Inside Grenke #chess win, viral no-handshake incident, and more Gukesh, Praggnanandhaa among top awardees Gukesh won an individual silver medal and helped India secure silver in the Open team event. His parents, Rajinikanth and Padma, collected the award on his behalf. Praggnanandhaa received the same amount after winning an individual bronze medal on Board 1 and contributing to India's team silver. Savitha Shri earned Rs 10 lakh for her individual gold medal and her role in India's bronze medal-winning women's team. Vaishali, who was also part of the women's team, received Rs 10 lakh. Her father, Rameshbabu, and Praggnanandhaa collected the award on her behalf. title: Asian Games 2026: 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi was India's youngest medallist; do you know who was the oldest?
text: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi and Mairaj Ahmad Khan The Asian Games 2026 took place in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, from September 19 to October 4, with athletes from 46 nations competing across various sports. India finished fourth in the medal table with 85 medals, including 21 golds, 27 silvers and 37 bronzes. India enjoyed several memorable performances, with the menâs and womenâs teams winning gold medals in cricket, kabaddi and hockey. It was also the first time both Indian hockey teams won gold at the same Asian Games . Among the standout individual performers was 17-year-old archer Kumkum Mohod, who became the first Indian woman to win individual recurve gold. Watch Lovlina Borgohainâs golden birthday: Asian Games medal after comeback She finished the Games with two golds and a silver. Pranavi Urs also created history by winning Indiaâs first individual golf gold, while Neeru Dhanda became the countryâs first womenâs trap shooting gold medallist. Vaibhav becomes Indiaâs youngest medallist At just 15, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi became Indiaâs youngest-ever Asian Games gold medallist. The teenage batting sensation was part of the Indian menâs cricket team that defeated Pakistan by 19 runs in the final to win gold. Sooryavanshi made an aggressive start, hitting two consecutive sixes, before Saim Ayub dismissed him for 15 off nine balls. Despite his early exit, India went on to win the final and secure a memorable gold medal. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Mairaj makes history at 50 Two-time Olympian Mairaj Ahmad Khan became Indiaâs oldest medallist at the 2026 Asian Games at the age of 50. He won bronze as part of the menâs skeet shooting team alongside Anantjeet Singh Naruka and Bhavtegh Singh Gill. Khan has competed internationally for more than 20 years and is a three-time ISSF World Cup gold medallist. However, the bronze in Aichi-Nagoya was his first Asian Games medal. Overall, Japanâs 11-year-old eSports player Yuki Kurihara became the youngest gold medallist in Asian Games history after winning the Puyo Puyo Champions title. title: âI was a daughter of Himachalâ: Ritu Negiâs heartbreak after home state drops Asian Games gold medallist from Rs 1 crore reward list
text: Indian women's Kabaddi player Ritu Negi. (ANI Photo) Former India captain Ritu Negi has represented the country at three consecutive Asian Games, won two gold medals and a silver, and led the women's kabaddi team to the top of the podium at the 2023 edition in Hangzhou. Yet, after being part of India's gold-medal-winning squad again at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, the Arjuna Awardee has found herself at the centre of an unexpected controversy in her home state of Himachal Pradesh. Negi's name was missing from the state's list of athletes announced for a cash reward of Rs 1 crore following India's women's kabaddi triumph in Japan. The decision has left the veteran player disappointed and raised questions about whether an accomplished sportsperson should lose recognition from her home state simply because she is married in another state. Watch Harita Bhadra Exclusive | 2 Asian Games Medals, Now the 22.45s World Championships Chase Negi hails from the Shillai region of Sirmaur district but is married in Panipat, Haryana. The omission has been particularly difficult to understand because she received a cash reward from Himachal Pradesh after India's women's kabaddi team won gold at the 2023 Asian Games, when she was the captain. This time, however, her name was left out while three other players from the state were included in the reward list. "Until a week ago, I was a daughter of Himachal and the CM shared a congratulatory message on Facebook, while former CM Jairam Thakur and Member of Parliament Anurag Thakur had called to congratulate me," Negi told the media while expressing her displeasure. "I simply cannot understand what changed so suddenly two days ago." âWhy is Himachal Pradesh behaving this way at this stage of my career?â The decision to exclude Negi has struck a particularly sensitive chord because of her long association with Indian kabaddi and her contribution to the state's sporting reputation. The veteran has represented India at three consecutive Asian Games, winning two gold medals and a silver. She captained the women's team to gold at Hangzhou in 2023 and remained part of the squad that successfully defended the title in Japan. India edged past Iran 37-34 in a tense final at the Aichi-Nagoya Games, holding on to its advantage in the closing stages to secure another Asian Games gold. The achievement should have been another moment of pride for the player and her home state. Instead, the omission from the reward list has left Negi questioning the recognition being extended to her. She pointed out that although she is employed by Indian Railways , she has consistently represented Himachal Pradesh, rather than Haryana, in domestic competitions. "Why Himachal Pradesh is behaving in such a way at this stage of my career?" she asked. For Negi, the issue goes beyond the financial incentive. It is about recognition for years of representing India and maintaining her sporting association with the state from which she hails. India women's kabaddi team after winning the Asian Games gold medal in Japan. Her father asks: Does a daughter stop belonging to her state after marriage? Negi's father, Bhavan Singh Negi, has also questioned the decision, asking whether a daughter ceases to belong to her home state simply because she gets married elsewhere. Speaking from Shillai in Sirmaur district, he pointed out that his daughter had received a cash reward from the Himachal government after the 2023 Asian Games, despite being married in Haryana. That precedent has made the latest omission even harder for the family to comprehend. They believe marriage should not erase an athlete's roots or diminish her contribution to the state she continues to represent in domestic competitions. The controversy has since drawn reactions from political leaders and people associated with sports in Himachal Pradesh. The debate has consequently become about more than a reward announced after a sporting achievement. It has raised questions about how states recognise athletes who continue to bring them distinction despite changes in their personal circumstances. Why three kabaddi players were awarded Rs 1 crore each The controversy emerged after Himachal Pradesh Chief Minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu announced a cash reward of Rs 1 crore each for three players from the state who were part of India's women's kabaddi gold-medal-winning squad at the Aichi-Nagoya Games. The recipients were Pushpa Rana, Jyoti Thakur and Bhawna Thakur. Indian women's cricket player Renuka Thakur was also announced as a recipient of Rs 1 crore in recognition of her achievements. The announcement followed an earlier disagreement over the amount offered to the kabaddi players. Initially, the three players had been informed that they would receive Rs 33 lakh each, a figure they felt was below their entitlement under the state's sports policy. They subsequently met Sukhu to raise their concerns over the cash incentives and employment opportunities. Pushpa Rana said the players were disappointed by the original announcement. "Look, we were very disappointed because according to the sports policy, we were not being given the amount that was due to us. So literally, anyone would be disappointed," she told IANS. Following the meeting, the Chief Minister assured the players that the reward would be increased to Rs 1 crore each. The state government also announced government employment for the three kabaddi players, with options in the police department or the Youth Services and Sports Department. While the revised announcement addressed the players' concerns over the amount, Negi's omission from the list brought a fresh controversy into focus. Government promises to review the decision The Himachal Pradesh government has not publicly provided a definitive explanation for why Negi's name was removed from the list. Sports Minister Yadvinder Goma said he was unaware of the reason behind the change and would examine the file before discussing the matter with the Chief Minister. Meanwhile, sources in the state government indicated that officials were monitoring the Haryana government's position on the matter. They suggested that Himachal Pradesh could consider a decision later, particularly since Haryana had not yet announced a cash award for Negi. The sources also indicated that her employment with Indian Railways was not a factor in the matter. The distinction is important because Negi has maintained that she has continued to represent Himachal Pradesh in domestic competitions despite her marriage and employment outside the state. Whether the government ultimately revises its list remains to be seen. For now, the Sports Minister's assurance that he will review the matter offers a possible route towards resolving the dispute. Another gold medal, but a different kind of disappointment For Negi, the timing of the controversy is especially poignant. At the 2023 Asian Games in Hangzhou, she captained the women's kabaddi side to gold and received recognition from her home state. At the Aichi-Nagoya Games, she again stood among the Indian players who helped defend the title, contributing to a campaign that ended with another gold medal for the country. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Her sporting journey has been built around representing India at the highest level while continuing to identify with Himachal Pradesh. The latest controversy has placed that connection under an uncomfortable spotlight. Negi's case also highlights a broader challenge in Indian sport: ensuring that recognition for athletes reflects their achievements and contributions, rather than becoming entangled in questions about residence, marriage or administrative eligibility. The government has yet to make its final position clear, and the possibility of reconsideration remains open. Until then, the former India captain's disappointment stands as a reminder that recognition can matter as much as the reward itself. title: When will Team India's ODI squad for New Zealand tour be picked? Details inside
text: Shubman Gill and Gautam Gambhir (BCCI Photo) MUMBAI: The Indian team for the five-match ODI series for India's upcoming tour of New Zealand will be picked âin the next two-three days,â BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia told TOI on Wednesday. âWe will select Indiaâs ODI team in the next two or three days,â Saikia told this paper. It's understood that pacers Prasidh Krishna and Harshit Rana will undergo a Return to Play (RTP) tests on Oct 24 or 26 at the BCCI's Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru, after which the selectors are likely to announce the Indian team for the two-Test series, set to start in Wellington from Nov 19. Watch Sanju Samson press conference: On India's loss vs West Indies and the turning moment On Thursday, both the Indian menâs and womenâs teams will be felicitated by India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi following their gold medal-winning campaigns at the 2026 Asian Games in Japan. The Pragyan Ojha-led selection committee has already picked Indiaâs T20I squad for the five-match T20I series in New Zealand, which will start from Oct 22. The five-match ODI series will start on Nov 4 in Auckland. It's understood that Ojha met Team India captain Shubman Gill and head coach Gautam Gambhir, celebrating his 45th birthday, in Hyderabad on Wednesday, for the first time since the BCCI asked him to take over as the interim chairman of the national selection committee. Amongst the newcomers, one of the strong contenders for a berth is Mumbaiâs seam-bowling all-rounder Suryansh Shedge, who has emerged as a strong contender to earn his maiden ODI call-up following a couple of impressive performances in the recently-concluded List A series against Australia A in Puducherry. The 23-year-old Shedge, who played three T20Is for India in England, recently returned to competitive cricket after recovering from a hamstring injury and, replacing injured senior India allrounder Hardik Pandya, impressed with both bat and ball, taking four 40 four wickets with his seam bowling, and then scoring 66 in a winning cause in the final One-dayer. Pandya's prolonged absence from competitive cricket due to a spate of injuries, and the drop in performance and Pandya's next-best alternative, seam bowling allrounder Nitish Kumar Reddy, may work in favour of Shedge, who is set to join the Mumbai team for its second 2026-27 season Ranji Trophy match against Himachal, which will start from Oct 18 in Bilaspur.
