title: 20 Hangzhou golds gone, 13 new routes to gold: How Indiaâs Asian Games medal map changed
text: Indiaâs Medal Route to Gold NEW DELHI: India won 28 gold medals at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou. Four years later, the question in Aichi-Nagoya was how many of those titles it could retain. The answer? - Eight, out of the 28 Hangzhou golds. Thatâs 28.6 per cent of the total. Twenty titles changed hands. The biggest changes came in the sports that had driven India's record campaign in Hangzhou. All seven shooting golds were lost, while all six athletics titles changed hands and, India also failed to retain either of its two individual compound archery golds. But just the gold-medal count does not tell the whole story. India retained the three compound team archery titles, both kabaddi golds, both cricket titles and the men's hockey crown. Watch Lovlina Borgohainâs golden birthday: Asian Games medal after comeback The other golds came from a different mix of events and athletes. Some had won silver or bronze in Hangzhou and moved up to gold in Japan. Others won titles in events where India had not been on the podium four years earlier. So while 20 of India's 28 Hangzhou champions failed to retain their titles, the gold medals themselves were replaced from a much wider pool. The Aichi-Nagoya campaign, in that sense, was less about defending the Hangzhou haul and more about how India's medal map had changed in four years. Indiaâs Gold Defence Shooting: from seven golds in Hangzhou to three in Aichi-Nagoya While Shooting had produced seven golds and 22 medals for India at Hangzhou, In Aichi-Nagoya, the overall medal tally fell to 15. The gold count dropped from seven to three, while silver moved from nine to eight and bronze from six to four. The biggest change was that none of India's seven Hangzhou golds was defended in the same event. Instead, India found gold elsewhere. Neeru Dhanda won the women's trap individual title and then partnered Kynan Chenai to win mixed trap. Kamaljeet and Suruchi Singh added the mixed 10m air pistol gold. The rifle teams that had delivered two of India's Hangzhou golds - men's 10m air rifle and men's 50m rifle 3 Positions - returned with silver in Japan. There was also a new medal in mixed skeet. Anantjeet Singh Naruka and Parinaaz Dhaliwal won bronze, giving India its first Asian Games medal in the event. So while India's shooting haul was smaller in Aichi-Nagoya, the change was not just in the numbers. The seven golds from Hangzhou were gone, and the three titles in Japan came from a different set of events. Shooting Medal Journey: Hangzhou to Aichi-Nagoya Athletics: The medals stayed, the golds disappeared While India won 29 athletics medals in Hangzhou, Four years later, the tally in Aichi-Nagoya was 24. The bigger change, though, came in the gold count. Six golds in Hangzhou became one in Japan and that lone title came in the women's 4x400m relay, four years after India's men's relay team had won gold in Hangzhou. Silver medals fell from 14 to nine, while bronze medals increased from nine to 14. There was still plenty of continuity among India's medallists. Murali Sreeshankar again won silver in the long jump. Tajinderpal Singh Toor, the Hangzhou gold medallist, finished with silver this time. Tejaswin Shankar moved from silver to bronze in the decathlon, while Ancy Sojan retained her long-jump silver. Vithya Ramraj again won bronze in the 400m hurdles. Gulveer Singh improved on his Hangzhou performance in the 10,000m, moving from bronze to silver. He also added silver in the 1500m and bronze in the 5000m. So the athletics podium did not disappear in Aichi-Nagoya. India still won 23 medals outside gold. The difference was that performances that had produced six titles in Hangzhou produced only one gold four years later. Athletics Medals: Golds Disappeared Archery: The tally remains the same, but in different events India matched its Hangzhou tally in archery, winning nine medals again - five gold, two silver and two bronze. The medal distribution, however, changed considerably. The three compound team golds were retained and beyond those events, India had a different set of medal-winning performances in Aichi-Nagoya, particularly in the women's recurve events. Kumkum Mohod won individual recurve gold, while the women's recurve team moved from bronze in Hangzhou to gold in Japan. That left the overall numbers unchanged, but the events behind those numbers were different. The individual compound events also saw a change. India had won medals in both the men's and women's individual compound events in Hangzhou. In Aichi-Nagoya, the men's individual compound event was the notable gap. Archery: The Tally Stayed the Same Boxing: From no gold in Hangzhou to three in Aichi-Nagoya Boxing went in the opposite direction to shooting and athletics. India had returned from Hangzhou with four medals - one silver and three bronze - but no gold, but In Aichi-Nagoya, the haul rose to six, including three gold medals. Lovlina Borgohain upgraded her silver in the women's 75kg category in 2023, to gold four years later, while Parveen Hooda and Ankush Panghal added two more titles in categories where India had not won gold at Hangzhou. The bronze tally remained unchanged at three. Boxingâs Medal Leap to 2026 Wrestling: Six medals again, but two golds this time Wrestling also finished with six medals, the same tally as Hangzhou. But the distribution changed completely. India had won one silver and five bronze medals in 2022, without a gold. In Aichi-Nagoya, that became two golds, two silvers and two bronze medals. Aman Sehrawat and Sujeet Kalkal supplied the two freestyle golds, while Nitesh, added a historic silver in Greco-Roman, and Antim Panghal upgraded her bronze from the 2022 Games to silver in 2026. The bronze tally fell from five to two (Sunil Kumar and Deepak Punia), but India added two golds and one silver. Wrestlingâs Medal Comeback Squash: Five medals again, but both golds are gone Squash finished with five medals in both Hangzhou and Aichi-Nagoya. But the two golds from 2022 were gone. India's tally changed from two gold, one silver and two bronze to two silver and three bronze. Abhay Singh retained the men's singles silver, replacing Saurav Ghosal on the podium. Anahat Singh added a women's singles medal. The men's team and mixed doubles titles from Hangzhou slipped to bronze in Japan. The women's team retained its bronze, while the mixed-team bronze was not repeated. The overall medal count stayed at five. The two golds did not. Squash Medals: Five Again, Golds Gone Kabaddi & Cricket: Four titles, no change India had won all four golds available across the two sports in Hangzhou - the men's and women's cricket titles and the men's and women's kabaddi titles and it repeated that sweep in Japan. In the kabaddi double, both Indian teams came through against Iran in the finals, with the women winning 37-34 and the men 40-34. For the women's team, the victory extended an impressive Asian Games record. India has now won the women's kabaddi gold at every edition it has entered except the 2018 Jakarta Games, when Iran took the title and India settled for silver. The 2026 victory was therefore its fourth gold in five appearances. The men's side has an even longer record. India's 40-34 win over Iran was its ninth Asian Games gold in the men's event across 10 editions. The only time it failed to win the title was in 2018, when Iran took gold. India had returned to the top at Hangzhou and retained the crown in Nagoya. Cricket followed with its own repeat. India's women's team opened the 2026 Games by defending the title it had won at Hangzhou, beating Sri Lanka in the final. The men's team then completed the cricket double on October 3, beating Pakistan to retain the men's gold as well. Indiaâs Four-Title Sports Triumph Hockey: Men's gold defended, women's bronze turned into gold Hockey produced two very different stories in Aichi-Nagoya. The men's gold was defended. The women's bronze became gold. For the men's team, the 2026 title was significant beyond the medal itself. India beat Malaysia 5-1 in the final to retain the Asian Games crown for the first time, becoming only the second country after Pakistan to win consecutive men's hockey golds. The victory also secured direct qualification for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics. The women's title was a different story altogether. India had finished with bronze in Hangzhou. In Japan, it beat defending champions China 1-0 to win the Asian Games gold for the first time since 1982. The victory ended a 44-year wait for gold and also secured direct qualification for LA 2028. It also produced a first for Indian hockey at the Asian Games. For the first time, both the men's and women's teams won gold at the same edition. Indiaâs Hockey Gold Rush Golf: A new gold, and a new first for Indian women At Hangzhou, Aditi Ashok won silver, giving India its first women's golf medal at the Asian Games. Four years later, Pranavi Urs went one better. She won individual gold, becoming the first Indian woman to win an Asian Games golf title. Urs then joined Aditi Ashok and Diksha Dagar to win India's first women's team medal in the sport. India's overall golf haul doubled from one medal in Hangzhou to two in Aichi-Nagoya. The individual gold also ended a 24-year wait for India. Shiv Kapur had won the men's title in 2002; Pranavi became the first Indian golfer since then to win an individual Asian Games gold. Golf: A New Gold for India Sailing: Three medals again, but different events Sailing produced the same number of medals in both editions. India won three medals in Hangzhou and three again in Aichi-Nagoya. But the events behind those medals changed. Two new skiff events produced podium finishes in Japan, replacing the men's windsurfer and men's dinghy medals from Hangzhou. The women's dinghy medal also changed colour, from silver to bronze. Badminton: Three medals became one Badminton saw one of India's biggest drops between Hangzhou and Aichi-Nagoya. The medal tally fell from three to one. India's 2022 haul included Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty's men's doubles gold, the men's team silver and HS Prannoy's singles bronze. Four years later, the men's team remained India's only podium finisher. But even that medal changed colour, with the silver becoming bronze. Neither of the two individual medals from Hangzhou was defended. There was no individual podium finish in Aichi-Nagoya, leaving India with just one medal from a sport that had produced three in the previous edition. Badminton Medals: Hangzhou to Aichi Rowing: Five medals fell to one Rowing's fall was even more pronounced. Five medals in Hangzhou became one bronze in Aichi-Nagoya. In 2022, India had taken two silver and three bronze medals across five events. In Japan, only Satnam Singh and Salman Khan's men's double sculls reached the podium. None of the five events that had delivered medals at Hangzhou did so again. And the build-up itself was unsettled, with last-minute changes to crew combinations and event entries. Arvind Singh, a 2022 silver medallist in the lightweight double sculls, was moved into the quadruple sculls, while Balraj Panwar shifted from the quadruple to the single sculls. Tennis: Two medals became none, and a 36-year streak ended Tennis went from two medals in Hangzhou to none in Aichi-Nagoya. The bigger change was the end of India's 36-year medal streak at the Asian Games. India had continued to find tennis medals across different generations, from Leander Paes and Mahesh Bhupathi to Sania Mirza, Rohan Bopanna and the current doubles players. That run ended in Japan. India had three quarterfinal opportunities but could not convert any of them into a medal. Sumit Nagal went out in the singles quarterfinals, while India did not have a women's singles entry. The result was India's first medal-less Asian Games tennis campaign since 1986. Tennis Medal Streak Ends Equestrian: Two medals became none Equestrian went from two medals in Hangzhou to none in Aichi-Nagoya. India had won one gold and one bronze in 2022. There was no podium finish this time. The campaign was also affected by selection disputes, the absence of an approved show-jumping team and a setback in eventing. The result was a complete reversal from Hangzhou, with a two-medal haul turning into none in Japan. Equestrian Medals: From Two to None MMA and Soft Tennis: Two new entries on India's medal map Aichi-Nagoya also added two new sports to India's Asian Games medal list. Suchika Tariyal won bronze in the women's traditional MMA 60kg category, giving India its first Asian Games medal in mixed martial arts. Jay Meena added another first in soft tennis, winning bronze in men's singles. For Meena, the medal came after two previous Asian Games appearances without a podium finish. He had competed at the 2018 and 2022 Games but returned without a medal on both occasions. In Nagoya, he finally reached the podium. Neither medal replaced a gold lost from Hangzhou. They came from sports that had not previously contributed an Asian Games medal to India. Indiaâs New Medal Map Weightlifting: 28 years later, Mirabai completes the collection Weightlifting produced another long-gap story. Mirabai Chanu's silver in the women's 49kg category was India's first Asian Games weightlifting medal since Karnam Malleswari's silver at Bangkok 1998. There was also a personal milestone. Chanu had Olympic and World Championship medals and Commonwealth Games titles, but an Asian Games medal had remained missing. The silver in Nagoya completed the collection. Kurash: Back on the podium India had not won a kurash medal at the previous Asian Games. Pincky Balhara put the sport back on India's medal list in Aichi-Nagoya, winning bronze in the women's -78kg category. It was a return to the podium rather than a title defence, adding another sport to India's 2026 medal tally. Wushu, Table Tennis, sepak takraw: Medals from the wider field Wushu again produced a medal through Roshibina Devi, who won silver in the women's 60kg sanda - her third Asian Games medal. Table tennis added bronze through Diya Chitale and Manush Shah in mixed doubles, while World No.3 menâs pair of Manush Shah and Manav Thakar flattered to deceive. India also retained its bronze in sepak takraw, with the men's quadrant team finishing on the podium again. The other side: Four sports drop out of India's medal list The Hangzhou-to-Aichi-Nagoya comparison also has a different side. Some sports that had contributed medals in 2022 did not produce one in Japan. Chess, bridge, roller sports and canoeing had together contributed six medals to India's Hangzhou tally - two silver in chess, one silver in bridge, two bronze in roller sports and one bronze in canoeing. None of those four sports were part of the Aichi-Nagoya programme. Firsts for India at Asian Games 2026 The changing medal map also showed up in the number of firsts India recorded in Aichi-Nagoya. Suchika Tariyal: Won India's first Asian Games medal in mixed martial arts, taking bronze in the women's traditional -60kg division. Jay Meena: Became India's first Asian Games medallist in soft tennis after reaching the semi-finals in men's singles. Neeru Dhanda: Won India's first individual gold medal of the Games in the women's trap event. Baranica Elangovan: Became the first Indian pole vaulter to win an Asian Games medal, taking bronze. Ankita Bhakat, Kumkum Mohod and Kirti Sharma: Won India's first women's team recurve gold at the Asian Games Kumkum Mohod: Became the first Indian woman to win individual recurve gold at the Asian Games. Pranavi Urs: Became the first Indian woman to win an Asian Games gold medal in golf. Sawan Barwal: Won India's first marathon medal since 1982, while setting a national record. Sarvesh Kushare: Ended India's 56-year wait for a high jump medal at the Asian Games. Anahat Singh: Became the first Indian to win a women's singles silver medal in squash at the Asian Games. Lovlina Borgohain: Became the second Indian woman boxer after Mary Kom to win Asian Games gold. India women's hockey team: Won the Asian Games title for the first time in 44 years. Mirabai Chanu: Won India's first Asian Games weightlifting medal since Karnam Malleswari's silver at Bangkok 1998. Seema Kumari: Ended a 16-year Indian medal drought in the women's 10,000m. Vithya Ramraj: Broke a 42-year-old national record in the women's 400m hurdles while winning bronze. The gold rush was not simply a repeat Thirteen of India's 2026 gold medals came from events in which India had either won silver or bronze at Hangzhou, or had not won a medal at all. That included three shooting golds. The mixed 10m air pistol moved from silver to gold, while Neeru Dhanda won the women's individual trap and mixed trap titles in events where India had not won gold in Hangzhou. Athletics produced another upgrade, with the women's 4x400m relay moving from silver to gold. Archery's women's recurve team went from bronze to gold, while Kumkum Mohod added the individual recurve title. Boxing produced three more. Lovlina Borgohain moved from silver to gold in the women's 75kg category. Parveen Hooda and Ankush Panghal won titles in categories where India had not taken gold in Hangzhou. Wrestling followed the same pattern. Sujeet Kalkal won the men's 65kg title, while Aman Sehrawat moved from bronze in 2022 to gold in the 57kg category. In golf, Pranavi Urs turned Aditi Ashok's women's individual silver from Hangzhou into gold. Women's hockey completed another major upgrade, moving from bronze in Hangzhou to gold in Aichi-Nagoya. India Found 13 New Golds Taken together, these 13 golds explain why the 2026 campaign cannot be judged simply by counting how many Hangzhou champions retained their titles. India did lose 20 of its 28 Hangzhou golds, but several of those losses were replaced by athletes who had finished lower on the podium in 2022, or had not reached it at all. The fact that India defended only eight of its 28 Hangzhou golds does not mean the 2026 campaign simply replaced the previous one with a broader or better model. Hangzhou had a heavy concentration of gold at the top. Shooting won seven. Athletics won six. Archery won five. Together, those three disciplines accounted for 18 of India's 28 gold medals in 2022. That made Hangzhou's medal profile very different from Aichi-Nagoya. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines And the disciplines that lost the most golds in Japan did not disappear from the podium. Shooting remained one of India's biggest medal contributors with 15 medals. Athletics produced 24, while archery matched its Hangzhou total of nine. So the change was not that India's traditional strengths stopped producing medals. They simply produced fewer golds. title: Sujeet Kalkal wins India's first wrestling gold at Asian Games 2026
text: Sujeet Kalkal (Image credit: X) NEW DELHI: Sujeet Kalkal ended India's wait for a wrestling gold at the Asian Games 2026 with a stunning comeback in the men's freestyle 65kg category on Friday. The 23-year-old Indian defeated Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiyev 10-9 in a dramatic final at the Nagoya City Inae Sports Center. Kalkal was trailing 2-9 for most of the bout and looked set to miss out on the gold. But he produced a remarkable late fightback, scoring eight points in a row to turn the match around and seal India's first wrestling gold at the Games. Watch Asmita Dey Unfiltered: Favourite Food, Match-Day Music & More | Rapid Fire | TOISA Dominant run to the final Kalkal had already beaten tough opponents from Afghanistan, Iran and Japan on his way to the final. He began his campaign against Afghanistan's Sayed Omar Zazai and fell 0-3 behind early. Kalkal then changed the match with a push-out and a shoulder throw to take a 5-3 lead. He added four more points with another throw and a roll before completing a 13-3 win by technical superiority to move into the quarterfinals. Kalkal then produced another clinical performance against Iran's Abbas Ebrahimzadehsavadkouhi. He won by technical superiority without conceding a single point. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Beat Olympic champion The biggest test came in the semifinal against Japan's Olympic champion Kotaro Kiyooka. Kalkal trailed 0-2 after the first period but fought back in the second. He scored three points while Kiyooka managed only one, leaving the bout tied 3-3. Kalkal won the contest on criteria to book his place in the final. Eight straight points for gold Kudiyev made a strong start in the final and built a 9-2 lead. The Tajik wrestler appeared to be close to winning the gold, but Kalkal refused to give up. The Indian then produced a sensational finish, scoring eight points in a row to overturn the deficit and win 10-9. The victory gave Kalkal his first Asian Games gold medal and India's first wrestling gold at the 2026 Games. title: Why Bangladesh replaced Pakistan at the last minute in Asian Champions Trophy hockey
text: Pakistan hockey team during the Asian Games 2026. (Reuters Photo) NEW DELHI: Pakistan have officially withdrawn from the men's Asian Champions Trophy Punjab 2026, with Bangladesh stepping in as their replacement for the six-team continental hockey tournament scheduled from October 27 to November 5. The decision sets up an India-Bangladesh clash on the opening day after the Asian Hockey Federation announced the full match schedule on Friday. Pakistan's withdrawal comes amid uncertainty over the team's participation in India, with the Pakistan Hockey Federation (PHF) previously stating that the tour would depend on government clearance. The development follows a September report by Dawn, which quoted PHF president Mohyuddin Ahmed Wani as saying the federation would follow the government's instructions regarding the team's visit. Watch Asian Games: India's gold medal-winning kabaddi teams return to Delhi With Pakistan pulling out, Bangladesh will join defending champions India, Malaysia, Japan, South Korea and China in the tournament. The replacement comes less than three weeks before the opening match, leaving Bangladesh to prepare for a late entry into the competition. Pakistan's decision also comes against the backdrop of sporting exchanges between the neighbouring countries being affected by cross-border travel restrictions. While some bilateral and multi-team competitions involving India and Pakistan have used neutral venues, hosting the Asian Champions Trophy at a neutral location was not part of the announced arrangements. India to open campaign against Bangladesh Fresh from defending their Asian Games gold medal in Japan, India will enter the tournament as the highest-ranked side and the most successful team in Asian Champions Trophy history, with five titles to their name. The hosts will begin their campaign against Bangladesh on October 27, shortly after the opening ceremony. India will then face China on October 29, Japan on October 30, Malaysia on November 1 and South Korea on November 2. All five of India's league matches are scheduled to start at 7 pm IST. The six teams will play a single round-robin league phase, with each side facing the other five. The top four teams will advance to the semi-finals, scheduled for November 4, while the bronze-medal and gold-medal matches will take place on November 5. India's previous Asian Champions Trophy triumphs came in 2011, 2016, 2018 â when they shared the title with Pakistan â 2023 and 2024. The team will look to extend that record in front of a home crowd after its recent success at the Asian Games. Gold medallist India's players during the medal ceremony for the men's hockey event. (PTI Photo) Punjab to host tournament across two venues The tournament will be staged at two venues in Punjab â the Olympian Surjit Singh Hockey Stadium in Jalandhar and the Olympian Balbir Singh Senior International Hockey Stadium in Mohali. Jalandhar will host all league-stage matches from October 27 to November 2, before the tournament moves to Mohali for the semi-finals and medal matches. October 28, October 31 and November 3 have been designated as rest days. The event carries special significance for Punjab, widely regarded as a nursery of Indian hockey and home to generations of players who have shaped the country's hockey legacy. The tournament's return to the state is expected to bring international hockey closer to its passionate fan base. We are delighted to welcome the teams from across Asia to Punjab and look forward to witnessing some high-quality hockey,â Hockey India president Dilip Tirkey said. Hockey India secretary general Bhola Nath Singh added: âWith the schedule now announced, the countdown to the Hero Asian Champions Trophy Punjab 2026 has truly begun. Hockey India is proud to host the participating nations and showcase the passion and hospitality of Punjab. title: Silent fight to glory: Aishwin wins 4 medals for India
text: Karan Sharma Ludhiana: For years, Aishwin Kaur dreamt of standing on an international podium with the Tricolour flying high above her. In Malaysia this week, that dream came true. The 20-year-old table tennis player from Ludhiana returned from the Asia Pacific Deaf Multi-Sport Championship 2026 with an impressive haul of four medals, including two gold and two bronze, making it the biggest achievement of her sporting career. Aishwin Kaur displays the four medals, including two gold, that she won at the Asia Pacific Deaf Multi-Sport Championship in Malaysia Aishwin won gold medals in the team event and womenâs doubles, besides securing bronze medals in the individual and mixed doubles categories. In a video message shared with TOI through sign language and interpreted by her father, Aishwin said the medals had only strengthened her resolve. âThese medals motivate me to work harder, improve my performance and continue bringing glory to India. I will keep working towards my dreams and making my country proud,â she said. Born with a hearing impairment and having battled metachromatic leukodystrophy, a rare neurological disorder, Aishwin overcame formidable challenges to pursue table tennis. With unwavering support from her family, the sport became her passion and eventually her route to representing India on the international stage. Her father, Bikramjit Singh, said the achievement was about much more than medals. âThe dream was never just to win. It was to win for India and hear the national anthem on an international podium. In Malaysia, with the gold medal around her neck and the Tricolour above her, that dream finally came true,â he said. Aishwin has previously won medals at the Deaf Asian Games and World Deaf Table Tennis Championships and is regarded as one of Indiaâs leading deaf table tennis players. title: Asian Games 2026 MVPs: Meet teenage sensation Yu Zidi and sprint king Puripol Boonson
text: Yu Zidi and Puripol Boonson (Reuters/AP Photo) The Asian Games have found two new superstars. China's 13-year-old swimming sensation Yu Zidi and Thailand's 20-year-old sprinting powerhouse Puripol Boonson were named the Female and Male Most Valuable Players of the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Games by the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) on Sunday. The pair were rewarded for spectacular campaigns in which they combined multiple gold medals with a string of Asian Games and Asian records, emerging as two of the brightest young stars of the continental showpiece. Watch Harita Bhadra Exclusive | 2 Asian Games Medals, Now the 22.45s World Championships Chase Yu and Boonson will each receive USD 25,000 from the OCA for their performances. Yu Zidi: Teen sensation makes history Yu was one of the breakout stars of Aichi-Nagoya, winning three individual gold medals at just 13 years of age and becoming the youngest MVP in Asian Games history. Her golden run began in the women's 200m butterfly, where she clocked 2:05.08 on September 20 to set a new Games Record. A day later, she produced an even more impressive performance in the women's 200m individual medley. Her time of 2:06.10 set a new Games Record and lowered the Asian Record. Yu completed her hat-trick on September 23, winning the women's 400m individual medley in 4:28.56, another Games Record. Three events, three golds and four records made the Chinese teenager one of the defining faces of the Games. Yu Zidi of China (AP Photo) Boonson: Thailand's sprint king If Yu ruled the pool, Boonson owned the track. The 20-year-old Thai sprinter stormed to a 100m-200m double, setting four Asian Games Records and equalling an Asian Record during his campaign. In the men's 100m, Boonson first broke the Games Record with 9.91 seconds in the semifinal before going even faster in the final, clocking 9.90 seconds to claim gold on September 25. Two days later, he completed the sprint double in the 200m. His winning time of 19.88 seconds broke his own Games Record of 20.10 seconds and equalled the Asian Record. He also added a silver medal in Thailand's mixed 4x100m relay, further underlining his impact in Aichi-Nagoya. Thailand's Puripol Boonson celebrates after winning the men's 200m final. (Reuters Photo) Stars with Los Angeles in sight The OCA MVP Awards Panel said the selection was particularly difficult because of the exceptional quality of performances across the Games. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Tayyab Ikram, chair of the five-member panel, said Yu and Boonson had established themselves as "Asian sports superstars" and backed them to achieve even greater success at the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics. Their selection places them alongside a distinguished list of previous Asian Games MVPs, including Japan's Koji Ito and Kosuke Kitajima, China's Lin Dan and Rikako Ikee, and the 2022 winners Qin Haiyang and Zhang Yufei. For Yu, still only 13, and Boonson, at 20, Aichi-Nagoya could prove to be only the beginning. The Asian Games gave the continent two spectacular new stars â and a glimpse of what could lie ahead on the Olympic stage. title: Centre grounds Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann foreign travel again; govt moves HC
text: Mann and his cabinet members have repeatedly been denied political clearance by the ministry of external affairs (MEA) for foreign visits CHANDIGARH: The Centre has yet again denied political clearance to Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann to travel abroad. And this time, Punjab govt has moved Punjab and Haryana high court. On Thursday, Justice Tribhuvan Dahiya directed Union govt to file a response to Punjab govtâs petition by Oct 16 on why it denied Mann clearance to travel to France from Oct 15 to 21. The Punjab CM has been invited to a Paris food festival, featuring a Markfed exhibition stall, but his travel plans were grounded by the Centreâs denial. âWhat do we do?â an exasperated Mann told mediapersons in New Delhi on Thursday. âWe received an invitation from French govt, and Markfed has put up a stall in Parisâ¦ but they (Centre) simply refuse to give me permission (to travel abroad). It seems only PM Modi can tour the world â visiting the most obscure places like Papua Guinea, âManglesia,â or âChanglesiaâ,â the Punjab CM said. He was earlier denied permission for a three-day trip to Japan, too, he said. âI wanted to watch the Asiad hockey semi-finals and finals. Since we are hosting the menâs Hockey Asian Champions Trophy from Oct 27, we wanted to extend a formal invitation to them in person but couldnât go,â Mann said. âWe have now moved high court, and hope to receive approval tomorrow. Our goal in traveling is strictly to benefit Punjab. We want to attract investors and create employment opportunities for our youth,â the CM said. Punjab govtâs petition challenges Centreâs decision as âarbitrary, without authority of law and violative of the federal structure of the Constitutionâ, and wants it quashed. According to the petition, Punjab govt had filed an application for the visit of a state delegation, led by the CM, to France for promotion of trade. It approached MEA through letters on Sept 3 and Sept 8 and submitted an online application on Sept 9. On Oct 12, Punjab govt found its application had been denied. The petition says no reason was assigned for the denial and neither was Punjab govt given an opportunity to clarify any concerns. It points out that Markfedâs participation in SIAL Paris 2026 had been confirmed under the APEDA India Pavilion and that the visit was intended to promote Punjabâs agricultural and processed food products in international markets. Punjab govt has sought a direction to the respondents to grant political clearance for the visit and asked for complete records relating to the application and the decision taken on it. This is not an isolated incident. Mann and his cabinet members have repeatedly been denied political clearance by the ministry of external affairs (MEA) for foreign visits. In Aug 2024, the Centre blocked Mannâs proposed trip to Paris to attend the Olympics and cheer on the Indian menâs hockey team, citing diplomatic and administrative reasons. Prior to that, Mann and then industries minister Sanjeev Arora were denied approval for an investment outreach tour to the UK and Israel ahead of Progressive Punjab Investorsâ Summit. More recently, MEA refused him clearance to travel to Japan for the Asian Games on security grounds. In Sept 2022, cabinet minister Aman Arora was refused approval for an official knowledge-sharing tour to Germany, Belgium, and the Netherlands. Also, assembly Speaker Kultar Singh Sandhwan was denied clearance to attend a legislative speakersâ conference in the United States in Aug 2024. And minister Harbhajan Singh was blocked from representing Punjabâs governance model at a conference in Boston in Aug last year. The Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) leadership has termed these rejections politically motivated, alleging partisan political discrimination by the Centre toward Punjab. In contrast, neighbouring Haryanaâs chief minister Nayab Singh Saini has consistently been granted prompt political clearances for his international delegations and investment tours. Recently, Saini led a state delegation to Singapore to pitch investment, urban infrastructure, and trade partnerships. Shortly after that, on Oct 14, he went on another four-day tour to Sweden to engage with international trade ministers and global investors. title: Asian Games 2026: Curtain comes down in Aichi-Nagoya as Doha receives flag for 2030 edition
text: India contingent during the athletes parade at the closing ceremony. (Reuters Photo) The 20th Asian Games came to a glittering close on Sunday, bringing down the curtain on more than two weeks of sporting action in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, as Qatar received the flag for the next edition in Doha in 2030. Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) President Sheikh Joaan bin Hamad Al Thani officially declared the Games closed at Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium, marking the end of a sporting spectacle that celebrated Asia's athletic excellence. Thousands of athletes, officials and spectators gathered for the closing ceremony, which carried the theme 'One Asia'. The proceedings also featured the formal handover to Qatari representatives, with Doha preparing to host the continent's premier multi-sport event four years from now. Watch Harita Bhadra Exclusive | 2 Asian Games Medals, Now the 22.45s World Championships Chase India's Neeru Dhanda, who enjoyed a memorable campaign with two gold medals and a silver in shooting, carried the national flag at the ceremony, capping a landmark outing for the Indian contingent. India finishes fourth with 85 medals India signed off with 85 medals â 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze â to finish fourth in the overall standings, behind China, Japan and South Korea. The campaign featured significant performances across shooting, athletics, boxing, hockey and other disciplines, underlining India's growing depth across sports. Neeru's outstanding haul was among the highlights, while India's gold-medal-winning hockey campaigns secured qualifications for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics. India's performance also continued a broader trend of consistent medal hauls at recent Asian Games, following the historic 100-medal milestone at Hangzhou 2023. The Aichi-Nagoya edition offered further evidence of the country's expanding presence across the continental sporting landscape, even as the final tally fell short of the previous edition's overall medal count. India's flag bearer Neeru Dhanda and others during the closing ceremony. (PTI Photo) Doha receives the baton for 2030 The closing ceremony formally shifted attention to the next host city, with Doha set to welcome Asia's sporting community in 2030. The handover marked the beginning of preparations for Qatar's second Asian Games, following its hosting of the event in 2006. The Aichi-Nagoya Games featured 469 gold-medal events across a record programme of 43 sports, with around 17,000 athletes and officials participating. Several disciplines, including padel, mixed martial arts, teqball and surfing, made their Asian Games debuts, reflecting the event's evolving sporting landscape. China dominated the standings with 169 gold medals among 341 medals overall, recording its best gold-medal haul at an Asian Games held outside its home territory. Hosts Japan finished second with 83 golds and 269 medals, surpassing their previous gold-medal record at Hiroshima 1994. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Qatar equestrian athlete Jassim Al Kuwari rides with the Olympic Council of Asia flag during the closing ceremony. (AP Photo) Sporting brilliance amid organisational challenges Despite the on-field excitement, the Games faced criticism over accommodation and transport arrangements. Organisers opted against building a dedicated athletes' village, instead using hotels, modular accommodation and a cruise ship to house participants. Registration delays, room-allocation problems and unreliable shuttle services affected several delegations, while diplomatic and ceremonial mix-ups added to the difficulties. Attendance was also subdued at several venues, with accessibility issues contributing to disappointing crowds. Nevertheless, the competition produced several remarkable individual performances, led by China's teenage swimming sensation Yu Zidi and seven-gold winner Zhang Zhanshuo, alongside standout displays in athletics and other disciplines. As Aichi-Nagoya handed over the baton to Doha, the Games closed with a celebration of sporting achievement, even as the organisational shortcomings offered important lessons for the next edition. title: Asian Games 2026 Medal Tally: How archers, shooters powered India into top 10
text: Neeru Dhanda and Kynan Chenai won gold in the mixed team trap event (PTI Photo) NEW DELHI: India moved up to eighth place in the Asian Games medal standings after reaching the 10-gold mark on Wednesday, with a golden sweep by the compound archers and another gold in shooting powering a big jump in the table. India now have 60 medals - 10 gold, 21 silver and 29 bronze. Watch Asmita Dey Unfiltered: Favourite Food, Match-Day Music & More | Rapid Fire | TOISA The compound archers won gold in all three team events, while Neeru Dhanda and Kynan Chenai added another gold in the mixed team trap event. Three boxing bronzes and Sunil Kumar's wrestling bronze also contributed to India's tally. India move to eighth India's 10 gold medals have lifted them to eighth in the standings, with Bahrain seventh on 11 golds. India have 60 medals overall, while Kazakhstan are ninth with 56 medals, including nine golds. China continue to lead the table with 275 medals - 150 gold, 66 silver and 59 bronze. Japan are second with 199 medals, while South Korea are third with 102. Compound archers complete golden sweep The compound archers were the stars of the day, winning gold in the men's, women's and mixed team events. Jyothi Surekha Vennam, Chikitha Taniparthi and Prithika Pradeep started the gold rush by winning the women's team title. They defeated China's Wunier, Yue Wang and Fangyao Wei 238-234. The Indian trio matched the world record with their score as they successfully defended their Asian Games title. Chikitha and Sahil Jadhav then won the mixed team gold after a thrilling final against South Korea's Jungyoon Park and Choi Eun Gyu. The Indian pair won 158-157 after a shoot-off. Kushal Dalal, Sahil and Ganesh Mani Ratnam Thirumuru completed the sweep by beating China's Jiahao Liao, Jinyi Liu and Jingyu Shi 238-237 in the men's team final. Chikitha and Sahil finished the day with two gold medals. The mixed team victory also secured an Olympic quota for India. India became the first country to qualify for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics compound mixed team event, which will make its Olympic debut. She had also helped India win silver in the women's team trap event. With two golds and a silver, Neeru has become the most successful Indian athlete at the ongoing Games. The four gold medals on Wednesday took India's gold tally to 10 and helped the country climb two places to eighth in the overall standings. Sooryavanshi made history earlier this year when he became the youngest Indian to play international cricket. He made his T20I debut against England at the age of 15 years and 99 days, breaking Sachin Tendulkarâs long-standing record. Watch IND vs WI: Shubman Gill on Indiaâs bowling concerns and fielding lapses He then became the youngest player to score a half-century in menâs international cricket when he reached the milestone against Zimbabwe at 15 years and 118 days. Gambhir explains Sooryavanshiâs wait Despite his early success, Sooryavanshi did not get a game during the entire Afghanistan series or the one-off T20I against Japan ahead of the Asian Games . The 15-year-old returned to the India XI in the Asian Games semifinal against Sri Lanka. He made a bigger contribution in the game, scoring 38 off 21 balls. Gambhir said he had explained to Sooryavanshi that being in good form does not always mean a player will immediately get an opportunity. "It was a new experience for me as well. Yes, he was in good form, but I made him understand that sometimes, because of the players who have done well for a long time, he will have to wait for his opportunity. And there's one more thing, social media or outside noise doesn't decide the playing eleven," Gambhir said on JioStar. âWe can't suddenly ignore a combinationâ Gambhir said the playing XI is picked based on what the coach and captain believe is the best combination to win a match. "It depends on who in that dressing room, or who the coach and captain feel can win us the match, or what is the best playing eleven, and who have done well for such a long time. Because if Vaibhav plays today, then it's going to be a tough conversation between me and whoever we leave out, whether it's Abhishek or Sanju. "So, we can't suddenly ignore a combination that has created such an impact over the last one and a half or two years, and after three or four failures, drop them and play a young player who is very talented, who is also in very good form. So, sometimes you will have to wait for your opportunity because we want to create that security in that dressing room," he added. He scored a quick 15 off nine balls in the final as India beat Pakistan by 19 runs to retain the gold medal. At 15 years, six months and six days, Sooryavanshi also became the youngest Indian to win an Asian Games gold medal. He surpassed shooter Saurabh Chaudhary , who was 16 years, three months and nine days old when he won the menâs 10m air pistol gold medal at the 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta. title: No tennis medal for India at Asian Games for first time in 40 years
text: Sumit Nagal (Image credit: X) India's tennis campaign at the Asian Games ended without a medal on Thursday, with Sumit Nagal 's quarterfinal defeat bringing the curtains down on a disappointing outing for the country. Nagal, India's top-ranked singles player, was the last Indian left in the medal race after the doubles pairs were knocked out on Wednesday. But the 29-year-old lost 4-6, 4-6 to China's Yibing Wu in one hour and 38 minutes. Watch Asmita Dey Unfiltered: Favourite Food, Match-Day Music & More | Rapid Fire | TOISA It means India will return from the Asian Games without a tennis medal for the first time since 1986. Since 1990, India had won at least one tennis medal at every edition of the continental event. This time, however, the country could not continue that run despite entering the competition with hopes of winning at least three medals. Nagal's exit ends India's hopes Nagal had carried India's singles hopes into the quarterfinal after beating Hong in the previous round and then overcoming Fomin. But Wu proved too strong for the Indian, who fought hard but could not convert his chances. India coach Ashutosh Singh said the team wanted better results, especially given the experience in the squad. "We obviously would have wanted stronger results, particularly given the quality and experience within the team." Singh admitted that the competition was "extremely high" but felt India's singles players needed to make more of their opportunities. "Sumit Nagal competed hard in his matches. First beating Hong for the first time in his career, then overcoming Fomin, he did what was required. Even today, Sumit managed to create multiple opportunities but somehow was unable to convert them. "DK (Dhakshineswar) has shown his playing level on the Tour but needs more work to sustain his short bursts into good performance through a physically demanding multiple week national campaign if he sees himself as being the torch bearer of the team," Singh said. Doubles pairs also fall short India had hoped that its doubles players would keep the country's medal tradition alive after Nagal's exit. However, Yuki Bhambri and N Sriram Balaji also failed to reach the podium. Balaji and Anirudh Chandrasekar, as well as Bhambri and Dhakshineswar Suresh, lost in the quarterfinals. Dhakshineswar had also exited in the third round of the men's singles. The women's doubles and mixed doubles combinations also could not convert their opportunities into medals. Talking about the doubles, Singh said, Bhambri and Bhosale got a tough Taipei team. "The doubles combinations were finalised based on the overall team requirements and the performances and circumstances leading into the event. Unfortunately, we could not convert that opportunity into medals. "Yuki and Rutuja were beaten by the Grand Slam champion Hseih who brought all her high level experience and her partner too was playing very attacking tennis." Singh added," As a team, we take responsibility for the results. There is no point in looking for excuses. At the same time, a proper assessment has to consider the conditions, scheduling, preparation and the quality of opposition rather than looking only at the final scorelines." India had a strong medal tradition India's last singles medals at the Asian Games came in 2018, when Prajnesh Gunneswaran and Ankita Raina won bronze medals in Jakarta. The country also had a major doubles presence through Rohan Bopanna, who rose to the world No. 1 ranking and helped India win gold medals at the Asian Games. After Bopanna's retirement, the responsibility was expected to be carried by players such as Bhambri and Balaji. But neither could make it to the podium in Japan. India also missed out on singles medals at the 2023 Hangzhou Asian Games, where Nagal lost in the quarterfinals and Ramkumar Ramanathan went out in the third round. Focus turns to the next generation Nagal is already 29, which means he will be 33 when the next Asian Games are held in Doha in 2030. The result has once again brought the focus on India's next generation of tennis players and the need to prepare them for the international stage. AITA interim Secretary General Sunder Iyer said the players had given their best but accepted that the federation needs to do more. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines "Players have tried to do their best. We reached three quarter-finals and were close to medals. As an association we need to see how to give more support to our players, juniors and professionals enabling them to do better," Iyer told PTI. Coach praises team spirit Despite the disappointing results, Singh said the players remained together throughout the campaign. The coach signed off by acknowledging "the way the players stayed together as a group." "There were difficult moments, selections and combinations that naturally bring pressure but the team maintained professionalism and supported one another throughout the campaign," he said. title: Para cyclistsâ protest enters Day 2, even sole Asian Para Games pick joins stir
text: The cyclists continued their sit-in outside Jawaharlal Nehru stadium. (TOI Photo) NEW DELHI: With the Asian Para Games fast approaching, Indiaâs para cyclists are spending their days demanding answers instead of focusing on their preparations, as their protest against the team selection entered its second consecutive day on Friday. The cyclists continued their sit-in outside Gate No. 1 of Jawaharlal Nehru (JLN) stadium, braving the harsh sun and sitting on the pavement to demand justice and the inclusion of the athletes they say were overlooked despite meeting the selection criteria. Their grievance remains unchanged: six cyclists were recommended by the joint selection committee of the Cycling Federation of India (CFI) and Paralympic Committee of India (PCI), but only one â Arshad Shaikh â made the final contingent for the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Para Games. Watch Harita Bhadra Exclusive | 2 Asian Games Medals, Now the 22.45s World Championships Chase Even Shaikh, the lone cyclist selected, has joined the protest in solidarity with his fellow athletes. Instead of concentrating solely on his training and preparations for the continental event, he is standing alongside those questioning why they were left out. The athletes allege that their repeated appeals have failed to elicit a satisfactory response from the authorities. They want the selection decision reconsidered and a clear explanation of why the other recommended cyclists were excluded. The protesters say they will continue their agitation until their demands are met and the sidelined athletes are considered for selection. The dispute stems from the joint selection committeeâs August 28 meeting, at which six cyclists were unanimously recommended for the Games. The list comprised Shaikh (MC2), Pavan Kumar Kommoji (MC3), Sameer (MC4), Prashant Arkal (MH4), Vishva Vasani (WC3) and Lisha Das (WC4). According to the athletes, their recommendations were based on performances, minimum qualifying standards, Asian and Union Cycliste Internationale (UCI) rankings, and international qualification criteria. They have sought athlete-wise explanations and clarity on the basis on which the final list was reduced from six names to one. The cyclists have also pointed to the financial burden they have borne, claiming to have met expenses related to international participation, equipment and prosthetics themselves. With the Games looming, they argue that the uncertainty over their selection has added to the strain on athletes who should be preparing to represent the country. The Asian rankings cited by the athletes show that several of the excluded cyclists had competitive positions in their respective categories. In 2026, Shaikh was ranked second in road and third in track, while Kommoji was second and third, respectively. Sameer was eighth in road and fifth in track; Arkal was second in road; Vasani was third in road and second in track; and Das was sixth in road and second in track. Track rankings do not apply to the MH4 category. The athletes have also cited Indiaâs position in the Asian UCI Nations Rankings as part of their argument over qualification slots, seeking transparency on how the available places were allocated. The cyclistsâ protest comes amid wider discontent over selections for the Asian Para Games. Para-shooters have also continued to raise objections over the selection process. On Thursday, their protest at the Indian contingentâs send-off ceremony brought allegations of irregularities and favouritism into focus, with athletes questioning their exclusion from the squad. The allegations have been contested by officials, who have maintained that selection was based on the prescribed criteria. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines With both groups raising concerns over selection transparency, the protests have cast a shadow over Indiaâs preparations for the Games. For the cyclists outside JLN stadium, however, the immediate demand remains simple: an explanation for the decision, a fair hearing and a resolution before the team departs for Japan. âWe will continue our protest until our demands are met,â the cyclists have maintained. For athletes who should be sharpening their competitive edge ahead of a major international event, the question now is how long they will have to remain on the pavement before their pleas are heard. title: âDeeply honoured and humbledâ: Rajeshwari Kumari elected to OCA Athletes Commission
text: Rajeshwari Kumari Former India trap shooter Rajeshwari Kumari has been unanimously elected as a member of the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) Athletes Commission after the conclusion of the Athletes Committee elections at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya. Rajeshwari was nominated by the OCA Executive Board to represent the South Asian region. She becomes the second Indian to serve on the OCA Athletes Commission, joining Vice-Chairman Shiva Keshavan. She will represent athletes from South Asia on the Commission. Watch Class topper, wooden gun, Nano rides: How Shapath Bharadwaj reached the Asian Games Rajeshwari grateful for opportunity A silver medallist in Womenâs Trap at the 2023 Asian Games, Rajeshwari also represented India at the Paris Olympic Games. Widely known as Ria, she brings experience as an athlete and a strong understanding of the Asian Games movement. Speaking on her election, Rajeshwari said: "I am deeply honoured and humbled by this recognition. I am sincerely grateful to the Indian Olympic Association, its President, Dr. P. T. Usha, and the IOA for placing their trust in me and nominating me for this prestigious honour," Rajeshwari said. "I am equally thankful to the Olympic Council of Asia and the Athletes Commission for their confidence in me and for considering me worthy of this responsibility. This means a great deal to me personally, and I accept it with humility, gratitude and a deep sense of responsibility. Having experienced sport and competition as an athlete myself, I understand the aspirations, challenges and dreams that lie behind every athleteâs journey. I look forward to contributing with sincerity and commitment, and to doing my part to strengthen the voice of athletes and serve the Olympic Movement with integrity," she added. Kynan Chenai praises wife Rajeshwari Asian Games 2026 gold medallist and Rajeshwari's husband Kynan Chenai also heaped praise on Rajeshwari. Kynan Chenai with Rajeshwari Kumari Four members elected The newly elected members are Amir Maimuratov from Kazakhstan, Reem Al Sharshani from Qatar, Naoto Tobe from Japan and Thanyalak Chophibunsin from Thailand. title: From Asian Games glory to tractor duty, hockey star Jarmanpreet Singhâs message to youth
text: Jarmanpreet Singh recently shared a 17-second video of himself driving a tractor and ploughing his fields. AMRITSAR: From winning medals for India on the international hockey stage to ploughing his familyâs fields in his native village, Olympian Jarmanpreet Singh has shown that sporting glory does not diminish oneâs responsibilities at home. The defender, who hails from Razadan village near Baba Bakala in Amritsar district, recently shared a 17-second video of himself driving a tractor and ploughing his fields, captioning it âNation duty â home dutyâ. After representing the country at major international tournaments, the Income Tax officer posted in Bengaluru said he had returned home to fulfil his responsibilities towards his parents, delivering a simple message to young people about the importance of family and giving time to those who stood by them. Jarmanpreetâs sporting achievements include gold medals at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou, China, and the 2026 Asian Games in Japan, a silver medal at the 2022 Commonwealth Games in Birmingham and bronze at the 2024 Paris Olympics. His father retired from the Punjab Police. The video offered a glimpse of the hockey star away from the sporting arena, taking up an everyday agricultural task at home. For Jarmanpreet, the visit was not merely a break between tournaments but an opportunity to stand by his parents and share their responsibilities. He said children should understand that their duties towards their parents did not end when they moved away for jobs or achieved success in their respective fields. They should make time for their families rather than allow professional commitments to keep them constantly occupied, he said. âEvery child should fulfil their responsibilities towards their parents and spend enough time with the family,â was his message to the youth. His example also carries particular significance for young people who leave their villages to pursue education, careers or sporting ambitions. While professional success and financial independence are important, maintaining close family bonds and being available for parents should remain a priority. Jarmanpreet, who is employed with the Income Tax Department and represents India in hockey, will now return his focus to the sport as preparations begin for the next Asian Champions Trophy campaign being hosted by the Punjab government and 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. For a player accustomed to the pressure of international competition, the message from his village is straightforward - serving the nation is an honour, but caring for oneâs parents is a duty that should never be forgotten. title: EXCLUSIVE | âIn reality, it really isnâtâ: Asian Games gold medallist Pranavi Urs on golfâs ârich manâs sportâ image
text: Gold medallist India's Pranavi Urs celebrates during the women's individual stroke play medal ceremony REUTERS/Andy Chua "A lot of non-golfers don't know what the sport means or what it is. And they all just think that it's a rich man's sport. In reality, it really isn't." Pranavi Urs, the 23-year-old from Mysuru, has just returned from the Asian Games as the first Indian woman to win an individual golf gold . The medal has changed her place in Indian golf, but she is more interested in what it can do for the sport itself. "I think any medal for golf at this point in the golfing world is great for India. So I think any medal, whether it's on the men's side or the women's side, would have brought a lot more attention to the sport, which obviously, at the end of the day, is the goal for us - to give back to the sport and kind of make it global and grow it in India," she told Timesofindia.com from Mysuru. "Because I feel like in India, it's definitely picked up in the last few years, but it's not where it should be. And I think getting this gold home, or even the silver, I think is a good step and it's heading in the right direction." Women's golf in India : Pranavi Urs wants more attention That is a bigger ambition than the medal sitting in her collection. And Pranavi sees the women's game as an important part of it. "I think the girls are doing far better than the guys globally. Four or five years ago, there were only one or two girls on the LET (Ladies European Tour), with full status. Now there are five of us. "So I think to just go out there and tell everyone and make a statement that the girls are good, and that we're better than the guys, and bring a lot more attention towards women's sports in India; and it doesn't have to be golf." I feel like in this Asian Games, women in sport have done a lot better than the guys. And it just shows that girls don't just sit at home. Her own career offers an example of that progress . In December 2025, Pranavi became the first Indian woman to win a professional open-field tournament against male golfers when she won the IGPL Invitational Mumbai. She shot a bogey-free 8-under 60 in the final round and won by two strokes. Pranavi's Asian Games campaign also brought a team silver, with Aditi and Diksha Dagar joining her on the podium in the women's event. Aditi had won individual silver at Hangzhou in 2023, becoming the first Indian golfer to win an Asian Games medal. She was also the first Indian to win on the Ladies European Tour, has five LET titles, has played at three Olympics and finished fourth at Tokyo, one shot off the medals. Aditi Ashok 's influence and the support behind Pranavi Urs For Pranavi, Aditi has been a reference point since she was a junior. "Aditi is on a different level. She's my senior. I've looked up to her since I was a little kid, since I was a junior. We have quite similar careers, apart from the fact that I haven't won on the LET yet. She's still the greatest golfer in India." Pranavi's own career began much earlier, at a golf course in Mysuru when she was six. The route since then has taken her through junior golf, the professional ranks and the LET with support around her through all of it. Gold medallists China's Yan Liu, Zhang Weiwei and Yin Ruoning celebrate during the women's team medal ceremony along with silver medallists India's Pranavi Urs, Aditi Ashok and Diksha Dagar and bronze medallists Taiwan's Chien Pei-yun, Ya-ni Tseng and Hsu Wei-ling REUTERS/Andy Chua "I think I wouldn't have done it without my family. My family has been my biggest support. I've got a really good support system. I have my coach, my S&C coach, my psychologist, my physio. So I've got a really strong base, and I can lean on them whenever I need to. We've got a really good bond. Everyone gets along really well. So I think I've achieved what I've achieved because of my family and my support system." That support is what she points to when asked about the next generation, rather than rankings or prize money. "I just want young girls to pick up a sport, love it, enjoy it, and have fun with it." I didn't grow up playing golf because I wanted fame or money. I play golf because I love the sport. And money and fame is just a bonus. The money has, nevertheless, become hard to miss after the 2026 Games . Karnataka Govt. announced â¹1 crore for her individual gold and â¹75 lakh for the team silver. The IGPL announced another â¹1 crore for the individual gold, while the Indian Golf Union also announced a reward. For a young golfer looking at what is possible in the sport, Pranavi believes the rewards can be an incentive too. "For someone who thinks like make money or X, Y and Z ... if that motivates them, then sure, so be it. Iâm very happy that it's all out there in public for people to see what they can get if they achieve something. So let them be motivated by that. I think each to their own, right? I feel like everybody has a different goal and why they play the sport. " Mysuru rolled out a grand welcome for its golden girl Pranavi Urs on Wednesday, celebrating her historic Asian Games golf triumph with a felicitation and colourful procession through the city The triple bogey that tested Pranavi Urs in Nagoya For all the attention that came after the gold, the medal itself was in serious doubt on the third hole of the final round. Pranavi had started the day with a three-shot lead. A triple bogey on the third wiped it out. "I think I lost my lead, which was unfortunate, not because of a bad shot, but I just got unlucky on the third. It was out of my control where the ball ended up and what happened." She was one shot behind by the fourth, but her response was not to start chasing every lost shot. "I was like, 'You know what, it's fine. You've hit rock bottom.â I was one back on the fourth hole. And I was like, âYou always love chasing. You've already hit rock bottom. Just play fearless and you can do it.'" There was - she remembered - another golfer, a certain Rory McIlroy , who had been in a similar position. I did think about Rory because he had a bad start at the Masters when he won it for the first time. And I was like, âIf he can do it, so can you.â So, you know, just keep at it. Just stick to your process. The process, she kept coming back to, was simple: stay patient. "There was not a single moment when I didn't think I was not going to win. You just keep doing what you have to do, stick to your process, and just be patient, because it's 18 holes. If I didn't win on the third hole after what happened, that's fine. It's 18 holes." She eventually finished with a 70 for a 15-under 265, one shot clear of China's Yin Ruoning, a former world No. 1 and winner of the 2023 Women's PGA Championship, and Singapore's Shannon Tan, who plays on the Ladies European Tour. India's Pranavi Urs in action during the women's individual stroke play final REUTERS/Andy Chua "All I wanted to do was obviously hole the [final] putt. I don't remember most of it. I was just in the flow. I remember every shot, but I don't remember it as much as I remember the last part, because obviously there are videos and stuff now." And the ability to stay in that flow was something Pranavi learned by spending the last three years playing on the LET, moving between countries, courses and conditions. The travel itself has become part of the job. "I think I'm more experienced now because I play in Europe. It's different conditions week in, week out. You've got jet lag, you've got different places, different rooms. You've just got to go with the flow. Just going with the flow and adapting to whatever comes your way - whether it's nervousness or anything - just being able to deal with it and move on." From Asian Games gold to the search for an LET title At the 2023 Asian Games, Pranavi finished 13th individually, and the Indian women's team finished fourth. And that is where much of the difference between Hangzhou and Nagoya lies for her. "It's a mental sport. You've got to stay focused, you've got to stay patient." Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines "And, like I said, just kind of preparing yourself week in, week out and travelling around the world, fighting jet lag, fighting being homesick and all of that has helped me grow into a better person and a better golfer." she added. India's Pranavi Urs celebrates after winning the women's individual stroke play gold medal and women's team silver medal with Aditi Ashok and Diksha Dagar REUTERS/Andy Chua Now, the one thing still missing from her professional record is an LET title. She has had several high finishes in Europe, but no victory yet. âEvery golfer has their doubts. If you're not winning, you're like, 'Will I ever win?'", said Pranavi, but Aichi-Nagoya has given her belief that she will eventually win. "I beat a world No. 6, so if I can do that, I can win on the LET. Just be patient, keep doing what I'm doing, and eventually I will win. Every golfer goes to win. You give 100%, 200%. That's why golfers go to win. Eventually, I will win." And then there is one small matter of one more first that she wants. "An Olympic gold."
